The Arabic word behind guardian is *walī*, the one who takes charge of a person's affairs and defends him, and the whole force of the sentence lies in asking whether such a protector is available anywhere else.

A guardian is measured by what he can do when his client is in danger. The sūrah's audience had spent generations treating stones as protectors, and the question quietly asks them what a stone does on a battlefield or in a famine. The Book records the same test elsewhere: how can you worship, besides Allah, those who can neither harm nor benefit you (5:76)?

**Fāṭir: The Name That Means "Splitter"**

The translation renders the title Originator, and the Arabic behind it is *fāṭir*, from a root meaning to split or cleave. In the Qur'an the word appears inside one standing phrase, Originator of the heavens and the earth, and it is applied to God in the prayers of Joseph (12:101), in the preaching of the earlier messengers (14:10), in the opening of the sūrah of the angels (35:1), in a supplication (39:46), and in a declaration of God's uniqueness (42:11). The verbal form of the same root is used for the forming of human beings, and its noun gives the word *fiṭrah*, the natural disposition God instilled in people and which the verse on upright faith says must not be altered (30:30).

The name therefore carries a picture rather than a title: the heavens and the earth were opened out from something closed, in the way a seed splits and a bud separates. Whoever did that does not need a partner for maintenance.

**The God Who Feeds and Is Not Fed**

The second clause is economic, and it is aimed straight at the cult of Makkah. God provides for all and needs no provision from anyone. The Book states it as a first-person claim: I seek no provision from them, nor do I need them to feed Me (51:57). That single sentence removes the entire commercial logic of sacrifice, in which the deity is sustained by what is brought to the shrine and the worshipper expects the arrangement to be honoured in return.

The same argument is turned against the divinisation of holy figures. The Messiah and his mother both ate food, the Book observes, as a sign that neither could have been a god (5:75). Appetite is the mark of a creature. A deity who must be fed has worshippers and rivals at the same time, since someone else can always bring a better offering.

**A God With a Kitchen Is Not a God**

Makkan worship was a farming and trading arrangement as much as a theology. Offerings of grain and livestock were diverted to the idols, and the sūrah later discusses the shares people assigned to God and to their deities (6:136). The verse's clause about provision attacks the practice at its base: the parties who needed the sacrifice were the ones receiving it, not the one being worshipped.

Set beside the earlier clause about splitting open the heavens and the earth, the contrast is severe. The Creator of everything is described as needing nothing, while the objects of Makkan devotion were represented by statues that had to be anointed and fed by the priests who kept them. That is the whole case, and the verse makes it in one line about dinner.

**"The First to Submit"**

Having refused the compromise, the Prophet is told to declare his own position: he has been commanded to be the first of those who submit. Interpreters read the word in three ways — first among the people of his own time to submit, first in rank among the submitters, or the one uniquely singled out to receive revelation. Two other passages carry the same claim in his mouth: he is commanded to be the first of those who submit (39:12), and he is the first to submit (6:163).

Each reading keeps the sense of priority in a sequence rather than superiority in a hierarchy. Abraham, raised among idolaters, is the model of the same submission (16:120), and the faith being claimed here is presented as the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not a polytheist (6:161).

**The Command Not to Be Among the Polytheists**

The verse closes with a warning addressed directly to the Prophet: and not be one of the polytheists. That the Book warns its own messenger is not a slight; it is the clearest possible statement that the prohibition is universal and that no station is exempt from it. The same phrasing recurs across the sūrah, attached to Abraham (6:79), to the Prophet's declaration of faith (6:161), and to his final profession (6:163).

Anyone who heard the demand for compromise should notice what the answer actually says. The Prophet is not described as too important to associate partners with God; he is described as commanded, like every other submitter, to stand outside that category entirely. The position he takes is not a privilege he owns but an instruction he carries. In a city that negotiated its alliances by exchanging acknowledgements, the refusal to trade a single word of testimony is the whole answer, and it is delivered as obedience rather than as pride.
verses.15:
> Say, “I truly fear—if I were to disobey my Lord—the torment of a tremendous Day.”

**The Messenger Is Told to Announce His Own Fear**

The instruction here is not to warn the Makkans about the Day but to tell them something about himself. The man who has been threatened, mocked, and offered a compromise is commanded to state that he too stands under the threat: if he were to disobey his Lord, he would fear the torment of a tremendous Day. It is a startling thing for the founder of a movement to say in public, because every other kind of authority in Arabia was built on the assumption that the man at the top was the least exposed.

The confession also removes a suspicion his hearers might have carried. A preacher who announced judgment on others while standing visibly outside the judgment would be understandable, and would be no different from the tribal soothsayers who sold verdicts. By placing himself inside the warning, the Prophet makes his message expensive for himself as well as for them. The sentence is also a public refusal of the role his opponents kept offering him, which was to be a poet or a soothsayer whose words cost him nothing.

**The Same Line Repeated in Another Sūrah**

A nearly identical sentence appears in the sūrah of the Crowds: I truly fear, if I were to disobey my Lord, the torment of a tremendous Day (39:13). The repetition matters for how the verse should be read. This is not a momentary remark the Prophet improvised under pressure; it is part of the confession he was commanded to deliver, and the Book records it twice in the same form.

Repetition in the Qur'an usually signals that a statement carries structural weight. What is being established is the shape of prophethood: a man who carries a warning he believes, addressed first to himself, and then to everyone else. The Book does not permit its messenger to be the one figure exempt from what he announces.

**A Leader Standing Inside His Own Warning**

Elsewhere the same Prophet is told exactly what he does not possess: he does not say he holds God's treasuries, or knows the unseen, or is an angel; he only follows what is revealed to him (6:50). The verse in front of us continues that self-description. He is not a shareholder in the divine power and not a priest with privileged immunity; he is a servant with an instruction and a fear.

That combination is what makes his claim credible to an audience that knew him. Anyone can warn a city. A man who warns a city while describing his own exposure to the same danger has told his listeners that he is not selling them a product. The message costs him the thing he is telling them to protect: his own safety.

**The Day and Its Adjective**

The Book has many names and descriptions for the final reckoning, and one of its standing adjectives is size. The Day is called tremendous, formidable, and great, and the adjective is attached to its torment as often as to the Day itself. The language is deliberately disproportionate to anything in the audience's experience, because the argument requires them to weigh an unseen event against visible possessions.

An earlier passage uses the same register when it warns that if the addressed turn away, they are feared for the torment of a formidable Day (11:3). The vocabulary is not there to frighten for its own sake. It is there because the audience was being asked to trade a comfortable present for a claim about the future, and the Book refuses to make the trade look small.

Size language also keeps the comparison honest. The audience measured its security in things it could count: camels, wells, sons, and alliances. Against that inventory the verse sets a single adjective describing an event no ledger can absorb. The mismatch is the argument, and the adjective is doing the work of a proof.

**Fear That Lives Beside Hope**

The verse does not describe the Prophet as despairing, and the Book never puts fear in opposition to hope. The sincere are described as those who abandon their beds, calling on their Lord with hope and fear (32:16). The two travel together because each corrects the other: hope alone drifts into presumption, and fear alone curdles into a portrait of God that no one could love.

What the Prophet's confession supplies is a standard. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 20, when the Companions told him that God had already forgiven his past and future sins and that they were not like him, he became angry and said that he was the most God-fearing and the most knowledgeable of God among them. The point is not that he feared more than others as an achievement. It is that knowledge of God and fear of God increase together, and the man who knows most has the least reason to feel safe.

**Why the Verse Ends on the Warning Rather Than the Mercy**

Only one clause follows: a tremendous Day of torment. The sūrah has already said that God prescribed mercy for Himself (6:12), and the verse after this one describes being spared as the triumph. Between those statements the Prophet is told to hold up the frightening side of the matter without softening it, and to include himself in it.

That ordering serves a purpose in a city that had decided the Day was a joke. A warning delivered by someone visibly unafraid would have confirmed their suspicion that the whole thing was a performance. The fear of the messenger is the first piece of evidence that the Day is real, and the Book makes him supply it in his own name before he asks anyone else for anything.
verses.16:
> Whoever is spared the torment of that Day will have certainly been shown Allah’s mercy. And that is the absolute triumph

**The Day Known by Its Torment Before Its Relief**

The verse names the Day by what people fear in it. Before it is described as anything else, it is the Day of the torment, and the one who escapes the torment is described as having been shown mercy. That is the Book's usual manner of speaking about the Hereafter when the audience is still undecided: the danger comes first, because the danger is what a person must take seriously in order to be saved from it.

There is no attempt to soften the picture or to suggest that the threat was exaggerated. The sūrah's argument depends on the audience believing that a real account is coming, and the mercy offered in this sentence would be meaningless if the torment it names were merely a figure of speech.

**Safety Described as Mercy, Not as Wages**

Notice the grammar of the escape. The one who is spared has been shown mercy; he has not been described as having earned his exemption. That is a significant choice of words in a Book that insists deed counts for something, and it reflects the Book's consistent position that the accounting is exact while the outcome is a gift. Even a person whose good deeds outweigh his bad ones arrives at the Day carrying a debt he cannot settle on his own.

The same framing appears when the righteous are described as praying for protection from the consequences of their evil deeds, since whoever is shielded from the evil of his actions on that Day has been shown mercy (40:9). The prayer of the best of people is therefore a request for mercy rather than a request for a fair wage, and this verse states the outcome of that request.

That wording also explains why the Book never lets its readers treat the Day as a negotiation. A wage can be argued about, disputed, or reduced by a clever advocate; a gift is either received or refused. By describing salvation as mercy shown, the verse puts the outcome in the category of something given rather than something owed, and it leaves the accountable person with no claim to press and nothing to plead except his need.

**"That Is the Absolute Triumph"**

In the four words at the end of the verse, the Book redefines winning. Escape from the Fire is not a rescue from a misfortune; it is an attainment, and the phrase is used elsewhere for a reward measured in Gardens and forgiveness of sins (61:12), and for the ultimate triumph of the saved (3:185). The scale of the language shows how the Book weighs the stakes it is describing.

For an audience that measured success in livestock, lineage, caravan profits, and victories in tribal skirmishes, the claim is a direct challenge. The Quraysh would have understood triumph as a matter of reputation and acquisitions in this world. The verse assigns the word to an outcome that happens after death, when none of those assets can be carried, and it does so without conceding any comparison between the two.

**Why Only This Victory Deserves the Word**

The Book is blunt about the alternative. Whoever is spared from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has truly triumphed, while the life of this world is nothing but the delusion of enjoyment (3:185). The contrast is drawn with a word that implies illusion rather than smallness: the pleasures are real, but the belief that they constitute a life's achievement is not.

Read in that light, the absolute triumph of this verse is not a supernatural version of a worldly win. It is the one achievement that survives the loss of everything the other achievements depend on. A man's victories in battle, his herds, and his reputation all end at the same border, and the verse states plainly what remains valuable when a person crosses it.

**The Sentence That Says Two Things at Once**

Placed directly after the announcement of the Prophet's own fear, the verse supplies the destination of that fear. The one who escapes has been shown mercy, and the escape is the greatest thing that could happen to a person. Fear and mercy are therefore not two competing portraits of God; they are the two halves of one transaction, with the accountable creature standing in the middle.

The word "that" carries the whole weight of the sentence. It points back to the torment, forward to the mercy, and settles on the triumph, and it treats the three as a single event viewed from three positions: the danger that was real, the gift that was given, and the deliverance that results from it. The verse's shortness is part of its force.

**What the Verse Asks Its Hearer to Prepare For**

No instruction follows the promise, and no list of deeds is attached. The verse is a statement about how the Day will be settled, and its absence of a to-do list is intentional in this place in the sūrah, where the audience has been arguing rather than asking for guidance. What it offers instead is a description of the only outcome worth arranging one's life around.

The arrangement itself has been described in the surrounding verses: submit, and do not join others with God (6:14); fear the Day if you disobey (6:15); and know that escape from it will come as mercy rather than as a settlement (6:16). The verse's quiet generosity depends on the reader having taken the earlier sentences seriously — mercy is offered, but only to those who needed to be spared.
verses.17:
> If Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him. And if He touches you with a blessing, He is Most Capable of everything

**Two Directions, One Hand**

The verse takes the two experiences that define a human life — injury and benefit — and assigns both to a single source. Harm cannot be lifted by anyone else once it arrives, and the second clause adds the mirror: blessing comes from the same hand, and that hand is capable of everything. Between them the two halves leave no space for a competing power, whether an idol, a star, a healer, or a tribal patron.

That is the argument the sūrah has been building from the start. Ownership of the heavens and the earth, knowledge of the hidden, and mercy prescribed for Himself are large claims; this verse makes them personal. The question a man in pain actually asks is not who owns the universe but who can remove this. The answer is given in the second person: if He touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him.

**Why the Book Says "Touch" Instead of "Strike"**

The verb chosen here describes contact, the light laying on of a hand, and the Book uses it for both harm and good in the same sentence. That choice does two things. It keeps the divine action close and immediate rather than remote and institutional, and it allows one verb to carry both halves of the verse, so that the reader feels the same nearness in the blessing and in the wound.

The alternative vocabulary was available. The Book can speak of striking, of smiting, of sending down, and it does so where severity is the point. Here the softer word fits the argument, which is about who is nearest rather than about how hard the blow lands. A person touched by something is in contact with whoever touched him, and the verse denies that any other hand was there.

**The Same Sentence Elsewhere in the Book**

The wording of this verse recurs almost identically in the sūrah of Jonah: if Allah touches you with harm, none can undo it except Him; and if He intends good for you, none can withhold His bounty, granting it to whom He wills of His servants (10:107). The Book repeats it because the audience kept needing it, and the repetition is itself the argument — a claim this central is stated in more than one sūrah in nearly the same words.

A second passage makes the same point from the opposite direction: whatever mercy God opens up for people, none can withhold it, and whatever He withholds, none but Him can release it (35:2). Two sūrahs, the same doctrine, and both place every gain and every loss inside a single decision that no intercessor can move.

**The Objects That Could Not Respond**

The idols of Makkah were credited with the power to hurt and to help, and the Book dismisses the claim from several angles. How can you worship, besides Allah, those who can neither harm nor benefit you (5:76)? Of the calf that the Israelites fashioned, the question is put with heavy irony: did they not see that it could not respond to them, nor protect or benefit them (20:89)? And the lords taken besides God are described as unable to benefit or protect even themselves (13:16).

Set beside that catalogue, this verse is compact and decisive. The complaint against the idols is not that they are weak in comparison with a stronger god. It is that the category of harm and benefit — the two levers by which a person's life is actually steered — is closed to them entirely, and belongs to one power alone.

**The Messenger Does Not Own the Power He Announces**

An obvious suspicion follows from such a claim, and the Book addresses it in the Prophet's own voice. He is told to say that he has no power to benefit or protect himself except by God's will, that he is only a warner and a bringer of good news to believers (7:188). He is told to say that he does not claim the treasuries of God, or knowledge of the unseen, or angelic status, and that he only follows what is revealed to him (6:50).

The two verses belong together. The messenger announces that God alone can harm and help, and then explicitly removes himself from that power. Arabia was used to men who claimed a share of the sacred; the Prophet's testimony is designed to be unusable as a claim of that kind. He is the announcer, not the dispenser.

**Even Sorcery Sits Under the Same Claim**

Makkan anxiety about magic was real, and the Book does not simply ridicule it. It places sorcery inside the doctrine of this verse: the practitioners of magic in the story of Babylon could not harm anyone except by Allah's will, and the harm they caused was ultimately to themselves (2:102). The verse's claim about harm therefore extends over the very practice the audience feared most.

That inclusion is a quiet mercy. People who live in fear of curses and charms are usually offered a stronger charm in exchange. The Book refuses to sell one. It tells them that the harm that reaches them was permitted by the One who alone can lift it, and that the cure is therefore addressed to Him and not to a counter-spell.

**Why the Verse Ends With Capability, Not Comfort**

The closing attribute is not mercy but capability: He is Most Capable of everything, able to do all things. The ending is deliberate. The second clause concerns blessing, and a person asking for blessing needs to know that the One being asked is able to grant it; the attribute supplied is precisely the one the request requires.

Mercy has already been settled in the sūrah: God prescribed it for Himself (6:12). With mercy established and capability stated at the end, the verse leaves its hearer in a position where neither fear nor hope has been left without a foundation. What the sentence rules out is the middle ground of going to a stone for the removal of a harm that only God can lift.
verses.18:
> He reigns supreme over His creation. And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware

**The Summit of the Argument So Far**

The sūrah has been climbing through its first verses, and this short sentence states the result. Ownership of the heavens and the earth (6:12), control of harm and benefit (6:17), and now unqualified dominance: He reigns supreme over His creation. The Arabic root behind the phrase carries the sense of overpowering and subduing, the way a thing is held down by something stronger than itself. Nothing in the created order stands outside that grip.

The word for creation here is the word for servants, which links the claim to loyalty rather than to raw force. A maker has authority over what he made; the verse states that authority in the language of ownership over those who serve, and the two senses run together deliberately. The sūrah is arguing with a city that had assigned shares of divine authority to other beings, and the sentence leaves no gap in which such a share could be lodged.

**The Same Claim Beside the Recording Angels**

Five verses later the phrase returns with an addition that shows what kind of dominance is meant. He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels watching over you, and when death comes the angels take the soul without neglecting the duty (6:61). The next sentence reports that people are returned to Allah, their True Master, to whom judgment belongs alone, and that He is the swiftest reckoner (6:62).

Dominance in the Book is therefore never blind force. It arrives with a ledger, and the powerful hand that holds the creature down is the same hand that keeps a careful account of the creature's days. The rulers of Makkah understood power as something exerted in public; the verse attaches it to an administration that never sleeps and never loses a file.

**Not Merely the Strongest**

If the verse stopped at dominance, it would have described a tyrant. The pair of names that follows prevents that reading. The All-Wise and the All-Aware are attached to overpowering rule so that the reader cannot separate the strength from the intelligence that directs it and the knowledge that records it. Power in the Book is always power with reasons.

That combination matters to an audience that had seen how unchecked strength behaves. Arabia's chieftains were not restrained by constitutions, and the sūrah's listeners had felt what it meant to fall into the wrong hands. The verse tells them that the supreme power over them is not arbitrary, and that its decrees are the product of wisdom rather than of appetite.

**All-Wise: Nothing Is Placed Wrongly**

Wisdom in the Qur'anic vocabulary means more than cleverness; it means everything set where it belongs, so that no arrangement in the creation is an accident. The suffering of the believers and the long prosperity of their tormentors are therefore not evidence against God's government, because the purpose behind both is known to him who set them in place. Time is part of the design, and the audience was being asked to wait inside it.

This is the doctrine the sūrah keeps needing. The Quraysh had asked why no angel came (6:8), why the punishment had not fallen, why the message had not been sent as a single book. Each complaint assumed that the current arrangement was a mistake. The name All-Wise answers all of them at once: the arrangement has an author, and the author has a reason.

**All-Aware: Nothing Escapes the Record**

The second name comes from the vocabulary of news; it describes one who has the report of a thing, not merely a general suspicion of it. In this sūrah, where the hidden and the declared have already been claimed by God (6:3), the name seals the argument. Deeds done in darkness, plans made in closed rooms, oaths taken in secret, and intentions never acted upon are all inside the report.

That is why the pair of names closes this particular verse rather than a verse about creation. The claim being made is that nothing in the universe can resist God's authority; the qualification is that nothing in the universe can escape His notice either. A person who has grasped both halves understands the shape of the life the sūrah is describing: absolute power, exact accounting, and a mercy already prescribed.

The Arabic word also carries the sense of a report received, which is worth pausing over. News is what reaches someone at a distance; the name says that nothing happening anywhere in creation is at a distance from God. The idols of the town had their local jurisdictions, and a man travelling between them could imagine business unobserved in the gaps. The name closes the gaps. Every journey, every private meal, and every unspoken design sits inside the awareness of the one who subdues, and the sūrah has already made that awareness personal to each reader in the second person.

**What This Rule Requires of the Creature**

A being who is dominated, watched, and dealt with wisely has only one reasonable posture, and the Book names it elsewhere: if Allah helps you, none can defeat you, and if He denies you help, who else could help you, so in Allah let the believers put their trust (3:160). The verse has argued away every other refuge — the stones and the stars cannot harm or help, the ancestors cannot negotiate, and the messenger claims no share of the power.

What remains is a creature standing before an overpowering, careful, informed authority that has already promised mercy. The response the sūrah will go on to state is submission, and this verse is the ground of it. Fear of such power is the beginning of sense, not the end of it.
verses.19:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Who is the best witness?” Say, “Allah is! He is a Witness between me and you. And this Quran has been revealed to me so that, with it, I may warn you and whoever it reaches. Do you ˹pagans˺ testify that there are other gods besides Allah?” ˹Then˺ say, “I will never testify ˹to this˺!” ˹And˺ say, “There is only One God. And I totally reject whatever ˹idols˺ you associate with Him.”

**A Question About Testimony Instead of Power**

The Makkans had been asking for evidence, and the sūrah now asks them a question about evidence: who is the best witness? The dispute between the Prophet and his people is being treated as a legal matter between two parties, and the verse goes to the largest possible authority, the one whose testimony cannot be doubted because nothing is outside his knowledge. In the preceding verse God is described as All-Aware; here that awareness becomes testimony in a case.

The move is shrewd in a society that ran on witnesses. Contracts, marriages, and blood-money settlements all rested on testimony, and a man's word was a public asset. By framing the argument this way, the verse puts the audience on familiar ground and then names a witness they had not been considering.

**The Witness Between Two Parties**

God is called Witness in several places, and the Book uses the title precisely where a dispute needs closing. The Prophet is told to say that God is sufficient as a witness between him and those who deny (17:96), and the title also appears in the account of the Day when witnesses testifies for every community (22:17; 85:9). The Book never offers this witness as a mere formality.

In this sūrah the parties are the messenger and his own people, standing in one marketplace with incompatible accounts of what is true. The audience had spent years asking the Prophet to produce a witness of their choosing — an angel, a book, a treasure — and the verse answers the demand for a witness by naming one that no party can cross-examine and no faction can bribe. In a city where a purchased testimony could decide a case, the choice of witness is the argument. Neither can produce an ordinary witness who saw revelation arrive, and that is the point. The only being present at the giving of the message, at the intention of the messenger, and at the secret reasoning of the deniers is the One who is now named as the witness between them.

**The Warning That Extends to Whoever It Reaches**

The verse then states why the revelation was given: so that with it the Prophet may warn you and whoever it reaches. The wording places everyone who hears the Book on the same footing as the first audience, which is how the sūrah's message becomes universal rather than a local announcement. Commentators read the phrase as evidence that the Qur'an's warning is addressed to whoever the text arrives at, generation after generation, not only to the Arabs of the Prophet's lifetime.

That universality changes the tone of the verse. If the warning stopped with the Quraysh, the argument about witnesses would be a closed historical dispute. Because it travels, the same question travels with it, and every later hearer is placed in the position of those who heard it first.

**The Turn: Do You Testify to This?**

Having established the witness and the warning, the verse pivots and asks the disbelievers whether they testify that there are other gods besides Allah. It is a carefully chosen question, because it forces the audience to move from practice to claim. Makkans performed rites for their deities; being made to say aloud, as testimony, that these were gods besides God was another matter.

The answer is supplied before they can speak. The Prophet is commanded to declare that he will never testify to it. That refusal is not silence, and it is not neutrality between two accounts. He has been asked to lend his word to the central claim of the society he lives in, and he declines to give it.

**"I Am Quit of What You Associate"**

The verse ends with the formula of dissociation that belongs to the messengers in the Book. Abraham, watching the sun set, tells his people that he totally rejects whatever they associate with Allah (6:78), and Hūd calls on God and the people together to witness that he rejects whatever they associate (11:54). The declaration is not merely that the associates are false; it is that the speaker has separated himself from the practice of associating them.

That separation is the difference between argument and allegiance. A man can debate whether a stone is a god; a man who declares himself quit of the association has told his tribe where he stands in the dispute that governs its life. The verse therefore ends with two statements held together: there is only One God, and the messenger has removed himself from the alternative.

**Why the Verse Replaces a Request With a Witness**

Everything the Makkans demanded — an angel, a written book, signs, a treasure — was a request for something visible. The answer they receive is a witness they cannot see but cannot avoid, and a Book that will serve as that witness in their own language for as long as it is recited. The sūrah does not deny them evidence; it redefines where the decisive evidence lives.

The last words leave the hearer with a choice that is also a testimony. In this verse nobody is asked to produce a miracle. They are asked what they say, and on what authority they would say it, which is a question that follows every reader of the passage out of the text and into his own life.
verses.20:
> Those to whom We gave the Scripture recognize him ˹to be a true prophet˺ as they recognize their own children. Those who have ruined themselves will never believe

**Recognition, Not Information**

The verb in this sentence is not the one used for intellectual knowledge in general; it is the one for recognizing something already known. The People of the Book are not described as encountering a new claim and being persuaded by it, but as seeing someone they had been expecting and identifying him. Their scriptures had described a messenger to come, and the sūrah reports that the identification is not difficult for them.

A covenant is on record elsewhere in which God took a pledge from the prophets that if a messenger came confirming what they had, they would believe in him and support him (3:81). Whether the audience of this verse were rabbis, monks, or traders who had picked up the language of the earlier scriptures, the Book's claim is that the tools for recognition were already in their hands.

**As They Recognize Their Own Children**

The comparison chosen is deliberately domestic. Nobody mistakes his own child for someone else's, and nobody needs an argument to establish the fact. The Book could have said that the People of the Book know him to be true, and it says something stronger: that the recognition is of the same order as the recognition of a face seen every day in one's own house.

The sentence is aimed at the Quraysh more than at the People of the Book. The Makkans were used to dismissing the Prophet as one more local preacher among people who had grown up with him. The verse points across the city to the neighbours who possessed the older books and reports what those books had prepared them to see.

**The Same Claim With an Uncomfortable Addition**

In the sūrah of the Cow the statement is repeated with a second sentence that this verse omits: a group of them hides the truth knowingly (2:146). Recognition and concealment appear side by side in the same report, and the pairing defines the accusation. It is not that the learned among the People of the Book failed to notice the signs; it is that some of them noticed and chose silence.

That is why the sūrah does not rest the argument on their testimony. A witness who has decided not to speak is worthless in court, and the Book never presents the recognition of the People of the Book as the proof of the message. It presents it as evidence against the people who recognized and said nothing.

**Why Recognition Is Not the Same as Acceptance**

Every reader of scripture brings interests to what he reads, and in Makkah those interests were social and economic as much as theological. To acknowledge a new prophet was to fold one's own standing into his, to accept correction from a man of a different clan, and to lose the authority that came from being the custodian of the older books. The Book names the motive plainly as knowledge, which makes the concealment a decision about status rather than a difficulty about evidence.

The verses about the People of the Book are read wrongly when they are taken as a complaint about scholarship. The complaint is about a class of experts who held their position by knowing more than others and who recognized in the new message a claim that would redistribute that position.

**Those Who Ruined Themselves Will Never Believe**

The sentence closes with the refrain the sūrah has already used once: those who have ruined themselves will not believe (6:12). Placed after the recognition of the People of the Book, the clause reads as an explanation of how recognition can fail to become faith. Something in the person is spent, and the loss is his own — the ruin comes first, the unbelief follows, and both are described as the same event seen from two angles.

The Book is careful not to make this a general verdict on every Israelite or Christian who did not accept the message. It speaks of those who have ruined themselves, a category defined by what it does rather than by what it is born into. The verse leaves the category open and lets each hearer decide whether the description fits.

**What the Verse Does for Its First Hearer**

A man being rejected by his own city is told that another community recognizes what his own does not. Read coldly, that could sound like a threat; read in the context of the sūrah's consolations, it is closer to a diagnosis. The refusal of his people is not proof that he is wrong, because the criteria for judging him are available to anyone who has read the earlier scriptures.

The sūrah will return to this comfort more than once, but its placement here matters. The verse stands directly after the great testimony, in which God is named as the witness between the Prophet and his people. In that courtroom the People of the Book supply the material evidence, and this verse reports, flatly, what the evidence shows.

It also settles a question the sūrah's audience would have found confusing. If the earlier scriptures came from the same God, why should a new messenger be a surprise? The verse answers that the earlier books themselves created the expectation, so that the arrival of the messenger is a fulfilment rather than an innovation. The Quraysh could dismiss the Prophet as a man from their own town, but they could not dismiss the fact that the communities with older books had been told to expect someone like him.
verses.21:
> Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His signs? Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed

**A Question That Ranks Wrongdoing**

The sentence is put as a question with no answer available, and the form appears across the Book whenever a particular offence is being placed at the top of the list. Who does more wrong than the one who fabricates lies against Allah (11:18; 18:15; 61:7)? Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah or deny His revelations (7:37; 10:17)? The same interrogative is used of those who bar God's name from being mentioned in His places of worship (2:114) and of those who hide testimony they received from God (2:140).

Ranking wrongs is not the Book's usual habit, and the device is a reminder that the two crimes named here are not moral slips. They are attacks on the source of the whole moral order, and they are committed by people who know the stakes, since the audience hearing this verse had already heard the message of the First Sūrah and the one who was named there as the "Lord of all worlds" (1:2).

**Fabricating a Lie Means Claiming Divine Guidance**

The Arabic phrase is specific. To fabricate against God is to invent a religious practice or belief and present it as God's command, which is why the Book attaches the charge to the ritual customs of the Makkans. When they commit a shameful deed they say, "We found our forefathers doing it and Allah has commanded us to do it," and the reply cuts them off: God never commands what is shameful (7:28). The same charge is laid against the invented cattle categories, the baḥīrah, sā'ibah, waṣīlah, and ḥām, which the sūrah itself treats at length: God never ordained them, but the disbelievers fabricate lies about Him (5:103).

An invention is not a harmless opinion, because a person who adds a rule to the religion has appointed himself a legislator beside God. He is not merely mistaken about the law; he is claiming the authority to make one.

**The Other Crime: Denial of the Signs**

The second half of the verse names the opposite operation. Denial does not add to God; it removes what He has already shown, refusing the evidence that the sky, the harvest, and the record of ruined nations were said to supply. Both are named together in 7:37 and 10:17, and the pairing is deliberate, because the two offences describe the same act of rearranging authority: one party edits the message, the other deletes it.

Between them, the two clauses close the exits. A person cannot escape into tradition, since tradition is where the inventions were lodged, and he cannot escape into scepticism, since scepticism has already been named as a crime rather than a method. The verse leaves the reader standing between the two doors with nothing on either side.

Denial also has a working form in the audience's own city. Signs were not met with silence; they were reassigned. The recitation was called magic, the messenger a poet or a soothsayer, and the warnings of the earlier scriptures were treated as material that had been borrowed and polished. Each reassignment let the sign be counted as something else, so that the person doing the counting never had to answer the question the sign raised. That is why the Book treats denial as an activity rather than an opinion, and why the crime is put on the same level as inventing a religion.

**What "Success" Means in the Book's Vocabulary**

The verb at the end of the verse is the one the Book uses for salvation. Believers are described as successful because they believe in the unseen, keep the prayer, and spend from what they are given (2:5); the people of the Gardens are described with the same word. When the verse says the wrongdoers will never succeed, it is not promising a business failure or a lost battle. It is denying them the only success the Book recognises.

That denial is total in both directions. Commentators explain that the wrongdoers will not find what they seek in this world or the next, which is why the same verb is used where the wrongdoers are seen to have failed after their apparent prosperity was stripped away (28:82). The Makkans would have read the word differently, since their own success was measured in caravans and shrines.

**The Audience That Recognised Its Own Customs**

Nothing in the verse is abstract for the people first addressed by it. They practised the invented restrictions, they petitioned the stones, they repeated the ancestral justifications, and they dismissed the recitation as old stories. The verse asks them which wrong could be greater than what they were doing while they were doing it.

This is the sūrah's method throughout, and it explains why the charge is stated in the present tense of a question rather than the past tense of a report. The verse has no interest in convicting a dead generation. It puts a live audience in front of a live accusation and waits.

**Why the Accusation Is Followed by the Gathering**

The verse refuses to leave the crime without a hearing. The sentence that follows opens with the Day when all of them will be gathered and asked where the gods they claimed have gone. The order is the sūrah's own logic: an offence against God's authority cannot be judged inside a life, because a life is too short to contain its consequences.

What the verse establishes is jurisdiction. If the crime is to take God's authority, the trial must belong to God, and the Book therefore moves from the question about wrongdoing to the scene of the gathering, where the answer will be given by the accused themselves.
verses.22:
> ˹Consider˺ the Day We will gather them all together then ask those who associated others ˹with Allah in worship˺, “Where are those gods you used to claim?”

**An Interrogation Rather Than an Announcement**

The scene opens with a question addressed to the polytheists, and the question is not about what they did. It asks where the gods are. In a trial, that kind of question is not an attempt to obtain information, since the one asking knows the answer. It is the device a judge uses to make the accused confront the object of his own claim, and it works by requiring him to look.

The Book returns to this question with a frequency that suggests it was the most effective thing that could be said to a people who had built their lives around shrines. On the Day of Judgment He will humiliate them and say, "Where are My associate-gods for whose sake you used to oppose the believers?" (16:27). The same challenge is reported in the sūrah of Stories twice over (28:62; 28:74), and again in the sūrah of the Believer (40:73), and once in Fussilat (41:47).

**The Gathering That Comes Before the Question**

All of humanity is assembled first: We will gather them all together. The Book insists on the totality of that assembly because the Makkan argument had rested on a small society of important people. In this world a shrine belongs to the strong, who can prevent questions from being asked and shut down the ones who ask them. At the gathering, the audience is every human being who has ever lived, and the tribe can no longer determine who speaks or when.

That is why the verse says "all together" rather than naming the guilty group. The polytheists are addressed by name afterwards — those who associated others with Allah in worship — but they are addressed inside a crowd that removes every advantage they had enjoyed on earth.

**The Word "Claim" Puts the Charge in Their Own Mouths**

The verse does not say "those gods you used to worship"; it says the gods you used to claim. The substitution is pointed. A claim is a public assertion a person advances, and the Book treats the theology of the Makkans as exactly that: a proposition maintained by a community, defended in councils, and financed by the offerings made at its shrines. There is no suggestion anywhere in the verse that the gods had an independent existence which the audience had discovered.

Everything in the sentence reduces the deities to an assertion. They were claimed into being as objects of worship, kept alive by repetition, and defended by social pressure. That is why the question at the end can be so short. If the gods owe their existence to a claim, the collapse of the claimants ends them.

**Where the Absent Are**

The answer is silence. In the parallel passages the accused cry out that their gods have failed them and confess that they had invoked nothing real (40:74); elsewhere the associates are said to fail their worshippers and the worshippers realise there is no escape (41:48). The question therefore works as a demonstration rather than a rebuke. Everyone present sees, in the same instant, that the whole apparatus was empty.

Nothing is reported about their gods arriving to defend them, and nothing is reported about their intercession, which is exactly the point the verse wants to press. The Book allows the idols every kind of dignity except presence at the moment when presence would matter.

**Why the Scene Is Rehearsed So Often**

A Makkan listener could dismiss a claim about the Hereafter as a story from elsewhere, since no one had returned to confirm it. He could not dismiss what the claim implied about his own confidence. Each time the Book stages this question, it invites its hearer to imagine a situation in which the things he relies on can no longer help, and to notice what he would then have left.

The frequency of the scene also tells the reader something about how the Book argues with idolatry. It could have listed the idols' deficiencies one by one, and it does that elsewhere. Here it does something sharper: it takes the audience to a moment when no deficiency has to be explained, because the objects of worship simply are not present. Nobody in the crowd needs a lesson in theology when the defendants fail to appear.

That exercise is available to any reader in any century. The gods may be stones, or markets, or the opinion of a family, or a standing among neighbours, and the question keeps its shape: the things relied on are the things that will be asked about, by name, in front of everyone, and the answer will be given by the person who staked his life on them.

**The Question Left Standing for the Hearer**

The verse places the reader in the position of the judge's assistant: he watches the interrogation and hears the question before the accused does. That arrangement is deliberate, and it is the reason the sūrah says earlier that God knows what is concealed and what is revealed (6:3).

Nothing in this verse is settled by argument, and nothing is settled by force. A question is put, a claim is quoted back to its owner, and the answer is left to arrive in due course. The verse ends on the question mark, which is where the audience's own thinking has to begin.

It is also worth noticing what the verse does not ask. There is no request for an explanation, no demand for repentance, and no negotiation about terms. The question concerns the location of a set of objects that the accused had treated as divine, and the only honest answer available to them is the one the Book records in the parallel passages, where the gods are said to have failed them and the worshippers admit they had invoked nothing real (40:74).
verses.23:
> Their only argument will be: “By Allah, our Lord! We were never polytheists.”

**The Defence That Convicts Its Speaker**

Facing a question they cannot answer, the accused produce one sentence, and the sentence is a lie sworn in the name of the God they spent their lives ignoring. They do not plead that the idols were powerful, or that they had misunderstood the message, or that their ancestors misled them. They deny the charge entirely, and they do it under oath, in the presence of the One they are swearing by.

The verse presents the reply as their "only argument," which strips away every version of the defence a person might expect from a people who had reasoned about religion for decades. The skill they displayed in the marketplaces of Makkah, the rhetoric of their poets, and the traditions of their elders all disappear, and nothing remains but an oath. A city that had produced negotiators, genealogists, and keepers of shrine custom finds itself in front of the gathering with one sentence to say.

That sentence is also, on its face, a denial of the plainest facts about their own conduct. They had made pilgrimages to the stones, slaughtered for them, distributed shares of their harvests to them, and argued in the market about their standing. To call all of that by another name in front of the One who recorded it is to attempt a change of legal category at the last possible moment.

**Swearing by the God They Denied**

There is a bitter irony in the formula they choose. Their oath is taken in the name of Allah, and they attach the word "our Lord" to it, which is an acknowledgement of the lordship they had refused to live by. The Book notes elsewhere that the Makkans already knew who created the heavens and the earth and would say so if asked (31:25; 43:9). In the moment of judgment they say it again, with the name they had avoided, to deny the practice they had maintained.

That confession is wrung out of them and used against them. They have just testified to the authority of the God in whose presence they are standing, which makes the denial that follows harder to file as an error of judgement.

Swearing in God's name was not, for this audience, an unusual thing to do in a tight corner. The Book records that they swore their most solemn oaths that a warner would make them better guided than any other community, and that when the warner came it only drove them further away (35:42); they swore that God would never raise the dead (16:38); they swore that a sign would bring them to belief (6:109). The oath of 6:23 is the last of that series, and the sūrah of the Argument reports the same behaviour on the Day of Resurrection, when people will falsely swear to God as they used to swear to their leaders, thinking they have something to stand on, and are named in the report as the total liars (58:18).

**Why They Believe Their Own Denial**

A person who spends forty years among idols does not necessarily experience himself as a polytheist. The Makkan position, as the Book describes it, was that the stones were intermediaries — a position that allowed its holder to think of himself as honouring the supreme God while approaching him through lesser powers. Under that description, the accusation of associating partners with God can be sincerely denied, because the worshipper never thought of his intermediaries as divine in the same sense as the Creator.

The verse takes that self-image and holds it against the record of what the people did. Their hands performed the rites, their money funded the shrines, and their leaders opposed the Prophet on the ground that he was attacking their gods. Whatever their theory of the stones was, their actions had already filed the case.

**The Disclosure That Comes First**

The Book describes a moment before the lying begins: what they used to hide becomes clear to them (6:28). The verse at hand sits inside that disclosure. They are not being asked to remember an event from long ago; they are standing in front of a record that has been produced, and the denial is spoken against what they themselves now see.

That is the terrible shape of the scene. A person who has been shown the truth of his own case and still denies it has crossed out of the category of the mistaken and into the category of the liar, and the Book names the result plainly: see how they lie about themselves (6:24).

**The Gods Who Refuse to Back Them Up**

Elsewhere the Book lets the false deities speak. When the polytheists call on their associate-gods, the gods throw the accusation back at them and say that they are definitely liars (16:86), and on that Day they offer full submission to Allah while everything they had fabricated falls away (16:87). Even their allies from the unseen do not defend them. Satan himself announces at the end that he had no authority over them, that he only called and they answered, and that they should blame themselves (14:22).

The Makkans had expected supporters. What they get is a courtroom where every witness, including their own gods and their own leader, declines to speak on their behalf. The oath in the verse is therefore the sound of a man abandoned by everyone he had relied on.

**A Sentence That Describes a Permanent Human Habit**

The specific denial concerns idol worship, but the pattern is broader than the seventh century. A person who has arranged his life around something other than God will often insist that he has done no such thing, because his own definition of the offence excludes the thing he does. The Book does not argue with that definition. It records the oath, notes that the gods have failed, and leaves the reader to notice that the final verdict belongs to the One being sworn by.

The verse that follows turns to that discovery, and the sūrah uses the same formula later in describing a different audience. Here the courtroom is still in session, and the accused has just finished his testimony.
verses.24:
> See how they will lie about themselves and how those ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them

**An Order to Look at a Specific Moment**

The verse begins with a command to observe: see how they will lie about themselves. It is the same instruction the sūrah gives later when it describes those arraigned before the Fire (6:27) and when it reports what the disbelievers will say when they stand before their Lord (6:30). The reader is not asked to form an opinion about the Hereafter in general. He is placed at a precise point in a scene and told which detail to notice.

The device appears throughout the Book as a way of settling an argument that a general statement cannot settle. Denial in this life is cheap, because the denier holds the initiative and can keep changing the subject. The verse asks its hearer to watch what denial looks like when the initiatives have all been taken away.

**The Third Target of Their Lying**

Earlier in the passage the lies were aimed outward. They fabricated against God and they denied His signs (6:21), so their untruth was directed at their Lord and at the evidence He had supplied. Here the lie turns and strikes the speaker: they lie about themselves. The sentence they swore in the previous verse was intended to protect their standing, and it does the opposite, because a denial spoken in the presence of full knowledge is a verdict on the person who speaks it rather than on the case.

That movement is worth tracking, since the Book maps the damage of lying in concentric circles. A lie against God corrupts the religion, and a lie against the signs corrupts the evidence, while a lie about oneself corrupts the only thing a person carries out of this world.

**Why the Damage Lands on the Liar**

Commentators explain the phrase as a realization that arrives in the Hereafter, when the consequences of deeds are displayed and the truth about the person becomes visible to him. The Book names that day the day when the secrets are tested (86:9), which is precisely the function of the scene here: the hidden thing is produced, and the false story collapses against it.

No one has to expose these people and no witness has to accuse them. Their own record is the refutation, and their oath is the proof that they knew what they were doing. The verse's verb of lying is not a comment about their ignorance but about their choice to speak against what they could see.

**The Fabrications That Walk Away**

The second half of the verse states the consequence: the gods they fabricated fail them. The Book uses the same expression repeatedly at the end of scenes like this one. Coming back to God all alone as He created the first time, a person finds that his intercessors have vanished, his ties broken, and his claims brought to nothing (6:94); every soul faces what it has done, and whatever gods they fabricated fail them (10:30).

The failure is not described as an act of punishment. It is described as absence. The systems that were built to carry a person through the judgment simply do not arrive, and the worshippers who had spent their lives maintaining them are left carrying nothing. The sūrah of the Heights uses the identical closing formula in the same setting: those who ignored the warning ask for intercessors or for a second term, and the report ends by noting that they have ruined themselves and that whatever gods they fabricated have failed them (7:53).

What disappears with the gods is the entire chain of dependence that had been arranged around them. No patron steps forward, no offering is remembered as a credit, and no lineage carries weight. The verse that reports the collapse at the beginning of the Hereafter, when people come back alone as they were created the first time and every tie is broken (6:94), describes the same vacuum from a different angle.

**Idolatry's Ordinary Disappointments in This Life**

The Makkans did not need to wait for the Hereafter to test the reliability of their gods. The Book points out that the objects of their worship neither respond nor protect nor benefit (20:89), and it asks how anyone can worship, besides God, what can neither harm nor benefit him (5:76). The complaint is not that the idols are weaker than another deity. It is that they are not participants in the transaction at all.

Read that way, the verse's demonstration has already been running in the audience's own experience. A stone that fails in a famine will fail at the judgment; the difference is only that at the judgment nobody can leave and go home.

**What the Reader Is Meant to Take Away**

The instruction to look is not aimed at the men in the scene. It is aimed at the person holding the text, who is still alive, still able to choose, and still in a position to examine what he relies on. The sūrah will go on to describe people who listen without hearing (6:25) and leaders who block the way (6:26), and this verse stands before them as the preview of where that road ends.

Two things are being shown: an accusation that convicts by its own utterance, and a support that stops supporting. The reader who has understood both has understood the case the sūrah intends to make before it moves to anything else.

There is also a difference between regret and change, and this verse marks the border between them. The men in the scene have understood their position completely, and their understanding produces nothing but a denial. That distinction between knowing the truth and letting the truth redirect a life is what the sūrah examines next, in a passage about people who hear the recitation and leave it still deciding about the recitation rather than about themselves.
verses.25:
> There are some of them who ˹pretend to˺ listen to your recitation ˹of the Quran˺, but We have cast veils over their hearts—leaving them unable to comprehend it—and deafness in their ears. Even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them. The disbelievers would ˹even˺ come to argue with you, saying, “This ˹Quran˺ is nothing but ancient fables!”

**Listeners Who Do Not Hear**

The verse opens with attendance. Some of them do listen to the recitation, and their bodies are present in the gathering, which makes their condition the more revealing. What reaches them is not a rumour but the text itself, recited in their own language. Nothing arrives; the sentence reports the veil over their hearts and the deafness in their ears, and it does so without suggesting that either came from a shortage of recitation on the Prophet's side.

The Book uses the same language for the same condition elsewhere. Their hearts are sealed along with their hearing, and their sight is covered (2:7); veils are cast over the hearts and deafness placed in the ears, and when the Lord alone is mentioned they turn their backs in aversion (17:46); they are described as those who turned a blind eye to the reminder and could not stand listening to it (18:101).

**The Two Impediments and What Each Blocks**

The veil over the heart prevents understanding, and the deafness in the ears prevents reception. The pairing is exact, and it distinguishes two separate failures that a casual observer would merge. A person may hear words without grasping them, and a person may grasp a meaning without accepting the words he heard. The verse closes both routes at once, and it locates the obstruction inside the listener rather than in the message.

Commentators describe the veil as a darkness of the soul that obscures the light of the message, which fits the sūrah's opening statement that God made darkness and light (6:1). What is at stake in the verse is thus not the quality of the recitation. It is whether the lamp can be seen by a person who has closed the shutters.

**The Question of Who Closed the Shutters**

Since God is the one said to have placed the covering and the deafness, the verse raises the question every reader of the Book eventually asks. Some commentators take it as proof that belief and disbelief are decreed, and the veil as a sign of a fixed disposition toward denial. Others object that this would make the call to believe meaningless for those so described, and would give the disbelievers an argument against God, since no soul is tasked beyond its capacity (2:286).

The stronger reading, and the one the surrounding verses support, is that the covering follows the refusal rather than preceding it. The Book states the sequence where it says that God leaves to stray those who are already in a state of disbelief and wrongdoing, and where it describes a person who takes his own desire as a god and is then left to stray knowingly (45:23). The hardening is the consequence of a decision, not the cause of it, and the same chapter that reports the veil reports the deliberate turning away in the verse immediately before (18:57).

**Signs Would Not Change the Outcome**

Having described the impediment, the verse removes the last comfort available to the sceptic: even if they were to see every sign, they still would not believe in them. The Book repeats this in several places with a firmness that leaves no room for negotiation (7:146; 10:96). The clearest case is recorded in the sūrah of the Moon, where the splitting of the moon, granted in answer to a demand for a sign, produced the reply that this was the same old magic (54:1–2).

A demand for evidence therefore cannot be taken at face value when it comes from this quarter. The sign would arrive, be examined, and be renamed, because the obstacle was never the strength of the proof.

**The Debate That Follows the Recitation**

The verse's last clause records what happens after the listening. The disbelievers come to argue, and the argument they bring is that the Qur'an is nothing but ancient fables. The same charge appears in a series of reports — the recitation is familiar, they could produce something like it, and the material is old (8:31); it is what the Lord has revealed, they are told, and they answer that it is ancient fables (16:24; 68:15); and others allege that it was written down and rehearsed morning and evening (25:5).

The charge is not a counter-argument, since it says nothing about whether the material is true. It is a social verdict dressed as a literary one, and the Book quotes it because it shows what the arguing was for. People who have decided not to accept a message do not need to refute it; they need a phrase that makes it uninteresting to their neighbours.

**Who the Verse Was Reported to Concern**

Some commentators report that this passage concerned leading figures of the Quraysh, including Abū Jahl and Abū Sufyān, who sat near the Prophet and heard the recitation without accepting it. The attribution is reported in the tafsīr literature rather than established by a firm chain, so it is given here as a report and not as a fact about named individuals.

What can be established from the text itself is the shape of the condition: attendance without comprehension, comprehension without submission, and submission replaced by a slogan. The verse describes a class of listeners rather than a single occasion, and it ends by naming what they carry away from the recitation instead of what they heard in it.
verses.26:
> They turn others away from the Prophet and distance themselves as well. They ruin none but themselves, yet they fail to perceive it

**Two Refusals in One Sentence**

The verse describes a double movement: turning others away from the Prophet, and standing back from him. The first half is social and the second is personal, and together they form a policy rather than a mood. The leaders of Makkah did not simply decline the message; they made sure the people around them did not get near it, and then kept their own distance so that no association with the Prophet could be held against them.

The Book records the operational version of this policy in another sūrah: the disbelievers advised one another not to listen to the Qur'an, but to drown it out with noise so that they might prevail (41:26). That is a meeting, a decision, and a method. Noise was the earliest instrument of censorship available in Makkah, and the verse in front of us describes the two halves of the same decision, one aimed outward and one aimed inward.

**Why Blocking the Road Was a Business Decision**

Makkan hostility to the message was not detached theological dislike. The standing of the city rested on the sanctuary, the pilgrimage seasons, and the network of shrines and offerings that made Quraysh a broker between tribes. A message that made the idols functionally worthless threatened revenue, prestige, and the regional arrangement in which the clan's authority was grounded. The Book describes the pattern in general terms when it speaks of those who hinder others from the way of Allah, striving to make it appear crooked (14:3), which is deliberate distortion rather than passive unbelief.

The refusals in the verse therefore belong to people with something to protect. The tribal notables were not free to accept the Prophet without dismantling the basis of their own standing, and the sūrah's argument repeatedly exposes the interests behind the doctrine.

**The Reading That Points to Abū Ṭālib**

Some early exegetes read the first clause differently, taking the thing forbidden to be harm to the Prophet rather than the message itself, and applying the verse to Abū Ṭālib, the Prophet's uncle and early protector, who shielded him from the notables while not accepting the message. The interpretation is transmitted from several commentators.

Its weakness is the sentence that follows. The verse censures those it names as people who ruin none but themselves, and shielding the Prophet was a service, not a ruin. The commentators who report the Abū Ṭālib reading also note that it sits awkwardly in a passage aimed throughout at the leaders who persecuted the Prophet, and the Shia tradition rejects the attribution altogether, holding that Abū Ṭālib died a Muslim. The obstructionist reading is the stronger one, because it gives both halves of the verse a single hostile meaning and keeps the censure where the passage has placed it.

**"They Ruin None but Themselves"**

The verse then turns the policy back on those who designed it. Whatever they believed they were protecting by keeping the message away from their people, the Book reports the loss as their own. The followers they turned away are not excused, and the leaders are told elsewhere that they will carry their burdens in full on the Day of Judgment along with some of the burdens of those they misled without knowledge (16:25).

A principle stated repeatedly in the Book holds the two truths together: no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another (6:164; 17:15; 35:18). The led answer for their own choices and the leaders answer for theirs, which include the choices they cultivated by blocking the road. What no leader can do is hand his loss to the people he obstructed.

**Why the Damage Stays Invisible**

The closing phrase explains how such a policy survives for years: they fail to perceive it. Nobody assembles in a council and resolves to ruin himself. Those notables believed they were defending the standing of the city, the customs of their fathers, and the position of their families. The Book's diagnosis is that a man can spend a lifetime defending an arrangement without noticing that the arrangement is consuming him.

That is what makes the verse permanent rather than local. Every generation produces people who cannot be shown their own losses because the losses are dressed as loyalty. Naming the damage plainly is a mercy toward them, and the difficulty of the verse is that the people it describes would not have recognised the description as theirs.

**The Barrier That Trapped Its Builders**

A wall built across a road keeps other people out, and it also fixes the builder on one side of it. The notables who turned others from the Prophet had committed themselves to a position they could no longer leave without humiliation, since a man who spends years discrediting a message cannot quietly accept it afterwards without conceding that his whole campaign was wrong. The Book describes the same trap elsewhere in the story of those who planned their strategies and found that God's own planning was ahead of it (86:16).

This is the practical sense in which they ruined none but themselves. Their followers could still hear the message from another quarter, and many of them eventually did, while the leaders had staked their authority on the message being false and were therefore unable to reconsider it. The turn away in the verse is not only an act they performed on others; it is the door they closed on themselves.

A question hangs over the sentence. If the notables turned the people away and the people went, what becomes of the ones who obeyed? The Book answers elsewhere by distinguishing those who followed without knowledge from those who taught them error, and it assigns responsibility to both rather than excusing either. This verse names only one party because its subject is the turning away itself.

What it leaves is the picture of a road with a barrier across it, guarded by men who think the barrier is protecting them. The verses that follow turn to a different group, people who came to argue after listening, carrying conclusions that had been settled before they arrived, and the two passages describe the same city from two floors of the same building.
verses.27:
> If only you could see when they will be detained before the Fire! They will cry, “Oh! If only we could be sent back, we would never deny the signs of our Lord and we would ˹surely˺ be of the believers.”

**A Scene Shown to the Prophet**

The Book several times asks the Prophet to picture a moment he cannot witness, so that its weight enters his argument. If you could see when the wrongdoers are in the throes of death while the angels stretch out their hands (6:93); if only you could see when they will be detained before their Lord (6:30); if only you could see the wicked hanging their heads in shame before their Lord, crying that they have now seen and heard and asking to be sent back (32:12). The device takes a claim about the future and gives it the force of a scene already in progress.

Its placement here matters. The verse before it described leaders who turned people away from the Prophet and kept their distance while ruining themselves, and this scene shows where that road ends. Nobody in the picture is debating theology, and nobody is guarding a shrine.

**Detained, Not Yet Thrown In**

The Arabic verb describes being held back and made to stand in front of something, which shapes the whole passage. These people are not yet inside the punishment, and they are not on their way back to the ordinary world either. They are held at the point where the truth about their lives is visible in front of them and nothing can be done about it, which is precisely the position the sūrah has been telling its audience they refuse to imagine.

Standing rather than burning means the scene is about knowledge before it is about pain. What is recorded in it is not a sensation but an understanding, and the request that follows is produced by that understanding rather than by the heat.

**The Reading That Changes the Grammar**

The sentence they speak admits two vocalisations, and the difference matters. On the reading followed by the translation, they promise: if we were sent back, we would never deny the signs of our Lord, and we would surely be of the believers. On the other reading, the sentence is a regret about the past rather than a pledge about the future: would that we had not denied the signs of our Lord, and that we had been among the believers.

Commentators who weigh the two prefer the first, because the verse that follows explicitly rejects the pledge: even if they were sent back, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden. A regret about the past would leave that rebuttal without a target, while a promise about the future gives it something to refuse. The disagreement is grammatical, and its resolution is that one reading supplies the next sentence with its subject.

**The Request Every Generation Makes**

Begging for a return is a fixed feature of these scenes, and the Book repeats it because the request never becomes less common. The wrongdoers plead, as they face the torment, to be shown any way back (42:44); people scream to their Lord to take them out so they may do good rather than what they used to do (35:37); the wicked ask to be sent back, promising good conduct and claiming sure faith (32:12); and the misled followers, seeing the fate of the leaders they obeyed, cry out that with a second chance they would disown them as they were disowned (2:167).

The repetition shows what the discovery of truth does to a person who lived around it without submitting to it. It also shows the reader this scene in advance, since the request is granted to nobody in the Book.

**Why the Wish Cannot Be Honoured**

Nothing in the scene is arbitrary. The life being asked for was already given, and the answer to a direct request for return is recorded: were you not given lives long enough for whoever wished to be mindful to be mindful, and did the warner not come to you (35:37)? A second term would add no information to the case, because the information had been delivered. What it would add is a different motive, and a virtue produced by the sight of the Fire is not the virtue the test was designed to produce.

That is the difference between a life built on conviction and a life adjusted to consequences. The sūrah's argument has been that the signs were sufficient for anyone willing to weigh them; a second term would replace weighing with arithmetic.

**The Voice of Panic, Not of Faith**

Commentators observe that the promise is made out of fear of the Fire rather than from any real desire for belief, which is why it carries no benefit. That judgement sounds harsh until the words are examined. A person who wants to be sent back so that his situation may be improved is asking for relief; a person who wants to be a believer is asking for a change in himself, and the sentence in the verse is the first kind of request.

The Book has already recorded what happens to a promise of belief made at the sight of punishment, in the case of Pharaoh as the sea closed over him. He declared his faith, and was told that it came too late, after a lifetime of disobedience and corruption (10:90–91). The verse in front of us is that moment, multiplied into a crowd, and spoken before the reader has to reach it.

There is one further difference worth noticing between the two scenes. Pharaoh spoke when the water arrived and there was still a heartbeat in which to speak, while the men in this verse are detained in a place where the ability to act has been withdrawn entirely. Both confessions cost their speakers nothing, which is precisely why the Book reports them and refuses to count them as faith. A confession whose price is zero cannot be evidence of anything about the person making it.
verses.28:
> But no! ˹They only say this˺ because the truth they used to hide will become all too clear to them. Even if they were to be sent back, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden. Indeed they are liars

**The Refusal That Opens the Sentence**

The verse begins with a word of correction, a blunt denial of what the previous sentence reported. The promise made in front of the Fire is struck down before it can be examined, and the striking down happens in a single syllable. The Book uses this device when it wants a claim cancelled rather than argued with, and the cancellation here is total: what the speakers offered as evidence of their sincerity is dismissed as a symptom.

The word also tells the reader how to hear the rest of the verse. What follows is not a debate with the people in the scene but an explanation of them, given to whoever is listening now. The Book explains why men promise reform in the fire of the Hereafter while they never reformed in the safety of the world.

**What Was Hidden Becomes Plain**
