The reason given is knowledge rather than honesty: the truth they used to hide will become all too clear to them. What was concealed in life, whether the realities of the resurrection and the judgment that the leaders dismissed in public, or the deeds that were kept out of sight, is displayed on the day the secrets are tested (86:9). Their promise is therefore not a change of heart. It is what a person says when he can no longer say anything else.

Commentators offer several identifications of what was hidden: the disbelief that hypocrites concealed, the truth about the Prophet that the People of the Book suppressed, or the evil deeds that the wrongdoers kept from view. The Makkan context favours the last two readings in combination, since the sūrah's opponents had both concealed their own conduct and worked to keep the message from circulating.

**The Counterfactual the Book States With Confidence**

The verse then makes a claim about a world that did not happen. Even if they were sent back, they would certainly revert to what they were forbidden. This is not a prediction about individuals whose future is unknown, since the Book elsewhere records that a return to the world would have produced the same conduct (32:12), and it reports the pattern of a generation that swore the most solemn oaths to believe if a warner came, and then was driven further away when he did (35:42).

That swearing is the key to the sentence. The Makkans had already been given a version of the second chance: they asked for a sign, swore they would believe on its arrival, and when signs came they renamed them. A return with better information would not produce better character, which is why the verse refuses the request on grounds of character rather than of evidence.

**Why the Promise Was a Lie**

The judgement at the end of the verse is severe: indeed they are liars. The promise is a lie, and the Book is not accusing them of insincerity at the moment of speaking. They meant the words as they said them. But a promise made under the pressure of pain and abandoned the moment the pressure lifts is a lie in the only sense that counts, because it was never grounded in the person's own will.

That distinction is the difference between regret and repentance. Regret is a response to consequences, and repentance is a response to the act. The scene records the first in its purest form, and the verse reports that the men who produce it are telling the truth about their feelings and a lie about their intentions.

**The Second Chance That Would Not Work**

Some commentators take the verse as evidence that the destiny of such people was already fixed, and read the return as pointless by decree. Others read the same sentence as a statement about character and habit: a person who returns to the same conditions, with the same appetites and the same social pressures, will repeat the same choices, and the Book's confidence reflects what it knows about human beings rather than about an abstract schedule.

The second reading keeps the verse connected to the world the audience knew. The leaders of Makkah had been offered the message for years, under no compulsion, and had chosen repeatedly. A return would restore the same freedom with the same appetites, and the Book states what use they would make of it.

**What the Book Does With Its Hypotheticals**

The counterfactual here is unusual in the Book, and its rarity is instructive. Ordinarily scripture sends its listeners to the past — ruining towns, destroyed generations, the fate of those who mocked the messengers — and lets the record do the arguing. This verse does the opposite. It invents a future that will never happen, puts the disbelievers in it, and reports what they would have done. The Book is so certain of the outcome that it can conduct the experiment on paper and publish the result.

That certainty is itself a claim about human nature. Appetite, habit, and social position do not change when a person is given a second trip through the same conditions, and the Book states elsewhere that the hearts are alike across generations, so that the demands of one age are the demands of another (2:118). Knowing this, God still grants the span of a life, and the granting is mercy rather than oversight. The men in the scene mistake the delay for an invitation to negotiate, and the verse states in advance why the negotiation would have gone nowhere.

The passage has been describing men who, on the day their options run out, promise to be different. The reader who holds the text is in the position they no longer occupy: still able to change, still able to be different, with the plain words of the message in front of him. That is the purpose of these verses in the sūrah, which is not describing the afterlife for its own sake but using it to make the present urgent.

The sentence that follows takes the reader to the same detained crowd and records a different question, asked by a different speaker, waiting for a different answer. The verse in front of us explains why the answer cannot be the one the crowd was hoping for.
verses.29:
> They insisted, “There is nothing beyond this worldly life and we will never be resurrected.”

**The Claim That Explains All the Others**

The verse names the position underneath every other objection in the sūrah. Requests for signs, arguments about the ancestors, mockery of the warnings, and the obstruction described a few verses earlier all rest on this one conclusion: there is nothing beyond this life, and no return to a judgment. The Book reports the same position in the mouths of other audiences, and it repeats it because it is the foundation on which a whole approach to life can be built.

Elsewhere the denial appears with the same edge: they say that once they are dead and reduced to dust and bones, they will not be resurrected (23:82); they ask whether, when they die and become dust and bones, they will really be judged (37:53); and the disbelievers claim the Hour will never come to them (34:3), a claim answered with an oath by the Lord of the unseen.

**A Sentence About the Boundaries of Reality**

The wording is not "we doubt the resurrection." It is a statement about what exists: nothing beyond this worldly life. That is a complete metaphysics delivered in nine words, and its confidence is worth noticing, because the people asserting it had no means of inspecting the boundary they were describing. A claim of that shape can be made only by a person who has decided what the limits of reality are and then allowed no evidence from outside them.

The Book treats the sentence as a boast rather than a finding. The verse says they insisted, which suggests repetition and reinforcement, the way a position is held by being restated among people who agree with one another.

**Why the Position Was So Useful**

Denial of the resurrection was not an unlucky guess that the Makkans had happened to make. It was the assumption that made their arrangements comfortable. Property, privilege, shrines, slave-trading, and inherited standing all lose their force if a person is going to be held to account for how he acquired and used them. The Book makes the connection explicit elsewhere, where the evil consequences of deeds unfold before people who had taken their religion as play and were deluded by worldly life (7:51).

The sūrah's next verses describe those who deny the meeting with God as the ones who will be caught by surprise, and the connection is the same in each place. A person who has removed the accounting from reality has removed the one limit on how he will treat the world.

**The Book's Name for This Denial**

Note the vocabulary the Book prefers. Rather than arguing about the mechanics of resurrection, it describes the position as denying the meeting with God (6:31); elsewhere as those who do not expect to meet their Lord (25:21). The choice of words places the issue where scripture wants it: not an argument about biology and dust, but a refusal that the account will ever be settled face to face.

That reframing explains why the Book answers this denial with evidence the audience already accepted. It points to the earth being revived after its death and says that people will be brought out in the same way (30:19); it points to the God who causes seeds to sprout and brings the living out of the dead (6:95). The audience had no quarrel with any of those observations. The quarrel was about where they led.

**Proof From the Ordinary World**

The Book's argument from nature is not a metaphor. It is the same Maker doing the same kind of work in front of witnesses every season, and the audience consisted of people who watched it for a living. Rain revives the ground, grain is produced from a seed, and a creature comes out of the dead matter of the earth, all of it under the same authority that the Makkans already conceded when asked who created the heavens and the earth.

The denial the verse reports therefore sits on top of a conceded premise. Acknowledging a Creator who can produce a harvest out of a dry field and then denying that He can produce human beings out of dust is a position that cannot be maintained on grounds available in the audience's own experience.

**The Claim Tested Against What the Audience Already Knew**

The Book does not treat the denial as an unanswerable position, and it does not ask the Makkans to accept a new principle in order to reject it. It asks them about the things they already granted. They accepted that God created the heavens and the earth; they accepted the rain, the harvest, and the span of a human life as coming from a power beyond the shrines. Against that backdrop, the sentence in this verse is not a cautious conclusion drawn from the evidence, and the Book says as much where it reports those who deny the meeting with God asking who will give life to decayed bones while forgetting that they were created in the first place (36:78).

A man who grants a first creation and denies a second has not followed his own premises to their conclusion. He has stopped where the conclusion became inconvenient, which is why the Book repeatedly reaches for the same argument and never bothers to look for a different one.

**First Creation as the Standing Proof**

The sūrah has already made the argument in its opening verses. The One who created human beings from clay appointed a term, and another term rests with Him, and the audience is asked why they still doubt (6:2). The reasoning runs from the creation the Makkans could see in their own bodies to the appointment they could not see, and it uses the visible fact as the guarantee of the invisible one.

That order is deliberate, and it matches the way the Book argues about the earth being revived for its harvest (30:19). The audience is not being asked to believe something without any analogue in experience. It is being asked to accept that the power which produced the analogue can repeat the operation on a larger scale, which is the smallest possible extension of what the Makkans already conceded.

**What the Denial Leaves in Its Wake**

Once the account is removed, the only remaining measure of a life is what can be enjoyed and shown to other people, and the verse that follows describes exactly that. It is worth reading the two sentences as a pair, since the first is the belief and the second is what happens when the belief runs its course. The sūrah will go on to describe how the world, arranged according to this belief, is play and amusement, and how the Home of the Hereafter is better for the mindful, and the argument continues from there.
verses.30:
> But if only you could see when they will be detained before their Lord! He will ask ˹them˺, “Is this ˹Hereafter˺ not the truth?” They will cry, “Absolutely, by our Lord!” He will say, “Then taste the punishment for your disbelief.”

**The Same Crowd, A Different Judge**

The verse opens with the formula used a few lines earlier when the wrongdoers were held before the Fire, and the scene is recognisably the same: people detained, no movement, and a question that will be answered. What has changed is the one asking. Earlier they were held before the punishment; here they are held before their Lord, and the question arrives from the authority they had spent their lives avoiding.

The crowd's own answer in the previous scene was a promise to behave differently if released. The answer now demanded is a straightforward acknowledgment, and the two responses are placed close together so the reader can measure one against the other. The men who promised reform in front of a fire are asked for a simple admission in front of the Lord they denied, and they give it.

**A Question the Answer Cannot Help**

Is this Hereafter not the truth? The question is not an examination, since the reality of what they see is not in dispute. It is the last opportunity to say out loud what their whole life was spent rejecting, and they take it. They say, by our Lord, that it is true. The confession is complete and correct, and it changes nothing, which is the point the Book wants its readers to feel.

The same exchange is reported in the sūrah of the Sand-Dunes with almost identical words: the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire and asked whether this is not the truth, they swear by their Lord that it is, and they are told to taste the punishment for their disbelief (46:34). Two sūrahs record the same script because the scene is fixed for everyone who arrives at it, whatever century they came from.

**The Confession That Comes Too Late**

The Book draws a firm line between believing because the evidence has been weighed and confessing because the evidence has become unavoidable. When Pharaoh's faith arrived as he was drowning, he was told that it came after a lifetime of disobedience and corruption (10:90–91). The same rule is stated for the disbelievers who cry out at the sight of the punishment that they now believe in God alone: their faith was of no benefit when they saw the torment, and that has always been the way God deals with His wicked servants (40:84–85).

Nothing about this is arbitrary. Faith at the sight of the punishment is not a decision about God; it is an adjustment to circumstances. The test in this world was designed for people who had to choose without seeing, and a confession wrung out of a person by force is not the thing the test was measuring.

**Tasting as a Form of Instruction**

The command to taste the punishment is used throughout the Book, and the verb is chosen for what it conveys about knowledge. Tasting is how a person learns what a thing is by experience, and the Book applies it to the consequences of deeds in more than two dozen places. Earlier in the same sūrah, the wrongdoers at the point of death are told they will be repaid with the torment of disgrace for telling lies about God and for being arrogant towards His signs (6:93).

The irony is deliberate. These were people who demanded signs, disputed evidence, and treated the warnings as fables, and their final lesson is delivered by experience rather than by argument. What they refused to know by report they are made to know by contact. The sūrah of the Women states the same law from the other side when it declares that repentance is not accepted from those who persist until they begin to die and then cry that they repent now (4:18).

**The Verse Behind the Verse**

Just before this passage the sūrah states that even if the angels had been sent down, the dead had spoken, and every sign the disbelievers demanded had been assembled before their eyes, they would still not have believed unless God so willed (6:111). The verse in front of us is that sentence carried to its conclusion. Every proof they asked for is now visible, and it produces a confession with no value.

The Book does not present this as a puzzle about God's will. It presents it as a fact about what kind of thing belief is. Belief that arrives after the outcome is known is no longer belief, and a confession that is simply the accurate report of what a person sees is no longer a confession. The sūrah will go on to describe the loss of those who denied the meeting with God, and this scene explains the shape of that loss.

**What the Question Asks the Reader to Admit**

A person reading the passage in a market or a courtyard in Makkah had not yet reached the point where the truth could not be denied, which is exactly why the passage was revealed then. The question in the verse, addressed to a crowd that can no longer benefit from answering it, is aimed over their heads at everyone who still can. The Book elsewhere states the same choice plainly when it reports the exchange between the residents of Paradise and the residents of the Fire, where both sides confirm that their Lord's promise proved true and the wrongdoers are then declared cursed (7:44).

The verse ends without comment on the crowd's fate, because what needed saying has been said. The acknowledgment is on record, the punishment has been ordered, and the sūrah turns next to a description of the people who insisted this day would never come.
verses.31:
> Losers indeed are those who deny the meeting with Allah until the Hour takes them by surprise, then they will cry, “Woe to us for having ignored this!” They will bear ˹the burden of˺ their sins on their backs. Evil indeed is their burden

**Loss Declared Before the Loss Happens**

The sentence passes the verdict in the present tense and then shows the scene that will produce it. Those who deny the meeting with their Lord are already described as the losers, and the description does not wait for the surprise that will make the loss visible. The Book makes the same move in its own compact way when it opens the sūrah of the Passing of Time: humanity is in grave loss (103:2). The verdict is announced in the language of a business account that has already been closed.

The Book's word for this kind of ruin is used elsewhere for the opposite of the successful soul. Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul, and doomed is the one who corrupts it (91:9–10). Loss in this vocabulary is not a penalty assessed from outside. It is the state a person has become, and the announcement comes early because there is still time for the reader to inspect his own account.

**"The Meeting With Allah" Is the Book's Name for It**

The denial is described as denying the meeting with Allah, not as denying a biological event, and the choice of words shapes the whole passage. The Book uses this expression consistently for the people it is describing: those who do not expect to meet Us, pleased with this worldly life and heedless of the signs (10:7); those who disbelieve in Allah's signs and the meeting with Him, who will have no hope in His mercy (29:23); and those who reject the signs and the meeting with their Lord, whose deeds are rendered void so that they will not be given any weight on Judgment Day (18:105).

The phrase places the issue where scripture wants it, which is the face-to-face accounting rather than the mechanics of revival. Its opposite is stated with the same brevity in the sūrah of the Cow, where the description of the guided includes those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return (2:46). The difference between the two groups is not information about the afterlife. It is whether the possibility was allowed to govern how they lived.

**The Hour That Arrives Without an Appointment**

The surprise is the detail that turns a denial into a personal emergency. The Book records it with the same verb in several places. The Hour will take them by surprise, leaving them stunned, unable to avert it or delay it (21:40); do they feel secure that an overwhelming torment will not overtake them, or that the Hour will not take them by surprise when they least expect it (12:107); are they waiting for the Hour to come upon them suddenly when they least expect it (43:66).

The Prophet himself is told to say that he has no power over his own benefit or protection except by God's will, and that if he knew the unseen he would have used the knowledge to his advantage (7:188). The concealment of the date is a deliberate arrangement, and it is precisely what the Makkan denial interpreted as evidence that no date existed.

**The Cry of the Delayed Buyer**

Then they will cry, woe to us for having ignored this. The cry is not a request and not a defence. It is the sound of a person recognising, all at once, what he had been in the middle of. The Book records similar cries in the later passages that describe the same discovery, including the plea of those who see the torment and ask whether there is any way back (42:44), and the man who wishes he had sent something forward for his true life (89:24).

The Arabic phrase suggests neglect of something that was present. What was ignored was not an unknown truth but a known warning, which is why the cry carries no complaint against God. Nobody in the scene says that the information was withheld.

**Al-Rāzī's Picture of the Investor Who Loses the Capital**

Al-Rāzī described this regret by borrowing the language of trade, and the metaphor is apt in a sūrah revealed to a merchant city. He compared it to the ruin of an investor who not only fails to earn a return but loses the principal he had put in. Applied to this verse, the faculties God gave a person — reason, hearing, sight, memory, and years of life — were the principal, and the expectation that they would produce an understanding of the truth was the return.

The picture explains why the Book calls these people losers rather than merely guilty. Nothing has been taken from them by force. They were issued capital, they were warned about the use of it, and they spent it on positions that had to be abandoned the moment the Hour arrived.

**Burdens Carried on the Back**

The verse ends with an image of physical transport: they will bear their sins on their backs. The Book uses the same picture for the burden of a warning refused, where the reminder becomes a load in the Hereafter for those who ignored it (20:100–101), and for the leaders who carry their own burdens in full as well as some of the burdens of those they misled without knowledge (16:25). The legal principle that no soul bears the burden of another (6:164) is untouched by the image, since what is being described is a load the person acquired through his own choices.

Evil indeed is their burden. The sentence is short, and it functions as a judgement on the load rather than a comment on its size. A person who has to carry his own record will find that the record weighs more than everything he had accumulated instead of it.
verses.32:
> This worldly life is no more than play and amusement, but far better is the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. Will you not then understand

**A Description of Attachment, Not of Creation**

The sentence is often misread as a condemnation of the world itself, and the Book itself closes that misreading. God did not create the heavens and the earth and everything in between without purpose (38:27), and the same claim is repeated where the creation is said to have been made for a purpose and an appointed term (30:8). The earth, the harvest, work, marriage, and play are not the problem. The problem is a life that reaches no further than they do and treats them as the whole account.

The sūrah of Iron lists the stages in a single verse — play, amusement, glitter, mutual boasting, and vying for increase in property and children (57:20) — which shows that the Book is describing a progression rather than a single activity. What begins as amusement matures into competition for standing, and that competition is what consumes a life.

**Why Play Is the Right Comparison**

Play differs from work in one respect that matters here: it has no product. A game produces nothing that survives it, and the satisfaction ends with the activity. The Book uses the comparison because the things the audience treated as ultimate — the size of a clan, the number of sons, the wealth of a caravan, the prestige of guarding a shrine — do not survive the person who holds them, and cannot be carried into the accounting that follows.

The same judgement is repeated in other sūrahs, where this worldly life is described as no more than play and amusement, while the Hereafter is called the real life (29:64), and where the world's attractiveness is set against the Home of settlement (40:39). The vocabulary is stable because the doctrine is: what perishes cannot be the point of a creature who does not.

**The Comparison Stated Without a Formula**

The verse then states the alternative in the plainest terms: the Home of the Hereafter is far better for those mindful of Allah. The Book repeats this comparison across several sūrahs, sometimes with the added reassurance that the eternal Home is an accommodation from God and that what is with Him is best for the virtuous (3:198), and sometimes with a warning aimed at those who trade the Hereafter for the present life so that their punishment is neither reduced nor averted (2:86).

The qualifier is what keeps the sentence from being a slogan. The Hereafter is better for the mindful, not automatically for everyone who acknowledges its existence. The Book does not offer the next world as a consolation prize for a life spent ignoring it, and the sūrah's own argument has been that the denial of the meeting is what removes hope (29:23).

**What the Mindful One Actually Does Differently**

The word translated as mindful carries the sense of guarding oneself, and the Book attaches it to conduct rather than to feeling. Those described by it treat the world as a place of work with a fixed number of days, which changes small decisions: how a debt is settled, how an employee is treated, how an inheritance is divided, whether a wrong is avenged. None of that is withdrawn from the world; all of it is performed with an eye on what outlasts it.

That practicality is the reason the verse does not need to list commands. A man who believes the accounting is real will adjust his behaviour without being told each item, and the sūrah's audience knew exactly which of their customs would come under pressure if that belief took hold.

**The Saying About the Prison and the Paradise**

The Prophet expressed the same relationship in a sentence reported in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2956: this world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever. The image is memorable because it explains why the two groups experience the same circumstances so differently. A believer who is wealthy, healthy, and comfortable still treats his situation as a waiting room, while a disbeliever with far less has nowhere else to go and treats the present as the whole of his prospects.

Read that way, the verse is not asking anyone to hate the world. It is telling a person who has decided that this life is everything that his own position is the one being described as play, and that the seriousness he brings to the game does not change what the game is.

**The Question That Closes the Verse**

Will you not then understand? The verse ends by appealing to the faculty it has been addressing, and the appeal is the same one the Book uses when it points to the alternation of night and day, the revived earth, and the record kept of every deed. Understanding, in this vocabulary, is not the ability to grasp an idea but the willingness to act on one.

The question is put to a city that prided itself on sharp dealing and clear judgement. The argument is that a people this good at weighing a caravan's worth should have no difficulty weighing a life, and the verse's refusal to argue further is itself part of the case. It hands the matter over to the reader's own sense of proportion and asks him to use it.

The Book repeats the appeal in other settings — will you not then be mindful, after describing a man who took his own desires as his god (45:23), and will you not then understand, after pointing to the earth and the sky as signs (12:109). The formula marks the place where an argument stops being an argument and becomes a test of the reader. Everything the sūrah has said about creation, mercy, and the coming gathering has been laid out; the last step is the reader's.
verses.33:
> We certainly know that what they say grieves you ˹O Prophet˺. It is not your honesty they question—it is Allah’s signs that the wrongdoers deny

**The Grief Is Acknowledged Before It Is Answered**

The verse begins by naming a private experience and confirming it from the highest authority. God knows that what they say grieves the Prophet, and the knowledge is stated before any instruction or consolation is offered. The Book does the same elsewhere: We certainly know that your heart is truly distressed by what they say (15:97); do not let their words grieve you, for all honour and power belongs to Allah (10:65); and be patient, for your patience is only with Allah's help, and do not grieve over those who disbelieve (16:127).

The acknowledgement itself carries weight. A man being mocked in the streets of his own city is told that the effect on him is known, and the first thing he receives is not a lesson about patience but the fact that his distress has been seen. The reassurances come after, and they come as a consequence.

**The Distinction That Makes the Verse Famous**

The sentence then draws a line the Prophet could not have drawn for himself: it is not you they are denying, but the signs of Allah that the wrongdoers deny. The denial is real, and it is aimed at the message rather than at the messenger's credibility, because the audience had already settled the question of his credibility years before. The man they were disputing with was the one they had named the trustworthy, and the Book itself points to his record when it has him say that he had lived a whole lifetime among them before the revelation came (10:16).

The distinction appears in other forms where the Book ties the treatment of the messenger to the treatment of the One who sent him. Those who pledge allegiance to you are actually pledging allegiance to Allah (48:10), and the Prophet is told to say that if they sincerely love Allah they should follow him (3:31). The message and its bearer can be separated in analysis, and the Book separates them so that the rejection is correctly located.

**What It Means to Reject a Sign**

The thing being denied is not an idea the audience found improbable. The sūrah uses the word signs for the created order as well as for the recited verses, and the Makkans had been living inside both. Their caravans navigated by the stars the Book describes as guidance through the darkness of land and sea (6:97), and they were addressed in a language they loved by a man they respected. To reject the signs is to refuse the route those things point to, not to dispute that the things exist.

The Book states the consequence of that refusal in a form that fits this passage: when a people is arrogant in the land, God turns them away from the signs, so that even if they see every sign they will not believe in it (7:146). The denial is thus an activity of the will rather than a failure of the mind, which is why the Prophet's honesty is not really in question.

**Why This Comfort Is Unique**

The Prophet receives many consolations in the Qur'an, but this is the only place where he is told that the denial is not directed at him personally. Commentators point out that this makes the verse the strongest of the reassurances, because it removes a burden he had been carrying rather than simply telling him to bear it. The grief of a rejected preacher is partly the fear that he has failed, and the verse settles that fear with a fact.

That fact is also a warning to the audience. If the denial bypasses the messenger, it lands on the signs of God, and the wrongdoers are the ones named as denying them. By telling the Prophet where the rejection actually lands, the verse simultaneously tells the deniers.

**The Wrongdoers Named in the Sentence**

The verse does not say that the disbelievers deny the signs. It says the wrongdoers deny them, using the term that throughout the sūrah describes those whose conduct corrupts what it touches. The substitution fits the reasoning established earlier, where denial of the signs and fabrication against God were paired as the two crimes ranked above all others (6:21). A person who denies a sign that has reached him has not merely declined an argument; he has refused something that was owed to the one who sent it.

That is the sense in which the denial is a wrong rather than a mistake. The evidence available to the Makkans was sufficient, the messenger was trustworthy, and the message was in their own tongue. What remained was a decision, and the verse names the decision where it belongs.

**The Comfort Given to Everyone Who Speaks After Him**

The line has outlived its first application. Any person who carries a message and is mocked for it can be tempted to hear the mockery as a verdict on himself, and the verse keeps that from happening by separating the bearer from the message. The Book goes further in the same direction where it tells the Prophet not to grieve himself to death over their denial (18:6; 26:3), since he is not responsible for an outcome he cannot control.

The sūrah does not leave that statement floating. The verse that follows explains how the pattern of rejection has run its course through every previous messenger, and it supplies the patience the Prophet needed by showing him what patience had already produced. The Book's customary way of handling grief in its messenger is to widen the frame until the personal injury becomes one instance of a pattern with a known ending, and that is exactly the shape of the passage that comes next.
verses.34:
> Indeed, messengers before you were rejected but patiently endured rejection and persecution until Our help came to them. And Allah’s promise ˹to help˺ is never broken. And you have already received some of the narratives of these messengers

**Rejection as the Standing Condition of the Work**

The verse hands the Prophet a fact about his own office: the messengers before him were rejected. The Book states it flatly in several places, naming the messengers generally rather than complaining about any single people. If you are rejected by them, so too were messengers before you who came with clear proofs, divine Books, and enlightening Scriptures (3:184); if you are rejected by them, so too were messengers before you, and to Allah all matters will be returned (35:4).

Those earlier messengers are named by community in other passages, where the people of Noah, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh of the mighty structures are listed among those who denied the truth (38:12), and where every community is described as having plotted against its prophet to seize him and argued in falsehood to discredit the truth (40:5). The pattern is not a series of unfortunate incidents. It is the ordinary reception of a message by the society it challenges.

**Patience Until the Help Arrived**

The second clause defines the shape of that patience with a time limit: they endured until Our help came to them. The Book insists on that order in every account. Our help came to the messengers at the moment when they and their followers had reached the end of their resources (12:110); We certainly help Our messengers and the believers both in this worldly life and on the Day the witnesses will stand forth (40:51); and the believers are told that they will not enter Paradise without being tested as those before them were, until they ask when Allah's help will come, and are told that it is always near (2:214).

The wording keeps the Prophet from measuring his position by the middle of the story. A messenger standing in the middle of his mission can see only the rejection, and the verse tells him where the account is going, in the same way the Book tells the whole community that its help is guaranteed in the end.

**The Promise That Cannot Be Broken**

Then the verse states the guarantee without any conditionality: Allah's promise to help is never broken. The Book records the promise itself in the sūrah of the Ranged Ranks, where God's word has gone forth to His servants, the messengers, that they would surely be helped and that His forces would prevail (37:171–173), and again in the sūrah of the Pleading Woman, where God has decreed that He and His messengers will certainly prevail (58:21).

The same guarantee is given about God's word in general, where the Word of the Lord is perfected in truth and justice and none can change His words (6:115), and where the Book tells its readers that there is no change in the promise of Allah and that this is the ultimate triumph (10:64). What the verse offers the Prophet is therefore not encouragement but information. The outcome was announced before the dispute began.

**What the Help Looked Like**

Help in these accounts was not always a military victory or an immediate reversal. For the messengers it came as rescue: We then saved whoever We willed, and Our punishment is never averted from the wicked people (12:110). For the Prophet's own community the deliverance took the form of the eventual establishment of the religion, after years in which the believers were fewer than their opponents and could not protect themselves. The Book also counts the endurance itself as part of what was being perfected, since it tells the believers that they will be tested as those before them were tested, and that the help comes after the shaking rather than instead of it (2:214).

That range matters for anyone reading the verse in a period of weakness. The promise does not specify the date or the method, and the Book deliberately leaves both open, while binding itself on the fact. What the Prophet was entitled to conclude from the histories was that no messenger was abandoned, not that every messenger was vindicated on the timetable he would have chosen.

**Why He Had Already Received the Narratives**

The verse closes by pointing to what the Prophet already possessed: some of the narratives of these messengers. In the Makkan period a substantial body of those accounts had been revealed, and the Book states their function plainly when it says that the stories of the messengers are related to reassure the heart, and that in these stories there is the truth, a warning for the disbelievers, and a reminder for the believers (11:120; 12:111).

So the consolation in this verse is not an abstraction. It is a library the Prophet could open in his own recitation, listing men who were mocked, imprisoned, hunted, and dismissed, and reporting in each case what happened next. The Book treats those reports as equipment for the mission rather than as history for its own sake.

**The Use of a Pattern Rather Than a Promise of Ease**

Nothing in the verse tells the Prophet that his difficulties are about to end. What it tells him is that his difficulties are a repetition, and that the repetition has a known ending. That is a different kind of comfort: it does not remove the hardship, and it removes the uncertainty about what the hardship means.

For the Makkan audience the sentence quietly makes the same point from the other side. A city that had decided the Prophet's struggle was evidence against him was being told to look at how the previous rejections turned out. The verse is addressed to the messenger, and it is heard over his shoulder by the men who were making his life difficult.
verses.35:
> If you find their denial unbearable, then build—if you can—a tunnel through the earth or stairs to the sky to bring them a ˹more compelling˺ sign. Had Allah so willed, He could have guided them all. So do not be one of those ignorant ˹of this fact˺

**A Challenge Built to Be Impossible**

The verse offers the Prophet a way out of his distress and then closes it in the same sentence. If the denial is unbearable, he may go underground and dig his way out, or climb a stairway into the sky, in order to bring them a sign they cannot dismiss. The conditional "if you can" leaves no doubt that he cannot, and the rhetorical shape of the instruction is the argument: no effort available to a human being can produce the outcome he wants.

The Book uses the same device elsewhere with the same intention. Ask them whether, if God made the night perpetual for them until the Day of Judgment, any god besides Allah could bring them sunlight (28:71), and the same question is repeated about perpetual day and the gift of night to rest in (28:72). The impossibility is not stated as a limitation on God. It is stated as a limitation on the audience's demand.

**The Sign That Was Already in Their Hands**

The demand for a more compelling sign had already been answered in a way the Makkans could examine. The Book challenges them directly: if they are in doubt about what was revealed to the servant of God, let them produce a sūrah like it and call their helpers besides Allah, if what they say is true (2:23); let them produce ten fabricated sūrahs like it (11:13); and if all humans and jinn were to combine to produce the equivalent of this Qur'an, they could not produce its equal, no matter how they supported one another (17:88).

So the tunnel and the stairway are not the only routes to a sign. The sign was reciting in the streets and marketplaces of Makkah in their own language, and the challenge to match it stood open for anyone who thought the message was human work.

**The Grief That Is Being Addressed**

The verse does not rebuke the Prophet for being sad. It reasons with him about what his sadness is asking for. Elsewhere the Book treats the same distress with tenderness, telling him that he will perhaps grieve himself to death over their disbelief (26:3), and asking whether he will destroy himself with grief if they do not believe in this message (18:6). The emotion is understood, and its limit is explained.

The limit is that the outcome belongs to God. A messenger is responsible for delivering the message clearly, and he is not responsible for whether a particular listener accepts it. Without that boundary, a preacher's love for his people turns into a demand he cannot meet, and the Book sets the boundary before the demand can do damage.

**"Had Allah Willed, He Could Have Guided Them All"**

The middle of the verse states the fact that settles the question: had God willed, He could have guided them all. The same claim appears in several places with variations. Had Allah willed, He could have easily made all humanity into a single community of believers, but He admits into His mercy whoever He wills (42:8); had He willed, He could have made the whole earth believe, so no one is asked to force people into belief (10:99); and had He willed, they would not have associated partners with Him, and the Prophet is told that he has not been appointed as their keeper or their maintainer (6:107).

Commentators drew opposite conclusions from such verses. Some read them as evidence that God creates human acts and determines the moral destination of each person, while others read them as a statement that God could have compelled everyone into one community but chose instead to let them choose, so that their religious destiny would be genuinely theirs. The second reading accounts better for the sūrah's steady assumption that its audience is being addressed as responsible agents and not as prisoners of a decree.

**The Instruction Not to Be Ignorant**

The verse ends with a warning to the Prophet: do not be one of those ignorant of this fact. The ignorance in view is not a lack of education. It is the failure to understand how guidance works, which would lead a messenger to measure his own worth by the number of people who accept his message, or to believe that the outcome is within his power to force.

The same warning is given to him elsewhere in the sūrah where he is told not to drive away those who call on their Lord, and where he is told that God knows best who is rightly guided. A messenger who understood the mechanism would work without either despair or coercion, because both responses come from the same misunderstanding of where the decision lies.

**What the Verse Leaves the Messenger With**

Once the tunnel and the stairway are taken away, one thing remains: the message itself, delivered with patience for as long as God grants. That is the position the verse pushes its reader toward, and the sūrah immediately turns to the different responses of different hearers. Some will respond, and the dead will be raised to be returned to their Lord, which is the subject the next verse takes up.

The passage leaves no room for a prophet who resigns, and no room for one who forces. What the sentences before and after this one supply is the working conditions of a mission whose results are not in the missionary's hands.
verses.36:
> Only the attentive will respond ˹to your call˺. As for the dead, Allah will raise them up, then to Him they will ˹all˺ be returned

**The Division Drawn by the Answer Rather Than by the Messenger**

The verse states a limit that the previous passage has already prepared. After the impossible tunnel and stairway, and after the reminder that God could have guided everyone had He willed, the sūrah now says who actually responds: the attentive. The word describes people who use the hearing they have, and it puts the difference between the two groups in the listener rather than in the message or in the one delivering it.

The Book draws the same line in several places. Those who respond to the call of their Lord will have the finest reward, while those who do not respond would offer everything in the world twice over to ransom themselves (13:18); and in the sūrah of Yā-Sīn, the Prophet is told that he can only warn those who follow the reminder and stand in awe of the Most Compassionate without seeing Him (36:11). Response in this vocabulary is a faculty in use, not a temperament.

**Hearing With Something Other Than the Ears**

The Book's use of hearing for spiritual comprehension is consistent enough to be called a doctrine. The sūrah has already described listeners with veils on their hearts and deafness in their ears, who hear the recitation and leave it unchanged (6:25). Elsewhere the imagery is the same: those who deny the signs are wilfully deaf and dumb, lost in darkness (6:39); the worst of all beings in the sight of God are the wilfully deaf and dumb who do not understand (8:22).

So the attentive are not an intellectual elite. They are people who permit what they hear to reach the place where decisions are made, and the verse treats that permission as the whole difference between response and refusal. A man can be present at the recitation, understand the words, and still be counted among those who did not hear.

**Who the Dead Are in This Sentence**

The second half of the verse turns to the dead, and commentators read the word in two ways that are not mutually exclusive. Some understand it as a reference to the disbelievers, meaning that they will be raised along with everyone else and judged for their disbelief. Others read it as a description of spiritual death, since a person who has cut himself off from revelation is, in the Book's vocabulary, dead while still walking.

The two readings meet in the Qur'anic image where the Prophet is told that he cannot make the dead hear the truth, nor make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and walk away (27:80; 30:52), and where the dead and the living are explicitly said not to be equal, with the added explanation that God alone makes whoever He wills hear (35:22). The verse in front of us uses the same pairing of attention and death, and then attaches the resurrection to it.

**Resurrection Stated as a Fact About Both Groups**

The clause about resurrection is not a threat aimed only at the deaf. To Him they will all be returned, and the Book puts the guarantee of that gathering in terms of ownership: the One who raises the dead is the One who holds the property rights over everyone who dies. The sūrah has already asked its audience who created them from clay and appointed terms for their death, and it noted the second term that rests with God alone (6:2).

Placing the resurrection here serves a purpose in the argument. The people being addressed had denied the meeting with their Lord (6:31), and the answer to their denial is not an argument from nature or from the ruins of earlier nations. It is the statement that the gathering is happening, together with the observation that the same authority governs both who hears in this life and who comes back in the next.

**The Comfort Inside a Hard Sentence**

Read as a whole, the verse tells the Prophet something he needed after being told that no sign he could bring would ever be enough. It tells him that his work has a defined audience and that the definition is not his to supply. The Book states the same principle where it tells him that he is not a keeper over the people (6:107), and where the duty given to him is described as reminding rather than compelling.

That limit is a mercy to the messenger, since a man who believes the result depends on him will exhaust himself trying to produce faith by force. It is also a mercy to the hearer, since a message delivered by compulsion would have no value in a religion whose central claim is that a person turns to God by choice.

**The Transition the Verse Makes**

The next sentences in the sūrah report a demand for signs, and this verse supplies the ground for the answer they receive. It also holds the two halves of the audience's objection together. A person who says he would believe if a sign arrived has just been told that belief does not work that way, because attention is not produced by the size of the spectacle. If only the attentive respond, then the production of a spectacle would not increase the number of the attentive; it would only increase the number of those who saw it. The verse therefore closes the discussion about evidence in the order it was raised, and it prepares the sūrah's next movement, in which the demand is answered briefly and the argument returns to the audience's own situation.
verses.37:
> They ask, “Why has no ˹other˺ sign been sent down to him from his Lord?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah certainly has the power to send down a sign”—though most of them do not know

**A Demand That Keeps Coming Back**

The request is recorded in the Book more often than any other objection to the Prophet's mission, and it always arrives in the same form: if only a sign could be sent down to him from his Lord (13:7). The same demand appears where people with no knowledge ask for God to speak to them or for a sign to come to them (2:118), where they ask why no other sign has been sent down (10:20), where they demand a sign from his Lord as though the previous ones did not exist (20:133), and where they say that if signs had been sent down, they would certainly have believed (29:50).

The Book also records the oaths the demanders attached to their requests: they swore their most solemn oaths that if a sign came they would believe in it, and the answer they received was that signs belong to God, and that even the sight of one would not produce belief in them (6:109). The demand in this verse therefore arrives with a history attached, which is why the response is so brief.

**The Answer Concedes the Power and Withholds the Sign**

Nothing in the reply denies the ability to do what is asked. Allah certainly has the power to send down a sign, and elsewhere the Book states that if He willed, He could send down upon the people a compelling sign from the heavens, leaving their necks bent in submission to it (26:4). The withholding is not a matter of capacity, and the verse makes that explicit so that the argument cannot be shifted to a question about divine strength.

What the answer does refuse is the assumption that a sign arrives on demand, at the discretion of the people who request it. The Book states the reason for the refusal in another place: nothing keeps God from sending the demanded signs except that earlier peoples denied them, and the sign granted to Thamūd was rejected all the same (17:59). A sign that has already been priced in the ledger of previous generations is not a neutral gift.

**The Precedent That Makes a Sign Dangerous**

The sūrah has already treated this subject in its discussion of the demand for an angel. Had an angel been sent down, the matter would have been settled at once and no further time for repentance would have been granted (6:8). The table sent down to the disciples of Jesus carries the same warning in a different register: whoever denies it afterwards will be subjected to a torment never inflicted on anyone else in creation (5:114–115).

So the sign is not simply evidence. It is an increase of accountability, and the Mercy that withholds it is the same Mercy the sūrah has already said God prescribed for Himself (6:12). A people who demanded a proof they had already decided to reject were asking for something that would remove the interval in which they were still able to change.

**The Sign That Was Standing in the Room**

The Book repeatedly names the Qur'an itself as the sign that was already available. If they are in doubt about what was revealed to the servant of God, let them produce a sūrah like it and call their helpers besides Allah, if what they say is true (2:23). Let them produce ten fabricated sūrahs like it (11:13). If all humans and jinn were to combine to produce the equivalent of this recitation, they could not produce its equal, however they supported one another (17:88).

That challenge was addressed to people whose whole culture was built on the value of words, which is why the Book treats their inability to meet it as decisive. The demand for a different sign asks for something other than the evidence already supplied, and the sūrah has shown earlier what the audience did with the evidence in its hands.

**"Most of Them Do Not Know"**

The verse closes with a statement about the demanders rather than about the sign. Most of them do not know, and the ignorance is not about the mechanics of revelation. It is about the purpose of signs, the reason for delay, and the way belief actually works in a human being. The Book makes the same observation after describing all the evidence God could assemble, where it says that even with angels sent, the dead speaking, and every sign assembled before their eyes, they still would not believe unless God so willed (6:111).

Within the argument of the sūrah, this clause puts the whole discussion on a different footing. The question was asked as though the problem were a shortage of proof in the world, and the answer relocates it to a shortage of understanding in the asker.

**The Consistency of the Sūrah's Answers**

Every demand that has been raised in this passage receives the same kind of answer. The request for an angel was answered with the fact that the angel's arrival would end the opportunity to repent (6:8). The request for a written book was answered with the audience's verdict on it before it arrived (6:7). The request for a compelling sign is answered here with a statement of God's power and a comment on the askers' knowledge.

The pattern is deliberate, and the Book names it in another sūrah where the Prophet is told to say that he only follows what is revealed to him and that the recitation itself is insight, guidance, and mercy for those who believe (7:203). The signs were never the variable. What the audience did with what had already come was.
verses.38:
> All living beings roaming the earth and winged birds soaring in the sky are communities like yourselves. We have left nothing out of the Record. Then to their Lord they will be gathered all together

**"Communities Like Yourselves"**

The word translated as communities is *ummah*, a term the Book normally uses for religious communities formed by a shared relationship to God — the believing community addressed as the best community brought forth for humanity (3:110), and every community having a messenger sent to it (10:47). Applying the word to birds and crawling things widens its range in a way that has no parallel in the sūrah, and the choice of vocabulary is the claim.

The verse does not say that animals resemble human beings in appearance or intelligence. It says they form communities, which in the Book's usage means groups defined by the way they stand before their Creator, and the following verses elsewhere make that relationship explicit. What is asserted here is that human beings are not the only organised creatures with a standing before God.

**What the Rest of the Book Says About Them**

That reading is not an inference from a single word. The Book reports that God revealed to the bees how to build their hives and produce their honey, and it calls the product a healing for people (16:68–69); it states that everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, and that human beings do not understand their glorification (17:44); and it records that the mountains and the birds joined David in praise (38:18–19). The same claim appears where all creatures in the heavens and the earth are said to declare His praise (24:41).

Some commentators concluded from such passages that at least some animals are aware of God, while others held that the description in this verse is simply a way of saying they are God's creatures. The first reading accounts better for the term community and for the glorification passages, and it is the reading the verse itself invites by joining the community claim to the gathering.

**"We Have Left Nothing Out of the Record"**

The middle clause places every creature inside a written account. Elsewhere the Book describes the Preserved Tablet (85:22), and it says that with God are the keys of the unseen, that He knows what is in the land and the sea, and that not a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth, but is written in a perfect Record (6:59).

The clause also answers a practical worry. A person who looks at the world sees enormous suffering among creatures that have no voice and no account: animals killed for no purpose, birds whose nests are destroyed, beasts that are hunted and eaten. The verse states that the record is complete and that no creature is outside it, which is the Book's way of saying that nothing in the creation lives or dies unnoticed.

**Gathered to Their Lord**

Then to their Lord they will be gathered all together. The verb is the one used for the resurrection of human beings, and it is also used of the Day when the wild beasts will be gathered (81:5). Commentators differed over what the gathering of animals means, with some holding that it refers to their resurrection and judgment and others that it means they will be gathered to their deaths. The reports that are authentic on the subject support the first reading in substance.

The most cited is transmitted from Abū Hurayrah in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2582, where the Prophet said that rights will certainly be restored to those entitled to them on the Day of Resurrection, to the point that even the hornless sheep will lay claim upon the horned one. The same report appears in Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 2420, where Abū ʿĪsā grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. What the hadith establishes is that the divine reckoning extends to wrongs that no human court would ever consider.

**What the Verse Requires of Human Beings**

If all creatures are communities with a relationship to their Creator, then the permission human beings have to use animals for food, transport, and labour is a delegation with terms rather than an unrestricted title. The Book does say that the earth and its contents have been subjected to human beings (14:32; 16:14; 22:65), and the same Book says that every creature's provision rests with God (11:6) and that there is no creature on earth whose provision God does not guarantee (29:60).

Those two sets of verses were not treated as contradictory by the scholars who read them together; they were treated as the terms of a trust. The report about the hornless sheep makes the same point from the other direction, since cruelty and waste in the use of creatures are named in the Book among the things that will be answered for.

**Two Ways the Commentators Took It**

Ibn Kathīr reported the disagreement about the gathering, recording the view that animals will be resurrected and judged and the view that they are gathered to their death. Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah, as reported in al-Rāzī, read the beasts and birds as figures for different moral types among human beings, so that the verse becomes a description of people who have come to resemble the animals in their habits.

The second reading has the disadvantage of turning a plain statement about creatures into an allegory, and it leaves the term community without its meaning. The first keeps the verse where it stands, and it explains why the passage appears exactly here, between an argument about signs and a series of warnings about the judgment. The Book follows the smaller creature to its accounting in order to make the larger one unavoidable.

**The Argument From the Smaller to the Greater**

The placement of the verse does the arguing. The audience had been told that the dead will be returned to their Lord (6:36) and that those who deny the meeting will discover their loss (6:31). To that claim the passage now adds that the accounting reaches even the birds, whose lives nobody had ever thought to keep an account of.

If God records the fall of a leaf and the claim of a sheep against another sheep, then the human being who believes his own deeds will go unchecked has misjudged the scale of the administration he is living inside. The verse ends on the gathering because that is the fact the sūrah has been establishing: nobody with a Lord is without an appointment.
verses.39:
> Those who deny Our signs are ˹wilfully˺ deaf and dumb—lost in darkness. Allah leaves whoever He wills to stray and guides whoever He wills to the Straight Way

**Three Conditions in One Sentence**

The verse describes the deniers with three images that cover the whole of a person: hearing, speech, and sight. They are deaf, so the message does not enter; dumb, so no truthful word comes out; and in darkness, so nothing around them can be seen. The Book uses the same combination elsewhere, where those who are wilfully deaf, dumb, and blind will never return to the right path (2:18), and where the example of the disbelievers is a flock that comprehends nothing of the shepherd's calls and cries, deaf, dumb, and blind with no understanding (2:171).

The three conditions are linked rather than listed. A person who hears nothing speaks about what he does not know and walks where he cannot see, so the images describe one condition from three angles, and the Book uses them together because none of them explains the others away.

**Darkness in the Plural**

The sūrah opened by saying that God made darkness and light (6:1), and the Book consistently renders darkness in the plural while light stays singular. The disbelievers are led out of light into darkness, and their false gods are the ones doing the leading (2:257); the Book was revealed to bring people out of darkness into light (14:1); God showers His blessings so that He may bring the believers out of darkness and into light (33:43).

The plural fits the sense of the verse. A person in the dark does not merely lack a direction; he has as many directions as there are paths that go nowhere, and each of them looks plausible at the moment of choosing it. What the verse says about the deniers is not that they lost the map but that they are standing in a place where maps cannot be read.

**The Wilful Element in the Translation**

The rendering supplies the word wilfully, and it is not an embellishment. The Book elsewhere explains the condition as the result of what the person did: those whose hearts are sealed with their hearing, and whose sight is covered, are the ones who suffer a tremendous punishment (2:7); when they are reminded of the revelations and turn away, forgetting what their own hands did, veils are cast over the hearing and the hearts (18:57); and those who take their own desires as a god are left to stray knowingly, with their hearing and hearts sealed and a cover placed on their sight (45:23).

The same sequence appears in the story of the punishment that did not produce humility: instead of humbling themselves when suffering came, their hearts hardened and Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them (6:43). The covering in these passages is described as following on a decision, which is why the translation can fairly say that the deafness is chosen.

**The Deeper Question the Verse Raises**

Since God is said to leave some to stray, the sentence opens a question the scholars of the Book took seriously. The Muʿtazilites argued that God's leading astray cannot be a direct act of misguidance, since that would make the punishment of the misguided unjust, and they read it as the withholding of a grace that would have made the person receptive. The Ashʿarites held that God creates all acts, including human choices, and that guidance and misguidance are determined by His will.

The verses that settle the question most cleanly are the ones that connect the straying to what the people were already doing: the ones who break the covenant and spread corruption are left to stray (2:26); the wrongdoers are left to stray after they took the wrong course (14:27); and Joseph's people were left to stray after they continued doubting what he had brought (40:34). The Book attaches the leaving to a prior condition in every case, and it never describes a person as misled before he chose.

**Guidance as a Straight Way**

The second half of the verse names the alternative as the Straight Way, the phrase that opens the prayer of the Fātiḥah and that the sūrah uses for the path the Prophet was guided to (6:161). The image of the road makes the sentence complete: the deniers are lost in darkness without a path, and the guided are placed on a way with a direction.

Commentators who emphasise human responsibility read the pair as a description of consequences rather than of decrees issued at random. On their reading, God guides the person who turns to Him and leaves the person who turns away, which is exactly what the Book says when it describes the leaving as following on wrongdoing. The sūrah's own audience is being told which side of the sentence they are standing on.

**What the Verse Tells the Listener to Check**

The sentence is not addressed to a hypothetical group from the distant past. It describes a condition that the preceding verses have located precisely: people who asked for signs while signs were present, who called the recitation old stories, who turned others away from the Prophet and kept their distance. Anyone hearing the verse in Makkah could measure the description against a specific list of behaviours he had witnessed or participated in.

That is the practical function of the image. A man can argue about whether he is convinced, and he cannot argue with deafness, muteness, and darkness once he recognises the symptoms in himself. The verse names the symptoms and leaves the diagnosis to the patient, and the sūrah moves next to a question put to the same people about a moment when their sight would be perfectly clear.
verses.40:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if you were overwhelmed by Allah’s torment or the Hour—would you call upon any other than Allah ˹for help˺? ˹Answer me˺ if your claims are true

**A Question That Uses the Audience's Own Experience**

The verse takes the Makkans to a situation every traveller in Arabia knew: a moment of overwhelming danger. Facing the punishment of God or the arrival of the Hour, the question asks whether they would call on anything besides Allah. It is not a question about their theology. It is a question about their conduct in the one situation where conduct becomes involuntary, and the answer is demanded with an oath-like challenge: answer me, if your claims are true.

The Book uses this form repeatedly, and it is one of the sharpest arguments in the Makkan sūrahs because it requires no new information from the audience. They are not being asked to accept a premise; they are being asked to remember what they did.

**The Sea That Made Them Monotheists**

The Book records the answer in several places. When they are touched with hardship at sea, they forget every deity they normally invoke, except Him, and when He brings them safely to shore, they turn away (17:67). When a gale overwhelms a ship and the passengers assume they are doomed, they cry out to Allah alone in sincere devotion, promising gratitude in exchange for rescue (10:22). Waves like mountains produce the same result: they call on Him alone, and once delivered, only some remain grateful (31:32). The same pattern is reported in the sūrah of the Spider, where after rescue they associate others with Him once again (29:65).

The sūrah of al-Anʿām itself has already asked the question in a similar form: who rescues you from the darkest times on land and at sea, the One you call upon in humility, openly and secretly, saying that if He rescues you, you will be grateful (6:63). The answer supplied there is that only Allah rescues from this and any other distress, and yet they associate others with Him (6:64).

**Why Emergency Produces Sincerity**

The phenomenon the verse relies on has a simple explanation. A person in a storm has run out of intermediaries. The stone in its niche cannot still the wind, the tribal patron cannot reach the ship, and the star cannot alter the course of the water. What remains is the One the Makkans had never denied as the Creator, and the instinct that reaches for Him under those conditions is the plainest evidence that the deeper knowledge was never actually lost.

That is why the verse can be called an argument from the audience's own nature. The Book elsewhere notes that even the idolaters, when asked who created the heavens and the earth, answer that Allah did (31:25; 43:9). The crisis on the water simply dismantles the layer of practice that had been built over that confession.

**"If Your Claims Are True"**

The challenge at the end of the verse places the burden of proof on the people making the claims. The Makkans claimed that their deities had standing and could be approached for help. The verse puts the claim into the only test the claimants had never had to face, and asks them to supply the evidence from their own experience.

There is a pointed restraint in the demand. The Book does not ask them to abandon the idols on the basis of a revelation they did not accept. It asks them to notice what they themselves do when revelation is the last thing on their mind, and to draw the conclusion from the one moment when their practice and their belief were forced to agree.

**Torment or the Hour: Two Ways for the Test to Arrive**

The verse names the two forms the reckoning could take: a punishment in this world, or the Hour itself. The Book treats both as legitimate possibilities for its audience, and it describes the first as having already happened to earlier nations while the second remains fixed for everyone. The next verse in this sūrah addresses the same subject from the side of the wrongdoers and their fate when it comes.

For the sūrah's argument the pairing matters, because it removes the escape of a distant deadline. A person who reasoned that the judgment was far away still had to reckon with the possibility of a tribulation in the middle of his own life, and the Book tells its audience elsewhere that they might be taken while travelling on a road or asleep in a house.

**What the Verse Establishes for the Argument Ahead**

Once this question is asked, the sūrah has closed the gap between the audience's beliefs and their conduct. Whatever a man may say about the idols when he is safe and surrounded by his clan, the verse has secured his admission that in the moment of real need he would call on Allah alone. Every later argument in the sūrah about the absurdity of associating partners is built on that confession.

The Book therefore treats the rest of the discussion as unnecessary. If the One who is called in the storm is the One who answers, then the question of who deserves worship has already been answered by the worshippers themselves, and the next sentence simply states the conclusion they have been avoiding.

There is a further implication the audience would have felt. A deity who is not called upon in the emergency is not performing the function of a god at all, whatever his shrine receives during the seasons of pilgrimage. The verse does not dispute the idols' existence; it points out their total absence from the one moment in which the word god has any content.
verses.41:
> No! He is the only One you would call. And if He willed, He could remove the affliction that made you invoke Him. Only then will you forget whatever you associate with Him ˹in worship˺.”

**The Answer Supplied Before the Audience Speaks**

The verse opens with a refusal that is also the answer to the previous question. No, they would not call on anyone else; He is the only One you would call. The Book frequently supplies the answer on behalf of the people it questions, and it does so because the answer is not in dispute. Everyone in the audience knew what happens to a man in a storm, and the verse simply records it as a fact about them.

What makes the sentence forceful is its second-person address. The Prophet is told to say "you," not "they." Each person listening is described to himself in the moment of his own greatest need, which is a more difficult position to argue from than a general statement about idolaters in the abstract.

**The Removal That Depends on His Will**

The next clause preserves God's freedom in the answer: if He willed, He could remove the affliction that made you invoke Him. The Book states elsewhere that God responds to those who call on Him (2:186), and that He has proclaimed that His servants should call on Him and that He will respond (40:60), and it also refuses to make the response a mechanical consequence of the request.

Commentators drew different conclusions from this. For the Ashʿarites the clause supported their position that God's response depends entirely on His will, while the Muʿtazilites read it as meaning that God answers in whatever way serves the greater good. The text itself keeps the request and the answer distinct, which is the posture the Book recommends throughout: ask with urgency, and leave the outcome with the One being asked.

**The Forgetting That Follows Rescue**

The verse closes on a diagnosis of the rescued: only then will you forget whatever you associate with Him. The Book documents this pattern in the same detail in several places. When hardship touches people they cry out to their Lord, turning to Him alone, and as soon as He gives them a taste of His mercy, a group of them associate others with their Lord again (30:33). The gratitude promised at sea is not delivered on land, as the sūrah itself has stated a few verses earlier (6:64).

The word "forget" is exact. The idols were not refuted in the storm; they simply were not there, and once the danger passes the memory of their absence fades with it. The Book treats that forgetting as the real problem, because a person who has seen the truth and lost it is in a different position from a person who never saw it.

**What the Confession Proves About the Idols**

The verse functions as a demonstration of the idols' standing, and the demonstration uses the audience's own conduct rather than an argument about the stones. The Book presses the point elsewhere in a challenge addressed to the same people: those you invoke besides Allah are created beings like yourselves, so call upon them and see if they will answer you, if your claims are true (7:194). It then asks whether those objects have feet to walk with, hands to hold with, eyes to see with, or ears to hear with (7:195).

A deity with no capacity to answer is not a lesser god; it is not a participant in the transaction at all. Once the audience conceded, in the storm, that only Allah is called upon, the whole system of association had been stripped of its function by the people who maintained it.

**The Warning in the Closing Clause**

Read as a warning, the last clause is the most serious part of the verse. A person who calls on God in danger and returns to his old practice once delivered has not merely relapsed; he has made the mercy the reason to continue. The same reversal is described in the sūrah of the Spider, where those rescued from the waves associate others with Him again (29:65), and where the pattern is called out as a mark of the ungrateful.

The sūrah will turn next to a different aspect of the same problem: communities that were tested with hardship and did not humble themselves, and what was done to them in the end. The verse in front of us supplies the moral mechanism, and the verses that follow supply the historical record.

**What the Audience Could Do With This Sentence**

The question had been put to the Makkans about a moment of crisis. The answer told them what they already knew about themselves, and the last clause told them what they usually did with the knowledge once the crisis ended. There was no room in the verse for the comfortable position of a man who has been saved and has not drawn any conclusion from being saved.

The sentence therefore works as a test rather than as an accusation, and the sūrah uses the same test again when it addresses the sailors, the travellers, and the people of the towns that were punished after long prosperity. The pattern is fixed, and the verse leaves the hearer to place himself inside it.

The Book also records what happens when the call from the depths is sincere. The Man of the Whale cried out in the veils of darkness that there is no god worthy of worship except God, and that he had certainly done wrong, and the answer came: So We answered his prayer and rescued him from anguish, and so do We save the true believers (21:87–88). The rescue in that account arrived while the man was still inside the problem, which is the mercy this verse's audience had never seriously asked for, since they called on God only when the water was already at their throats and returned to the shrines as soon as the shore appeared.
verses.42:
> Indeed, We have sent messengers before you ˹O Prophet˺ to other people who We put through suffering and adversity ˹for their denial˺, so perhaps they would be humbled

**A History of the Same Mission**

The verse places the Prophet's work inside a long sequence, and it does so with the messengers rather than with the prophets' biographies as the main subject. Communities before this one received messengers, and the pattern of sending has not changed; what changed in each case was the treatment of the warning. The Book states the same claim in other sūrahs, where messengers were sent to communities before and Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them (16:63).
