The point of the sequence is not repetition for its own sake. It tells the Prophet that his situation is a case within a rule, and it tells the Makkans that their response is being compared to the responses of peoples whose endings they already knew.

**Suffering and Adversity as Instruments**

The verse names two forms of hardship, and commentators distinguish between them: the first involving loss of wealth and straitened circumstances, and the second illness and physical suffering. Others read the pair as covering the whole range of affliction that befalls a community, from famine and drought to defeat and disease. The sūrah of the Heights describes the same programme in almost identical words: whenever a prophet was sent to a society, its people were afflicted with suffering and adversity so that they might be humbled (7:94).

Both forms are described in the Book as tests rather than as punishments, and the same two experiences are named among the marks of the righteous, who are said to be patient in times of suffering, adversity, and battle (2:177). That dual use of the vocabulary matters. The same event can be a purification for one person and a summons for another, and the verse is concerned with how a people responds to being shown its own helplessness.

**Why Hardship Was Thought to Produce Humility**

A community that has grown comfortable tends to treat its prosperity as a verdict on its conduct. When the rain fails, the caravan is lost, and the children fall ill, the arrangement that supported that confidence has been interrupted, and the interruption is meant to be noticed. The Book says elsewhere that God tested the dispersed tribes with prosperity and adversity so that they might return to the right path (7:168), and that testing with good and evil is the standing condition of human life (21:35).

The affliction is therefore not evidence of God's anger in every case. It is a message delivered in a language that a comfortable person can still read, and the whole point of the verse is that the message was delivered to these earlier peoples in exactly that form.

**The Hope Attached to the Sending**

The verse ends with a purpose clause: so that they might be humbled. Commentators read this as the objective God intended for the communities, and the Book's many accounts show that the objective was not always achieved. Some responded and were saved with their messengers, and others hardened and were destroyed, which is the subject the next verse takes up.

Read carefully, the clause tells the Prophet something about his own work as well. The test of a community is not only the warning it receives in words; it is also the pressure applied to its comfort, and God applies both so that a people cannot say it was never given an opportunity to reconsider.

**What Hardship Does and Does Not Do**

The Book is careful not to claim that suffering automatically produces humility, because it does not. Some people are driven deeper into resentment, and others emerge from a crisis more arrogant than before, convinced that their recovery was deserved. The next verse names that outcome for the communities in question, and the sūrah of Jonah describes a people who responded in time and were spared for a while.

The verse therefore sets up a contrast it does not yet resolve. Hardship was sent with the hope that the people would be humbled, and the question that follows is why the hope was not realised. The answer the sūrah gives is about what the people did with the opportunity rather than about what was missing from it.

**The Consolation for the Messenger**

For the Prophet, the verse carries the same message as the passage about rejected messengers a few lines earlier. The difficulties of the mission are not unique events; they are the ordinary shape of a summons that a society does not want to hear. The Book consoles its messenger by showing him the pattern and telling him that the outcome of every previous case is known.

That pattern also removes a burden he might have carried. If earlier communities had suffered as his own people were suffering, then the suffering was not evidence that he had failed or that God had withdrawn from him. The verse adds the Makkans to a list that already included communities whose stories the Prophet had been reciting, and the next sentence asks why the list ends the way it does.

The universality of the pattern is stated elsewhere in the Book in a form that leaves no community outside it. Every community has had a warner (35:24), a messenger was sent to every community with the call to worship God and shun false gods (16:36), and once a community's messenger has come, judgment is passed on it in fairness and it is not wronged (10:47). The Makkans were therefore not being singled out for hardship. They were being treated at the point in the sequence where their own messenger had arrived.
verses.43:
> Why did they not humble themselves when We made them suffer? Instead, their hearts were hardened, and Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them

**The Question That Expects No Answer**

The verse asks why the people did not humble themselves, and the question is not seeking information. It is the form the Book uses when a response was available, expected, and refused. The suffering had been sent with a declared purpose, and the purpose was not achieved, so the failure belongs to the people who lived through the affliction and used it for nothing.

The Book records the same reproach in the sūrah of the Believers, where God says that the people were seized with torment and yet never humbled themselves to their Lord, nor appealed to Him submissively (23:76). The complaint is not that they lacked a reason to turn; it is that the reasons kept arriving and nothing in them moved.

**Hardening as a Response to the Wrong Kind of Relief**

Hardness of heart is described in the Book as a condition that can develop in anyone who receives a great deal of something without being changed by it. The sūrah of Iron warns the believers not to become like those who were given the Scripture before them, who were spoiled for so long that their hearts became hard (57:16). The children of Israel are said to have hardened after the covenant was broken (5:13), and their hearts are compared to rock, or harder than rock (2:74).

The process described is gradual rather than sudden. A person who prays during a crisis and then forgets the prayer afterwards has not returned to his previous state; he has added to it the habit of not being changed by what he has seen. Each cycle leaves the heart less responsive, and the verse reports the result as a fact about the people rather than a punishment imposed on them.

**How Misdeeds Come to Look Beautiful**

The second half of the verse names the mechanism by which the hardening is rewarded: Satan made their misdeeds appealing to them. The phrase recurs in the Book with remarkable frequency, and it is used for the entire range of conduct that a society persuades itself is normal. Satan made their deeds appealing to them and hindered them from the way (27:24); he made their deeds appealing to them in the battle of Badr and then abandoned them (8:48); evil associates were set on the wrongdoers and made their past and future misdeeds appealing to them (41:25).

The same phrase is used of Pharaoh, whose evil deeds were made so appealing that he was hindered from the right way (40:37), and of the pagans who were made to see the killing of their own children as acceptable (6:137). In each case the misdeed is not denied. It is renamed, decorated, and made into a practice with reasons attached.

**The Partnership Between the People and Their Tempter**

The verse names Satan as the agent, and it does not thereby excuse the people, since the question in the first half was directed at them. The Book treats the relationship as one in which both parties are active: Satan tempts (15:39), and the person who follows him has chosen to follow. The Book also states that the delusion is a general tendency of human beings who prefer the immediate (2:212), where the life of this world has been made appealing to the disbelievers, and where desires of every kind have been made attractive to people (3:14).

That combination is what gives the verse its weight. The people wanted what they were being shown, and they wanted the reasons that made it acceptable. The tempter supplied the vocabulary; the appetite was already in place.

**Hardening as a Consequence of What Was Refused**

Commentators read this verse together with the passages about failure to respond to earlier warnings. The sūrah of the Heights describes the sequence directly: hardship, then a change to prosperity, until the people flourished and argued that their forefathers had seen the same pattern, and then they were seized by surprise while they were unaware (7:95). The hardening in the verse is thus a stage in a process that begins with a warning received and set aside, and it is the stage in which the warning loses its power to disturb.

That reading also explains why the verse uses the past tense for something the audience could watch happening around them. The Makkans had been living with the message for years and were still untouched by it, and the description in the verse is the diagnosis of their present condition presented as history.

**What the Verse Leaves the Reader Holding**

The sentence ends without comfort, and it does so deliberately, because the point is the closing of a door. A community that is suffering has the option of humbling itself, and the verse reports that these communities took the other option and that the option became progressively harder to take. The verses that follow describe what happened to them, and the description is the answer to the question the sūrah has just asked.

A reader living in the middle of his own life can still do what these people did not. That is the function of the verse in the sūrah's argument, and it is why the next sentence, which reports the sudden seizure of a people at the height of their confidence, is placed immediately after it.

The Book gives a detailed example of the hardening in the story of Pharaoh's people, and the detail shows how a community talks itself out of a lesson. When famine and crop failure struck them (7:130), their response was to divide the events by their own convenience: in prosperity they said that what they had was what they deserved, and in adversity they blamed it on Moses and those with him, while the Book notes that all of it was destined by Allah and that most of them did not know (7:131). The test produced an accountant's argument rather than humility, which is precisely the outcome this verse reports in general terms.
verses.44:
> When they became oblivious to warnings, We showered them with everything they desired. But just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise, then they instantly fell into despair

**The Word "Became Oblivious" and What It Covers**

The verse describes a people who forgot what they had been reminded of, and the reminder in view is the lesson written into their own suffering. Commentators read the phrase in two ways: either they forgot the message the prophet had brought them, or they forgot the lesson their own hardship should have taught them about their complete dependence on God. Both readings point to the same failure, which is that an experience of need was not converted into knowledge.

The Book states the same charge elsewhere when it describes people who call on God while lying on their side, sitting, or standing, and who then return to their old ways as soon as the hardship is lifted, as if they had never cried for help at all (10:12). The forgetting is not an accident of memory. It is the disposal of a lesson that has become inconvenient.

**The Gifts That Arrive Instead of the Punishment**

What comes next is the hardest part of the verse: We showered them with everything they desired. Adversity had failed to produce humility, and the response was not a heavier punishment but an opening of the gates. The Book calls this drawing a person on gradually, and it states the mechanism plainly when it says that those who reject the message will be drawn to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend, and that their end is delayed while God's planning remains flawless (68:44–45).

The interweaving of hardship and ease is described by commentators as the work of a wise guardian who uses both, and the clause in this verse shows how easily the second stage is misread. A people who had failed the test of poverty were given a test of wealth, and wealth is the harder of the two because it arrives dressed as approval.

**The Hadith About Prosperity Without Obedience**

A report quoted in the tafsīr literature on this passage states that when you see that God has given much to one of His servants in this world despite his disobedience, it is only a temptation. The Book makes the same point in its own voice when it tells the disbelievers not to imagine that living longer is good for them, since they are only given more time in which to increase in sin (3:178).

The principle is not that prosperity is bad. It is that prosperity is not a certificate, and the Book returns to that point repeatedly because it is the error most likely to be made by successful people. The Makkans were successful, and their success was the argument they used for the truth of their religion.

**Seized at the Moment of Exultation**

Then the seizure comes: just as they became prideful of what they were given, We seized them by surprise. The timing is precise. It is not during the hardship, when the people were still asking, but at the peak of the recovered confidence, when the lesson had been fully forgotten and the prosperity had been fully credited to their own merit.

The Book uses the same sequence in several accounts of destroyed nations. The people of the Heights argued that their forefathers had seen adversity and prosperity, and then they were seized while they were unaware (7:95); earlier societies were destroyed while they were settled in their comfortable living (28:58). The seizure by surprise is the standard ending, and it is chosen at the point where the warning would have had the least chance of being believed.

**Despair as the Final Condition**

The verse ends with the people in a state the translation renders as despair. The Arabic word describes someone dumbfounded, unable to produce an argument, and it is connected by commentators to the name of Iblīs, the being cast out. What the people lose in that moment is not hope alone but the ability to account for themselves.

The word also measures the distance travelled. This is a people who were confident, comfortable, and certain of their position, and they arrive at a condition in which nothing can be said in their defence. The Book ends them there, and the next verse declares what has happened to them in a single sentence.

**The Test That Runs in Both Directions**

The overall shape of the passage is a test that ran twice, once through adversity and once through ease, and the people failed both halves. The Book names that double testing as the standing condition of humanity, since they are tried with good and evil alike and then returned to their Lord (21:35). What makes the passage so uncomfortable is the observation that the second half of the test is the more dangerous, because it feels like a reward.

Read against the Makkan situation, the verse is a warning aimed at the city's most confident men. They had the wealth, the standing, and the inherited prestige, and they were being told exactly what their comfort was measuring. The verse does not tell them to give it up; it tells them what it is.

The Book gives this procedure its own name and repeats it as a settled pattern. Those who deny the signs are drawn gradually to destruction in ways they cannot comprehend, and their end is delayed while God's planning remains flawless (7:182–183). The Quranic term for the drawing-on carries the sense of a person being led forward step by step, each stage feeling like an ordinary advance, until the moment when he discovers what the path was for. The verse in front of us is that process described from its conclusion, which is why the seizure comes at the point of greatest confidence rather than at the point of greatest need.
verses.45:
> So the wrongdoers were utterly uprooted. And all praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds

**A Sentence of Removal, Not of Battle**

The verse reports the end of the peoples described in the preceding passage with a verb of cutting off. The image is agricultural as much as military: a people is described as uprooted, removed from the ground entirely, so that nothing of it continues. The Book uses the same verb for the destruction of those who denied the signs in the time of Hūd (7:72), for the disbelievers at Badr (8:7), and for the decree given to Lot about the sinners of his city, that they would be uprooted in the morning (15:66).

The choice matters for how the audience is meant to read the passage. These communities were not defeated in a war; they were removed from the record as communities, and the uprooting is described as a consequence rather than an event. The Book describes the wind that destroyed ʿĀd in the same register, leaving its people like trunks of uprooted palm trees (69:6–7).

**Who Is Being Described**

The wrongdoers in this sentence are the peoples of the previous verses: those who were sent messengers, tested with hardship, hardened by the testing, given ease when the lesson was lost, and then seized at the height of their confidence. The verse closes their account with a single verb, and it does so without naming a single one of them, because the pattern is the subject.

The Book names communities elsewhere for the same reason and with the same effect: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and the towns of Lot. The Makkans would have known those names, and the suppression of the names here is a way of pointing forward. What had happened to the named peoples was the general law, and the general law was still in force.

**Why Praise Follows Judgment**

The most striking feature of the verse is its second half: and all praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds. The formula is the one that opens the Fātiḥah and the one the sūrah itself uses at its own opening (6:1). Placing it directly after a report of destruction is a deliberate theological statement, and the commentators explain it as praise for God's justice and for the patience He showed before the punishment fell.

Read that way, the praise is not a celebration of the destruction. The Book's own account of these episodes stresses the length of time the messengers spent among their peoples, the warnings issued, and the afflictions that preceded the end. Praise after judgment acknowledges that the judgment was right, that no one was wronged, and that the door had been held open far longer than the offenders deserved.

**The Two Vocabularies Held Together**

The sentence joins mercy and severity in a single breath, and the sūrah has been doing that from the beginning. It opened with praise for the Creator of the heavens and the earth and of darkness and light (6:1); it stated that God prescribed mercy for Himself while announcing the gathering for judgment (6:12); it described the wrongdoers as people who ruin only themselves while their Lord could have guided everyone (6:35). The final clause of this verse is the formula that holds the two together.

The Book returns to the pairing in other places where nations are destroyed and praise is given to God for His judgement, and it does so because the alternative is worse. A universe in which the oppressor is never removed is not a universe in which mercy means anything, and the praise is the recognition that the removal is part of the mercy.

**What the Verse Does for the Prophet**

The Prophet had been consoled a few verses earlier with the fact that earlier messengers were rejected and endured until help came (6:34), and with the impossibility of forcing his people to believe (6:35). The passage about the hardened communities supplies the other half of the picture: what happens when a people continues past the point at which the warning has been exhausted.

For a messenger in the middle of a hostile city, that is a difficult and necessary piece of information. It tells him what the end of the story is for a community that refuses, and it tells him that the ending is not arbitrary. The verse does not invite him to look forward to it. It tells him that the matter is in hands that handle it correctly.

**The Praise That Teaches the Reader How to Read the Passage**

Every element of the verse prepares the reader to receive the following passage, which returns to the argument about signs, evidence, and the revelation itself. The sūrah moves from the historical record of ruined communities to the specific objections of the Makkans, and the transition is the praise.

The reader is told to accept the account of the uprooted peoples as part of the goodness of God's government, not as a difficulty to be explained away. A person who can say that praise while reading about the destruction of a nation is a person who has understood the sūrah's argument about who owns the world, who sets its terms, and who is entitled to close an account when the last warning has been delivered.

The Book places the same formula at the beginning of this sūrah, where praise is given to the One who created the heavens and the earth and made darkness and light (6:1), and at the end of this section, where the wrongdoers are uprooted. Read as a frame, the repetition tells the reader that the two statements belong to the same subject. The God who is praised for the creation is the God who is praised for the judgment, and the sūrah offers no version of the first that can be held without the second. The whole of the argument that follows sits inside that frame.
verses.46:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Imagine if Allah were to take away your hearing or sight, or seal your hearts—who else other than Allah could restore it?” See ˹O Prophet˺ how We vary the signs, yet they still turn away

**The Faculties Named One by One**

The verse takes three gifts the audience used every hour and asks who could return them if they were withdrawn. Hearing, sight, and the heart are named because they are the whole apparatus of understanding: the ear receives, the eye observes, and the heart is where a person decides what the information means. The Book elsewhere treats the heart as the seat of comprehension rather than of emotion, and the sealing of hearts appears in several places as the end of that comprehension (2:7; 16:108; 45:23).

The question is put as a hypothesis rather than as a threat. Nobody is being told that the faculties have been removed; they are being asked to imagine the situation and to name a candidate who could undo it. The Book has already answered that question about harm and benefit in general a few verses earlier, where it said that none can undo harm except Him (6:17), and it repeats the answer elsewhere with the same firmness (10:107).

**The Question the Sūrah Has Asked Before**

This is the third time in the sūrah that an appeal of this shape has been made, and the repetition builds a case rather than padding one. Earlier, the audience was asked who rescues them from the darkest times on land and at sea (6:63), and a few verses before this one they were asked about being overwhelmed by the punishment (6:40). Each question uses something the audience already knows, and each one strips away another layer of the claim that the idols had standing.

The pattern in this verse is more exacting, because the loss described is not an external danger. It is the loss of the means by which a person could notice the danger at all. A man who cannot hear, cannot see, and cannot understand has no resource left, and the verse leaves him with a question that no shrine in Makkah could answer.

**The "Varying" of the Signs**

The second half of the verse turns to the method of revelation itself: see how We vary the signs, yet they still turn away. The Book uses this vocabulary repeatedly, and the sūrah names the practice in more than one place. To vary the signs means to bring the same truth through different arguments, images, and parables, so that an audience cannot claim it was offered only one kind of proof, or that the message depended on a single demonstration.

The idea appears where God says that every kind of example has been set out for people in this recitation, though most of them persist in disbelief (17:89), and where the sūrah says the parables and warnings are presented in various ways (18:54; 20:113). The verse therefore presents the diversity of the message as an act of care by God, and the audience's turning away as a response to a generosity they have no ground to complain about.

**Two Readings of What the Signs Are**

Commentators observe that the word for signs can refer both to the recited verses and to the created order, since both are called by the same term. On that reading, the varied signs include the alternation of day and night, the revived earth, and the ordinary facts of human dependence, alongside the arguments presented in the revelation itself. The sūrah of Fussilat supports the wider reading when it says that God will show people His signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that this message is the truth (41:53).

The two readings do not compete. A person who has heard the recitation has already seen the signs in his own body, and the verse's closing complaint is that he turns away from both at once, which is the reason the sūrah's descriptions of denial keep returning to the use a person makes of what he already possesses.

**The Emphasis on Sight at the End**

The verse closes with the Prophet as the observer of the turning away: see how they still turn away. The same instruction was given earlier in the sūrah, where the command to travel through the land and look at the fate of the deniers was followed by the observation that it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts inside the chests (22:46). Here the object of sight is not a ruin but a living refusal that the Prophet encounters daily.

That emphasis carries a message for him. The refusal is visible and it is habitual, and the verse treats it as something to be looked at rather than something to be argued away. The sūrah then continues with the subjects of punishment, warning, and the treatment of the poor, as though to show the Prophet what the argument looks like when it is translated into the practical decisions of a community.

**What the Question Does to the Audience**

A sentence that asks who could restore your hearing if it were taken is difficult to answer with the name of a stone. It puts the audience in the position of a person imagining the loss of everything he uses to make sense of the world, and it leaves him with only one possible reply. The Book does not require the reply to be spoken; it supplies the conclusion through the question mark.

The verse therefore functions as a demonstration rather than as a threat, and the demonstration lands on a matter of fact. Whatever else the Makkans disputed with the Prophet, they had no story about who gave them their eyes, and the sūrah records their answer to a similar question in another passage, where they concede that it is Allah who created the heavens and the earth (29:61). The verse simply brings that admission home to their own bodies.
verses.47:
> Ask, “Imagine if Allah’s punishment were to overwhelm you with or without warning—who would be destroyed other than the wrongdoers?”

**Two Ways for a Punishment to Arrive**

The verse names the two possibilities an audience would have feared: a punishment that comes without warning, and one that comes openly. Commentators explain the pair as covering the night and the day, or as covering a coming that is felt before it strikes and a coming that arrives unannounced. The Book uses both patterns in its accounts of destroyed peoples, and it records towns in the Qur'an as having been destroyed at night while their inhabitants slept, or in the morning while they were playing (7:4; 7:98).

The choice presented in the question is therefore not between two punishments but between two timetables. Neither option leaves a gap in which a person could claim he did not see it coming, since even the open arrival gives only enough time to recognise what is happening rather than to change anything.

**The Question That Answers Itself**

Who would be destroyed other than the wrongdoers? The interrogative form is the same device the sūrah has used for the greatest wrong (6:21) and for the greatest of religious inventions. Here it is used to deliver a conclusion the audience had no interest in resisting, and the conclusion is that the punishment is aimed rather than indiscriminate.

That is the sense in which the sentence is a mercy as much as a warning. A person who has understood that God's destructive acts are directed at wrongdoing, and not at whoever happens to be standing nearby, has been told that he can remove himself from the target by removing the conduct that draws it.

**The Difficulty the Verse Leaves Open**

The Book also records worldly destruction falling on whole societies, righteous and wicked alike, as in the case of Noah's people and the towns of Lot, and it warns the believers about a trial that will not befall only those among you who do wrong (8:25). Commentators acknowledged the difficulty and answered it in different ways, with some restricting the verse to the destruction of the guilty in the Hereafter, and others holding that the righteous who are destroyed in this world lose nothing, because their reward with God is secure.

Al-Rāzī's treatment of the question is the one that fits the following verses best. He argued that even when a worldly punishment wipes out a people together, the righteous receive their reward with God in the Hereafter, while the wrongdoers have lost both this world and the next. The verse's verdict about who is destroyed concerns what each group ends with rather than who was standing in the street on a particular morning.

**Why the Timetable Was Left With God**

The sentence is addressed to a people who were pressing the Prophet to hasten something, and the answer removes the question from his hands entirely. The Book records their demand in another sūrah where they called for stones to rain down from the sky if the message was true (8:32), and it reports people asking why the torment is not sent down (29:53). The verse treats the demand as a symptom of unbelief rather than as a request for information.

The Book states the underlying reason plainly: the postponement is not a sign that nothing is coming but a period in which the wrongdoer is given time, and the Book elsewhere describes the delay as a rope rather than as an acquittal (3:178). The verse in front of us supplies the warning side of that arrangement, and the next one describes the messenger's only role.

**What the Words "With or Without Warning" Imply About God**

A deity who warns at all is a deity who does not want the destruction to be a surprise, and the Book treats the warnings sent through messengers as exactly that. The same pattern runs through the sūrah's earlier passages, where messengers were sent and the people were tested with hardship so that they might be humbled (6:42), and where the destruction followed only after the reminders had been forgotten (6:44).

So the question in this verse carries an implicit account of God's conduct. If the punishment can come at night or in broad day, the difference between the two for a guilty community lies only in how much time it is given to reconsider, and the Book holds that the warning had already been delivered in either case.

**The Two Groups Named in the Future**

The verse ends by naming the wrongdoers as the ones who will be destroyed, and the term is not accidental. The sūrah has been describing conduct rather than a label: obstructing others from the message (6:26), disputing after listening (6:25), demanding signs while rejecting the signs already given (6:37), and hardening after suffering (6:43). The wrongdoers in this sentence are those whose record contains those items, and the verse leaves each hearer to check the list against himself.

The next sentence describes the mission that had been given while that check is still possible. Messengers come as bearers of news and warnings, and the Book's habit of stating the messenger's role immediately after a threat is its way of keeping the door visible.

The demand behind this question is recorded elsewhere in a form that shows how the Makkans actually phrased it. They prayed that if the message was truly from God, He should rain down stones on them from the sky or bring a painful punishment upon them (8:32), and the Book also notes that the wrongdoers have a share of torment like that of their predecessors, with an instruction not to ask for it to be hastened (51:59). The verse in front of us answers the tone of such demands rather than their content. A person asking for the punishment to come early is not requesting justice; he is testing whether anyone is listening.
verses.48:
> We have sent messengers only as deliverers of good news and as warners. Whoever believes and does good, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve

**Two Functions and Nothing Besides Them**

The verse defines the office of the messenger in two words, and the construction is restrictive: messengers were sent only to bring good news and to warn. The Book repeats the pairing across many sūrahs, describing the prophets as bearers of glad tidings and warners (2:213; 4:165; 18:56; 25:56; 33:45; 34:28; 35:24). The Prophet himself is told to say that he is only a warner and a bringer of good news to people who believe (7:188).

The restriction answers the demands the sūrah has been recording. A messenger who is only a news-bearer cannot be required to produce a treasury, to know the unseen, or to turn the world upside down on request. Each of those demands assumes an office larger than the one described here, and the verse closes them off before the next verse states the outcome for those who accept and those who reject.

**Why Both Words Are Necessary**

The pairing is carefully balanced. Good news without warning would produce a religion of comfortable expectations, in which the mercy of God is separated from the seriousness of the accounting. Warning without good news would produce despair, and the Book states its own refusal of that result when it describes people who call upon God with hope and fear at once (32:16), and where it says that God has taken upon Himself to be merciful (6:12).

The two words therefore hold the messenger's task in a single direction. What he announces is not a general religious atmosphere but a specific news item with two aspects: the possibility of a good outcome and the reality of a bad one, and the audience is told plainly which conduct belongs to which.

**The Two Conditions Attached to the Promise**

Whoever believes and does good is the Book's standard formula for the saved, and it uses two verbs where a modern reader might expect one. Belief is inward and amendment is outward, and the Book consistently refuses to separate them. Elsewhere it states the same pairing where it speaks of those who believe in God, the Last Day, and do righteous deeds, and says that they will have their reward with their Lord, with no fear for them and no grief (2:62; 2:262).

The Book's moral psychology is visible in the pairing. Faith that produces no change in conduct is not treated as a weaker faith but as a doubtful claim, and conduct that has no faith underneath it is treated as an account that will not balance. The verse in front of us states the combination as the condition of the promise without commenting on the exceptions, and the sūrah elsewhere handles the exceptions directly.

**What It Means to Have No Fear or Grief**

The two words cover the two directions of human anxiety. Fear concerns what is coming, and grief concerns what has gone; the Book's promise removes both, which is why the formula recurs so often in descriptions of the Hereafter (7:35; 10:62; 46:13). Those who are promised it are told that the arrival of the judgment holds nothing for them to dread, and that the losses of their earthly lives are not the end of the account.

The Book also treats the promise as a present possession in some measure, since the people described as mindful are those who have no fear concerning their future and no regret over their past dealings with God. That is the practical form of the good news the messenger brings, and it is delivered in the same sentence as the warning to the people who reject him.

**The Messenger's Freedom From the Outcome**

Read together with the verses around it, this sentence also relieves the Prophet of a burden. He had been told that the punishment is not in his hands (6:47), and now he is told that his task is the delivery of news rather than the production of results. The Book repeats the point when it tells him that his duty is only to remind (88:21), and when it refuses to make him a keeper over the people (6:107).

That arrangement protects the message as well as the messenger. A prophet who could compel acceptance would destroy the moral content of the decision, and a prophet who carried the responsibility for other people's choices would be crushed by them. The verse states the boundary, and the next sentence states what happens on the other side of it.

**The Value of Naming the Office So Plainly**

The verse is a small definition with a large reach. It tells the audience what they may expect from the man addressing them and therefore what they may not demand, and it tells the messenger what he may and may not attempt. Everything the sūrah reports about the Makkan demands for signs, angels, and written books is answered in advance by the narrow job description given here.

That description also puts the audience on notice about what they are being held to. The message has been delivered as news and warning; the response is now theirs, and the following verse states what the response costs when it goes the wrong way.

The Book widens the same description beyond the Prophet's own people when it says that he was sent only as a deliverer of good news and a warner to all humanity, though most people do not know (34:28), and when it says that no community has ever lacked a warner (35:24). The wording of this verse is therefore a definition of the office in general rather than a description of one mission. Every messenger who came to a people came with the same two items and the same absence of coercive power, and the Makkans were dealing with an instance of a pattern they had already heard about.
verses.49:
> But those who deny Our signs will be afflicted with punishment for their rebelliousness

**The Mirror of the Previous Verse**

The sūrah has just named the promise attached to belief and good conduct (6:48), and this sentence supplies the counterpart. The structure is exact: two conditions on the favourable side, and on the other side the denial of the signs together with the reason given for the punishment, which is a word the translation renders as rebelliousness. The Book frequently pairs the two outcomes in this way, so that the reader receives mercy and warning in the same breath.

The pairing is not a literary symmetry for its own sake. It tells the audience that the two roads being described are the only ones available, and that each has been marked with the same clarity. The sūrah has spent thirty verses assembling evidence and answering objections; this sentence states the consequence of ignoring all of it.

**The Word Behind "Rebelliousness"**

The Arabic term describes the conduct of someone who steps outside a boundary he was meant to keep, and the Book uses it for people who break covenants and corrupt what they touch. The same root appears where the Book describes those who spread corruption in the land and violate their pledges (2:27), and where the people who cross the limits set for them are described as the ones who ruin themselves (2:229). The word indicates conduct rather than an inherited condition.

That distinction matters in a sūrah that has been arguing that denial is an activity. The verse does not say that the deniers were born outside the boundary; it says that they put themselves there and remained, and the punishment is attached to the choice rather than to a label applied from the outside.

**Denial and Conduct Held Together**

The verse names two things about the people it describes: they deny the signs, and they have crossed the boundary. The Book's habit is to join belief with righteous action and denial with transgression, and it does so because the two belong together in its understanding of a human being. Faith that has no effect on conduct is not the faith the verse is describing, and misconduct that has no connection to belief is not the fault it is naming either.

That view is stated plainly in the passage where the Book describes the righteous as those who keep their pledges, are patient in hardship, and give from what they have (2:177), and where it describes those who break the covenant, cut the ties God ordered to be maintained, and spread corruption as the true losers (2:27). The pairing runs through the whole Book, and this verse is a compact instance of it.

**Why the Punishment Is Attached Rather Than Described**

The verse does not describe what the punishment consists of, and this restraint is typical of the Makkan passages. Earlier in the sūrah the description was more explicit, with the wrongdoers at the point of death surrounded by angels stretching out their hands (6:93), and later the sūrah will describe the scene where the wrongdoers are held before the fire (6:27). Here the sentence ends at the fact.

The restraint keeps the focus on the cause rather than on the penalty. What the audience needed to understand was the connection between the way they were living and the outcome, and the Book describes that connection with a single word before moving to the wider argument about what the messengers are and are not.

Elsewhere the same sūrah fills in what is left out here. The wrongdoers are told at the point of death that they will be repaid with the torment of disgrace for lying about God and for being arrogant toward His signs (6:93), and those who take their faith as play and amusement are described as facing a boiling drink and a painful punishment for their disbelief (6:70). The absence of such detail in this verse is a matter of placement rather than of information. The sūrah states the two roads first and describes the destinations later, once the audience has been brought through the argument that makes the description bearable to hear.

**The Proportion Between the Two Sentences**

The favourable sentence in the previous verse describes an inner state and an outward conduct, and then removes fear and grief. The unfavourable sentence describes denial and a crossing of boundaries, and then states that a punishment follows. Nothing in either sentence mentions quantity, and nothing suggests that the two outcomes are comparable in weight.

The reader is left to work out the proportion for himself, and the Book helps him elsewhere when it says that God's mercy encompasses all things (7:156) while His punishment strikes whoever He wills. The pairing in these two verses is deliberately unequal in tone, and the inequality is part of what the sūrah is telling its audience about the One they are dealing with.

**What the Verse Requires the Reader to Decide**

Both sentences in this pair are about groups, and neither one asks the reader to place himself in a group. The sūrah treats the reading itself as the point at which a person begins to decide, and the verses that follow turn immediately to the practical shape of the community being addressed, including the Prophet's treatment of the poor among his followers.

That shift is not a change of subject. Having stated the two outcomes, the sūrah shows the audience what the two roads look like inside a living community, where the worth of a person is measured by God rather than by his family or his wealth. The next passages handle that question directly.

The sentence also matches the Book's description of what happens when the same promise is given from the other side. In the sūrah of the Heights, the children of Adam are told that whoever shuns evil and mends his ways will have no fear and no grief when messengers recite God's revelations to them (7:35), and in the sūrah of the Cow the promise is attached to belief, good deeds, prayer, and alms (2:277). The two halves of the contrast are composed of the same materials in every passage: inward belief, outward conduct, and the consequences that follow from each.
verses.50:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not say to you that I possess Allah’s treasuries or know the unseen, nor do I claim to be an angel. I only follow what is revealed to me.” Say, “Are those blind ˹to the truth˺ equal to those who can see? Will you not then reflect?”

**Three Claims the Prophet Is Told to Give Up Before They Are Made**

The verse lists three things the Prophet does not claim: the treasuries of God, knowledge of the unseen, and angelic status. Each one corresponds to a specific demand recorded elsewhere in the Book. The disbelievers asked why a treasure had not been sent down with him (11:12); they asked to see an angel, or for the messenger himself to be an angel (15:7; 17:94–95); and they demanded to know about the Hour (7:187; 43:53). The verse removes all three of the goods they were asking him to supply.

The order is deliberate. The first two would have made him a dispenser of power, and the third would have made him something other than a human being. What remains after the three are removed is a man with a message, which is exactly the position the sūrah has been defending since the demand for an angel was first raised (6:8).

**Noah Said the Same Thing First**

The wording of the denial is not unique to this Prophet, and the Book records it almost identically on the lips of Noah when his people accused him of seeking wealth and status through his message. He told them that he did not ask them for money, that his reward was with God, and that he was not going to drive away the believers (11:29; 11:31). The parallel places the Makkan demand inside a long history in which the same demands were made of the same kind of man.

The comparison also answers a suspicion the Makkans were fond of raising. If the Prophet had claimed control of provisions or foreknowledge, his message would be a claim about himself rather than about God, and the Book's habit of making its messengers renounce such claims is a mark of what kind of mission they carried.

**"I Only Follow What Is Revealed to Me"**

The positive half of the sentence is the important half. After removing the three claims, the Prophet states what he does possess: revelation, and the practice of following it. The Book uses the same formula elsewhere when it has him say that he is nothing new among the messengers and that he does not know what will be done with him or with his people, and that he only follows what is revealed to him (46:9).

The phrase also defines the authority of everything he says about God. He speaks from a text he did not compose, and the criterion of his teaching is its conformity to what arrived rather than his personal judgement. That is the doctrine the sūrah has been pressing on an audience that kept trying to negotiate the terms of the message.

**The Unseen Belongs to God**

The Book states the principle behind the second denial in several places. With God are the keys of the unseen, and no one knows them except Him (6:59); He alone knows the unseen and reveals it to no one except the messengers of His choice (72:26–27); and the unseen is known only to God (10:20; 27:65). The revelation given to the Prophet contains news of the unseen, as when the Book tells him stories he could not have known, such as the account of Mary's guardianship (3:44) and the story of Joseph's brothers (12:102).

The distinction is between possessing knowledge and receiving it. A messenger is informed of what God chooses to disclose, and he is not a source of disclosure in himself. The sūrah's audience was demanding a fortune-teller's knowledge of hidden matters, and the verse refuses the demand on behalf of the man they were asking.

**The Challenge About Blindness and Sight**

The verse ends with a question that draws the line between two kinds of people rather than two kinds of faculty: are those blind equal to those who can see? The Book uses the same question in several places, including where it contrasts the one who stands on clear proof from his Lord with the one whose evil deeds have been made appealing to him (47:14), and where it asks whether the blind and the seeing can be equal, or the darkness and the light (13:16).

The imagery refers to spiritual perception, and the Book makes that explicit when it says that it is not the eyes which go blind but the hearts inside the chests (22:46). The question is therefore not about the faculties a person happens to possess. It is about what he does with them, which is the same argument the sūrah has made in its earlier discussion of veiled hearts and deafened ears (6:25).

**What the Verse Leaves as the Prophet's Position**

After the three denials and the one affirmation, the Prophet's position in the argument is complete. He cannot be asked to produce wealth, to disclose the future, or to appear as something other than a human being, and everything he has said rests on what was revealed to him. The sūrah's audience is left with the message itself, which is where the Book has been trying to place them from the beginning.

The final question asks them to reflect, and the reflection is not difficult to perform. Either the guidance is real and the difference between seeing and blindness is worth attending to, or it is not, and the verse's refusal to argue further is the strongest form of the claim it makes.
verses.51:
> Warn with this ˹Quran˺ those who are awed by the prospect of being gathered before their Lord—when they will have no protector or intercessor besides Him—so perhaps they will be mindful ˹of Him˺

**A Warning Aimed at a Specific Kind of Listener**

The previous verses defined the messenger's office as news and warning, and this verse says who the warning is for. It is not addressed to the confident deniers who have been arguing throughout the sūrah. It is addressed to people who already fear the gathering, and the Book identifies its audience by that fear rather than by their religious label.

Commentators listed several groups as candidates for the description: believers who accept the resurrection but are negligent in their works, People of the Book who believe in the Day of Judgment but have not accepted this Prophet, and idolaters who carry a private unease about what comes after death. The breadth of the list is the point. The Book is not sorting people by community but by the condition of the heart.

**The Fear That Makes a Person Reachable**

The Book treats fear of the gathering as the beginning of usefulness to the message, and it states the same principle elsewhere when it tells the Prophet that he can only warn those who follow the reminder and stand in awe of the Most Compassionate without seeing Him (36:11). The phrase "without seeing Him" matters, because it describes a fear that operates in the absence of evidence at hand, and it is the form of fear the Book commends.

That is why the verse's instruction is directed at this group and not at the men who kept demanding signs. A person who has already granted that he will be summoned to account has given the message something to work with, and the Book's method with such people is to increase their awareness rather than to argue them into an admission.

**No Protector and No Intercessor**

The verse describes the scene those listeners fear, and it describes it with two denials: apart from Him there is no protector and no intercessor. The Book makes the same statement in several places, including the passage where God says that there is no protector and no intercessor besides Him (32:4), and the one where the Prophet is told to warn a people who have no one to protect them from God (42:7).

Intercession is treated carefully in the Book rather than dismissed outright. The majority position among the scholars is that intercession exists by God's permission and for those He permits, which is why the verse's denial is expressed as a denial of any intercessor besides Him rather than of intercession as such. What the sentence removes is the assumption that led the Makkans to build their religious practice around intermediaries.

**An Intercessor That Is a Text**

Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, the sixth Shia Imam, read the word differently and gave it a form that has been quoted widely. He said that the command means to warn by means of the Qur'an those who anticipate the meeting with their Lord, and to make them long for what awaits them there, because the Qur'an itself is an intercessor that will plead on their behalf. The interpretation is reported in the tafsīr literature and gives the verse an unexpected shape: the warning and the advocate are the same object.

Whether or not one adopts that reading, it captures something the verse carries. The Book is being described as an instrument the Prophet uses, and the people who benefit from it are the ones who let it work on them in advance of the meeting rather than at the meeting itself.

**Awaiting a Meeting in Order to Prepare for It**

The phrase the translation renders as being gathered before their Lord is literally a meeting, and the Book uses that vocabulary deliberately both for the saved and for the lost. Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return are described among the guided (2:46), while those who do not expect the meeting are described as pleased with the present life and heedless of the signs (10:7).

So the difference between the two groups is not information about the event. It is expectation, and expectation is what produces preparation. A man who is expecting an appointment arranges his affairs accordingly, and the verse assumes that the listener who expects the meeting will act on the warning he receives.

**The Closing Purpose Clause**

The verse ends with the same formula the sūrah has used for the sending of messengers: so perhaps they will be mindful of Him. The word describes guarding oneself against something, and the Book attaches it to conduct rather than to sentiment. A person who is mindful of God orders his life around the awareness that he will be questioned, and the verse presents the warning as the means by which that state is reached.

The Book repeats the purpose clause in the passage about the Prophet's own instruction, where he is told to remind because his duty is only to remind (88:21), and it uses the same word when it tells him who can be warned at all. The identical phrase appears in the sūrah of the Cave, where the Prophet is told that he can warn only those who follow the reminder and fear their Lord unseen, and that he should give them news of forgiveness and a generous reward (36:11). The verse therefore closes the discussion of the messenger's role with a description of the listener who can receive it, and the sūrah turns next to the practical question of who was being kept away from the message.
verses.52:
> ˹O Prophet!˺ Do not dismiss those ˹poor believers˺ who invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. You are not accountable for them whatsoever, nor are they accountable for you. So do not dismiss them, or you will be one of the wrongdoers

**An Instruction About Seating Arrangements**

The verse addresses a practical pressure rather than a doctrine. A group of prominent Makkans had indicated that they were willing to sit with the Prophet, and they did not want to be seen in the company of his poorer followers, some of them freed slaves. The reports describe two versions of the request: that the Prophet should send those followers away entirely, or should move them to the back rows so that the notables would not be visible standing behind people of lower social standing.

The wording of the verse fits either version. Do not dismiss them is an instruction about who may be kept at a distance from the message, and it settled a question the society had been making on the basis of birth and wealth. The Prophet is told that the arrangement of his gathering is not a matter of social convenience.

**What the Poor Believers Were Doing**

The verse describes the people in question by their practice: they invoke their Lord morning and evening, seeking His pleasure. The Book uses the same description in the sūrah of the Cave, where the Prophet is told to keep himself patient with those who call on their Lord morning and evening and not to let his eyes go past them toward the trappings of worldly life (18:28). Commentators note that the phrase covers the five daily prayers, the recitation of the Qur'an, and voluntary remembrance, or all of them together.

The description does the arguing. The people being asked to leave the room were the ones occupied with the worship that the message had come to establish, and the people requesting their removal had offered no such practice. The Book's reversal of the social order is complete in a single clause.

**"Seeking His Pleasure"**

The phrase translated as seeking His pleasure refers to a motive rather than an outward act, and the Book uses it repeatedly to describe sincerity. Those who give their wealth are described as doing so seeking God's face (2:272; 30:38–39), and the same phrase appears where the Prophet is told to stay with the poor rather than to court the powerful. Commentators read it as sincerity of intention, and some note that the literal sense concerns the hope of seeing God, which is what an honest worshipper's desire ultimately reaches toward.

The criterion that emerges is worth stating plainly. What qualified these people to be near the Prophet was not their lineage, their wealth, or their standing in the market. It was the direction of their intention, which is precisely the thing the notables could not see and were trying to assess anyway.

**The Line About Accountability**

The verse then removes a practical worry from the Prophet's shoulders: you are not accountable for them, nor are they accountable for you. The Book states the general principle elsewhere, that no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another (6:164; 17:15), and it applies it here to a specific social anxiety. If the poor believers turned out to have mixed motives, that was God's assessment to make, and if their poverty offended the Makkans, their own accounts would be examined without reference to it.

Commentators read the sentence in two ways, with some taking the reckoning to concern the poor believers' inner sincerity, which the Prophet is not required to audit, and others taking it to concern the notables, whose acceptance of the message the Prophet should not pursue at the cost of the community he already had. Both readings converge on the same instruction: the door of the gathering is not his to narrow.

**The Warning Attached to the Instruction**

The verse closes with a warning that is remarkable for being addressed to the Prophet himself: if he sends them away, he will be one of the wrongdoers. The Book issues such warnings to its messenger in several places, and the sūrah of ʿAbasa records the incident in which he showed displeasure at being interrupted by a blind man while he was engaged with the notables.

The warning is not evidence of a fault in the Prophet's character. It is evidence of the seriousness of the principle, and the Book states it in the second person so that no reader can take the protection of the weak to be optional. A community that arranges itself around the status of its wealthiest members has made a decision about what it values, and the verse names that decision as a species of wrongdoing.

**What the Passage Does for the Rest of the Sūrah**

The instruction is placed in the middle of a long argument about idolatry, and its placement is not incidental. The sūrah has been exposing the fabricated hierarchies by which the Makkans divided their world, including the shares they assigned to their gods and to their own clans. The verse applies the same critique to the community the Prophet was building, where a distinction between first-class and second-class believers had been proposed to him.

The next verses continue the subject directly, describing how God tests people by means of one another, and stating what the wealthy questioners would say about the poor. The passage holds together as a single treatment of a single problem: who decides the worth of a person, and on what evidence.

The same scene is recorded from the other side in the story of Noah. His people argued that they could not believe in a man followed only by the lowest among them (26:111), and Noah answered that their judgment rested with his Lord and that he was not going to expel the believers (26:113–114). The disbelieving chiefs made the same complaint to him that the Makkan notables were making in this sūrah, and Noah asked his people who would protect him from God if he were to dismiss them (11:27; 11:30). The repetition of this argument across the sūrahs shows that the pressure being applied to the Prophet was not a local peculiarity; it was the standard demand made against a messenger by the powerful of every community.
verses.53:
> In this way We have tested some by means of others, so those ˹disbelievers˺ may say, “Has Allah favoured these ˹poor believers˺ out of all of us?” Does Allah not best recognize the grateful

**Inequality as a Test Rather Than an Accident**

The verse states that the differences between people are arranged as a trial, and it states it in the first person: We have tested some by means of others. The Book treats disparities of wealth, strength, and status as part of the design rather than as faults in it, and it says in another place that if God had willed He could have made humanity a single community, but the will is to test people with what they have been given (5:48).

The testing runs in both directions. The wealthy are tested by their responsibility toward the needy, and the needy are tested by their trust in God and by the patience required to accept help from those who have less standing. Neither condition is a verdict on the person living in it.

**The Question the Disbelievers Ask**

Those who disbelieved look at the Prophet's followers and ask whether God has favoured these poor believers out of all of them. The question relocates the argument from truth to status, which is the move the sūrah has been dismantling since its opening verses. The Makkans had assumed that if a message came from God it would arrive among the powerful and be accepted by them first, and the composition of the Prophet's following was being used as evidence against him.

The Book records the same reasoning in the story of Noah, where the notables demanded that he drive away the believers of low standing, and he refused on the ground that he could not expel those whose account rested with God (11:29; 11:31). The assumption that spiritual worth follows social rank was old before Makkah, and the Book treats it as a recurring error.

**The Question Posed From Both Sides**

Commentators note that the question may equally be asked by the poor, looking at the wealth of the disbelievers and wondering why God continues to grant them prosperity while the believers remain poor and exposed to persecution. Under that reading the sentence covers both directions of the same bewilderment, and the verse's answer serves both groups at once.

The Book deals with the second question in several places. The disbelievers should not imagine that living longer is good for them, since they are only given more time to increase in sin (3:178), and the wealth of an enemy is not evidence about his standing with God. The answer to both versions of the question is the same: the present distribution of comfort is a field of testing rather than a table of verdicts.

**What the Grateful Are and Why the Word Is Chosen**

Does Allah not best recognize the grateful? The question at the end defines the quality that distinguishes one person from another in this arrangement, and the quality is gratitude. The Book links gratitude to perception of the giver, and it describes the person who uses his abundance to acknowledge God rather than to congratulate himself. The opposite failure is described in the same sūrah a few verses later, where people in prosperity credit themselves and in adversity blame God's messenger (7:131, in the sūrah of the Heights).

The choice of word also answers the disbelievers' question about favour. God's favour is real, and it is recognized by its fruits in the person who receives it. What the proud could not see was that the poor believers were displaying the fruit that the arrangement was meant to produce, while their own wealth was producing the confidence that kept them from the message.

**Testing by Means of One Another in Practice**

The mechanism described here shapes the daily life of every community. A person's treatment of those below him in status tests his character more reliably than his treatment of those he needs, and the Book's legislation is full of provisions for people whose standing made them easy to overlook: orphans, the poor, travellers, debtors. The sūrah itself turns next to the greeting and the promise of mercy that the Prophet is to extend to the believers who approach him.

Read that way, the verse is a portrait of the community being built rather than a comment on the society being left behind. The differences between people are permanent features of the world, and the Book's response is not to abolish them but to make the arrangements through which they are held a matter of conscious and tested conduct.

**The Answer Given to a Hard Question**

The verse does not comfort the poor by telling them their poverty is meaningless, and it does not console the rich by insisting they are secretly better off. It states that the whole arrangement is a test and that gratitude is the criterion God recognises. Everything the audience wanted to know about the meaning of rank and wealth is answered in that one word, and the answer is a question, which is the Book's preferred way of leaving the reader with something to work out for himself.

The verses that follow turn to the practical consequences of the principle in the Prophet's own circle, instructing him to greet the believers with peace and to announce the mercy his Lord has placed upon Himself. The theory of testing is immediately applied to how people are to be treated.

The sūrah names the same principle once more later in its account of the idolaters' practices, where the pagans are said to have killed their own children out of a confusion in their faith, and where the Book states that had God willed they would not have done it (6:137). The distribution of ranks, wealth, and even understanding among people is presented throughout the sūrah as an arrangement with a purpose, and the purpose is never to establish which human being matters more.
verses.54:
> When the believers in Our revelations come to you, say, “Peace be upon you! Your Lord has taken upon Himself to be Merciful. Whoever among you commits evil ignorantly ˹or recklessly˺ then repents afterwards and mends their ways, then Allah is truly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

**A Greeting That States a Doctrine**

The verse instructs the Prophet to greet the believers with the words of peace, and then to follow the greeting with the reason it can be said: their Lord has taken upon Himself to be merciful. The greeting is the one the Book records as the welcome of the people of Paradise (7:46; 14:23; 16:32; 19:62), and it is also the form of address used between the prophets and their guests, as when Abraham's visitors greeted him with peace (15:52; 51:25).

Putting the two together makes the instruction more than a courtesy. A person entering the Prophet's gathering is met with a claim about God's own commitment, and the claim is stated in the same breath as the welcome. The message the community carries about God is the first thing a believer receives when he approaches.

**The Reason for the Instruction After the Previous Passage**

The verse follows immediately on the treatment of the poor believers and the demand that they be kept at a distance. Commentators connect the two, noting that the instruction may have arisen from a specific request by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and others that the Prophet accommodate the notables, and others relate it to a separate incident in which believers confessed serious sins to the Prophet and received this verse as the answer.

Either way, the placement matters. A community that had just been told not to sort itself by status is now told how to receive anyone who comes to it: with peace and with the announcement of mercy. The instruction restores the dignity of the person coming in, and it places the assessment of his record with God rather than with the gathering.

**The Mercy God Prescribed for Himself**

The sentence repeats a claim the sūrah made earlier, where God is described as having taken upon Himself to be merciful (6:12), and it is the only attribute the Book says God prescribed for Himself. The earlier verse stated the fact in the context of a warning about the gathering; this verse states it in the context of forgiveness for a person who has sinned and repented, which shows the doctrine at work.

The Book keeps the two contexts together in other passages, where mercy is described as encompassing all things while punishment falls on whoever God wills (7:156). The verse in front of us gives the practical reason for the self-imposed obligation. A community of human beings will contain people who fail, and the arrangement had to include a route back.

**"Commits Evil Ignorantly or Recklessly"**

The phrase describes the ordinary way in which people do wrong: not as a deliberate campaign against God but as a lapse, a failure of attention, or a decision made without weighing what it means. The Book uses the same description where it speaks of those who commit evil out of ignorance and then repent (4:17–18), and where it says that God accepts the repentance of the one who does wrong and then turns back.

That wording keeps the door wide while it keeps the requirement firm. The ignorance does not excuse the act, and it does not remove the need for repentance, but it puts the act inside the category of the foreseeable rather than the unforgivable. What the verse will not do is remove the conditions attached to the promise.

**Two Conditions and Their Order**

Whoever repents afterwards and mends their ways is the phrase that closes the verse's conditions, and the two halves are not redundant. Repentance is a turning from the act, and amendment is a turning toward a different practice, and the Book regularly requires both. Elsewhere the same sequence appears in the sūrah of the Cow, where the instruction to the believers is followed by the announcement that God is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful toward those who repent and do right.

The order matters because regret alone can be a passing emotion. The Book treats the change of conduct as the evidence that the turning was real, and it does not ask the person returning to prove himself to the community first. The two names that close the verse, All-Forgiving and Most Merciful, state what he will find when he does return.

**The Report About God's Right Over His Servants**

The tafsīr literature connects this passage with a hadith in which the Prophet asked his Companions whether they knew the right of God over the servants, and answered that it is that they worship Him and do not associate partners with Him, and then asked whether they knew the right of the servants over God if they do that, and answered that He will not punish them. The report is quoted in the commentaries on this verse to show the reciprocal nature of what God has bound Himself to.

Read with the verse, the report explains the phrase about the Lord taking mercy upon Himself. The obligation is not something God owed anyone by nature; it is a commitment He announced, and the Book treats it as the ground on which a person may approach him with hope rather than despair.

**What the Believer Receives on Arrival**

The verse gives the community its welcome and its first doctrine in a single instruction. The person who comes is greeted with peace and told that his Lord has bound Himself to mercy and that the way back is open to whoever takes it. The sūrah then continues its argument with the disbelievers, but it does so having first described what happens at the door of the believing community, which is where the rest of the message has to be lived.
verses.55:
> This is how We make Our signs clear, so the way of the wicked may become distinct

**Clarity as a Deliberate Act**

The verse states that the signs have been made clear, and it states it as something God does rather than as something that happens. The Book uses this vocabulary repeatedly, and the sūrah alone names it several times, including where the signs are explained for people who know (6:97) and where the Prophet is told to follow the road that has been made plain (6:126). The same formula appears in the sūrah of Fussilat, which takes its title from the word.

The claim matters because the Makkans had been complaining about ambiguity. They wanted a sign that would settle the matter beyond argument, and the verse answers that the Qur'anic method is to make the truth clear by accumulated explanation, argument, warning, and illustration. What they were asking for was not clarity but the end of the discussion.

**The Purpose Named: Distinguishing a Road**

Then the verse states why the clarity is given: so that the way of the wicked may become distinct. The phrase is spatial, and the Book's imagery of two roads runs through it. There is a path and there is a deviation, and the Book's work of explanation is what makes the difference visible. The sūrah earlier used the same image where it asked whether the blind and the seeing could be equal (6:50), and where it described being guided to a Straight Way in contrast to being left to stray (6:39).

That purpose is easy to misread as hostile. The point is not that God marks out a group of people in order to condemn them but that the clarity of the message makes the course of conduct visible for what it is. A road can only be avoided by a person who can see where it goes.

**The Book's Insistence That the Message Is Not Cryptic**

The Book returns to this point in several places because it was a live complaint. It says that it has set out every kind of example for people in the recitation, though most of them persist in disbelief (17:89); it states the same in the sūrah of the Cave (18:54) and in the sūrah of Ṭā-Hā (20:113); and it describes the revelation as a Book whose verses have been perfected and then explained in detail (11:1). The clearest statement of the principle is that the message is a clarification from God rather than a puzzle.

The Makkan objection, in the sūrah's own account, was not that the message was unclear. It was that the message was unwelcome, and the Book's response is to keep making the same points in fresh forms rather than to make them obscure.

**Why the Word "Wicked" Is Used Here**

The Arabic behind the translation describes a person who steps out of bounds, the same vocabulary the previous verse used for the people who deny the signs and are punished for their rebellion. Its appearance here connects the passage: the clarity of the signs has the effect of showing where the boundary lies, and the person who crosses it does so with knowledge.

The word does not describe people who have never heard. The whole point of the sentence is that the explanation preceded the conduct, and the Book's insistence on the clarity of its own message is what makes the responsibility of the reader what it is.

**The Verse as a Closing Statement of Method**

The verse functions as a pause after a long stretch of argument that has covered creation, the terms of life and death, mercy, the fate of earlier peoples, the treatment of the poor, and the greeting owed to believers. The sentence states what all of that material was doing: making the signs clear.

It also states what the clarity cannot do. It cannot remove the will of the person hearing, and the sūrah has shown in several places what happens when clarity meets a settled refusal. The verse therefore closes one section of the argument and opens the next, which consists of the Prophet's own declarations about what he has been forbidden to worship and what he stands on.

**The Reader Left With the Two Roads**

A person reading the sentence is left with the choice the sentence describes. The clarity has been supplied, and the two paths have been laid out: the one that the believers walk with their Lord morning and evening (6:52), and the one the wicked take by crossing the bounds that the signs have marked. The sūrah does not present the matter as unresolved, and it does not present it as a question the reader is free to leave open.

The verses that follow give the Prophet the words to declare where he stands, and they give the audience the sight of a community that has already chosen its road.

**Clarity for People Who Already Know**

The sūrah attaches the same phrase to a specific audience when it says that the stars have been made as guides through the darkness of land and sea and that the signs have already been made clear for people who know (6:97). The Book's explanations are not delivered into a neutral space. They are given to people who are travelling through their own lives and who can recognise what they have been told when it matches what they see.

That is why the verse here ends with the distinction between the two roads rather than with a celebration of the explanation itself. The clarity serves a purpose, and the purpose is that a person should be able to see the difference between the way of the wicked and the way of the guided while he still has time to choose between them.
verses.56:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I have been forbidden to worship those you invoke besides Allah.” Say, “I will not follow your desires, for I then would certainly be astray and not one of those ˹rightly˺ guided.”

**A Prohibition Stated in the First Person**

The verse begins with the Prophet announcing that he has been forbidden, and the passive construction carries the authority without requiring him to name himself as the source of the rule.
