The prohibition concerns the objects the Makkans invoke, which the sūrah has already examined from several angles: they can neither harm nor benefit (5:76), they cannot respond or protect (20:89), and they are created beings like the people who worship them (7:194).

Making the announcement in the first person is a public act of separation. The Prophet is not reporting a difference of opinion between himself and his people; he is declaring a boundary that has been drawn for him by someone else, which leaves no room for negotiation and no room for the political compromise the Makkans had been seeking.

**What "I Have Been Forbidden" Does Not Say**

The formulation is worth noticing for what it declines to claim. The Prophet does not say that he finds their gods unworthy through his own reasoning, though the sūrah has supplied the reasoning, and he does not say that the matter is open to discussion. He states the instruction and leaves the audience with the source of the rule, which is the pattern the Book follows in every dispute between a messenger and his people.

The Book uses the same construction elsewhere for the community, where the believers are forbidden certain things by the same authority. The effect is to keep the question where it belongs, since a prohibition from God cannot be renegotiated by the people it inconveniences and cannot be weakened by the fact that a majority disagrees with it.

**The Second Command and the Word "Desires"**

The verse then adds a separate instruction: I will not follow your desires. The Arabic word describes inclination and appetite rather than reasoned preference, and the Book uses it for the impulses that pull a person away from a considered decision. The same warning is given to the Prophet repeatedly, including where the Book tells him not to follow the desires of the People of the Book (5:48–49) and where it warns him against their wish that he compromise (17:73).

The word also explains what the Makkan position actually amounted to. They were not offering an alternative account of God that could be examined in the light of argument. They were asking the Prophet to accommodate the practices they were attached to, and the verse names the attachment for what it is.

**The Two Results of Following Desire**

The verse then states the consequence of the decision the Prophet refuses to make: for then I would certainly be astray and not one of those rightly guided. He is not describing a possible lapse in his own function as a messenger; he is describing what happens when a person with knowledge allows appetite to set the course. The Book states the same principle for all people when it describes those who take their own desire as a god and are then left to stray with their hearing sealed and a cover over their sight (45:23).

The language of straying and guidance returns here because the sūrah has just used it for the two roads (6:55). A person who follows desire has left the road, and the Book does not soften the description by suggesting that departure can be partial.

**The Political Shape of the Refusal**

The Makkans had asked for a reciprocal recognition: their gods acknowledged by the Prophet, and his God acknowledged by them. The sūrah records the suggestion in other places, where they sought a compromise and were told that the Prophet's position could not be traded in that market. This verse's refusal is the same answer in two sentences, addressed to the whole city.

The refusal also had consequences the audience would have understood. A public declaration of this kind closed the path of tribal reconciliation and made the Prophet's position an identifiable cause, which is precisely why the sūrah puts the declaration in his mouth rather than leaving it as a private conviction.

**What the Two Sayings Establish**

The pair of commands establishes two facts about the Prophet that the rest of the sūrah will build on. He does not worship what his people worship, and he does not accept their criteria for judging religious questions. Both statements are given as instructions rather than as preferences, and both remove the possibility that the message could be adjusted to fit the audience.

The next verses continue with the Prophet's declarations about the proof he stands on and the punishment his people were demanding he hasten. The sūrah is putting the whole of his position on the record in his own voice, so that no one could claim afterward that the terms had been left vague.

The Book shows what the compromise would have looked like in other passages, and none of them make pleasant reading. The Prophet is told that his opponents wished him to accommodate them so that they would accommodate him (68:9), and the sūrah of al-Isrāʾ reports that they nearly lured him from what had been revealed to him, in the hope that he would attribute something to God that had not come from Him (17:73), a scheme the Book says would have brought him a double punishment in this life and the next (17:75). The same refusal is stated in the shortest terms in the sūrah of the Disbelievers, which ends the matter with the declaration that each party has its own way (109:6).
verses.57:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Indeed, I stand on a clear proof from my Lord—yet you have denied it. That ˹torment˺ you seek to hasten is not within my power. It is only Allah Who decides ˹its time˺. He declares the truth. And He is the Best of Judges.”

**A Claim Several Messengers Have Made**

The declaration that the speaker stands on a clear proof from his Lord is placed on the lips of several prophets in the Book. Hūd announced it twice to his people (11:28; 11:63), Shuʿayb said the same when he was accused of seeking his own advantage (11:88), and the Book describes the believers generally as those who stand on clear proof from their Lord (11:17). The statement is therefore not a personal boast on the part of one man but the standing of every messenger in relation to the message he was given.

The clear proof in this context is the Qur'an itself, together with the demonstrative arguments the sūrah has been building. The Prophet is not claiming a private experience that others cannot evaluate. He is pointing to something the audience also possessed and could examine, which is what makes the next clause so grave.

**"Yet You Have Denied It"**

The sentence states the situation without softening it. The proof stands and it has been denied, and the two facts are placed next to each other in a single breath. The Book's descriptions of denial nearly always have this structure, since what is being described is not a lack of evidence but a response to evidence that is present.

That is why the sūrah's earlier verses kept returning to the same complaint in different words, asking who could restore hearing, sight, and hearts if God withdrew them (6:46), and naming the wrongdoers as the ones who deny the signs (6:49). The denial in this verse is not the beginning of the story but a settled response recorded after a long argument.

**The Demand to Hasten What Cannot Be Hastened**

The verse then names the thing the Makkans had been pressing for: the punishment they were seeking to hasten. The Book records the styles of that demand in several places. They asked, if the message was true, for stones to rain down on them from the sky (8:32); they asked when the promise would come to pass if it was true (27:71); and the Book answers once that perhaps some of what they were seeking to hasten was close at hand (27:72). Elsewhere the Prophet is told that the wrongdoers have a share of torment like that of their predecessors and that they should not ask for it to be brought forward (51:59).

The request was not a sincere inquiry. It was a challenge issued in public, on the assumption that nothing would happen, and the Book treats the tone rather than the content. The answer given here removes the question from the Prophet's authority entirely, which is the point the audience most needed to hear.

**Judgment Belongs to God Alone**

The sentence states that it is Allah alone who decides the time, and the Book states the same principle for judgment generally. The sūrah itself says a few verses later that all authority belongs to God and to Him people will be returned (28:88), and it says elsewhere that no one shares in His rulings (12:40). The Book makes the point repeatedly because the Makkans' demand assumed that the messenger or his God could be manipulated into a display on request.

The verse's effect is to state a limit on the messenger's function, and the sūrah will state that limit again in different terms when it asks the Prophet to say that he follows only what is revealed to him (6:50). The man who delivers the warning has no control over the timetable of the thing he is warning about.

**"He Declares the Truth"**

The phrase is translated from a verb that can be read with a slight change of letters to mean that God decrees the truth, and some commentators preferred that reading in a passage about judgment. Either way, the sentence states that God's relation to the truth is active: He declares it, establishes it, and makes the outcome follow from it.

The Book uses the same verb to describe God's narration of events, as when it relates the accounts of the prophets to the Prophet himself, and it uses the noun for the truth across the whole of the message. The verse is claiming that the truth is not a matter of opinion that the audience is free to negotiate but a fact that God states about the world and the Hereafter.

**"The Best of Judges"**

The verse closes with a name that appears at the end of several passages. Shuʿayb told his people to be patient until God judges between them, calling Him the Best of Judges (7:87); the Prophet is told to follow what is revealed to him and to be patient until God passes judgment, with the same name attached (10:109); Noah used it when he appealed to his Lord about his son (11:45); and the eldest brother of Joseph used it when he refused to leave the land (12:80). The Book ends the whole recitation with the same question: is Allah not the most just of all judges (95:8).

Putting the name at the end of a verse about the punishment the Makkans were demanding means the answer to their challenge is already settled in principle. A judge who is the best of judges does not need assistance or prompting from the parties before him, and the timing He has chosen is not something the accused can schedule.

**What the Verse Establishes About the Prophet**

Two things are established about the Prophet in this sentence. He has a proof, which means his position is not arbitrary, and he has no power over the punishment, which means his position is not coercive. The middle of the verse holds those two facts together, and the next sentence draws the conclusion the audience should have drawn for themselves.

That conclusion is put in the form of a conditional statement about what would have happened if the timing had been left to the Prophet, and it is stated in the plainest words available.
verses.58:
> Say ˹also˺, “If what you seek to hasten were within my power, the matter between us would have already been settled. But Allah knows the wrongdoers best.”

**A Sentence That Answers the Challenge by Granting It**

The verse takes the Makkan demand seriously for one clause and then shows where it leads. If the timing of the punishment had been in the Prophet's hands, he tells them, the matter between us would already be finished. The sentence is built as a hypothetical, and the hypothetical is the argument: it demonstrates what the audience's own request would have produced if it had been granted.

Nothing in the sentence needs elaboration for the Makkans to feel its force. They had been crowding around the Prophet asking him to bring down what he was warning them about, and the verse lets them imagine a world in which he could. Their next breath would have been their last, and the fact that they were still arguing was evidence about who held the decision, not evidence about the message.

**What the Hypothetical Reveals About the Delay**

The sentence explains the delay as the product of a decision that has not yet been reached rather than as a failure of the threat. The Book makes the same point at length when it describes how the wrongdoers are drawn on step by step in ways they cannot comprehend, and how their end is postponed while the planning proceeds (7:182–183). The delay is described elsewhere as a period in which people are given time, and the Book warns against reading the postponement as approval (3:178).

For the Prophet's own audience, that meant the shouting matches of the Makkan market were still possible because they were being tolerated. The verse turns the delay into a fact about God's patience rather than a fact about the Prophet's weakness, which is the whole purpose of putting the statement in his mouth.

**The Verse Pair and the Difference Between Them**

The two verses stand together as a single answer. The first says that the punishment is not in the Prophet's power and that judgment belongs to God, who declares the truth and is the best of judges (6:57). The second says what would have happened if the first statement had been false. Together they form a demonstration that the audience had asked for, delivered in the form of a condition.

That structure is a favourite of the Book: it makes the audience's own demand the instrument of their correction. A question raised against the messenger is answered by showing what the answer would cost, and the audience is left with the only conclusion available.

**"The Matter Between Us Would Have Been Settled"**

The phrase describes a dispute brought to its end by a ruling, and the sūrah has just described God as the one who decides. The Book uses similar language where it speaks of judgment being passed between people in fairness, with no one wronged (10:47), and where it says that God will judge between those who differ. The settlement in view here is final and total, and it includes the people who are asking the questions.

The expression also implies that the dispute was real and that it had two sides. The verse does not present the Makkans' position as a misunderstanding to be cleared up, and it does not present the Prophet's position as a preference. It treats the matter as a case awaiting a decision, which is exactly how the Book describes the relation between a messenger and a people who reject him.

**"Allah Knows the Wrongdoers Best"**

The closing clause might look like a step down from the high statement of judgment that preceded it. It is not. The sentence states that the parties to the dispute are known, and that the one who will judge has the full record of every one of them. The Book uses the same construction where it says that God knows the wrongdoers best, and elsewhere when it says that He knows best who has strayed from His path and who is rightly guided (6:117).

Knowledge of that kind removes the last remaining hope that any party could argue its case on the day. The Makkans could accuse the Prophet in the market, and he could answer them, and the Book's response to the whole exchange is that the judge already knows what both sides have done.

**The Prophet's Position After the Two Verses**

After making these two declarations, the Prophet has said publicly that he stands on evidence, that his people have denied it, that the punishment is not in his hands, that God decides its time, that God declares the truth, that God is the best of judges, and that the punishment would already have fallen if the timing had been left to him. There is nothing left for the audience to ask him for, and the sūrah moves straight from this point into one of its most expansive statements about the reach of God's knowledge.

That statement begins with a claim no creature shares, and it is introduced without any transition, since the audience has just been told that the decision rests with the One who knows everything that exists.

The difference between the two positions is stated by the sūrah a few verses later, where God is described as knowing best who has strayed from His way and who is rightly guided (6:117). The Makkans judged by the standards of their market and their ancestry, and the Prophet spoke from a proof he had received. The verse's last words place the assessment of both parties in the hands of the one who needs no evidence to reach a conclusion, which is the reason the passage can end on a note of confidence rather than on a threat.
verses.59:
> With Him are the keys of the unseen—no one knows them except Him. And He knows what is in the land and sea. Not even a leaf falls without His knowledge, nor a grain in the darkness of the earth or anything—green or dry—but is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record

**The Only Place the Keys Are Named**

This is the only verse in the entire recitation that says God possesses the keys of the unseen, and the phrase gave its name to works of scholarship across the centuries, including the great commentary of Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī. The Book states elsewhere that God alone knows the unseen, as in the verse where He tells the Prophet to say that none in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except God (27:65), and in the passage where He says that the unseen belongs to Him alone (10:20).

The word for keys describes the instruments that open what is closed, and the commentators understood the phrase as a reference to the storehouses from which everything created is brought forth. What the verse is doing in context is answering the demand the Makkans had just made. They wanted the Prophet to disclose the future and the timing of the punishment, and the answer is that the keys of that domain are held by someone else.

**The Five Keys in the Reported Tradition**

The commentaries connect the phrase with a report transmitted from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, in which the Prophet said that the keys of the unseen are five and then recited the verse in the sūrah of Luqmān: with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour, He sends down the rain, He knows what is in the wombs, no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die (31:34). The report is recorded by al-Bukhārī in his Ṣaḥīḥ in the book of the rain prayer, and it is reported from Buraydah in the Musnad of Aḥmad with a chain the scholars judged sound.

ʿĀisha used the same material to correct a claim about the Prophet himself, saying that anyone who told her that Muhammad had seen the unseen was a liar, because God says that none has knowledge of the unseen but He, and then quoting the Prophet's statement about the five keys. The point of the tradition is not to restrict God's knowledge to five items but to name the matters people most wanted disclosed and to place them beyond every created claimant.

**Knowledge That Reaches the Smallest Things**

The verse then widens its scope from the hidden to the visible: He knows what is in the land and sea. The statement moves from the general to the minute, and the two examples chosen are a falling leaf and a grain buried in the dark of the earth. Neither object has any importance to a human observer, and both are beyond observation altogether, which is precisely why the Book selects them.

The same argument appears in the sūrah of Yūnus, where the Book says that not even an atom's weight is hidden from the Lord on earth or in heaven, nor anything smaller or larger than that, but that it is written in a perfect record (10:61). The sūrah of Naml makes the same point about what is hidden in the heavens and the earth being recorded in a clear book (27:75), and the sūrah of Sabāʾ states that nothing escapes the Lord's knowledge by so much as an atom's weight (34:3).

**The Argument Against Those Who Limited God's Knowledge**

This verse was used by the theologians against certain Muslim philosophers who held that God knows universals but not particulars. The claim was that a God whose knowledge reached every individual thing would be affected by change, and the response was that the Book's own wording leaves no room for the distinction. A leaf that falls, a grain in the dark, a seed in the ground: the verse names the particulars, not the categories.

The sūrah states the point in a form that makes the objection impossible to maintain, since the falling of a single leaf is the most contingent event imaginable. Whoever knows that knows a particular, and the Book says the knowledge extends to everything green or dry, which is another way of saying that nothing at all lies outside it.

**The Clear Record and What It Means**

The verse ends by saying that all of this is written in a perfect record. Commentators identified the record with the Preserved Tablet, of which the Book speaks when it describes the Qur'an as inscribed on a tablet well preserved (85:22), and some held that the expression refers to God's own knowledge rather than to a created object. The Book uses the same phrase for revealed scripture in several places, which shows how flexible the image is in its hands.

What the phrase accomplishes in this verse is to add permanence to knowledge. The leaf is not merely watched as it falls; it is recorded, and the record keeps the account of a thing that no human being ever noticed. The Book's readers were being told that the details of their own lives are kept in the same way, which is the practical consequence the sūrah draws from it a few verses later.

**What It Means for a Person's Own Account**

The verse that follows this one describes God taking the souls of people by night and knowing what they do by day, and the one after that describes the recording angels who watch over every person. Read together, the three verses establish the whole apparatus of accountability, beginning with the One who holds the keys and ending with the point at which a life is closed and its account returned.

For a reader, the consequence is that nothing is hidden which will not be produced, and nothing is trivial which will not be weighed. The verse's leaf and grain are not incidental details chosen for their poetry. They are the claim that the smallest event in the world is known and written, which makes every deed of a human being a matter of record.
verses.60:
> He is the One Who calls back your souls by night and knows what you do by day, then revives you daily to complete your appointed term. To Him is your ˹ultimate˺ return, then He will inform you of what you used to do

**Sleep Described With the Language of Death**

The verb the verse uses for what happens at night is the same verb the Book uses for death, and the commentators noticed it. Yatawaffā is the word that appears when a person's life is taken at the end of his term, and here it describes the ordinary experience of falling asleep. In sleep, the senses and the limbs stop functioning, and what continues is something inward, which is why the Book can use one vocabulary for both states.

The Book makes the comparison explicit in the sūrah of al-Zumar, where it says that God calls back the souls of people at their death and the souls of the living during their sleep, keeping those for whom death has been decreed and releasing the others until an appointed time (39:42). The sūrah of al-Furqān describes the night as a covering, sleep as rest, and the day as a rising (25:47), which is the same three-part sequence this verse follows.

**Waking as a Daily Resurrection**

Then by day He resurrects you: the verse uses resurrection language for the ordinary morning. The point is not decorative. The Book argues for the reality of the final resurrection by pointing to events within human experience that resemble it, and sleep and waking are the most immediate of those events. A person who accepts that he was conscious yesterday, lost that consciousness, and had it returned to him this morning has already accepted the structure of the argument.

The same method appears with the revived earth. The Book describes God sending the winds and driving clouds to a dead land so that rain falls and fruit comes forth, and then says that in the same way He will bring the dead to life (7:57). It repeats the image in the sūrah of the Bee (16:65), the Pilgrimage (22:5), the Spider (29:63), the Romans (30:24), and Fussilat (41:39), and the audience is told in one of those passages that even the idolaters admit who sends the rain.

**The Appointed Term**

Then the verse says that people are revived each day so that a term appointed may be fulfilled. The Book attaches an appointed term to individuals and communities alike, saying that every community has its term and cannot delay or advance it by a single hour (7:34; 10:49), and describing the sun and moon as running their courses for a set period (13:2; 31:29; 35:13; 39:5). The whole creation is described as having been made with a purpose and an appointed term (46:3).

The phrase places the small cycle of sleep and waking inside the larger cycle of a life. Each day that a person is revived is a day added to the course he is running, and the verse treats the supply of days as provision for a task rather than as an entitlement. The Book states that the span is fixed, which is why the demand to hasten a punishment made no sense to a community that could not extend its own lives by a moment.

**The Return and the Reporting**

To Him is your ultimate return, and then He will inform you of what you used to do. The Book uses this closing formula across many sūrahs, sometimes attached to the warning that the guilty will be told what they did, sometimes to the promise that those who did right will be shown their deeds. The sūrah of the Cave states it in almost the same words in the middle of a comparison between two groups of people, and the same ending appears in the sūrahs of Joseph, the Spider, and Luqmān.

The informing is not a formality of the court. The Book describes the record of each person being handed over on that day, with those who receive it in their right hand reading it with joy (17:71; 69:19), and the Book says that every deed, whether small or large, is written down for exactly this purpose. What the verse establishes is that the knowledge described in the previous verse has an outcome: it is not only that God knows, but that the person will be told.

**The Cycle as Provision and Warning at Once**

Read with the verses around it, this one describes the whole apparatus of human life as a loan. The night returns a person to a state like death, the morning gives him back out of mercy, and the days are counted until the term runs out. The Book states the same about the earth, which is revived by rain so that people and animals might eat from it, and it draws the natural conclusion that all of it belongs to the One who runs it.

For an audience that had just been told that the keys of the unseen belong to God and that nothing green or dry escapes His record, this verse explains the practical shape of that knowledge. Every day the account is open, and every night the ledger is held by the One who will read from it at the end.

**The Comfort in the Ordinary Cycle**

The passage also carries a note of mercy that a reader should not miss. Sleep is described in the Book as a mercy, and the sūrah of the Cave explains that God kept the young men of the cave asleep as protection from the city that would have stoned them. A person reading this verse is being told that the ordinary rhythm of every day he has ever lived was maintained by the One who has bound Himself to mercy, and that the same power that returned him to the world each morning will return him to his Lord at the end of the term.
verses.61:
> He reigns supreme over all of His creation, and sends recording-angels, watching over you. When death comes to any of you, Our angels take their soul, never neglecting this duty

**A Statement the Sūrah Makes Twice**

The opening clause of this verse repeats almost word for word a sentence the sūrah used earlier, where God is described as reigning supreme over His creation and as being All-Wise and All-Aware (6:18). The repetition is not accidental, since the two statements sit inside the same argument, and the second adds the machinery that makes the first concrete: not only does God hold authority over what He has made, but there are appointed agents watching what every human being does.

The Arabic phrase describes a mastery that leaves nothing outside it, and the Book uses the same root for the overwhelming of a people by water, for the descent of an irresistible punishment, and for the crushing realization of a truth one had denied. The verse's claim is that God's authority over His creatures is of that order: complete, present, and unopposed.

**The Angels Who Write**

Then the verse describes the recorders: vigilant, honourable angels who note everything and know what people do (82:10–12). The sūrah of Qāf describes two of them sitting on the right and the left and states that no word is uttered without an observer ready to write it down (50:17–18). The Book refers to the same system when it says that every soul has successive angels before and behind it, protecting it by God's command (13:11).

Commentators discussed whether these are the same angels as the scribes of a person's deeds, and the common view is that the record of deeds is kept by two witnesses at all times. What matters for the verse is that the watching is described as an office assigned by God rather than as a power the angels hold by themselves, so the whole apparatus leads back to the One the audience was being asked to acknowledge.

**Protection and Observation in One Sentence**

Read carefully, the clause describes two functions that pull in opposite directions: the angels guard, and they record. The Book holds both ideas without tension, since the same presence which notes a person's conduct also shields him from harms he never knows about, and the sūrah of the Cave speaks of protection when it says that God brought the truth before anyone could see it.

For the Makkans, this sentence carried a correction to a familiar belief about the jinn and the invisible world. The Book's position is that the unseen is administered, not chaotic, and that no spirit has a private claim on a human being's fate. The angels in this verse do nothing on their own initiative, which is why the account they keep is trustworthy.

**The Moment of Death**

When death comes to any of you, Our angels take their soul, never neglecting this duty. The verse moves from the ongoing record to the single moment in which the record is closed, and the phrasing about the angels never neglecting their task is a reassurance to the friends of God and a warning to everyone else. No one dies unattended, and no one dies at a moment other than the one that was fixed.

The Book describes the taking of the souls of the wrongdoers in harsher terms elsewhere. When the angels seize the souls of those who wronged themselves, they ask them what they were doing, and the reply from the people who claim they were oppressed in the land is met with the question of whether God's earth was not wide enough to move within (4:97). Another passage describes the angels striking the faces and backs of those who disbelieve (47:27), and the sūrah itself will describe the same scene with the angels stretching out their hands (6:93).

**A Reassurance That Cuts Both Ways**

The sentence about the angels fulfilling their duty is addressed to a community in which the manner of a person's death carried heavy social meaning. A death far from home, or an early death, or a violent death, was read as a judgment on the person and his tribe. The verse removes that reading by stating that the taking of the soul is performed by appointed agents who never fall short, which means the circumstances of a death are not a verdict on the one who dies.

That is the mercy in the sentence. The same clause also establishes the point the Book repeats in several places: the moment cannot be moved. The sūrah had said earlier that every community has its appointed term and cannot delay or advance it (7:34; 10:49), and here the application is made to a single person. Neither the physicians of the city nor the idols at the shrine have any part in the timing.

**What Follows the Angel**

The verse stops at the taking and leaves the next sentence to describe what happens after it, which is where the sūrah's argument about accountability reaches its conclusion. The reader is left with a chain of events that has no gap in it: keys with God, knowledge of every leaf, souls taken at night, deeds known by day, an appointed term completed, then the return.

The word the verse uses for the return is a term of ownership, and it opens the question the next verse answers in four words about who the Master is. The record kept by the two angels and the moment of death are the two ends of a single process, and the sūrah is now ready to describe what comes after both.

**What the Sentence Teaches About the Hidden World**

The Book mentions the angels in this verse and in the two on either side of it, and it never once describes them as acting on their own authority. They record, they guard, and they take the soul when the order comes. The uniform picture is a world in which every invisible power is an employee rather than a partner, and the sūrah's audience, which had assigned shares of the unseen to the jinn and the idols, is being shown the actual chain of command.
verses.62:
> Then they are ˹all˺ returned to Allah—their True Master. Judgment is His ˹alone˺. And He is the Swiftest Reckoner

**The Claim of Ownership**

The verse describes the return of every soul to God and calls Him their true Master, and the word translated as Master is one the Book uses for the person who owns, protects, and manages the affairs of another. Slaves in Makkah had such a master, and clients attached themselves to a patron, and the whole city was organised around relationships of that kind. The verse states that the relationship which actually covers every human being is the one that most people treat as a matter of law and property.

The Book uses the same word in a passage about intercession, where it says that the believers have God as their Patron while the disbelievers have no patron at all (47:11), and the sūrah states plainly that apart from Him no one has a protector and no one has an intercessor (6:51). The Makkans' patrons could not carry a client past death, and the verse tells them whose clients they have been all along.

**A Question Asked on That Day**

The Book describes a scene in which the ownership of everything is publicly announced. On the day when all appear before God, nothing about them will be hidden from Him, and the question will be asked: who does all authority belong to this day? The answer given is to Allah, the One, the Supreme (40:16). The Book says elsewhere that true authority on that day will belong only to the Most Compassionate, and that it will be a hard day for the disbelievers (25:26).

That scene explains what this verse means by a true Master. On the day of the question, every title that a person relied on will be shown to have been delegated at best and imaginary at worst, and the Book's word for it is that authority belongs to God alone. The Makkans' clan loyalties, their property, and their names would all have been visible as borrowed things.

**Judgment Is His Alone**

The sūrah has already said once that the decision belongs to God, when the Prophet was told to say that he had no power over the timing of the punishment and that God is the best of judges (6:57). The same claim returns here as the conclusion of the passage on knowledge and death. What began with God knowing every leaf and every grain ends with God alone passing sentence on what every soul has done.

The Book states that God will pass judgment between people on that day in fairness, without the least injustice, and it says that every soul will then be rewarded for what it did, with no wrong done at all (40:17). The two claims belong together: the judge who knows everything has no need of witnesses, and the judge who is the best of judges has no need of advocates.

**The Swiftest Reckoner**

The name that closes the verse appears in several places in the Book, usually in the context of a settlement that takes no time to reach. The sūrah of the Cow uses it when it says that some people receive their reward and that God is swift in reckoning (2:202), and the sūrah of Ghāfir uses it in the announcement that every soul will be repaid in full (40:17). The name is not about haste for its own sake; it describes an accounting that requires no deliberation, since the record is complete and the judge is the one who wrote what the record contains.

The Book also describes the fear that this swiftness produces in the guilty, when their descendants and neighbours and the entire crowd watch the books being distributed. The speed of the reckoning is a mercy for one party and a disaster for the other, and the same attribute is used for both, which is the way the Book regularly speaks about the attributes of God.

**The Chain That Ends Here**

Follow the verses as a unit. God holds the keys of the unseen and knows every falling leaf and buried grain (6:59). God takes the souls of people by night and knows what they do by day, reviving them each morning until the appointed term is complete (6:60). God has appointed angels who record everything and angels who take the soul at death without fail (6:61). Then the souls are returned to their Master, who alone judges and who settles accounts without delay (6:62).

Read that way, the four verses give the complete account of a human life in the order in which it happens. The audience wanted to know about the hidden and the future, and the sūrah has answered by describing the process that connects this world to the next without leaving out a single step, and without giving the audience any access to the timings they were asking about.

**The Contrast With Earthly Masters**

The closing sentence of the passage is deliberately stark. On the one side stands the judge who knows everything, holds everything, and needs nothing; on the other side stand people whose patrons could not answer for them and whose gods had no share in the making of the world. The Book records the idolaters themselves conceding that their gods are names they gave (12:40), and it reports God's challenge for them to show anything their associate-gods had created (35:40).

The verse does not answer that contrast with argument. It states the fact of the return and leaves the audience to reckon with the master they had chosen. The next verses turn from the general scene to the specific behaviour of people in danger, who call upon God alone and then forget Him the moment they are safe.
verses.63:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who rescues you from the darkest times on land and at sea? He ˹alone˺ you call upon with humility, openly and secretly: “If You rescue us from this, we will be ever grateful.”

**The Prayer of the Tight Corner**

The verse asks the Makkans about a moment every one of them knew: the point at which a situation has become hopeless and the only remaining act is to call out. The Book returns to this scene repeatedly because it is the one place where a human being's actual beliefs become visible. The idolaters could argue in the market about their gods, and in the dark they abandoned them without discussion.

The Book describes the same behaviour elsewhere, sometimes with the vivid detail that a person in danger calls on God with sincere devotion but then returns to his old associations once he is safe (29:65), and sometimes with the observation that when people are asked who saves them, they answer that it was God (31:32). The verse in front of us turns that knowledge into a question and lets the audience supply the answer the Book already knows they will give.

**Land and Sea**

The pairing of land and sea covers the two great fears of a trading city, and the merchants of Makkah knew both. A caravan crossing the desert faced thirst, sandstorms, and raiding; a ship faced the possibility that the water would simply close over the crew, with no grave and no witness. The Book uses the sea in several places as an image of helplessness, describing the drowning of the people of Noah and the rescue of Jonah, and it describes people in a ship as calling upon God with sincere faith until He brings them safely to land, at which point they begin to associate others with Him (17:67).

Commentators note that the verse names the two settings because each produced a different kind of fear. On land a person may still run, and at sea there is nowhere to go. The question is designed to reach a memory and not an argument, and the Book's method with its stubborn audience is often exactly this.

**Calling With Humility, Openly and Secretly**

The verse describes the manner of the call before it describes its content, and the description is precise. The person in danger prays with humility, meaning with a lowered voice and a subdued self, and he prays openly and secretly, which the commentators explain as praying aloud in company and quietly alone, or as the visible and hidden forms of supplication.

The two adverbs reveal how thin the Makkan position was. A person who prays in secret has admitted where the power lies, and he cannot then claim that his public position represents his belief. The Book recorded this inconsistency long before: those who call upon God in fear and hope, and those who cry out when harm befalls them, and then attribute a share of what they have been given to others (16:53; 39:8).

**The Vow Made in the Dark**

The verse gives the actual words used in that moment: if You rescue us from this, we will be ever grateful. Gratitude is the promise, which is the opposite of the response the Book says most of them produced. The sūrah of Yūnus describes the pattern exactly, saying that when God rescues people they immediately transgress in the land unjustly, and then addresses them with the reminder that their transgression is against their own souls (10:23).

The vow is the proof the verse needs. Nobody promises gratitude to a stone in a storm, and nobody offers a bargain to an image. The words used at the moment of danger are the audience's own testimony that they know who the rescuer is, and the Book uses their testimony against them rather than against an outsider.

**Why the Question Is Put to the Prophet to Ask**

The command begins with Say, which places the question in the Prophet's mouth rather than in God's. The effect is that the audience is being answered by the man they were disputing with, using material they cannot deny. The sūrah uses this device repeatedly, as it did with the question about hearing and sight (6:46) and the question about being overwhelmed by the punishment (6:47).

The interrogative form also keeps the audience responsible for the conclusion. The Book does not say that every one of them knows the answer; it asks them who rescues, and the answer arrives in the next verse as a verdict rather than as a speculation.

**What the Verse Establishes Before the Rebuke**

By the time the rebuke arrives, the audience has already granted the whole premise of the message. They have been asked who alone can answer a call from a sinking ship, and the answer they must give is the same one the Prophet gives. The following verse states it and then names the contradiction that their own religious practice represented, which is why the rebuke lands where it does.

The sequence is worth noting for how the Book argues with an unwilling audience. It does not begin by declaring them wrong; it leads them to the edge of a conclusion they already believe and lets them stand there, and the sentence that follows is short because the work has already been done.

**The Same Scene in the Sūrah of Yūnus**

The Book tells this story elsewhere with details that make the Makkan setting unmistakable. In the sūrah of Yūnus, people are described boarding a ship that sails with a favourable wind while the passengers rejoice, and then the wind turns, the waves come from every side, and the travellers are certain they are about to die. At that point they cry out to Allah with sincere devotion and promise that if they are saved they will certainly be grateful (10:22). The wording of the prayer in that account is virtually the same as the wording preserved in this verse, which is a sign of how closely the two passages are related in the Book's argument.

The sūrah of the Ant carries the same question in the form of a challenge: who responds to the distressed when they cry to Him and relieves their affliction, and who makes people successors in the earth? Is it another god besides Allah, asks the verse, before noting that people are hardly mindful (27:62). The Book's audience is asked to answer its own question in three separate sūrahs, and the answer is never disputed.

**The Mercy Hidden in the Question**

There is a further point in the way the verse is framed. The question does not ask what a person believes in general, nor does it test him on the fine points of doctrine that the Makkans were disputing. It asks only about the one moment when no human being can maintain a pretence, and it treats the honesty of that moment as a foothold.

The following verse rebukes the inconsistency, and the rebuke would be unanswerable if there were nothing else in the passage. But the Book's habit of returning to that same scene across many sūrahs suggests something further. The call made in the dark is treated as the recollection of a truth the person already carries, and the reminder of it is meant to make the recovery of that truth possible before the next crisis arrives.
verses.64:
> Say, “˹Only˺ Allah rescues you from this and any other distress, yet you associate others with Him ˹in worship˺.”

**The Answer Stated as a Verdict**

The previous verse asked who rescues from the dangers of land and sea, and this one answers without waiting for the audience's reply. The answer is Allah alone, and the wording makes the exclusion total: no partner, no intercessor, no shrine receives credit for the rescue. The Book frequently supplies the answer to its own questions in this way, and it does so because the audience did not need information about the identity of their rescuer. They needed to hear it named in public, in the words of the man they were resisting.

The sūrah of Yūnus contains a similar question about who provides from heaven and earth, who owns hearing and sight, and who conducts every affair, and it records that the answer people give is Allah, followed immediately by the question of whether they will not then be mindful (10:31). The Book treats the audience's own admissions as the strongest evidence available, and it produces them for the record.

**"And Any Other Distress"**

The sentence widens the scope deliberately. The rescue described in the previous verse concerned the most desperate situation conceivable, but the answer here states that the same God rescues from that and from every other hardship as well. The Book makes the same point where it says that whatever blessings people have are from God, and that whenever hardship touches them it is to Him alone they cry for help (16:53).

The widening removes the last defence available to a person who prayed at sea. Some might say that the extremity of the situation produced an instinctive cry rather than an acknowledgment, which would leave the normal conditions of life in the hands of the gods. The verse rejects the separation. The power that answered the cry in the waves is the power that runs everything, which is what makes the next clause a charge rather than an observation.

**What the Prayer Did Not Include**

The verse also exposes the difference between what the audience said and what they practised. The prayer described a person who calls on God alone, who asks God alone for rescue, and who promises God alone his gratitude. Nothing in the moment of crisis left room for the associate-gods, and the verse notes that they were added afterwards, when the danger had gone and the story was being told.

The Book describes the same sequence with a sharper image when it says that a person touched by hardship cries out to God lying on his side, sitting, or standing, and then returns to his old ways once the hardship is relieved, as though he had never called at all (10:12). The Book's conclusion is that the misdeeds of such people were made to look attractive to them, which is a statement about how a habit of ingratitude becomes a settled way of life.

**The Meaning of Associating Others With Him**

The charge in this verse is that they associate others with Him in worship, and the sūrah has been dismantling that practice from every angle. The associated beings were created things like the worshippers (7:194), they could neither harm nor benefit anyone (5:76), they could not respond or protect (20:89), and they had been given names by their own ancestors with no authority from God (12:40).

What this verse adds is the specific context of gratitude. The Book treats the blessing and the rescue as coming through channels that would be entirely the work of God even if the idols were real, and it treats the assignment of a share of thanks to a created thing as a falsification of the record. The person who thanks a stone for a rescue he received from God has made a mistake about what happened to him.

**The Book's Pattern of Testing Its Audience With Their Own Words**

The Book's practice of using the audience's confessions is a feature of its method, not an accident of this passage. It asks who created the heavens and the earth, and the answer recorded is Allah (29:61); it asks who sends down rain to revive the dead earth, and the answer is Allah (29:63); and in each case the question is followed by a rebuke that turns on the gap between the admission and the practice.

That method leaves no exit. A person who answers Allah to these questions has already accepted that the beings he invokes alongside God have no share in the matters he is asking about, and the verse in front of us closes the discussion by naming the inconsistency directly rather than by arguing about the idols' nature.

**What Gratitude Would Have Required**

The verse's charge also states what the correct response would have been. The rescue and every other deliverance come from one source, and the acknowledgment belongs with it. The Book describes gratitude as a form of recognition that produces conduct, and it pairs the ungrateful with those who reject the signs, as it does in the sūrah of Luqmān, where the Book says that none rejects the signs except the treacherous and ungrateful (31:32).

The sūrah then moves from this rebuke to a warning about the forms the punishment can take, and the transition is not sudden. A people who attribute their rescue to the wrong source have placed themselves in the position the next verse describes, in which the same power that saved them is the power that can reach them without any possibility of escape.

The Book states the rebuke in a compact form in the sūrah of the Bee, where it says that every blessing people have comes from God and that whenever hardship touches them it is to Him alone that they cry for help, and then asks why they turn away from the One who gave them what they have (16:53–54). The movement from gratitude to association is described there and here in the same order, which shows that the charge is a general diagnosis of human conduct rather than a complaint about one city.
verses.65:
> Say, “He ˹alone˺ has the power to unleash upon you a torment from above or below you or split you into ˹conflicting˺ factions and make you taste the violence of one another.” See how We vary the signs, so perhaps they will comprehend

**Three Ways for a Community to Be Punished**

The verse lists three possibilities, and the order matters. The first two are punishments that come from outside: a torment from above, and one from below. The third is not an external punishment at all but a condition the community brings upon itself, in which it splits into factions and each group makes the others taste violence. The Book places the self-inflicted one last, which is where the emphasis falls.

Commentators interpreted the torment from above as stones or a storm, or as domination by a tyrant, and the torment from below as an earthquake, a sinking, or being swallowed by the earth. The Book's catalogue of destroyed peoples fits both categories: some were struck by a storm of stones, some were overtaken by a blast, some were made to sink into the earth, and some were drowned (29:40). The sūrah of Sabāʾ states the same power in a conditional: if God willed, He could cause the earth to swallow the people or cause deadly pieces of the sky to fall on them (34:9).

**The Third Punishment and Why It Is the Worst**

The sentence about factions describes a community tearing itself apart, and the Book's choice of image is exact: each faction is made to taste the violence of the others. Civil conflict gives a person the opportunity to be both victim and perpetrator, and it destroys the ordinary structures of trust that hold a society together.

The Book warns about this kind of trial elsewhere in a form that applies it to communities generally. It says that people should guard against a trial which will not strike only the wrongdoers among them (8:25), which is the Book's way of saying that disorder does not restrict itself to the guilty. The sūrah of al-Anʿām has already stated the same warning in the story of the earlier peoples it describes as having been split into groups, and it will return to the subject of divisions among the believers later, when it tells the Prophet that he bears no responsibility for those who split their faith into sects (6:159).

**A Warning Delivered to the Prophet's Own Community**

The force of the list is that it applies to the audience, and the Prophet is told to deliver it as a public statement. The Makkans were confident that they were the strong party, protected by their alliances and their numbers, and the verse tells them that their strength was itself vulnerable to the third scenario. The Book's history is full of communities whose destruction began as an internal quarrel.

The warning also served the Prophet as a boundary. He had been refused the power to bring the punishment, and here he is told that God can bring it in forms that no alliance can resist. His task remained the delivery of the warning, and the verse keeps him inside that task even while it describes what God is able to do.

**"See How We Vary the Signs"**

The verse closes with the same formula that appeared earlier in the sūrah, where the Prophet was asked to see how the signs were varied while the people still turned away (6:46), and where the explanation of the signs was said to make the way of the wicked distinct (6:55). The recurrence is deliberate. The sūrah keeps a running account of the methods being used on its audience, and this verse places the warning about punishment among the variations.

The different reactions attached to the same formula mark the progression across the sūrah. At the earlier point the complaint was that the audience turned away; here the purpose clause is that they might comprehend. The Book's expectation is stated as a hope, and the hope is what keeps the warning from being merely a sentence.

**The Verb That Asks for Understanding**

To comprehend in this context describes the act of grasping something with the mind and turning it over, and the Book uses it for the kind of understanding that changes behaviour. A person who comprehends the argument of this verse has understood that the power which rescued him at sea (6:63) is the same power that can reach him on land, and that the quarrel he is pursuing may itself be the form the punishment takes.

That is the practical use of the list. The divine power described in the third scenario does not need to be exercised directly, since a community left to its own factions will produce the outcome on its own. The verse states the possibility and lets the audience see where their divisions were leading.

**A Final Word for the Prophet**

The verse ends the section that began with the demand to hasten the punishment, and it ends it by transferring the whole question out of human hands. The Prophet does not control the timing, he does not control the form, and he cannot prevent the third scenario from happening to his own people. What he can do is deliver the warning and let the variation of the signs do its work on whoever is willing to comprehend.

The sūrah then turns from these public warnings to a different kind of instruction, addressing the Prophet about how to deal with the people who attack the message and telling him what his own position is in relation to those who reject it. The tone changes, and the audience is offered a portrait of the messenger's own conduct for the first time in several verses.
verses.66:
> Still your people ˹O Prophet˺ have rejected this ˹Quran˺, although it is the truth. Say, “I am not a keeper over you.”

**A Statement That Acknowledges the Grief**

The verse does not open with an argument or a command. It states a fact about the Prophet's situation, and it states it in a way that acknowledges how heavy the fact was: your people have rejected this, though it is the truth. The Book speaks to its messenger here in the manner of one who knows what has been happening, and the sentence does not pretend that the rejection is small.

The sūrah has already recorded the accusations, the obstruction, the demands for signs, and the mockery, and the Prophet has been told that the people who did these things are not questioning his honesty but denying God's signs (6:33). This verse adds the element of personal grief, and the Book elsewhere shows how deep that grief went when it tells him that he might destroy himself with sorrow over people who would not believe (18:6; 26:3).

**"Although It Is the Truth"**

The clause about the truth is the pivot of the sentence. The rejection is not a matter of an unresolved dispute in which one party may turn out to be right; the Book has settled the question of what the Qur'an is, and the rejection is being recorded against that settled fact. The Book uses this construction repeatedly, placing the truth of the message next to the rejection of it as a way of naming the tragedy rather than merely the disagreement.

That pattern is worth seeing in full. The Book states the same combination in the sūrah of Yūnus, where the Prophet is told to say that the truth has surely come from his Lord and that whoever chooses guidance or straying does so for his own account, and then to say that he is not a keeper over the people (10:108). The sūrah of the Troops makes the identical statement when it says that the Book has been revealed with the truth for humanity and that the messenger is not a keeper over them (39:41). The claim is that the rejection happens in the presence of the truth rather than in its absence.

**The Office of Keeper and What It Excludes**

The Prophet is instructed to say that he is not a keeper over them, and the word used here appears twice more in this same sūrah. Earlier he is told to follow what is revealed to him and to turn away from the idolaters, in a passage that ends with the same denial of keepership (6:106–107), and earlier still he is told that his insight has come from his Lord and that he is not a keeper over the people (6:104). The repetition marks it as a settled feature of his commission.

A keeper in this sense is the person charged with the management and outcome of another's affairs. The Book denies that role to the Prophet in matters of belief, and it does so at the very points where the temptation to take that role would have been strongest. What is left to him is the delivery of the message and the reminder, which the Book describes in the sūrah of the Overwhelming when it says that his duty is only to remind (88:21).

**Why the Denial Is a Mercy to the Messenger**

Read in the context of the grief that the verse acknowledges, the sentence functions as a release. A man who believes that the fate of every person he speaks to depends on his own persuasiveness will be destroyed by the work, and the Book's answer to that condition is repeated in several places. The sūrah of the Cave asks whether the Prophet would destroy himself with sorrow over people who will not believe, and the sūrah of the Poets opens the same subject by mentioning the grief that eats away at him.

The Book's remedy is not indifference. The Prophet is told to be patient, to continue the reminder, and to keep the company of those who turn to their Lord, and the sūrah will give him instructions in the next verses about how to behave toward the people who mock the revelation. What is removed is the responsibility for the outcome, and the removal makes the work possible.

**The Boundary Between Warning and Force**

The verse also closes off a temptation on the other side. A messenger who is not accountable for results has no reason to pursue results through the methods that a custodian would use: pressure, bribery, alliance, or the manipulation of the community's social structure. The Makkans were offering exactly those instruments, and each of them required the Prophet to accept the role of keeper that the verse denies him.

That is why the Book's arguments against compulsion in religion are grounded in the doctrine of the messenger's office rather than in a general principle of tolerance. The man who delivers the news has no authority to force its acceptance, and the Book states the conclusion of that reasoning in terms of his own position: if he cannot secure belief, he cannot be blamed for its absence.

**What the Verse Leaves With the Audience**

The audience is left with a message that has been delivered and a messenger who will do what he can do and no more. The statement also leaves them with the fact of their own responsibility, since a warning that cannot be enforced by the one who delivers it places the decision entirely with the person who hears it.

The next verse states the timeline of that decision. The Book's habit in these exchanges is to move from the denial to the appointment, and the appointment is stated in words that leave the timing in God's hands while making the arrival certain.
verses.67:
> Every ˹destined˺ matter has a ˹set˺ time to transpire. And you will soon come to know

**A Sentence About Appointments**

The verse states that everything destined has a time at which it arrives, and the word used for the appointment comes from the same root as the terms and spans the Book applies to human lives and communities. The sūrah used it a few verses earlier when it said that people are revived each day so that an appointed term may be completed (6:60), and it used it for the communities whose fixed spans cannot be delayed or advanced (7:34; 10:49). Here the same structure is applied to the events the audience was impatient about.

The Book states the principle in almost this exact wording at the end of a passage about the demands for signs, where it says that no messenger could bring a sign except by God's permission and that every destined matter has a set time (13:38). Read together, the two verses answer the Makkan demand for a miracle and the Makkan demand for the punishment in the same currency: the timing of both rests with God.

**The Threat and the Promise in the Same Clause**

And you will soon come to know is a formula the Book uses in several tones. It appears where it warns people who reject the revelation that they will soon know (37:170), where the Prophet is told to bear with the mockers and answer them with peace because they will soon come to know (43:89), and where the Book tells the audience that they will certainly know the truth of the warning before long (38:88). The same words serve as a warning and as an assurance depending on who is hearing them.

That double edge is the point of placing the formula here, immediately after a verse that has acknowledged the Prophet's rejection and denied him the role of keeper. The audience is told that the delay in their case does not mean the matter will not be settled, and the Prophet is told that the settlement is coming and that he is not required to produce it.

**The Impatience of the Audience**

The sūrah has recorded the demand to hasten the punishment several times, and the Book treats that impatience as a feature of the human being rather than a considered position. It says in the sūrah of the Prophets that humanity is made of haste, and follows the observation with a warning that the signs will be shown and should not be demanded ahead of their time (21:37). The sūrah of Yūnus ends a discussion of the delay with the instruction to keep waiting, since the Prophet is also waiting (10:102).

The impatience has a function in the Book's argument. It shows that the audience knew the message was making a claim about the future and that the claim mattered to them, since nobody demands the hastening of a matter he regards as fiction. Their demand was a form of acknowledgment, and the verse's answer treats it as such while refusing to move the appointment.

**Waiting as a Form of Conduct**

The Book's instructions about waiting are never passive. The sūrah of Ṭā-Hā ends with the Prophet being told to say that each party is waiting and that the outcome will soon be known (20:135), and the context of that verse is a community being asked to continue in the conduct the message requires. Waiting in the Book's vocabulary means going on with the work while the appointment approaches.

The same structure appears in the sūrah of the Cave, where the audience is told that the message is the truth from the Lord and that whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve (18:29). What looks like a release from obligation is a statement about where the obligation lies. The reader is told that the outcome is fixed for a time of its own choosing, and that the interval belongs to him.

**The Coming of Knowledge**

The clause about coming to know deserves attention because knowledge is the thing the audience had been demanding on its own terms. They wanted to know when the punishment would arrive, and they were told that they would know at the time appointed. The Book's answer is not that the information is being withheld arbitrarily but that the schedule of knowledge is itself part of the appointment.

That principle runs through the Book's treatment of the Hour, whose timing is stated to belong to God alone, and whose arrival is described as something that will take people by surprise. The verse in front of us applies the same arrangement to the smaller events of judgment that the Makkans were demanding to see, and it places the whole subject inside the doctrine of a fixed term that the sūrah has been teaching since its account of the keys of the unseen.

**The Transition It Creates**

The two verses just completed move the sūrah from public argument to practical instruction. The Prophet has been told that he is not a keeper over his people (6:66), and the appointment of every matter has been stated (6:67). What follows is a set of directions about how the believers are to conduct themselves when the revelation is mocked, and how far their responsibility extends toward the mockers.

That transition is worth noting, because it shows what the Book does with the anxiety of a messenger who cannot compel belief. Having removed the responsibility for the outcome, the Book replaces it with a defined responsibility for conduct. The next verses state exactly where the limits of the believer's obligation lie.

The Book keeps a copy of the same appointment in its account of the Hour, where the Prophet is told to say that knowledge of the time belongs to his Lord alone and that it will take people by surprise (7:187). The two statements belong to one doctrine: what the audience was demanding to see was already scheduled, and the One who scheduled it had described the effect of its arrival as a surprise rather than as an announcement. The verse therefore leaves the makkans with certainty about the fact and no information about the date.
verses.68:
> And when you come across those who ridicule Our revelations, do not sit with them unless they engage in a different topic. Should Satan make you forget, then once you remember, do not ˹continue to˺ sit with the wrongdoing people

**An Instruction About Where a Person Sits**

The verse gives a rule about physical presence, which is the kind of instruction the Book issues when a principle needs a form a community can actually follow. The command is not to argue with the mockers, not to retaliate against them, and not to leave the city on their account. It is to get up and go if the mockery continues, and the Book treats that act of withdrawal as the answer.

The rule is stated in the second person singular, and its addressee is the Prophet, but the sūrah of the Women makes the same statement to the whole community in the same words, saying that when they hear God's revelations being denied or ridiculed they should not sit in that company unless the conversation changes, or else they will be like those who mock (4:140). The two verses together give the instruction a general application without removing it from the particular scene that produced it.

**The Reason for the Rule**

The reason given in the sūrah of the Women is that sitting with the mockers makes the listener like them, and that reasoning explains the shape of the rule in this verse. Presence at a gathering is a form of participation in it, and the Book does not treat a person's silence as neutrality when the revelation of God is being treated as a joke.

That principle is worth stating in full because it is the hinge of the passage. The Book is not asking the believers to avoid people who disagree with them, since the same Book tells the Prophet to argue gracefully with the People of the Book (29:46), and it tells him that the message has been sent as a mercy to all people. What is forbidden is attendance at an assembly whose purpose is to degrade the revelation.

**The Exception and What It Reveals**

The command allows for the conversation to change: unless they engage in a different topic. That exception shows the point of the rule is not social separation. If the same people begin talking about ordinary matters, the believer may stay, which means the objection is to the activity and not to the persons.

That distinction has consequences for the way the community was to live in a city full of people who did not accept the message. The believers were to trade, marry, and negotiate with the same Makkans who contested the Prophet, and the Book's rule only removes them from the one setting where the revelation is turned into entertainment. The verse draws a line around an activity, and the line leaves everything else intact.

**"Should Satan Make You Forget"**

The verse then allows for the failure to observe the rule. If forgetfulness happens and the believer later remembers, he is told that the obligation returns immediately: do not continue to sit with the wrongdoing people. The mention of Satan as the cause of the lapse is the Book's way of naming the ordinary source of distraction without turning the lapse into a mortal fault.

The Book uses the same device in the story of Moses and his companion, who explains that only Satan made him forget the fish (18:63). The pattern is consistent: the Book acknowledges that human beings lose track of their obligations, and its remedy for the everyday kind of failure is to resume the duty as soon as it comes back to mind, without treating the interim as a catastrophe.

**Where the Believers Were Not to Sit**

The phrase about the wrongdoing people at the end of the verse connects the instruction to the sūrah's larger argument. The sūrah has described the wrongdoers across the previous sixty verses: those who turn others away from the message (6:26), who deny the signs (6:49), who respond to God's rescue by associating partners with Him (6:64), and who were warned about the punishments that could reach them from above, from below, and through their own divisions (6:65).

The command to leave that gathering is therefore a command to leave the company of a group the Book has just finished describing, and the leaving has a doctrinal weight. The person who walks away from the mockery is performing the same refusal the Prophet was told to make when he was instructed to declare his rejection of the gods of his people (6:56).

**What the Instruction Protects**

The rule protects two things, and the second is easily missed. It protects the revelation from being treated as material for idle entertainment, which is the concern the verse states directly. It also protects the person who stays, since the Book's reasoning in the parallel passage is that the listener becomes like the mockers, and the Book knows how quickly a person's sense of the sacred can be eroded by watching other people treat it lightly.

The next verse addresses a question the rule raises, which is what responsibility the believers carry for the mockers themselves. The answer given there releases them from liability while leaving the duty of advice in place, and the two verses together form the Book's complete instruction about this particular social situation.

**What Kind of Discussion the Verse Is About**

Commentators drew a line between the discussion that this verse forbids and the deliberation that the Book encourages. The Arabic verb used for the mockers' activity describes argument that is disparaging and disrespectful rather than inquiry, and al-Rāzī rejected the reading that would ban religious discussion in general, since the Book elsewhere commands people to reflect and to reason about the signs. The distinction is between a conversation that treats the revelation as a target and one that treats it as a question.

The Book's own usage supports that reading. The believers are described among the successful as those who avoid idle talk (23:3), and the sūrah of the Cattle states that God has made enemies for every prophet from among the devilish humans and jinn, whispering elegant words of deception, and then tells the Prophet to leave them and their deceit (6:112). What is being excluded is a specific kind of speech, not the exchange of views.
verses.69:
> Those mindful ˹of Allah˺ will not be accountable for those ˹who ridicule it˺ whatsoever—their duty is to advise, so perhaps the ridiculers will abstain

**A Question the Previous Verse Raises**

Having been told to leave the company of the mockers, a believer might reasonably ask what he owed them afterward. The verse answers that the mindful are not accountable for the mockers in any respect, and the answer is paired with a duty that remains: to advise them. The sentence separates two things that people tend to confuse, which are responsibility for another person's conduct and responsibility for what one says to him.

That separation is stated as a general principle elsewhere in the Book, where it says that no soul burdened with sin will carry the burden of another (6:164), and where the sūrah of the Troops says that the messenger is not a keeper over the people. The verse in front of us applies the principle to the specific case of a man who has walked out of a gathering and may be worrying about what becomes of the people he left behind.

**The Word Translated as Mindful**

The sentence is addressed to those who guard themselves against wrongdoing, and the description serves as a qualification rather than as a formality. The people who receive the exemption are the ones already ordering their lives around God's commands, including the command they have just obeyed by leaving. The verse is not addressed to someone looking for permission to sit comfortably beside those who mock the revelation.

That is how the Book uses the description of mindfulness in other passages, where it is joined to a specific act of obedience or restraint. The effect here is that the exemption from liability comes with the duty of advice attached to it, which means the person who qualifies has already taken on a task.

**What the Duty of Advice Includes**

The word for advising describes a reminder delivered with the aim of correcting conduct, and it does not require a sermon. The Book uses the same idea when it tells the Prophet that his only duty is to remind (88:21), and when it describes the believers as those who call others to good and forbid what is wrong. The duty in this verse is narrower than a general obligation to reform the society; it concerns the mockers the believer has just left.

The Book's model of this advice is visible in the story of Noah, the most mocked of the messengers, who kept warning his people and calling them to their Lord for centuries while they laughed at him. The Book does not present that persistence as a failure, and it does not describe the mockers as beyond the reach of the invitation. The purpose clause attached to this verse carries the same expectation in a single word.

**"So Perhaps They Will Abstain"**

The clause states the aim of the advice rather than a guaranteed result. What the Book hopes for is that the ridicule may cease, and the hope is stated in the form used throughout the Book for outcomes that depend on human choice. The Book's use of this construction keeps the free will of the audience intact, since a certainty would leave no room for the decision the warning is meant to produce.

The clause also explains why advice is worth giving to people who are mocking. The person mocking the revelation may stop, and the Book's approach to the hardened is to keep the possibility open, which is why it tells the Prophet to bear with the mockers and answer them with peace (43:89). The stance the Book recommends is neither contempt nor cooperation but a persistent reminder delivered without hostility.

**The Two Verses Together**

Read as a pair, the last two verses give the community a complete rule for living beside a majority that ridiculed its scripture. They are told where not to sit, how to behave if they forget, and whom they are not answerable for. They are told to keep advising, and they are told that the outcome of the advice is not their possession.

That arrangement is characteristic of the Book's method in the Makkan sūrahs, where the believers are a minority with no power to enforce anything. The instructions they receive are about conduct, speech, and distance, rather than about authority, and the Book's confidence in the message is not built on the expectation of social success.

**What the Passage Establishes About the Community's Boundaries**

The passage also quietly establishes a boundary that later jurisprudence would elaborate. The community is defined by its adherence to the revelation rather than by its kinship, its city, or its class, and the people who mock what it holds sacred are described by their activity rather than by their tribe. The rule about leaving a gathering is the earliest form of a principle that appears in the sūrah of the Women as a general law.
