The next verse turns from the conduct of the believers toward the people the passage has been describing, and it gives the Prophet a further instruction about how to deal with them. The Book is still speaking to him about the same group, and the instruction that follows defines the limits of what a believer may do for them and what no one will be able to do for them at all.

**The Duty Stated Elsewhere in the Book**

The Book describes the messenger's obligation in the same terms in several places, and each statement narrows the task to the delivery of the message. The Prophet is told that if people turn away after the invitation, his only duty is to deliver (3:20); he is told that whether he sees the punishment or dies before it, his duty is to deliver and the judgment is God's (13:40); and the sūrah of the Spider states that the messenger's only obligation is clear delivery (29:18). The sūrah of the Women puts the same thought in the form of a promise, saying that whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God, and that whoever turns away has not been placed in the Prophet's keeping (4:80).

Read with the verse in front of us, those statements explain why the believers' duty toward the mockers is limited to advice. The task of the messenger and of the community that carries his message is to make the truth clear, and the Book repeats the boundary so often because the temptation to go beyond it is permanent.
verses.70:
> And leave those who take this faith ˹of Islam˺ as mere play and amusement and are deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life. Yet remind them by this ˹Quran˺, so no one should be ruined for their misdeeds. They will have no protector or intercessor other than Allah. Even if they were to offer every ˹possible˺ ransom, none will be accepted from them. Those are the ones who will be ruined for their misdeeds. They will have a boiling drink and painful punishment for their disbelief

**The Command to Leave and the Command to Remind**

The verse begins by telling the Prophet to leave a group and ends by telling him to remind them, and the combination states the Book's position on people who treat religion as entertainment. They are to be left alone with their chosen course, and they are not to be abandoned without a warning. The two commands are not in tension; the leaving is a refusal to argue further, and the reminder is the last form of care that remains.

The Book uses this combination elsewhere. The sūrah of the Cave tells the Prophet to say that the message is the truth from his Lord and that whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve (18:29), and the sūrah of the Troops ends a similar discussion by describing the messenger as a warner who is not a keeper. The Book's mode with the heedless is to state the fact clearly and then to let them face it.

**"Play and Amusement" as a Description of Conduct**

The phrase describes people whose relation to the message is that of an audience watching a performance. The Book uses the same language to describe the worldly life itself, saying that it is no more than play, amusement, luxury, mutual boasting, and competition in wealth and children (57:20), and it says that those who took the faith as amusement and play and were deluded by the life of this world will be told on the day of judgment that they are ignored just as they ignored the meeting of that day (7:51).

The two images belong together. A person who treats the revelation as entertainment has already accepted the priority the Book assigns to the worldly life, and the Book's description of that life as play is not contempt for the world but a statement about its duration. The same pair appears in the sūrah of the Kneeling, where people are told that they made a mockery of God's revelations and were deluded by the worldly life (45:35).

**"Deluded by Their Worldly Life"**

The word translated as deluded describes a person who is deceived by something that presents a good appearance, and the Book uses it for the deception worked by the present life and by Satan. The delusion in this verse is not a mistake about facts but a wrong estimate of value, in which the affluence of a man's surroundings is taken as evidence about his standing.

The sūrah has been dismantling that estimate since the passage about the poor believers. The Book told the Prophet not to dismiss the humble worshippers whose devotion the notables regarded as an embarrassment (6:52), and it said that the differences between people are a test by which God distinguishes the grateful (6:53). The people in this verse are the ones who failed that test, and their amusement is the form the failure took.

**The Reason for the Reminder**

So no one should be ruined for their misdeeds: the verse gives the motive for the warning, and the motive is a refusal to accept destruction. The Book states that God does not desire injustice for His servants, and it describes the sending of messengers as an act of mercy precisely because a people who were never warned would have had an argument on the day of judgment.

The reminder is therefore not a formality that precedes the sentence. It is the last stage of the invitation, and the Book's language about it is urgent: the same sūrah that declares the wrongdoers will be seized at the height of their confidence also records the sorrow of the Prophet over people who would not listen (6:33). The command in this verse shows the direction of the Book's own preference.

**No Protector, No Intercessor, No Ransom**

The verse then describes what the reminder is meant to prevent. They will have no protector or intercessor other than Allah, which is the same statement the sūrah made in connection with the warning given to those who fear the gathering (6:51), and even if they offered every possible ransom it would not be accepted. The Book repeats that image where it says that a disbeliever possessing everything in the world twice over could not ransom himself from the punishment of the day of judgment (5:36), and where it describes the wrongdoers offering what they have in the world in exchange for escape (39:47).

The sūrah of the Cow states the same three denials in a single verse about the day when no soul will help another and no intercession will be accepted and no ransom taken (2:48). The Makkans' religious system rested on the assumption that their patrons and their gods would negotiate on their behalf, and the Book closes that door in every sūrah where it describes the reckoning.

**The Drink and the Punishment**

The verse ends with a description of the outcome: they are ruined for their misdeeds, and they have a boiling drink and a painful punishment for their disbelief. The sūrah of the Cave mentions the same boiling liquid in its account of what those who take their faith lightly will be given when they cry for relief (18:29), and the Book refers to it in several descriptions of the Fire.

The final clause attaches the punishment to disbelief rather than to the mocked scripture, which is consistent with the sūrah's treatment of denial as an activity with consequences. The passage ends here, and the sūrah turns next to a series of arguments about God's exclusive right to worship, moving from the description of the heedless to the case against the gods they invoked.
verses.71:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Should we invoke, other than Allah, those ˹idols˺ which cannot benefit or harm us, and turn back to disbelief after Allah has guided us? ˹If we do so, we will be˺ like those disoriented by devils in the wilderness, while their companions call them to guidance, ˹saying˺, ‘Come to us!’ Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah’s guidance is the ˹only˺ true guidance. And we are commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds

**A Question Put in the First Person**

The sūrah has been answering the Makkans for seventy verses, and here the Prophet is told to put the argument in his own mouth as a question. Should we invoke, apart from God, something that can neither benefit nor harm us? The construction makes the proposal state itself, since the moment the objects of worship are described in those two words, the absurdity is on the surface and no further argument is needed.

The Book uses the same description repeatedly where it deals with the idols. The sūrah of the Table states that those whom the pagans worship besides God can neither harm nor benefit anyone (5:76); the sūrah of Yūnus describes people who worship beings of that kind and call them their intercessors with God (10:18); the sūrah of the Bee asks whether anyone would take besides God lords who cannot even benefit or protect themselves (13:16); and the sūrah of the Prophets records Abraham putting the same question to his people (21:66). The description is not a debating point invented for this verse but the Book's settled account of what an idol is.

**Turning Back on the Heels**

The second clause of the question is about the cost of the choice: should we turn back to disbelief after God has guided us? The Book states the danger of that reversal in the strongest terms, saying that whoever among the believers renounces his faith and dies a disbeliever has rendered his deeds void in this life and the next (2:217), and telling the community that if they yield to the disbelievers they will be dragged back to disbelief and become losers (3:149).

The imagery is of a traveller who has been put on a road and then walks back down it, and the sūrah will use the same figure of speech for a person who returns to his old ignorance. The question in this verse is therefore not only about what the idols can do. It is about what the believer would lose by going back, and the answer is stated in terms of a guidance he had already received.

**The Man in the Wilderness**

The verse then supplies a simile: like one bewildered, seduced by satans on the earth, though he has companions who call him to guidance, saying, Come to us! The picture is of a man who has lost his way in open country, is being pulled in the wrong direction by whispering companions, and is being called back by others. The Book's word for the seducers is plural and general, and the commentators noted that it can cover both the human and the unseen agents who do Satan's work, since the Book speaks elsewhere of devilish humans and jinn who whisper to one another with elegant words of deception (6:112).

The image earns its place because it captures the specific form of the danger. The man is not being argued out of his faith by better evidence; he is being drawn away, step by step, in a place where he has no landmarks. That is the situation the sūrah has described throughout its account of the Makkan response, in which the argument was settled and the dispute continued anyway.

**The Companions Who Call Him Back**

The detail about the companions is the mercy in the image. The man is not alone, and the people calling him are calling him to guidance rather than to their own advantage. Commentators read the companions as sincere and rightly guided people who try to bring him back, and some connected the verse with reports about the son of Abū Bakr, who was being lured toward idolatry while his father called him to the faith he had left.

A minority of commentators understood the callers to be inviting the man to a guidance that was itself false, since the Book elsewhere uses the word for the calling of those who have strayed. The reading is worth noting because it shows how carefully the commentators attended to the pronouns, but the more natural sense fits the verse's argument: the man has people who want his good, and he is still walking away.

**Allah's Guidance Is the Only Guidance**

The Prophet's answer to the imaginary proposal is short: Allah's guidance is the only true guidance. The statement appears in the same wording in the sūrah of the Cow, where the Prophet is told to say it after being pressed to follow the faith of the People of the Book (2:120), and in the sūrah of the Family of Imran, where the same claim is made against a claim of exclusive ownership of guidance (3:73). The sūrah of Fāṭir puts the same idea in a form that leaves no doubt: what God opens of mercy cannot be withheld, and what He withholds cannot be released (35:2).

The exclusivity is the point of the whole passage. Guidance in the Book is not one beneficial practice among several that might be compared on their merits; it is a specific instruction from the One who made the world, and the alternatives are not paths to the same destination. The commentators read the sentence as a claim that there is no guidance outside God's, and that everything else which calls itself a road leads elsewhere.

**Submission to the Lord of All Worlds**

The verse closes with the alternative to the proposal: we are commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds. The Book places the same declaration on the lips of the Prophet in the sūrah of Ghāfir, where he announces that he has been forbidden to worship what the people worship besides God, since clear proofs have come to him, and that he has been commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds (40:66). The two verses are almost parallel in structure and content, which shows that this sūrah's closing declarations belong to a fixed pattern in the Book.

Submission, in the Book's vocabulary, is the act that answers the whole argument of the sūrah. The Makkans had been invited to acknowledge a maker, a provider, a rescuer, a judge, and a recorder of deeds, and the response the Book asks for is the one that accepts all of those claims at once. What the Prophet is told to announce in this verse is not a philosophical position but an allegiance.
verses.72:
> establish prayer, and be mindful of Him. To Him you will all be gathered together

**The Sentence That Completes the Verse Before It**

This line finishes the declaration begun in the previous verse, and the connection is grammatical as well as thematic: the sentence started there does not end until here. That is why the passage has to be read as a unit. The Prophet announces submission to the Lord of all worlds, and then states what the submission consists of: the prayer and mindfulness of God, and the gathering that awaits everyone at the end.

The practice named first is the prayer, which the Book presents as the standing obligation of every community that received a messenger. The sūrah of Ibrāhīm records Abraham asking his Lord to make him and his descendants people who maintain the prayer, and the Book's descriptions of the righteous regularly include the establishing of it. The order in this verse places the ritual act before the interior state, which is the Book's ordinary way of describing religious life: the visible practice carries the inward one with it.

**Why Prayer Comes First**

The Book treats the prayer as the marker of a community's identity and the ordinary channel of its connection with God. The sūrah of Ṭā-Hā gives the command in the first person on God's behalf, telling Moses that He is God and that there is no deity but Him, and then instructing him to worship and to establish the prayer for the remembrance of his Lord (20:14). The sūrah of the Spider states that the prayer restrains people from indecency and wrongdoing (29:45), and the sūrah of the Cow tells the believers to seek help through patience and prayer (2:45).

Those verses show what the prayer was understood to do. It is not presented as an obligation discharged for God's benefit, since the Book states that God has no need of any of His creatures. It is presented as a discipline that builds the person who performs it, which is why the sūrah of the Spider attaches moral effects to it and why this verse attaches it to submission.

**Mindfulness as the Ground of Conduct**

The second item is to be mindful of Him, and the Book's word for mindfulness is one of its central concepts. It describes a person who orders his conduct around the awareness that God is present, sees what he does, and will hold him to account. The sūrah of the Cow opens by describing the Book as guidance for those who are mindful (2:2), and the Book commands mindfulness repeatedly in connection with specific acts rather than as a general sentiment.

Al-Rāzī arranged the three items of this passage into a scheme that shows how the Book's religion fits together: submission is the best of the acts of the heart, prayer is the best of the acts of the limbs, and mindfulness is the best of the acts of restraint, since it is the quality that keeps a person from what he should avoid. The arrangement is a commentator's, but it captures the verse's balance. The passage has given the audience an allegiance, a practice, and a disposition.

**The Gathering at the End**

The sentence closes with the statement that it is unto Him that you shall be gathered, which returns to the theme the sūrah has been developing since its account of the keys of the unseen. The Book states the gathering in dozens of places, and the sūrah has already described the return of every soul to its true Master (6:62). Here the statement comes at the end of a declaration of worship, which gives it a different weight: the person who prays and lives mindfully is not performing an isolated act but travelling toward an assembly.

That is why the Book joins the command to worship with the announcement of the gathering so consistently, and why the sūrah of the Cave reports the same linkage in the words of the Prophet's declaration. The end of the journey is a fact about the future that shapes the present, and the verse states it in the same breath as the obligations that fill the present.

**The Turn the Passage Makes**

Read together, the two verses mark a turn in the sūrah. The long argument with the Makkans about idols, signs, punishment, and mockery ends with the Prophet stating what he has been commanded to do, and the statement is a declaration of commitment rather than a rebuttal. The Book uses that movement repeatedly: after a section of contention comes a statement of the worship that distinguishes the community.

The next verse continues the declaration by describing the God to whom this worship is directed, and the description is drawn from the creation itself. The heavens and the earth, the command that brings things into being, the sovereignty that belongs to God on the day the trumpet sounds, and the knowledge that covers the unseen and the seen: those are the terms in which the sūrah now describes the One the Prophet has been commanded to serve.

**The Book's Instructions About the Prayer and Mindfulness**

The Book repeats the two obligations of this verse in forms that show what it expected of the community. The believers are told to observe the prayers, especially the middle prayer, and to stand in true devotion to God (2:238); they are described among the successful as those who humble themselves in their prayer (23:2); and they are commanded to be mindful of God in the way He deserves and not to die except in a state of submission to Him (3:102). The sūrah of the Mutual Disillusion adds the concession that the obligation is measured to a person's capacity, telling the believers to be mindful of God to the best of their ability (64:16).

Those verses place the passage in the middle of the Book's practical teaching rather than at its edge. What the Prophet declares about himself in this verse is the same programme the Book lays on the community, stated in the first person before it is imposed on anyone else.
verses.73:
> He is the One Who created the heavens and the earth in truth. On the Day ˹of Judgment˺ He will say, ‘Be!’ And there will be! His command is truth. All authority is His ˹alone˺ on the Day the Trumpet will be blown. He is the Knower of all—seen or unseen. And He is the All-Wise, All-Aware.”

**Creation in Truth Rather Than in Play**

The verse opens by describing God as the One who created the heavens and the earth in truth, and the phrase answers a question the Makkans had never posed but which the sūrah has been building toward. The Book states that the creation was not made as play, and it repeats the point in several places: the sūrah of the Prophets asks whether God took the heavens and the earth and everything in them as a pastime, and it answers that He did not; the sūrah of Ṣād denies that the creation of the heavens and the earth was in vain; and the sūrah of the Family of Imran describes the people of understanding as those who reflect on the creation and conclude that it was not made without purpose (3:191; 21:16; 38:27).

The same claim appears in the sūrah of the Smoke, where God states that He did not create the heavens and the earth and what lies between them as play (44:38). Put beside the sūrah's account of the idols, which can neither benefit nor harm their worshippers, the statement makes a comparison the audience could not miss. The created order has a purpose, and the gods of Makkah had none.

**The Command That Brings Things Into Being**

The verse then names the mechanism of creation: on the day He says, Be! and it is. The Book uses this formula repeatedly for the divine command, and it attaches it to the original creation of the heavens and the earth (2:117), to the conception of Jesus (3:47), to the creation of Adam (3:59), and to resurrection (36:82; 40:68). The phrase's function is to deny any gap between God's intention and its execution.

The commentators drew a theological conclusion from the wording, since if everything was created by God's word then the word itself must precede creation and cannot be a created thing. The discussion belongs to the long debate among Muslim theologians over whether God's speech is created or uncreated, and this verse was cited in it by those who held the second position. What the verse settles for a reader is simpler than the controversy: the world owes its existence to a command, and the One who gave the command remains its owner.

**Sovereignty on the Day the Trumpet Sounds**

All authority is His alone on the day the trumpet will be blown. The Book mentions the trumpet in many places as the herald of the resurrection, and it describes the sequence: the trumpet is blown and everything in the heavens and the earth falls dead, then it is blown again and they rise up looking on (39:68). The sūrah of Ṭā-Hā states that on that day God will gather the wicked, blue-faced from horror (20:102); the sūrah of Yā-Sīn describes people rushing from their graves to their Lord (36:51); and the sūrah of the Troops gives the same scene in the same terms as this verse.

Some commentators read the word for trumpet as forms, giving the sense that sovereignty belongs to God on the day when forms are given their spirit, but the majority reading is the trumpet that announces the end. Either way the conclusion is the same, and it is the conclusion this verse draws: the authority that the Makkans distributed among their gods will be concentrated on that day in a single hand, and the Book states that the question will be asked aloud: who does all authority belong to this day? The answer it supplies is: to Allah, the One, the Supreme (40:16).

**The Knowledge That Covers Both Sides of Reality**

The verse closes by naming God as the Knower of all, seen or unseen, and the pairing appears across the Book as a summary of His knowledge. The sūrah of the Thunder calls Him the Knower of the seen and the unseen, the All-Great, the Most Exalted (13:9); the sūrah of the Prostration gives the name at the head of a passage about His mercy (32:6); the sūrah of the Troops places it in a prayer for judgment (39:46); and the sūrah of the Gathering and the sūrah of Mutual Disillusion repeat the same pair (59:22; 64:18).

The pairing matters here because the sūrah has spent a long passage on things that human beings cannot see. The keys of the unseen belong to God (6:59), the leaf and the grain are recorded (6:59), the soul is taken at night (6:60), and the record is kept by angels (6:61). The verse now states the principle that covers all of those cases: nothing is outside the knowledge of the One who is described in the same sentence as the maker and the sovereign.

**The Closing Word of the Declaration**

The verse ends with two names, the All-Wise and the All-Aware, which are the same two names that the sūrah used near its beginning when it described God as reigning supreme over His creation (6:18). The repetition closes a ring in the sūrah's structure: the argument that began with the wise and aware Creator ends with the wise and aware Sovereign.

That structure is worth noticing because it explains the placement of the Abraham narrative that follows. Having stated the case in terms of creation, command, sovereignty, and knowledge, the sūrah turns to the man whom the Book presents as the model of a person who reasoned his way from the created order to its maker. Abraham's argument with his people is the human counterpart of everything the last three verses have stated about God.
verses.74:
> And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said to his father, Ȃzar, “Do you take idols as gods? It is clear to me that you and your people are entirely misguided.”

**The Beginning of a Narrative Section**

After seventy verses of argument, the sūrah turns to a story, and the story is the one the Book treats as the model of the case it has been making. Abraham is introduced in the middle of a declaration about the One God, and what follows is the account of a man who arrived at that declaration through the created world. The sūrah of Maryam calls him a man of truth and a prophet (19:41), and the Book elsewhere credits him with sound judgement given to him early (21:51).

The placement matters. The sūrah has just stated that God created the heavens and the earth in truth, that His command brings things into being, that authority belongs to Him alone, and that His knowledge covers the seen and the unseen (6:73). Abraham's story is the demonstration of what those statements mean for a human being who looks at the world honestly, and the sūrah will end the section by calling his argument the one God gave him against his people (6:83).

**The Address to a Father**

And remember when Abraham said to his father, Āzar. The Book names the father only here, and the commentators spent considerable effort on the name. In the Biblical account Abraham's father is Terah, and some held that Āzar was another name for the same man; others suggested that Āzar was the name of an idol and that Abraham was addressing his father by it as a rebuke; and a third group held that Āzar was an uncle who was called a father in the wider sense in which the Book uses the word for older relatives, citing the verse where Jacob names Ishmael among his fathers though Ishmael was his uncle (2:133).

The discussion behind that third view is worth noting, because some Muslims, particularly among the Shia, held that the father of a prophet could not have been an idolater, and they cited a report in which the Prophet says that God transferred him from pure loins to pure wombs and that he was never touched by the filth of the age of ignorance. The most literal reading of this verse, as al-Rāzī acknowledged, is that Āzar was Abraham's father and that he worshipped idols, and the Book's own account of Abraham's later dissociation from him gives the story its pathos.

**A Question Rather Than a Denunciation**

Do you take idols as gods? The question is the same device the sūrah has used throughout, and it works the same way here: the practice is named in a single clause and the hearer is left to see it. The Book records a harsher version of the same question in the sūrah of the Prophets, where Abraham asks his father and his people what the statues are to which they are so devoted (21:52).

What follows in the verse is not a personal insult. Abraham states that he sees his father and his people in clear error, and the sentence is about the error rather than about the man. The Book's prophets address their closest relatives in this way because the message begins at home, and the command given to the Prophet in the sūrah of the Poets to warn his nearest kin has a precedent in the first of the prophets to argue with his own household.

**The Tension Between Kinship and Conviction**

The verse introduces a theme that returns at several points in the Abraham story and that the community reading the sūrah would have felt immediately. The Book elsewhere praises those who honour their parents and forbids the believer to obey them if they press him toward idolatry, while requiring that he keep their company courteously in this world (31:14–15). Abraham's case shows how far the requirement of courtesy could be stretched and where it ended.

The Book records the end of that story in the sūrah of Repentance, where it says that Abraham's prayer for his father's forgiveness was only in fulfilment of a promise he had made, and that when it became clear to him that his father was an enemy of God he broke ties with him, while noting that Abraham was tender-hearted and forbearing (9:114). The Book's sympathy for the difficulty of that decision is visible in the wording, and the sūrah of Maryam preserves the words Abraham used when he left: peace be upon you, I will pray to my Lord for your forgiveness (19:47).

The same sūrah records how he spoke to the man. He called him dear father and asked him why he worshipped what could neither hear nor see nor benefit him at all (19:42); he told him that he had received knowledge his father had not received, and asked him to follow so that he could guide him to a straight path (19:43); he warned him against worshipping Satan, who is ever rebellious against the Most Compassionate (19:44); and he said that he feared his father would be touched by a punishment and become a companion of Satan in the Fire (19:45). Every sentence is an address of respect, and every sentence states the danger without softening it.

**What the Verse Assumes About the Audience**

The Makkans were the descendants of Abraham and knew it. The Book had already told them that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian but a man of pure faith, a Muslim, and not one of those who associate partners with God (3:67), and it uses his story here because the claim of descent gave the argument its edge. The ancestor whose name they invoked had begun his mission by rejecting idols of the same kind.

That is the force of the opening of this section. The sūrah is not introducing a distant figure from a foreign tradition; it is introducing the man the audience claimed as their founder, at the moment when he turned his face away from the objects their own city was built around. The verses that follow describe what he saw and what he argued, and the account is presented as the argument God gave him.
verses.75:
> We also showed Abraham the wonders of the heavens and the earth, so he would be sure in faith

**The Showing Attributed to God**

The verse states that God showed Abraham the wonders of the heavens and the earth, and the attribution is the point of the sentence. The case for the oneness of God can be made from observation, and the sūrah has been making it that way, but this verse says that Abraham's insight was given rather than merely achieved. The Book's invitation to reflect on the created order is addressed to everyone, and it states that signs are of no benefit to people who refuse to believe (10:101), so the difference between Abraham and his people was not access to the world but the use made of it.

The Book places the same kind of statement at the end of the sūrah of Fussilat, where God says that He will show people His signs in the universe and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that the message is the truth (41:53). The sūrah of the Scatterers states the same in two verses that begin with the signs on the earth for those with sure faith and end with the signs within the readers themselves (51:20–21). What Abraham received in this verse is what the Book offers to every reader of it.

**What the Wonders Were**

Commentators differed on what exactly Abraham was shown. One reading takes the phrase at face value: the wonders of the heavens and the earth are the phenomena everyone can see, the sun, the moon, the stars, the turning of the day and night, and the ordering of the world. On that reading the verse describes Abraham applying his reason to what was in front of him, and the Book credits the sound judgement he had been given early for that use of it (21:51).

The other reading, which appears in most of the commentaries, takes the showing to be an unveiling in which the heavens were opened so that Abraham saw their levels up to the Throne and the earth was laid bare so that he saw its depths. Al-Rāzī held that the manifestation of God's power in natural phenomena is always objectively available but is veiled from most people by error and by preoccupation with worldly affairs, and that Abraham received it with the inner eye of his understanding.

**The Sufi Reading of the Sequence**

The Sufi commentators read the star, the moon, and the sun of the following verses as stages in the growth of spiritual knowledge, and their interpretation of this verse sets the context for it. Al-Qushayrī took the star to represent the intellect that first witnesses the truth through demonstration, the moon to represent knowledge that grows clearer through reflection, and the sun to represent the light of direct knowledge of God. Abraham's movement from one to the next was, on this reading, the progress of a seeker who discovers the limits of each station and is led beyond it.

That reading has the merit of explaining the pattern of the narrative that follows, in which each celestial body is abandoned at the moment of its setting. The Book records the conclusion Abraham drew on each occasion, and the Sufi interpretation treats each setting as the collapse of a partial understanding rather than as an ordinary astronomical event.

**Certainty as the Purpose**

The verse gives the purpose of the showing: so that Abraham would be sure in faith. The Book's word for that certainty describes knowledge that has passed beyond doubt, and it is used for the assurance the believers seek about the meeting with their Lord and about the reality of the accounting. The same word appears in the sūrah of the Cow, where Abraham asks to be shown how God gives life to the dead and explains that he already believes but wants his heart to be reassured (2:260).

The comparison between the two passages is instructive. Abraham asked for the reassurance, and in this verse the showing is given without a request. The Book presents certainty as a state that can be sought, asked for, and granted, and it presents the created world as the material through which it is reached.

**The Argument and the Certainty**

The sūrah closes the Abraham section by naming the discourse with his people as the argument God gave him against them, and by stating that God elevates in rank whoever He pleases (6:83). Read with this verse, the two statements describe the same gift from two angles. The certainty given to Abraham in this verse is what produced the argument in the following verses, and the argument is credited to God rather than to Abraham's ingenuity.

That arrangement is the sūrah's answer to a question the reader may not have asked but which the commentators raised: if Abraham reasoned his way to the truth, where does revelation fit? The sūrah's answer is that the showing preceded the reasoning and the argument was supplied. The Book does not treat natural reflection and divine guidance as competing explanations; it treats the first as the field in which the second operates.

**What the Verse Teaches the Audience**

For the Makkan audience, the verse offered Abraham as the man their own tradition claimed, whose reasoning had led him out of the very practices they were defending. For a reader in general, it offers a description of how conviction is formed: an honest look at the world, a refusal to treat the familiar as exempt from examination, and the understanding that the ability to see clearly is itself a gift.

The sūrah now moves into the account of that reasoning, and it records Abraham's words as he watched the objects the audience revered appear and disappear across the sky. The demonstration in the next verses is built entirely from things the Makkans themselves could observe, and its conclusion is the declaration that Abraham made when the last of them set.
verses.76:
> When the night grew dark upon him, he saw a star and said, “This is my Lord!” But when it set, he said, “I do not love things that set.”

**The Setting of the Sky**

The verse opens with the night darkening over Abraham, and the scene is the one his people knew best. The Makkans travelled by the stars, divided their calendar by the moon, and associated the heavenly bodies with the deities they served, and the region's older religions had made the sun, the moon, and the stars objects of worship. The sūrah's audience would have recognised the setting immediately, and the argument that follows is built from the objects they considered sacred.

The Book elsewhere denies the heavenly bodies any share in divinity while maintaining their place in the created order. The sūrah of Fussilat says that among God's signs are the day, the night, the sun, and the moon, and commands the reader not to prostrate to the sun or the moon but to prostrate to God who created them (41:37). The sūrahs of the Bee, the Prophets, and Ibrāhīm all describe the sun, the moon, and the stars as subjected by God's command (7:54; 14:33; 16:12; 21:33), which is the position Abraham states in the verses that follow.

**"This Is My Lord" and the Difficulty It Raises**

When Abraham saw the star he said, This is my Lord, and the sentence raised a question for the commentators that they answered in more than one way. Some held that Abraham did not mean it sincerely but said it to draw his people into the argument, since the Book's purpose in the passage is to show how the argument against the heavenly bodies can be made using the heavenly bodies themselves. Others held that the words record a genuine process of reasoning in which Abraham tested each candidate and rejected it, and they placed that reasoning early in his life, before his prophethood and before he was accountable.

The sūrah itself resolves the question at the end of the section when it calls Abraham's discourse the argument God gave him against his people (6:83). Whichever reading of the individual sentences is adopted, the Book presents the sequence as a demonstration that belongs to Abraham's mission rather than as a record of a mistake he made and corrected.

**The Argument From Setting**

But when it set, he said, I do not love things that set. The argument is compressed into that phrase, and it takes the form of a test that anyone can apply: a god should not be subject to disappearance, change, or decay. The Book states the same principle about the created order when it describes the sun as travelling for its fixed term and the moon as passing through phases until it looks like an old curved palm stalk, and when it says that the sun cannot catch up with the moon and that the night cannot outrun the day, since each is travelling in an orbit of its own (36:38–40).

The audience's gods shared the defect of the objects they were identified with. Whatever could rise and set, appear and vanish, was a creature running its course, and a creature's course can be interrupted. The verse states the conclusion in the language of affection, which is why the phrase has stayed in the memory of every generation that has read it: what he rejected, he rejected as something he could not love.

**A Concession the Audience Would Have Made**

The Book records that the Makkans themselves admitted who had made the heavenly bodies when they were asked directly. The sūrah of the Spider says that if they were asked who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they would certainly say Allah, and it follows the admission with a question about how they could then be deluded (29:61). The sūrah of Luqmān and the sūrah of the Troops record the same answer to the same question (31:25; 39:38), and the sūrah of the Ornament adds that they would name the Almighty, the All-Knowing as the maker (43:9).

Those admissions are the ground on which Abraham's argument stands in this verse. The audience already accepted that the sun and the moon were creatures under God's command; what they had not done was follow the concession to its conclusion. The verse shows the founder of their tradition doing exactly that.

**The Star Among the Objects of Worship**

The star is the first of the three candidates and the smallest of them, so the argument begins with the least impressive and rises through the sequence toward the sun, which the verse after next calls the greatest. That order shows the method at work: Abraham moves from one object to the next, and at each stage the same defect appears, until the audience has been shown that the greatest of all the visible powers has the same weakness as the smallest.

The Book's account of the sun and moon's subjection gives the same argument a longer form, stating that both were created and commanded and that their regularity is itself a proof of the design they serve rather than of any authority of their own. Against the background of those verses, Abraham's nightly observation is not merely a story about an individual's search. It is the narrative version of the sūrah's claim that the created order points beyond itself.

**What the Verse Establishes Before the Argument Continues**

By the end of this verse the reader has watched Abraham test and reject one candidate, and the pattern is now available to be repeated with the other two. The sūrah has also established the connection between the demonstration and the reader's own situation, since the Makkans watched the same sky and their ancestors had drawn the opposite conclusion from it.

The next verse takes Abraham to the moon, and the language of the search is repeated with a difference: the conclusion this time is not a rejection but a plea for guidance. The sequence is building toward the declaration Abraham makes when he has finished with the greatest of the heavenly bodies, and the sūrah treats that declaration as the destination of his reasoning.
verses.77:
> Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, “This one is my Lord!” But when it disappeared, he said, “If my Lord does not guide me, I will certainly be one of the misguided people.”

**The Second Candidate**

The moon rises next, and the language of the search is repeated: This one is my Lord. The sūrah is building a sequence, and the pattern of the previous verse is preserved: the appearance, the identification, the disappearance, and the rejection. What changes is the scale of the object, since the moon is brighter and more regular than the star, and the audience that venerated it would have considered it the stronger candidate.

The Book repeatedly describes the moon as a creature under command. The sūrah of Yā-Sīn says that God ordained precise phases for it until it ends up like an old curved palm stalk (36:39); the sūrah of the Heights includes the moon among the objects subjected by God's command, together with the sun and the stars (7:54); and the sūrah of Ibrāhīm describes the sun and the moon as constantly orbiting by God's arrangement (14:33). Each description leaves the moon doing what it was told, which is the argument the verse has Abraham making.

**How the Rejection Changes**

When the moon disappeared, Abraham did not only reject it. He said that if his Lord did not guide him, he would certainly be one of the misguided people. The sentence keeps the possibility of error wide open for himself, and it is the reason the verse is important in the sequence: the man who has just dismissed two candidates has no account of his own to offer, and he says so.

That admission is the opposite of the position Abraham's people were in. They had inherited a system and defended it, whereas Abraham had discarded a system and was asking for the guidance that would replace it. The Book records the same posture in the sūrah of the Cattle's later description of him when it says that God showed him the wonders of the heavens and the earth so that he might be among those who possess certainty (6:75), which means the guidance he asked for had already been promised.

**The Moon and Its Place in the Calendar**

The moon had a particular hold on the region's religious practice, since its phases governed the months and the times of pilgrimage and sacrifice. A man who abandoned the moon as a god was therefore not making a small adjustment to the local pantheon; he was cutting off the object most closely bound to the rituals of the community. The sūrah's own audience would have felt the weight of that, and the Book records elsewhere that the new moon is appointed for the timing of pilgrimage and for the reckoning of time (2:189).

The Book states the rule that Abraham was invoking when it says that whoever God guides is truly guided, and that whoever He leaves to stray will find no guardian besides Him (7:178). The sūrah of the Cave repeats the sentence in the middle of its account of the sleepers, and the sūrah of the Night Journey gives it in a longer form that ends with the warning that such people will be dragged before their Lord deaf, dumb, and blind (17:97; 18:17). Abraham's plea is therefore not a formula of humility but an accurate description of where guidance comes from, and the Book states elsewhere that the Prophet himself cannot guide whomever he loves, since it is God who guides whom He wills (28:56).

The contrast the verse draws is between the calendar and its maker. The Book nowhere suggests that timekeeping is a fault; it presents the sun and the moon as marks by which people can count the years and the reckoning. The fault is in the worship, and the verse shows Abraham separating a useful creature from the Creator whom it serves.

**The Declaration That Follows**

The sequence reaches its third and final candidate in the next verse, where the sun appears, receives the strongest identification of the three, and sets like the others. Abraham's final statement is not a rejection but a declaration of disownment: he turns his face toward the One who originated the heavens and the earth, upright, and declares that he is not among those who associate partners with God (6:78–79).

Read with this verse, the progression is exact. The star produces a rejection, the moon produces a rejection and a plea for guidance, and the sun produces the abandonment of the whole category. The sūrah is not merely recording a man's reasoning; it is showing the stages by which an honest observer leaves the visible world behind as a candidate for divinity.

**The Sufi Reading of the Stations**

The commentators with a mystical orientation read the three objects as stages of knowledge, and their reading of this verse holds that the moon represents the understanding that comes with growing clarity and reflection. The disappearance of the moon is then not an astronomical event but the collapse of a station that a seeker must pass beyond, and the plea for guidance is the voice of a person who has learned the limits of what he has reached so far.

Al-Qushayrī described the progression in terms of seeing things through God, then for God, and finally losing everything in God, and he took Abraham's successive statements as the verbal record of that ascent. The reading is a commentary rather than a substitute for the plain sense, but it captures something in the sūrah's arrangement: each candidate in the sequence is more impressive than the last, and each one is let go.

**What the Verse Contributes to the Case**

The Makkans' claim to be the heirs of Abraham is the target of the whole section, and this verse is part of the answer. Their ancestor stood under the same sky and used the same words about the moon, and then he left it. The sūrah places the audience in a position where they must either take Abraham as their model or explain why the founder of their tradition was wrong about the objects their tradition revered.

The next verse brings the sequence to its conclusion with the sun, the greatest of the visible powers, and it lets Abraham speak the sentence the audience was refusing to say.
verses.78:
> Then when he saw the sun shining, he said, “This must be my Lord—it is the greatest!” But again when it set, he declared, “O my people! I totally reject whatever you associate ˹with Allah in worship˺

**The Greatest of the Three**

Then when he saw the sun shining, he said, This must be my Lord. The sūrah presents the sun as the strongest candidate in the sequence, and it says so in the text: it is the greatest. The audience venerated the sun as the most powerful visible thing in their world, and the verse allows the claim its full weight before it takes it away.

The description is worth noticing, because the argument in this passage does not proceed by belittling the objects. Abraham calls the moon his Lord and calls the sun the greatest, and each statement raises the candidate as high as the audience would have raised it. What defeats the argument is not a low opinion of the sun but the fact that the sun goes down.

**The Setting That Ends the Case**

But again when it set, he declared his rejection of everything his people associated with God. The sentence moves directly from the observation to the address, and the address is public: O my people! The earlier verses recorded Abraham's words to himself or to his father; this one records him speaking to the community that worshipped the sun, and he says that he is done with the whole set of their deities.

The Book's word for the setting describes disappearance or decline, and its use here clinches the argument the previous verses were making. Whatever is subject to the horizon cannot be the One who placed it there, and the Book states the same principle in its own voice when it commands the reader not to prostrate to the sun or the moon but to the God who created them both (41:37).

**The Public Break With the Community**

The declaration is not a philosophical conclusion but a social act, and the Book treats it that way. Abraham's announcement put him outside the religion of his city, and the Book later records the consequences: his people argued with him, threatened him, and eventually tried to burn him. The sūrah of the Prophets describes the response of the community when they heard his case and decided to act against him, and the sūrah of the Poets gives the summary of his mission in his own words.

The Makkans hearing this sūrah knew what such a declaration cost. The Prophet had been told in this very sūrah to say that he had been forbidden to worship what they invoked and that he would not follow their desires (6:56), and the passage about Abraham supplies the model of what that refusal looked like when it was made by the founder of their tradition.

**"Whatever You Associate With Allah in Worship"**

The phrase Abraham uses names the practice rather than the deities, and the Book does the same throughout the sūrah. The warning is about association as an activity, and the sūrah has described that activity in several forms: assigning to God partners in worship, invoking created things for benefit and harm, and treating the divine claim as divisible among objects the community had chosen.

The Book makes the same point where it reports the idolaters admitting that their gods were names they and their fathers had invented, with no authority from God (12:40). Abraham's declaration follows from that: what he rejected was not a set of powerful rivals but a set of names attached to creatures. The word he uses in this verse states the category, which is why the sentence applies to every generation that has made the same arrangement.

**The Pattern the Book Repeats**

The Book records this declaration of disownment in other places, and it holds Abraham up as the example of it. The sūrah of the Tested describes Abraham and those with him saying to their people that they dissociate themselves from them and from whatever they worship besides God, and that the enmity between them will last until the people believe in God alone (60:4). The Book also connects Abraham's descendants with the same posture when it tells the Prophet that those who follow him have Abraham as the closest of people to him.

The pattern has a cost that the sūrah does not hide. The Book records that Abraham's people answered him with argument and with force, and it records his patience under both. What the verse establishes is that the separation happened first, in public, and was stated in the plainest terms.

**Sun Worship in the Book's Accounts**

The Book records the worship of the sun as the practice of another ancient people, described in the report of the hoopoe that Solomon received: I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God, with Satan having made their deeds appealing and hindered them from the right way (27:24). The verse treats the practice as a familiar error rather than as an exotic one, and it places the sun where the sūrah has placed it, among the created things that human beings have taken as lords.

The Book also describes the end of the sun's course, since the objects the audience venerated are among the first to be extinguished on the day of judgment. The sūrah of the Resurrection says that the moon will be dimmed and the sun and the moon will be brought together (75:8–9), and the sūrah of the Folding Up opens with the sun being put out and the stars falling (81:1–2). Whatever a community has worshipped from the sky is thus shown in the Book to be waiting for its own end.

**From Observation to Allegiance**

Read as the end of the sequence, the verse shows the transition from a reasoning exercise to a religious position. Abraham began by watching the sky and asking what deserved his worship, and he ends by announcing to his people that he has left their religion. The sūrah treats the two halves as one act, and the next verse states the positive content of what he chose.

The declaration continues into that verse without a break, and the final words of the sentence state the identity Abraham claims for himself before his people. What he has chosen is described in the next line with a word that the Book uses for him more than for any other figure.
verses.79:
> I have turned my face towards the One Who has originated the heavens and the earth—being upright—and I am not one of the polytheists.”

**The Act of Turning**

I have turned my face towards the One Who has originated the heavens and the earth. The sentence is built on the image of a person who changes direction, and the Book uses the same verb for the act of turning to God in repentance and for the turning of a face away from what is false. Abraham's declaration begins with a movement rather than with a proposition, and the movement is the whole of his religious position in a single image.

The word for the One he turns to describes the originator, the one who brings a thing into being for the first time, and the sūrah has used it of God twice already in similar declarations. The Prophet is commanded to say that he will not take any guardian other than God, the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who provides for all and needs no provision (6:14), and the sūrah later uses the same title in the passage about God's having no offspring (6:101). The term anchors Abraham's declaration in the sūrah's account of creation.

**The Meaning of Upright**

The word the translation renders as being upright is the Book's technical term for the faith of Abraham, and the commentators explained it as a person who turns away from every deviation toward the straight path. Its root carries the sense of inclining and of deviation, and the term as the Book uses it describes a person whose whole orientation is set on one point rather than distributed among several.

The Book applies the description to Abraham in a series of passages that read like a refrain. Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he submitted in all uprightness and was not a polytheist (3:67); the believers are told that the faith of Abraham the upright, who was not a polytheist, is the answer to the claims of the People of the Book (2:135); and the Book describes him as a model of excellence, devoted to God, perfectly upright, and not a polytheist (16:120). The recurrence of the same sentence across sūrahs shows how much work the Book assigns to it.

**Affirmation and Denial Together**

And I am not one of the polytheists. The Book never allows the affirmation of God's oneness to stand alone, and Abraham's declaration is the model of that practice: he states what he has turned toward and what he has left behind in the same breath. The denial is not an afterthought, since the audience's error lay precisely in combining the acknowledgment of a creator with the worship of other beings.

That combination is the practice the sūrah has been dismantling all along, and it is the form of religion the Makkans actually held. They admitted that God made the heavens and the earth, and they still directed their devotion to the objects of the shrine. Abraham's sentence is the correction of that arrangement, stated by the man whose descendants they claimed to be.

**The Prophet and the Faith of Abraham**

The Book commands the Prophet to follow the same way, and it does so in the language of this verse. He is told that his Lord has guided him to a straight path, a perfect way, the faith of Abraham, the upright, who was not one of the polytheists (6:161); the Book commands him to follow the Way of Abraham the upright (3:95; 16:123); and it says that God revealed this instruction to him. The sūrah's Abraham section is therefore not only an argument against the Makkans but a statement about the identity of the community being formed.

The connection runs through the House as well. The Book records Abraham raising the foundations of the House with Ishmael and praying that it be accepted (2:127), and it recalls God assigning to him the site of the House with the instruction not to associate anything with God in worship and to purify it for those who circle it and bow and prostrate (22:26). The religion being restored was the one Abraham had practised at the same place, which is why the declaration in this verse matters for the city the sūrah is addressing.

**What the Declaration Cost**

The Book records what Abraham's people did with his religion in the sūrah of the Prophets, where he smashed their idols and left the greatest of them standing so that the people might turn to it for answers (21:58), and where his community concluded that they should burn him to avenge their gods (21:68). The sūrah of the Ranged records the same verdict in the words of the crowd that called for a furnace for him (37:97). The declaration of belief is followed in the Book's narrative by a trial of fire.

That sequence gives the sūrah's audience a frame for the verses they had just heard about the Prophet. He had been told to declare that he did not worship what they invoked (6:56), and the section that follows shows what such a declaration had meant for the man whose tradition they claimed. The Book is not presenting Abraham's story as a distant legend; it is presenting a precedent.

**The Sentence That Ends the Search**

The declaration ends the search that began with the star. Abraham had moved through the visible world and found nothing to rest on, and the verse states what he found instead: the One who originated the heavens and the earth, whom he faces with a settled direction, and whom he refuses to associate with any created thing.

The sūrah's next verses record his people arguing with him, and they record his answer, which is not a defence of himself but a statement of what his Lord has given him. The demonstration concludes with the Book's own verdict: this was the argument given to Abraham against his people (6:83).
verses.80:
> And his people argued with him. He responded, “Are you arguing with me about Allah, while He has guided me? I am not afraid of whatever ˹idols˺ you associate with Him—˹none can harm me,˺ unless my Lord so wills. My Lord encompasses everything in ˹His˺ knowledge. Will you not be mindful

**The Argument His People Made**

And his people argued with him. The sūrah does not record the terms of their argument, and that silence is informative. What the Book preserves instead is Abraham's reply, and the reply shows what the dispute was about: fear. The Makkans of his day were not defending a philosophical position but a relationship they believed they had with powers that could be offended, and Abraham's answer addresses that belief directly.

The Book describes the same style of argument among the polytheists of the Prophet's own time, who said that if God had willed they would never have worshipped anything other than Him, nor forbidden anything without His command (16:35). The sūrah of the Ornament records the same claim in almost the same words, and adds that the speakers have no knowledge in support of it and do nothing but lie (43:20). The dispute with Abraham belongs to that long-running argument about human practice and divine permission.

**"While He Has Guided Me"**

Are you arguing with me about Allah, while He has guided me? The clause places guidance at the centre of the dispute, and it does so before Abraham says anything about the idols. His position rests on something he has received rather than on something he has worked out, and the sūrah has already described that gift in its account of the showing given to him (6:75).

The Book treats guidance as the decisive element in every such dispute, and it states that whoever God guides is truly guided while whoever He leaves to stray will find no guardian besides Him (7:178). The two participants in this argument were therefore not equals exchanging opinions. One had been shown the wonders of the heavens and the earth, and the other had inherited a set of names.

**"I Am Not Afraid of What You Associate With Him"**

The sentence addresses the practical stake of the controversy, and it removes the fear that the community's religion was built on. Abraham's position is that the idols cannot harm him, and the Book makes the same claim in its own voice when it challenges the idolaters to consider whether their gods could undo a harm God willed or withhold a mercy He granted (39:38).

The concession that follows is important: unless my Lord so wills. The sentence does not claim that Abraham stands outside God's decree, and it does not describe the idols as having any power that God must restrain. The Book's position throughout is that everything that happens does so by God's permission, and the verse states that principle in the same breath as the refusal of fear.

**The Knowledge That Encompasses Everything**

My Lord encompasses everything in His knowledge. The sentence gives the reason Abraham can speak with confidence about a matter that involves the unseen, and it repeats one of the sūrah's central claims. The sūrah said earlier that God knows what is on land and sea and that not a leaf falls without His knowledge (6:59), and it described the record kept of every deed (6:61).

The same phrase appears on the lips of Moses in the sūrah of Ṭā-Hā, where he tells his people that their only god is God, and that He encompasses everything in His knowledge (20:98). The sūrah of the Divorce states that God encompasses all things in knowledge (65:12), and the sūrah of the Women says that God is fully aware of everything (4:126). The claim functions in these verses as a boundary on human speculation: the audience may not know what the gods are doing, but nothing is outside the knowledge of the One Abraham serves.

**The Question at the End**

Will you not be mindful? The verse ends with a question rather than a conclusion, and the question is the same one the sūrah has asked its audience several times. It asks whether the hearers will order their lives around the awareness of God, and it takes for granted that the material for that awareness has been supplied.

Read in place, the question is the sharpest thing in the verse. The people arguing with Abraham had just heard him say that his Lord encompasses everything in knowledge, and the natural response to that sentence is not an argument about which god should be feared but a change in how a person lives. The Book lets the question stand without an answer, and the next verse continues the comparison of fears that the question has opened.

**What the Reply Reveals About the Prophet's Situation**

The Book places this story in the middle of a sūrah addressed to a Prophet whose people were making the same argument to him. They had asked him to accommodate their gods, threatened him with the displeasure of those gods, and warned him that abandoning them would cost him the protection of the city. Abraham's reply supplies the answer he was to give: the question is not which powers might be offended but who has guided whom.

The sūrah draws the parallel tightly when it puts the same claim on the Prophet's lips in the declaration that he has been forbidden to worship what they invoke and will not follow their desires (6:56). Abraham's words and the Prophet's words are the same refusal, spoken in different cities and to different generations of the same argument.

**The Refusal to Certify What They Claim**

The Book gives the Prophet a further instruction in this sūrah that answers the same pressure: he is told to ask who the best witness is, then to answer that God is witness between him and them, and then to ask the idolaters whether they testify that there are other gods besides God, with the instruction to declare that he will never testify to that and that there is only One God (6:19). The refusal to certify the audience's claim is the practical form of the position Abraham states in this verse. A person who will not say that the idols have a right to fear has already answered the argument, and the Book makes the Prophet say so in the audience's hearing.
verses.81:
> And how should I fear your associate-gods, while you have no fear in associating ˹others˺ with Allah—a practice He has never authorized? Which side has more right to security? ˹Tell me˺ if you really know!”

**The Comparison of Fears**

And how should I fear your associate-gods, while you have no fear in associating others with Allah? The verse turns the audience's objection back on them, and it does so by comparing two fears. Abraham is being told that he should be afraid of the gods his people serve, and his answer is that they should be far more afraid of what they are doing with those gods. The question is not whether fear is appropriate but where it belongs.

The argument is built on a comparison of magnitudes that the audience would have accepted if they had been willing to state their beliefs openly. Their gods were objects they had made, inherited, or named (12:40); the One they associated with those gods had made the heavens and the earth (6:73). A person who fears a stone and does not fear its maker has made an error about proportions, and the verse lets the error speak for itself.

**Nothing Authorizes the Practice**

The clause about practice He has never authorized is the legal form of the same accusation, and the Book states it repeatedly. It says that the names the idolaters use are inventions that God never authorized (12:40), and it asks in the sūrah of the Romans whether God has sent down any authority that attests to what the people associate with Him (30:35). The sūrah of Yūnus records the claim that God has offspring and answers that the claimants have no proof and are speaking about God what they do not know (10:68).

The Book's point throughout is not that the audience had chosen badly among options but that they had no warrant at all. Nothing in the revelation, and nothing in the created order, gives a human being permission to assign a partner to God, and the verse describes the practice as unauthorized rather than merely mistaken.

**The Question of Security**

Which side has more right to security? The verse poses the question and asks the audience to answer it if they know. The question is a summary of the whole passage, since it asks what a person is entitled to feel safe about, and the Book's answer arrives in the following verse in a single sentence: those who believe and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood are the ones who are guaranteed security and are rightly guided.

The Book's word for security covers the sense of being safe from harm and fear, and the idolaters' religion was built on the pursuit of exactly that condition. They kept the gods on their side in order to be safe, and the question asks them to compare the safety of a person who worships the maker of everything with the safety of one who divides his trust among creatures.

**The Concept of Wrong That Tarnishes Faith**

The word used in this verse for association is rendered by the translation as falsehood and by many commentators as an act of oppression or wrong, and the Book's usage supports the wider sense. The following verse says that those who believe and do not tarnish their faith with wrong are the ones who are secure, and the commentators discussed at length whether the wrong in view is the specific wrong of associating something with God or any serious sin.

The strongest reading, and the one the passage's own argument supports, takes the wrong in question to be the association the previous verse has been describing. The Book uses the word for wrong across a wide range, and it defines the greatest of it elsewhere as the worship of something other than God. The sentence that follows the question therefore supplies the criterion the question asked for: security belongs to the believer whose faith has not been mixed with the assignment of partners to God.

**The Idiom of Right and Entitlement**

The phrase the translation renders as which side has more right, with the instruction to tell if you know, is an invitation to judge between two claims. The Book uses this form of challenge in several places where it asks the audience to arbitrate against itself, as when it asks whether the blind and the seeing can be equal or whether darkness and light are the same (13:16).

Those challenges work because the audience already knows the answer. The Makkans would not have claimed that a stone had as much right to their fear as the Creator of the sky, and the verse in front of us asks them to say so out loud. The final words, if you really know, carry the sting, since the sūrah has been demonstrating for eighty verses what they did not know.

**What the Two Verses Establish**

Read together, the two verses state Abraham's full position before his people: no fear of the idols, no acceptance of an unauthorized practice, and a question about where security is to be found. The next verse gives the answer as a statement of fact rather than as an argument, and the sūrah then names Abraham's discourse as the argument God gave him against his people (6:83).

The Book has thus presented the case for God's oneness in three forms across this sūrah: as a series of questions put to the Makkans, as a declaration commanded to the Prophet, and now as a story from the life of the man their tradition claimed as its founder. The last of the three is the one the Book calls God's own argument, which is why it stands at the centre of the sūrah.
verses.82:
> It is ˹only˺ those who are faithful and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood who are guaranteed security and are ˹rightly˺ guided

**The Answer to the Question of Security**

The previous verse asked which party had more right to security and told the audience to answer if they knew. This verse supplies the answer as a statement of fact: those who believe and do not tarnish their faith with falsehood are the ones guaranteed security and guided. The sentence names the two conditions and then attaches the two results, and the structure matches the pairing the sūrah used earlier when it described the believers and the deniers (6:48–49).

The Book states the same arrangement in other words when it says that whoever submits themselves to God and does good will have their reward with their Lord, and that there will be no fear for them nor will they grieve (2:112). The security in this verse is therefore not a general sense of safety but the specific condition of a person who has placed his trust where the power actually lies.

**The Word That Alarmed the Companions**

The condition about tarnishing faith with falsehood produced one of the most famous exchanges in the early community, and the Book's commentators record it in connection with this verse. According to the report in al-Bukhārī, when the verse was revealed the Companions were distressed by it and asked which of them had not mixed his belief with wrongdoing, since the word used here can mean any injustice or sin. The Prophet answered that the verse did not mean that, and directed them to the saying of Luqmān to his son: never associate anything with God in worship, for associating others with Him is truly the worst of all wrongs (31:13).

The report explains the verse's scope and shows how the earliest readers handled it. The wrong that tarnishes faith is the specific wrong of assigning partners to God, since the sūrah's whole argument has been aimed at that practice. The Companions' alarm came from reading a general word in a general sense, and the Prophet's answer narrowed it to the one offence the passage was about.

**Why the Word Is a Comfort as Well as a Warning**

Read with the report in view, the verse is one of the sūrah's clearest statements about what does and does not destroy a person's faith. Ordinary failure, repented of, does not put a believer outside the security the verse describes, and the sūrah gave the same assurance earlier when it told the Prophet to announce that God has taken mercy upon Himself and that whoever does evil in ignorance and then repents and mends his ways will find God forgiving and merciful (6:54).

What the verse will not allow is the opposite of the association it condemns: the assumption that a person may combine the worship of God with the worship of other beings and still hold the guarantee. The whole Abraham section has been devoted to showing that such a combination is not a form of religion but the abandonment of it, and this verse states the consequence in the vocabulary of security.

**Guidance as the Second Result**

The verse ends by saying that those who meet the condition are rightly guided, which adds the inward result to the outward one. The Book treats guidance as both a gift that precedes belief and a state that follows it, and the sūrah earlier described the Prophet as one whom God had guided while his people were arguing with him about God (6:80). The sentence here follows the same pattern: the person who holds to the faith without mixing it is confirmed in the direction he has taken.

The Book's description of the guided elsewhere attaches the same two marks. It says that whoever God guides is truly guided and that whoever He leaves to stray will find no guardian (7:178), and it describes the people of understanding as those who reflect on the creation and the alternation of night and day and are led by that reflection to the acknowledgment of their Lord (3:190–191). Guidance in the Book's usage is not a status conferred on a group but a condition that shows itself in conduct and in the direction a person is facing.

**The Verse as the Centre of the Pericope**

This sentence sits at the middle of the Abraham passage and gives the reader the point the whole passage has been arguing. The founder of the community's tradition asked which side had more right to security, and the answer names the two things Abraham did: he believed, and he purified his belief of everything his people mixed with it.

The verse that follows names Abraham's discourse as the argument God gave him against his people, and it states that God elevates in rank whoever He pleases (6:83). The two sentences belong together. The security promised here is what the argument in the previous verses was seeking, and the elevation named in the next verse is God's response to the one who held to it.

**What the Passage Now Leaves Behind**

With this verse the sūrah finishes the dispute with the Makkans about Abraham's legacy, and it does so by making the test consist of belief and purity rather than descent. The audience had claimed Abraham as an ancestor and used his name against the Prophet; the sūrah has taken the claim and turned it into a question about their own practice.

From this point the sūrah turns to the line of prophets who followed Abraham and to the pattern of guidance and reward that runs through their stories. The next verse states what God's treatment of Abraham demonstrates about His own practice, and the verses after it set that story inside a longer chain of revelation.
verses.83:
> This was the argument We gave Abraham against his people. We elevate in rank whoever We please. Surely your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing

**The Argument Credited to God**

This was the argument We gave Abraham against his people. The sentence closes the pericope with the Book's own verdict on the sequence just related, and it settles the question the commentators had raised about the star, the moon, and the sun. Whatever Abraham said and however the statements are read, the discourse as a whole is described here as something given to him rather than as something he produced, and the giving is attributed to God.

The Book uses the vocabulary of proof for the mission of the messengers generally when it says that they were sent as bearers of news and warnings so that humanity would have no excuse before God after their coming (4:165). That statement explains what the argument was for: the demonstration given to Abraham removed the ground on which his people could plead ignorance of their Lord, and the Book presents it as a case so well made that no answer to it was available.

**Abraham's Case Elsewhere in the Book**

The Book records Abraham making the same kind of case in other settings and in other forms. In the sūrah of the Cow he argues with the king who disputed with him about his Lord, and he answers the claim to give life and death with a demonstration that the king cannot perform (2:258); in the sūrah of the Prophets he questions his people about the statues to which they are devoted and then acts against them (21:52–58); and in the sūrah of the Poets he recites the catalogue of what his Lord has done for him, ending with the promise of forgiveness on the day of judgment (26:69–82).

Each version of the case is a demonstration from the created order or from the speaker's own dependence. The sūrah's version, which moves through the star, the moon, and the sun, is the one the Book places in the middle of this sūrah because it matches the sūrah's argument from the heavens and the earth.

**The Elevation of Whom He Pleases**

We elevate in rank whoever We please.
