The sentence states the principle that explains why Abraham could see what his people could not, and it repeats a formula the Book uses whenever it accounts for differences between people. The sūrah of Joseph uses the same words at the moment when Joseph's plan succeeds, noting that God elevates in rank whoever He wills and that above everyone with knowledge is the One who knows all (12:76). The sūrah of the Gatherings states that God will elevate those who believe and those given knowledge by degrees (58:11).

The principle also answers a question the sūrah raised much earlier, in the passage about the poor believers and the wealthy notables. The sūrah said that God tests people by means of one another (6:53), and here it states the same arrangement in terms of rank. Differences of understanding and of station are part of the design, and the sūrah's closing verse will return to the subject when it describes the ranks by which people are tested with what they have been given (6:165).

**The Two Names at the End**

The verse closes with the All-Wise and the All-Knowing, the same pair that ends the sūrah's declaration about creation and the trumpet (6:73) and that appears throughout the Book in statements about God's ordering of human affairs. The names fit the sentence they follow: the elevation of some over others is the act of a being whose knowledge covers what He is arranging and whose wisdom determines where each one is placed.

The Book attaches these names to the same subject in several passages. It says that the Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing at the end of the verse in which Abraham's case is described as God's argument, and it uses the pair in connection with the giving of scripture and the sending of messengers. The sentence therefore states the principle and then names the attributes that make it just.

**What the Verse Does for the Sūrah's Argument**

The verse is the hinge on which the sūrah turns from the dispute with the Makkans to the line of prophets. It states that the case for God's oneness which the sūrah has been building was given to Abraham as a gift, and it states that the gift was measured out by a wisdom that distributes its gifts as it will. The audience's objection to the Prophet's mission, which was that he was a man of no particular standing, is answered by the same statement.

That answer had already been given in the sūrah's discussion of the poor believers, where the Book said plainly that God knows best who is grateful (6:53). Here the same principle is applied to the greatest of the messengers, and the application shows how far the principle reaches. Neither poverty nor wealth, neither obscurity nor fame, determines who receives understanding from God.

**The Transition to the Prophetic Line**

The verses that follow list the men who inherited the same guidance: Isaac and Jacob, Noah and his descendants, David and Solomon, Job and Joseph, Moses and Aaron (6:84), and then Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias (6:85), and then Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot (6:86). The sūrah has placed Abraham at the head of a chain, and the gift of guidance is described as passing through it.

That arrangement gives the audience a way to read their own history. The Prophet being addressed in Makkah stood in a line whose members had all been given what Abraham was given, and the sūrah's next verses name them one by one so that the pattern cannot be mistaken for a claim about one exceptional man.
verses.84:
> And We blessed him with Isaac and Jacob. We guided them all as We previously guided Noah and those among his descendants: David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron. This is how We reward the good-doers

**The Gift of Descendants**

And We blessed him with Isaac and Jacob. The sentence follows the account of Abraham's trial with the announcement of what he received, and the Book pairs the two elsewhere in the same order. The sūrah of the Ranged records his prayer for righteous offspring (37:100), and the sūrah of the Prophets records its answer, saying that God blessed him with Isaac as a son and Jacob as a grandson, as an additional favour, and made all of them righteous (21:72). The addition of the words as an additional favour is the Book's way of saying that the gift exceeded what was asked.

The two names matter for the sūrah's audience as well as for Abraham. The tribes of Israel traced themselves to Jacob, and the Book elsewhere tells the Prophet that the believers make no distinction among the prophets and that they believe in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants (2:136; 3:84). The line that begins here is the line the sūrah will follow through the next two verses.

**"We Guided Them All"**

We guided them all as We previously guided Noah. The sentence places guidance rather than lineage at the centre of the gift, and it names Noah as the standard by which the others are measured for a reason that the next verse makes explicit: the men listed here are described as being among his descendants. The sūrah of Iron states the arrangement directly when it says that God sent Noah and Abraham and reserved prophethood and revelation for their descendants (57:26).

The Book's list of the guided in this verse includes Job, who does not belong to the Israelite line, alongside David, Solomon, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron. The point of the catalogue is that guidance is God's gift to those He chooses rather than an inheritance that runs through a single family, and the sūrah states that principle in the sentence that closes the verse.

**The Reward Attached to Good Conduct**

This is how We reward the good-doers. The sentence names the reward and the conduct it answers, and the reward in context is the guidance just described. The Book repeats the connection in several places: those who struggle in God's cause will be guided along His ways (29:69), and Noah is described as utterly grateful for God's favours, with the result that God chose him and guided him to the straight path (16:121). Guidance, in the Book's usage, is both the gift that starts a person on the road and the reward that follows the conduct it produces.

The sūrah of Consultation states the same principle in a form that ties it to the whole line of prophets, saying that God has ordained the way He decreed for Noah, for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, and that He chooses for Himself whoever wills and guides to Himself whoever turns to Him (42:13). The catalogue in this verse is a list of people who did what that verse describes, and the reward they received is the guidance the sūrah says belongs to God.

**The Character of the Men Named**

The list in this verse moves through the great figures of the Book's prophetic history, and each one carries the story the Book tells about him. David and Solomon received kingship and judgement; Job endured a trial that the Book holds up as an example of patience; Joseph passed through slavery and imprisonment to authority; Moses and Aaron were sent to the tyrant of Egypt. The Book mentions them here without detail because the audience knew their stories, and the shared element in those stories is what the verse is naming.

That shared element is the guidance of God, given to each of them in the circumstances of his own life. The Book's habit of listing the prophets in groups is not a genealogical exercise. It is a demonstration that the same gift has been given across different centuries, lands, and conditions, and that the pattern does not change with the circumstances.

**Why the List Matters to the Makkans**

The sūrah's audience had claimed Abraham and used the claim to argue that their religion was the religion of their fathers. The catalogue in this verse and the two that follow it widens the frame: the prophets who carried the same message include men from outside the Arabian peninsula and outside the audience's lineage, and the Book had already said that God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImrān above all people of their time (3:33).

The list therefore functions as an answer to the claim of exclusive descent. Among the figures named in this verse are men from every branch of the tradition that the audience would have recognised, and the point of naming them together is that they were all guided by the same Lord, with the same message, and were all rewarded for the same thing.

**The Transition Into the Next Verse**

The sūrah continues the list immediately in the next verse with Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias, and then in the verse after it with Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot. The catalogue is arranged in three groups, and the group in this verse begins with Abraham's sons and continues through the great names of the Israelite tradition.

The three verses together set the stage for the statement in the sūrah that follows them, which says that the guidance given to all these men is God's guidance, given to whoever He wills of His servants, and that if they had associated others with Him their deeds would have been wasted (6:88). The list has been assembled, and the sūrah now states what it demonstrates.
verses.85:
> Likewise, ˹We guided˺ Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias, who were all of the righteous

**The Second Group in the Catalogue**

Likewise, We guided Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias, who were all of the righteous. The sentence continues the list from the previous verse without introducing a new subject, and the connecting word makes the catalogues one continuous act of guidance. The four names belong to the later part of the Israelite prophetic tradition, and they sit in the same list as David and Moses with no distinction drawn between them.

The arrangement is deliberate. The sūrah's audience argued with the Prophet about the standing of particular prophets, and the Christians of the region had raised Jesus to a status the Book rejects. The verse places him in a line with Zachariah and John and gives the whole group one description: they were all of the righteous. The Book makes the same point in the sūrah of the Family of Imran, where the believers are told that they make no distinction between any of the prophets (3:84).

**The Pair of Zachariah and John**

Zachariah and John are named together because their stories are joined, and the Book tells that story in detail in the sūrah of Maryam. Zachariah prayed for an heir in his old age, the prayer was answered with John, and the Book describes the household as one that used to race in doing good, calling upon God with hope and fear, and humbling themselves before Him (21:90). The father and the son stand at the head of the group in this verse as an example of what the guidance produces.

John holds a particular place in the Book's account, described as chaste and as one who honoured his parents, and the sūrah of the Family of Imran names him among those who confirmed the word from God. The two men are therefore being presented to the audience as recipients of the same guidance the sūrah has been describing, given in answer to a prayer and rewarded with offspring who carried the message further.

**Jesus in the Line of the Righteous**

The mention of Jesus in this list is one of the sūrah's clearest statements about his standing, and it is placed in a passage aimed at the claims the region's Christians were making about him. He is named among the guided and described as one of the righteous, which is the Book's ordinary designation for the servants of God. The sūrah of the Table records his own declaration that he is a servant of God, and the sūrah of Maryam preserves his words from the cradle in the same terms.

The Book's treatment of Jesus throughout is consistent on this point: he is honoured, inspired, supported with the holy spirit, and given clear proofs, and he is not described anywhere as sharing the divine nature. The sūrah of the Women states that the Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of God, and the sūrah of the Family of Imran tells the Christians not to exceed the limits in their religion. This verse's placement of him inside a list of guided men is part of the same teaching.

**Elias and the Prophetic Tradition**

Elias appears in the Book in the sūrah of the Ranged, where he calls his people to be mindful of God and asks them whether they invoke Baal and abandon the best of creators. The sūrah records that his people rejected him and that he was among those brought near, and it closes the account by saying that peace be upon the family of Elias. His inclusion in this list connects him with the same line of messengers and with the same refusal of the worship of created things.

What Elias preached is therefore identical to what the sūrah has been presenting. He asked his people why they called upon an idol while abandoning the One who made them and their ancestors, and the account in the sūrah of the Ranged ends with the notice that the men who rejected him will be brought before their Lord. The Book's catalogue in this verse draws men from different centuries into a single description because they carried a single message.

**"All of the Righteous"**

The description that closes the verse is one word in the Arabic, and the Book uses it for those whose conduct and belief are sound together. The sūrah will use the same description in the next verse for the third group, and the Book uses it of the believers generally in passages about reward. The uniformity of the description is the point: whatever their rank and whatever the miracles attached to their stories, the prophets are grouped under the same moral category.

That category is also the one the sūrah has been recommending to its audience. The statement in the previous verse that God rewards the good-doers is followed by a list of men who were described as righteous, and the reader is being shown what the reward looked like in their lives. The Book's habit in these passages is to describe the prophets not by their extraordinary gifts but by the conduct that made them worthy of the guidance they received.

**The Function of the Two Verses Together**

The two catalogues in verses 84 and 85 serve the sūrah's argument in a way that a single name could not. They show the audience a continuous tradition of guided men spanning centuries and lineages, and they do it in a passage whose immediate subject is Abraham's argument for the oneness of God. The implication is that the teaching the Prophet was bringing had been the content of every mission in the list.

The sūrah then adds the third group of names in the next verse and follows the whole catalogue with a statement about what the guidance was and what would have destroyed it. That statement is the conclusion the list was assembled to support, and it appears in the very next sentence.
verses.86:
> ˹We also guided˺ Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot, favouring each over other people ˹of their time˺

**The Third Group of Names**

We also guided Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot, favouring each over other people of their time. The catalogue that began with Isaac and Jacob and continued through the later Israelite prophets now closes with four names, and the four come from different settings and different centuries. Ishmael is Abraham's first son and the ancestor the Arabian audience claimed; Lot is his nephew and the prophet of the cities that were destroyed; Jonah is the man of the whale; Elisha appears in the Book only in lists like this one and with the companions of Elijah.

Bringing these four together in a single sentence is the sūrah's statement about the breadth of guidance. The men named here did not belong to one family or one land, and their stories in the Book take place among different peoples and in different conditions. What they share is the favour the sentence names at its end.

**The Favour Named at the End**

The phrase translated as favouring each over other people of their time is the Book's language of election, and it is used for the prophetic calling in several places. The sūrah of the Family of Imran says that God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImrān above all people of their time (3:33); the sūrah of the Bee describes Abraham as a model of excellence whom God chose and guided to a straight path (16:121); and the sūrah of the Ranged records Lot being described as one of the messengers (37:133).

The wording also makes clear what the favour was not. Being preferred over the people of one's time is a statement about a mission and its reception, not a claim about the inherent superiority of one lineage over another. The sūrah has already said that God elevates in rank whoever He pleases (6:83), which removes the possibility of reading the catalogue as a genealogy of merit.

**Ishmael and the Arabian Line**

Ishmael's place in the list would have struck the sūrah's first audience with particular force, since the northern and central Arabian tribes traced their descent to him. The Book records him building the foundations of the House with Abraham and praying for acceptance (2:127), and it describes him as true to his promise and as a messenger and a prophet. The sūrah of Maryam gives him a place among those mentioned with honour, and the sūrah of the Prophets describes him with Enoch and Dhū al-Kifl as steadfast.

His inclusion in this verse means that the Arabian line is not absent from the prophetic catalogue. The audience could not claim that God had confined guidance to the descendants of Isaac, and they could not claim that their own ancestor had been passed over. The sūrah places Ishmael in the same list as the Israelite prophets and gives the whole group the same description.

**Lot and the Cities**

Lot's story is the Book's account of a community destroyed for conduct that the Book describes in detail, and his name in this list places him among the messengers who warned their own people. The sūrah of Hūd records the angels' arrival at his house and their instruction that he should travel with his family in the dark of night and not look back, with the exception of his wife, and it records their announcement that the appointed time of the cities was the morning (11:81).

The choice of Lot for this catalogue is significant because his community's destruction is one of the Book's starkest examples of a people who refused a messenger. His presence in a list of the guided means the sūrah is not presenting the prophets as men whose missions succeeded by human measures, and it prepares the reader for the statement in the following verses about those who were guided and those who turned away.

**Jonah and the Prayer From the Dark**

Jonah is the prophet whose story the Book tells in the sūrah of the Prophets, where he leaves his city in anger, is swallowed, and calls out from the veils of darkness that there is no god but God and that he has certainly done wrong (21:87). The Book records that his prayer was answered and that he was rescued from anguish, and it adds the sentence that this is how the believers are saved (21:88).

His name in this verse brings the theme of mercy into the catalogue. The Book's description of the prophets includes men who were rescued from their own errors as well as men who led their peoples to safety, and the sūrah's audience, which had been told that the punishment would reach the wrongdoers, is shown that the door remains open to the one who calls from the dark.

**The Whole List and Its Purpose**

The three verses of names have now covered the fathers of the tradition from Noah to Jesus, and the sūrah has inserted no ranking among them. The purpose of assembling them becomes explicit in the verses that follow, where the sūrah states that this guidance is God's and is given to whoever He wills of His servants, and where it warns that association with God would have voided the deeds of any of them.

The catalogue therefore serves two arguments at once. It answers the audience's claim to a special line by showing how many lines there were, and it answers their confidence in ancestry by stating that the deeds even of these men would have been wasted had they associated others with God. The next verse widens the circle once more by including the forefathers, descendants, and brothers of the men named, and the one after that states the principle behind all of it.
verses.87:
> And ˹We favoured˺ some of their forefathers, their descendants, and their brothers. We chose them and guided them to the Straight Path

**The Circle Widens Beyond the Names**

And We favoured some of their forefathers, their descendants, and their brothers. The verse extends the catalogue in three directions at once, and the three directions cover the whole of a family: the generations above the named prophets, the generations below them, and their contemporaries. The sūrah has listed specific men; this sentence says that the favour was not confined to them.

The Book uses the same threefold formula in its description of the descendants of Abraham and Jacob generally, and it uses it again in the sūrah of the Cattle's own account of the guidance given to the line. The effect of naming the three groups is to close off the possibility that the audience could argue from the catalogue that only exceptional individuals were favoured and that the rest were left outside. The favour moved through families and generations.

**The Two Verbs at the End**

We chose them and guided them to the Straight Path. The sentence states two distinct acts, and the Book uses both for the prophetic mission. To choose is to select a person for a purpose, and to guide is to set him on the road that leads to it. The sūrah of Maryam uses the same pair when it describes the prophets as those whom God has blessed among the descendants of Adam, of those carried with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and as those whom God rightly guided and chose (19:58).

The pairing protects a truth about the religious life that the sūrah has been teaching throughout. Election without guidance would be a status without a path, and guidance without election would be a road that no one had been appointed to walk. The Book's descriptions of the prophets consistently hold the two together, and the sūrah states both in a single clause.

**The Straight Path as the Common Destination**

The phrase the Book uses for the road here is the same one it uses for the Prophet's own path in the sūrah's later declaration, where he says that his Lord has guided him to a straight path, a perfect way, the faith of Abraham the upright (6:161). The recurrence is not incidental. The catalogue of prophets and the sūrah's final statement of the Prophet's religion end at the same phrase, which tells the reader that the road named in this verse is the road the sūrah has been describing from its opening verses.

The Book attaches the same description to the guidance given to the community of believers in several places, and the sūrah of the Fatihah makes the request for that road the central petition of the prayer. What the prophets received is therefore presented as the same thing that the ordinary believer asks for each day, and the difference between them lies in the mission rather than in the destination.

**Favoured Families and the Question of Inheritance**

The verse's mention of forefathers, descendants, and brothers raises the question of what the favour means for the families of the prophets. The Book's answer elsewhere is that proximity to a messenger is not a guarantee. Noah's son was among the drowned, and the Book records Noah's plea and the response that the son was not of his household in the sense that mattered. Lot's wife was left behind, and the Book records Abraham's father among the idolaters.

The sūrah's own catalogue is careful in the same way. It names the guided rather than the lineage, and the sentence that follows this one states that the guidance is given to whoever God wills of His servants. The favour that runs through families in this verse is therefore a statement about God's practice of raising messengers from particular houses, not a promise that every member of those houses will be saved.

**The Book's Wider Use of the Formula**

The Book uses the language of choosing and favouring for whole communities as well as for individuals, and the sūrah of the Cow records that God made Abraham a role model for the people (2:124). The sūrah of the Family of Imran states the principle that God chose certain families above all people of their time (3:33), and the sūrah of the Pilgrimage says that God named the community of believers the ones who submit in the earlier scriptures and in this recitation (22:78).

Read against those passages, this verse describes a process that runs through history: God selects, guides, and produces a line of men whose task is to carry the message to their peoples. The sūrah's audience is being shown that the line is long, that it includes their own ancestor, and that their quarrel with the Prophet was a quarrel with the pattern the line represents.

**The Sentence That Follows**

The guidance given to all these men is named in the next verse as God's guidance, given to whoever He wills of His servants, and the verse after it makes the startling statement that if they had associated others with God their deeds would have been wasted (6:88). The two sentences take the catalogue that has just been assembled and use it as the basis for the sūrah's final argument about what the audience's practice would have cost even the greatest of the men whose names they honoured.

The reader is therefore meant to carry the names forward into those statements. The prophets were chosen and guided, and the guidance was a gift rather than a possession, and it could be lost. That is the lesson the sūrah draws from the list, and it states it without qualification in the next sentence.
verses.88:
> This is Allah’s guidance with which He guides whoever He wills of His servants. Had they associated others with Him ˹in worship˺, their ˹good˺ deeds would have been wasted

**The Guidance Identified as God's Gift**

This is Allah's guidance with which He guides whoever He wills of His servants. The sentence states what the catalogue of names has been demonstrating, and it names the guidance as God's rather than as the possession of the men who received it. The Book uses the same construction when it describes the guidance given to the prophets of the line of Abraham, and the possessive form keeps the gift attached to its giver.

The statement also answers the question the sūrah's audience had been raising about the Prophet. If guidance is given to whoever God wills, then the identity of the man carrying the message is not the decisive question, and the Book had already said as much in the verse about the poor believers when it stated that God knows best who is grateful (6:53). The catalogue in the previous verses shows the same principle at work across centuries.

**The Conditional Sentence About the Prophets**

Had they associated others with Him in worship, their good deeds would have been wasted. The sentence is the sharpest in the passage, and it makes a claim about the men whose names the sūrah has just honoured. Even the prophets, if they had committed the one offence the sūrah has been describing, would have lost the value of everything they did.

The Book states the same rule elsewhere in the second person. The sūrah of the Troops records the revelation given to the Prophet and to the prophets before him, that if anyone associates others with God his deeds will certainly be void and he will be among the losers (39:65). The verse in front of us takes that rule and applies it hypothetically to the greatest figures in the catalogue, which is the Book's way of making the point impossible to evade by reference to ancestral standing.

**What the Sentence Is Not Saying**

The verse is not reporting a fault in the prophets, since the Book declares them protected in their mission and honours them throughout. What the hypothetical does is remove the audience's last refuge in genealogy. The Makkans were arguing that the religion of their fathers was sufficient because their fathers were the men of the tradition, and this sentence states that the tradition's own heroes would have been ruined by the practice the audience was defending.

The point lands with particular force because the sūrah has just included Abraham in the catalogue, and Abraham's declaration ended with the words that he was not one of the polytheists (6:79). The audience's claim to his legacy is thus met with a statement about what would have happened to him had he done what they were doing, and the sūrah supplies no room for negotiation on that point.

**The Doctrine of Wasted Deeds**

The expression about deeds being wasted appears repeatedly in the Book for those who mix association with belief, and it describes a loss that cannot be made up. The sūrah of the Family of Imran says of those who disbelieve and die as disbelievers that their deeds are wasted in this world and the next, and the sūrah of the Cow uses the same language for the works of those who deny the signs of God and the meeting with Him.

The Book's teaching on this subject explains what the sūrah's audience stood to lose and what it did not. Their generosity, their hospitality, their keeping of promises, and their care for their families were all real, and the Book does not say that God ignores the good that people do. What it says is that the value of a deed depends on the axis around which a life is built, and the deeds of a person who sets up partners with God are described as scattered.

**The Warning at the End of the Abraham Section**

The verse closes the pericope that began with Abraham's address to his father, and it closes it with a warning rather than with a conclusion about Abraham's greatness. The sūrah has taken the audience through the story of their ancestor, his reasoning, his declaration, his argument with his people, and the line of prophets that followed him, and it now states the one thing that would have destroyed all of it.

That is a rhetorical move the Book uses at the ends of its stories, and it leaves the reader with the practical question the passage was designed to raise. The line of men the audience honoured had all been guided by the same God on the same path, and the practice the audience had inherited was the one thing the sūrah says could have taken that guidance away from any of them.

**What the Sūrah Says Next**

The verse that follows this one describes the men of the catalogue as those to whom God gave the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood, and it warns that if the audience disbelieves in the message, God has already entrusted it to a people who will not disbelieve in it (6:89). The two sentences belong to one movement: the gift is named, the danger to its recipients is stated, and the message is passed to those who will carry it.

The sūrah is thus completing its treatment of the audience's reliance on lineage. Having shown the line, honoured it, and stated the condition attached to it, the sūrah now announces that the trust has been transferred, and it does so without naming the people in question and without softening the sentence. The next verses continue with the same theme, describing the men who were given the Book and the guidance that came with it.
verses.89:
> Those were the ones to whom We gave the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood. But if these ˹pagans˺ disbelieve in this ˹message˺, then We have already entrusted it to a people who will never disbelieve in it

**The Three Gifts Named Together**

Those were the ones to whom We gave the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood. The sentence summarizes what the catalogue of names had in common, and it names three gifts where a reader might have expected one. The Scripture is the revelation given to a messenger; wisdom is the understanding that allows it to be applied; prophethood is the office of carrying it to a people. The Book uses the same triple formula for the children of Israel generally, saying that God gave them the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood, granted them good and lawful provisions, and favoured them above the others (45:16).

The combination is important for the argument the sūrah has been making. The men listed in the previous verses were not honoured because of their lineage but because they received a message, understood it, and delivered it. The three gifts describe an office rather than a status, and the sentence that follows this one states what happened to the office when the audience refused it.

**Wisdom as a Distinct Gift**

The Book treats wisdom as a distinct gift from revelation, and it describes its own message as containing both. The sūrah of the Family of Imran says that it is not appropriate for a man blessed with the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood to tell people to worship him instead of God, but that he would instruct them to be devoted to the worship of their Lord (3:79). The sūrah of the Women describes the descendants of Abraham receiving the Book and wisdom along with great authority (4:54).

Those passages show what the sūrah is claiming for the men in its catalogue. They had the text, the understanding of the text, and the authority to teach it, and the combination is what the Book means when it calls a man a prophet. The audience in Makkah was hearing a man who claimed the same three things, and the sūrah places him in the line by naming the gifts he shares with them.

**The Transfer of the Trust**

But if these pagans disbelieve in this message, then We have already entrusted it to a people who will never disbelieve in it. The sentence announces a transfer, and it does so without naming the people who will receive it. Commentators took the community in question to be the believers of Madinah and the generations that carried the message afterward, and the Book states the same principle in several places: if the audience turns away, God will replace them with another people (47:38; 9:39).

The sūrah of the Table gives the promise in a form that describes the replacement community, saying that if any among the believers abandon their faith, God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble with the believers and firm toward the disbelievers, striving in His way and fearing no blame from anyone (5:54). The verse in front of us states the same fact in the past tense, as though the transfer had already been decided, which is the Book's way of expressing certainty about what God will do.

**Why the Warning Is Addressed to the Audience's Claim**

The sentence is aimed at the claim of inheritance that the sūrah has been dismantling. The Makkans assumed that the tradition of Abraham guaranteed their standing, and the verse answers that the tradition is carried by whoever receives it, not by whoever can claim descent from it. The previous verse made the same point by stating that even the prophets would have lost their deeds by association with God (6:88).

The Book's treatment of the Children of Israel in other sūrahs follows the same pattern. They received the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood, and the Book describes their failure to keep the covenant and the consequences that followed, including the transfer of favour to a community that would receive the final message. The sūrah's audience is being shown that the pattern they knew from the earlier communities was now applying to them.

**The Identity of the People Who Will Not Disbelieve**

The verse leaves the recipients of the trust unnamed, and the commentators offered several identifications: the emigrants and the helpers of Madinah, the people of the Book who accepted the message, the angels, or a community whose identity would be revealed by events. The Book uses the same formula when it says that God will replace a people with others whom He loves and who love Him (5:54), and in another place when it says that He has entrusted the message to a people who will never disbelieve in it.

What the verse establishes is that the message does not depend on any one audience. The sūrah's audience had been told in the previous verse that association with God would waste the deeds of the greatest men in their tradition; this verse tells them that the message would survive their rejection and find other carriers. The warning and the assurance are stated in one breath, and the assurance is about the message rather than about the audience.

**The Comfort the Sentence Gives the Prophet**

The sentence also addresses the Prophet's situation directly. He had been told that he was not a keeper over his people (6:66), that every matter has a fixed time (6:67), and that he would face mockery (6:68). The announcement of a people who would never disbelieve gave him something to look toward while the city he lived in refused the message.

The Book states the same comfort in other forms, including the promise that God is sufficient for the Prophet against those who mock him and the statement that the message is a reminder to the whole world (6:90, in the sentence that follows). The sūrah is moving from the argument with Makkah toward a declaration of the message's scope, and the next verse completes that movement by commanding the Prophet to follow the guidance of the men just catalogued.
verses.90:
> These ˹prophets˺ were ˹rightly˺ guided by Allah, so follow their guidance. Say, “I ask no reward of you for this ˹Quran˺—it is a reminder to the whole world.”

**The Command to Follow the Guidance of the Prophets**

These prophets were rightly guided by Allah, so follow their guidance. The command is addressed to the Prophet and through him to the community, and it treats the catalogue of the previous verses as a practical model rather than as a historical record. The line of men who received the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood are to be followed in the guidance they carried, and the book of their message is the same book the Prophet was reciting.

The Book issues the same command in connection with Abraham, telling the Prophet that God revealed to him to follow the faith of Abraham the upright (16:123), and telling the believers that they follow the way of their forefather Abraham (22:78). The sūrah of the Family of Imran states the same instruction twice, first as an answer to the claims of the People of the Book (3:95) and then in the declaration that God has guided the Prophet to the faith of Abraham (6:161, in this sūrah). The command in this verse extends the model to the whole prophetic line.

**What Following the Guidance Involves**

The Book describes the content of the guidance in the verses that precede this one: the worship of God alone, the declaration that He has no partners, the refusal to invoke what cannot benefit or harm, the argument against the worship of created things, and the conduct of patience and prayer. The Prophet is told to follow that guidance, which means that his message is not a departure from the tradition of the prophets but the restoration of it in the language of his own people.

The Book states the continuity explicitly when it says that God has ordained the way He decreed for Noah, for Abraham, for Moses, and for Jesus, and that the instruction given to all of them was to uphold the faith and make no divisions in it (42:13). The sūrah is therefore presenting the Prophet's mission as the final link in a chain whose earlier links the audience claimed to honour, and the command to follow the guidance of the earlier men is the practical form of that presentation.

**The Refusal of Payment**

Say, I ask no reward of you for this. The sentence detaches the messenger from any material interest in the response, and the Book repeats it in several sūrahs. The Prophet is told to say that he does not ask for any reward but that whoever wishes may take a path to his Lord (25:57); the sūrah of Sheba gives the answer that if he had ever asked for a reward they could keep it, since his reward comes from God alone (34:47); and the sūrah of Yūnus records the same declaration in the words of Noah to his people (10:72).

The Book's insistence on this point is a statement about the nature of the message. A prophet who profited from his mission would give his audience a reason to suspect his motives, and the Book's messengers are consistently described as men who worked with their hands and asked nothing of their peoples. The declaration also protects the message from the suspicion that it was tailored to produce a following.

**A Reminder to the Whole World**

It is a reminder to the whole world. The sentence states the scope of the message in the widest terms available, and the Book repeats it in the same words in other places, saying that the Qur'an is nothing but a reminder to the whole world (12:104; 38:87). The sūrah of the Prophets states the same universality in a different form, telling the Prophet that God has sent him only as a mercy for the whole world (21:107).

The claim has consequences for the audience's assumption about their own standing. A reminder addressed to the whole world cannot belong exclusively to one city, one clan, or one line of descent, and the sūrah has just said that the message would be entrusted to a people who would not disbelieve in it (6:89). The two sentences together define the message's reach and remove the audience's ability to treat it as a family possession.

**The Prophet's Position Among the Guided**

The verse places the Prophet in the line of the catalogue without diminishing his mission. He is told to follow the guidance the earlier men received, and the Book elsewhere says that God has elevated him in rank above the others and given him what the earlier messengers were given. The Book's teaching on the prophets is that they form a single community with a single message and that God has favoured some of them over others in particular respects (2:253).

The audience was being asked to consider what it means that the man addressing them stood in that line. The sūrah has named the men they honoured, shown what they received, warned of what could have ruined them, and announced the transfer of the trust. Now it commands the Prophet to follow them, which means the message he was bringing was their message, and the argument about who owned it was over.

**The Transition to the Next Subject**

The next verse turns sharply from the prophets to their opponents with a statement about those who have not shown God His proper reverence, since they said that God had revealed nothing to any human being (6:91). The contrast is deliberate: the line of men who received the Scripture, wisdom, and prophethood is set against a claim that revelation does not happen at all.

The sūrah has been building toward that confrontation for a long stretch of verses, and the two declarations in this verse supply the terms of it. The message is the continuation of a chain and the reminder is for everyone, and the next verses take up the argument with those who denied that any of it had been sent down.
verses.91:
> And they have not shown Allah His proper reverence when they said, “Allah has revealed nothing to any human being.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who then revealed the Book brought forth by Moses as a light and guidance for people, which you split into separate sheets—revealing some and hiding much? You have been taught ˹through this Quran˺ what neither you nor your forefathers knew.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah ˹revealed it˺!” Then leave them to amuse themselves with falsehood

**The Charge of Failing to Appraise God**

And they have not shown Allah His proper reverence. The Book uses this formula in two other places, and each time it is attached to a failure of understanding. The sūrah of the Troops uses it for people who cannot conceive of God's power to hold the earth in His grip and roll up the heavens on the day of judgment (39:67), and the sūrah of the Pilgrimage uses it in a passage about those who worship beings that can create nothing (22:74). Here it is attached to a claim about revelation, and the claim is that God has never revealed anything to any human being.

The severity of the sentence comes from what the claim implies. A person who says that God has never spoken to humanity has denied the whole of the tradition he claims to honour, and the Book's answer begins by naming the one book the audience could not deny.

**The Book of Moses as the Counter-Example**

Who then revealed the Book brought forth by Moses as a light and guidance for people? The question is addressed to people who acknowledged the Torah, and it leaves them with no answer except the one they were refusing to give. The Book uses the same method of argument elsewhere, appealing to the earlier scriptures as evidence that revelation happens, since the audience accepted those scriptures as genuine.

The sūrah of the Family of Imran states that God revealed the Book in truth confirming what came before it, as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel (3:3), and the sūrah of the Cow says that Gabriel revealed the Qur'an confirming what came before it, as a guide and good news for believers (2:97). The continuity between the earlier books and this one is the sūrah's theme in these verses, and the audience's own acceptance of Moses is the ground on which the argument stands.

**The Charge of Concealment**

Which you split into separate sheets, revealing some and hiding much. The sentence accuses the custodians of the earlier scripture of selective disclosure, and the Book makes the same accusation in several places. It says that the Messenger has come revealing much of what the People of the Book used to hide (5:15); it records the covenant taken from those given the Scripture to make it known and not hide it, and their casting it behind their backs in exchange for a fleeting gain (3:187); and it says that a group of them hides the truth knowingly (2:146).

The charge matters to the sūrah's argument because it explains how an audience could claim the tradition of Moses while denying revelation altogether. The sheets had been divided, the difficult passages set aside, and the result was a religion that could be honoured in name while its content was managed. The verse describes that practice as a failure to show God the reverence He deserves.

**"You Have Been Taught What Neither You Nor Your Forefathers Knew"**

The sentence continues with a statement of what the new revelation contains, and it names the new knowledge as a gift to the audience rather than a challenge to their tradition. The Book describes the Qur'an as teaching what neither the Prophet nor his people knew before, and the sūrah of Hūd records the same claim when it says that the stories of the messengers are related so that the Prophet's heart may be strengthened by them.

The sūrah's audience was therefore being told that the message brought content their tradition had never contained, and that this content had reached them through the man they were arguing with. The statement also pre-empts the objection that the message was merely a repetition of what earlier prophets had said, since the Book holds both things at once: it confirms the earlier scriptures and it brings what those scriptures did not.

**The Command to Declare the Source**

Say, Allah revealed it. The sentence is short, and the Book places it after a long question because the answer needed to be stated plainly. The Prophet is not asked to argue the point further but to name the source of the Book he was reciting, and the declaration is the same one the sūrah has been making since its opening verses about the revelation being sent down.

The Book uses this pattern repeatedly, placing a short declaration of divine origin after an extended argument. What the audience is left with is not a demonstration to evaluate but a claim to accept or reject, and the sūrah's concern throughout has been with the response rather than with the quantity of evidence.

**The Dismissal at the End**

Then leave them to amuse themselves with falsehood. The verse ends by withdrawing the Prophet from the argument, and the instruction uses the same vocabulary the sūrah used earlier when it told him to leave those who take the faith as play and amusement (6:70). The people who have just denied that God ever revealed anything to a human being are described in the terms of the earlier passage, and the sūrah declines to make their amusement the Prophet's responsibility.

The closing instruction also prepares the reader for the verse that follows, which presents the Book as a blessed revelation sent down to warn the Mother of Cities and those around it. Having stated that revelation is real and that the earlier books confirm it, the sūrah now describes the book in the Prophet's hands and the mission it carries.
verses.92:
> This is a blessed Book which We have revealed—confirming what came before it—so you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it. Those who believe in the Hereafter ˹truly˺ believe in it and guard their prayers

**A Blessed Book Sent Down**

This is a blessed Book which We have revealed. The description of the Qur'an as blessed is the Book's own term for its benefit, and it recurs in the verses that speak of the revelation's purpose. The sūrah of the Prophets calls it a blessed reminder sent down and asks its audience whether they will deny it (21:50), and the sūrah of the Cattle itself repeats the description near its end when it says that this is a blessed Book revealed so that people might follow it and be shown mercy (6:155).

The sūrah has been arguing about revelation for several verses, and this sentence introduces the revelation itself, laying it before the audience as an object. The Book's habit in these passages is to state what the text is and then to name what it is for, and the two purposes named in this verse are the confirmation of what came before and the warning of the cities around the sanctuary.

**The Confirmation of the Earlier Scriptures**

Confirming what came before it. The Book states this function of the Qur'an in many places and attaches it to the act of revelation itself. The sūrah of the Family of Imran says that God revealed the Book in truth confirming what came before it, as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel (3:3); the sūrah of the Cow says that Gabriel brought the revelation to the Prophet's heart by God's will, confirming what came before it (2:97); and the sūrah of the Table describes the Qur'an as a confirmation of previous scriptures and a supreme authority over them (5:48).

The claim is a claim about continuity rather than about competition. The Qur'an, in the Book's own description, does not come to abolish the earlier revelation but to confirm it and to stand as the criterion for what has been preserved of it. That is the answer the sūrah gives to the accusation that the Prophet was teaching something new, and it is the answer to the audience's refusal to accept a message that arrived in their own language.

**The Mother of Cities and Those Around It**

So you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it. The Book uses the same expression in the sūrah of Consultation, where it says that the Prophet is to warn the Mother of Cities and all around it about the Day of Gathering (42:7). The phrase identifies Makkah as the first city in the mission's scope, and the words that follow extend the warning outward without limit.

That expansion is worth noticing because the sūrah's audience might have taken the warning to be addressed to their city alone. The Book's statement that the message is a reminder to the whole world (6:90) has already fixed its scope, and this verse's reference to the cities around the sanctuary establishes the order in which the warning reaches them. The Book elsewhere describes the settlement at the sanctuary as established for the sake of all people, and it tells the Prophet that he was sent as a mercy to the worlds (21:107).

**The Sign of Belief in the Hereafter**

Those who believe in the Hereafter truly believe in it and guard their prayers. The verse gives the audience a test that distinguishes the two kinds of response, and it builds the test from two things the sūrah has been teaching: conviction about the coming judgment and the practice of prayer. The sūrah has already described the believers who call upon their Lord morning and evening (6:52) and it has stated that the Prophet has been commanded to establish the prayer and to be mindful of God (6:72).

The pairing appears throughout the Book. The sūrah of the Believers lists those who humble themselves in prayer among the successful and includes those who are properly observant of their prayers among the inheritors of Paradise (23:9). The sūrah of the Cow describes the Book as guidance for those who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer, and are certain of the Hereafter (2:3–4). The sūrah's description of belief in this verse uses the same two marks.

**Why the Hereafter Is the Test**

The choice of the Hereafter as the marker is not arbitrary, and the sūrah has spent many verses on the subject. Belief in the Hereafter is the conviction that requires a person to live by a standard other than his neighbours' approval, and the Makkans' resistance to the message was rooted in their assumption that death ended everything. The sūrah recorded their insistence that there is nothing beyond this worldly life and that they would never be resurrected (6:29).

A person who believes in the Hereafter has already accepted that the present arrangement of wealth and power is not the final one, and the sūrah has used that acceptance throughout as the dividing line. The Book states the same criterion in the verse about the warning given to those who fear the gathering (6:51), and it repeats it here as a description of those who will accept the Book.

**The Link to the Practising Community**

The second half of the test is conduct rather than conviction, and the Book joins the two because one without the other was not enough. A person who believed in the reckoning but neglected the prayer would have accepted a theory without taking on the practice, and the sūrah's descriptions of the two roads have consistently paired what a person holds with what he does.

The verse therefore closes the discussion of revelation with a portrait of the reader who receives it. The blessed Book has been sent down, it confirms what came before it, and it warns the city at the centre of the peninsula and everything beyond. What remains is the response, and the sūrah names the two things that will show what it is.

**The Transition Into the Next Verses**

The verses that follow turn to the arguments of those who reject the revelation, and the sūrah takes up the objection that the message contains nothing new or that it could have been produced by someone else. Having presented the Book and its scope, the sūrah now answers the objections to it.

The sūrah's movement in this passage is worth following as a whole. It named the prophets and their gifts, warned that even they would have been ruined by association with God, announced the transfer of the message to a people who would keep it, commanded the Prophet to follow the guidance of the earlier men, refused any reward for the message, described it as a reminder to all creation, and then answered the claim that revelation never occurred. The Book is now in the audience's hands, and the sūrah proceeds to answer everything they said about it.
verses.93:
> Who does more wrong than the one who fabricates lies against Allah or claims, “I have received revelations!”—although nothing was revealed to them—or the one who says, “I can reveal the like of Allah’s revelations!”? If you ˹O Prophet˺ could only see the wrongdoers in the throes of death while the angels are stretching out their hands ˹saying˺, “Give up your souls! Today you will be rewarded with the torment of disgrace for telling lies about Allah and for being arrogant towards His revelations!”

**The Greatest Wrong Restated**

Who does more wrong than the one who fabricates lies against Allah? The formula appears at several points in the Book, and each time it is attached to a particular offence. The sūrah used it near its beginning for the man who invents a lie about God or denies His signs (6:21), it appears in the sūrah of the Heights and the sūrah of the Spider in similar forms, and here it introduces a passage about people who claimed to receive revelation.

The sūrah has been dealing with the Makkans' claims about the Qur'an, and this verse turns the accusation around. The men who said that God had revealed nothing to any human being (6:91) were themselves accused of manufacturing revelation, and the verse's three examples show what that manufacture looked like in practice.

**Three Ways of Fabricating Revelation**

The verse names three offenders in one sentence. The first invents a lie against God, which the Book treats as the broad category covering false doctrine and false attribution. The second claims to have received revelations when nothing was revealed to him, and the third announces that he can produce something like what God has sent down. Each of the three is a claim to a share in the authority that belongs to the revelation, and the sūrah has been answering the audiences' own claims to authority for many verses.

Commentators connected the second and third categories with figures from the Prophet's lifetime, including men who claimed prophethood among the Arabian tribes and a scribe who had recorded parts of the revelation and then came to believe that he could produce its like. The verse is stated in general terms, and the sūrah's argument applies it to everyone who asserts a comparable claim.

**The Scene at Death**

If you could only see the wrongdoers in the throes of death while the angels are stretching out their hands. The sūrah has already described the taking of the soul by the angels who never neglect their duty (6:61), and it now supplies the scene that the earlier verse left implicit. The angels extend their hands and order the dying to give up their souls, and the order is accompanied by the announcement of what awaits them.

The Book describes the same scene elsewhere with harsher detail, recording the angels striking the faces and backs of those who disbelieve (47:27) and the angels seizing the souls of those who wronged themselves and asking them what they had been doing (4:97). The picture the sūrah paints here is of a moment when the claims made during a life of argument are answered by the arrival of the angels, and the answer takes the form of an order that cannot be refused.

**The Charge Attached to the Death**

Today you will be rewarded with the torment of disgrace for telling lies about Allah and for being arrogant towards His revelations. The sentence names two offences, and they correspond to the two sides of the audience's conduct throughout this sūrah. They spoke about God what they did not know, which is the charge the sūrah made in the passage about the idols and their false intercession, and they turned away from the signs that had been made clear to them.

The Book treats arrogance toward the signs as the more serious of the two because it determines what a person does with evidence. The sūrah's earlier verses described people who denied the signs and turned away from them while they were still able to see them (6:46), and this verse states what that conduct receives at the end.

**The Condition the Verse Describes**

The phrase that introduces the scene, if you could only see, is the Book's way of presenting a reality that the audience cannot observe and of asking them to consider it as though they could. The address is to the Prophet, and the effect of the construction is to place the reader in the position of a witness to something that has not yet happened.

The Book uses the same form in other passages about the day of judgment, and it consistently uses it to bring the outcome of a dispute into the present. The argument the sūrah has been conducting with the Makkans concerned matters they could not see, and this verse describes what the dispute will look like at the moment when the claims are checked.

**What the Verse Establishes in the Chapter**

The verse completes a section that began with the audience's claim that God had revealed nothing to anyone (6:91) and continues with the treatment of those who claimed to produce revelation themselves. The sūrah has moved from the gift of revelation to its denial and now to its counterfeiting, and it has placed all three in the same frame of accountability.

The next verse records the address given to the same people when they arrive before God with nothing in their hands, and the two passages belong together. What the angels announce at the deathbed is stated in full at the judgment, and the sūrah supplies both so that the audience can see the whole sequence at once.
verses.94:
> ˹Today˺ you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time—leaving behind everything We have provided you with. We do not see your intercessors with you—those you claimed were Allah’s partners ˹in worship˺. All your ties have been broken and all your claims have let you down.”

**The Address at the Resurrection**

Today you have come back to Us all alone as We created you the first time. The verse gives the content of what is said to the wrongdoers after their souls have been taken, and it states the condition they arrive in. The Book describes every person as standing alone before God, and it uses the fact of the original creation as the measure of the final one: the person who begins his existence with nothing returns with nothing.

The Book states the same isolation in other places, and its descriptions of the day include people who are so overwhelmed that each one is occupied with his own condition. The sūrah of Maryam says that every person will come to God on the day of resurrection individually, and the sūrah of ʿAbasa describes a day when a man will flee from his brother, his mother, his father, his wife, and his children, each of them having enough concern of his own.

**The Things Left Behind**

Leaving behind everything We have provided you with. The sentence names what has been stripped away, and it includes everything a person used to make himself secure: wealth, property, position, and the alliances that protected him in his city. The Book describes the goods of this world as provided for use in the present life, and it says that whatever is sent ahead for the soul is what a person will find waiting for him (73:20).

That contrast was a favourite of the commentators on this verse. Al-Rāzī observed that the connections between a person and his possessions are severed at death while the knowledge of God and virtuous conduct a person has acquired are sent ahead to be met in the Hereafter. The sūrah's audience, which measured a man by what he owned, is shown the moment when the measure stops working.

**The Intercessors Who Do Not Appear**

We do not see your intercessors with you, those you claimed were Allah's partners in worship. The verse takes the Makkans' own religious claim and tests it at the point where they expected it to pay off. The sūrah has described their belief that the idols were intercessors with God (6:51; 6:70), and it has described the impossibility of ransom or plea on that day (6:70).

The Book records the same scene in many other passages, saying that the beings the idolaters invoked will disown them and that the ties between them will be severed (6:24; 7:37; 14:22). The verse in front of us states the separation as a fact of the judgment rather than as a warning about it, and the sentence is spoken to the people who had built their lives around the claim.

**The Severing of Ties**

All your ties have been broken and all your claims have let you down. The Book's word for the ties is the one used for the connections between people and between a person and his patrons, and the sentence announces that the whole network has been dissolved. In a society organised around tribal protection, this was a total statement: the claims that gave a man standing in Makkah were precisely the ones that would not be available to him there.

The Book uses the same vocabulary when it says that the disbelievers will see the punishment and that every cause will be cut off from them (2:166), and when it describes the followers of the wrongdoers grieving over those they followed. The sūrah's audience is being told that the structures of loyalty on which their religion rested would not survive the transition, and the verse states it in their own language of ties and patrons.

**What the Verse Says About Intercession as a Doctrine**

The sūrah has mentioned intercession several times and has consistently denied it to anyone besides God. It said that those warned about the gathering will have no protector and no intercessor besides Him (6:51), and it said that those who take their religion as play will find no protector or intercessor other than God, even if they offered every ransom (6:70). This verse completes the sequence by showing the intercessors themselves absent from the scene.

The Book's teaching on intercession in other passages is that it occurs only by God's permission and for those He permits, which is why the sūrah's denials are phrased as denials of any intercessor besides Him. What the verse eliminates is the assumption the Makkans had built their religious practice on: that the beings they associated with God held a claim on Him that they could exercise for their clients.

**The Argumentative Force of the Scene**

The verse works as an argument by showing the audience what their own position would look like when the arrangement they relied on was checked. The Makkans were proud of their ancestry, their wealth, and their alliances, and they were confident in the intercession of their gods. The sentence strips away all three at once, and it does so in the voice of the One who is described at the end of the passage as the All-Wise and All-Aware.

The sūrah then moves to the signs of God's power in the created order, and the transition is one the Book makes often. Having described the isolation of the wrongdoer before his Lord, the sūrah turns to the evidence of the Lord's power that was available to him all along, beginning with the sprouting of the seed and the splitting of the dawn.
verses.95:
> Indeed, Allah is the One Who causes seeds and fruit stones to sprout. He brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living. That is Allah! How can you then be deluded ˹from the truth˺

**The Splitting of the Seed**

Indeed, Allah is the One Who causes seeds and fruit stones to sprout. The verse opens a series of signs drawn from the created order, and it begins with the smallest and most ordinary of them. A seed is buried, splits, and sends out a living shoot; a fruit stone does the same, and the process repeats itself in every field and orchard the audience walked past. The Book treats that daily event as one of the plainest arguments available for the power of God.

The choice of the image connects directly to the sentence that follows it. What happens when a seed splits is life emerging from what appears to be dead matter, and the Book uses that observation to make its case about resurrection. The sūrah of Yā-Sīn puts the two together when it says that there is a sign in the dead earth: God gives it life and produces grain from it for people to eat (36:33).

**The Name That Comes From Splitting**

Commentators noticed that the Arabic term for the One who splits the seed shares its root with the divine title the Originator, which the Book uses for God in the phrase Originator of the heavens and the earth. The title appears in the sūrahs of Ibrāhīm, Fāṭir, the Troops, Consultation, and elsewhere, and the sūrah used it in the declaration Abraham makes when he turns his face toward the One who originated the heavens and the earth (6:79).

That connection gives the image its theological weight. Creation in the Book's language is not assembly from existing parts but an originating, and the splitting of a seed is the visible form of the same power at work. The sūrah's audience, who watched the fields around their city come to life every season, was being shown the operation of the creating command in the ordinary course of nature.

**Bringing the Living From the Dead**

He brings forth the living from the dead and the dead from the living. The sentence states the cycle in both directions, and the Book repeats it in several sūrahs. The sūrah of the Family of Imran uses it in a prayer that addresses God as the one who causes the night to pass into the day and brings the living from the dead (3:27); the sūrah of Yūnus includes it in a list of questions the idolaters answer by naming God (10:31); and the sūrah of the Romans states it and then says that this is how people will be brought forth from the grave (30:19).

The commentators explained the two directions in several ways. The living coming from the dead covers the creation of a human being and the raising of the dead; the dead coming from the living covers death itself and the natural cycle by which a living plant produces a seed that must be buried before it grows. The two divine names that the theologians attach to these acts, the Giver of Life and the Bringer of Death, name the same pair of operations.

**The Argument From Ordinary Observation**

The strength of the verse's argument lies in its ordinariness. The audience did not need to travel or to be shown anything they had not seen. They lived from agriculture and from the produce of the soil, and every harvest repeated the demonstration that God brings life out of death. The Book makes the same point about rain when it says that God sends the winds and drives the clouds to a dead land so that the earth revives, and then states that this is how He will bring the dead to life (7:57).

The Book uses this form of argument repeatedly because it does not depend on accepting the messenger's authority. Long before the question of revelation is raised, the audience had watched the process they were being asked to accept as a sign, and the sūrah expects them to draw the conclusion from what they already knew.

**The Conclusion Drawn**

That is Allah! How can you then be deluded? The sentence states the conclusion and then asks how the audience could have missed it, and the Book's word for delusion describes being turned away from a clear path. The question is not an expression of surprise at the audience's ignorance; it is a statement about the evidence available to them.

The sūrah has been asking this form of question throughout. It asked how those who had been rescued at sea could then associate others with God (6:64), and it asked how the people who argued with Abraham could fail to be mindful of the One who encompasses everything in knowledge (6:80). The question here closes the first of a series of signs, and the same structure returns in the verses that follow.

**The Sequence the Sūrah Is Building**

The verses that follow continue with the dawn, the night, the sun, the moon, and the stars, and they form a catalogue of the created order similar to the arguments the sūrah has used against the Makkans throughout. What distinguishes this passage is its position in the sūrah: it comes directly after the description of the wrongdoers arriving before God with nothing, and it functions as the answer to the isolation described there.

The people who were stripped of their intercessors and their ties are the people who lived in a world full of signs of the power they had ignored. The sūrah does not leave that contrast implicit. It names the signs one by one, and it ends the series with a statement about how clearly they have been made for those who know.
verses.96:
> He causes the dawn to break, and has made the night for rest and ˹made˺ the sun and the moon ˹to travel˺ with precision. That is the design of the Almighty, All-Knowing

**The Dawn as a Sign**

He causes the dawn to break. The Book's word for the breaking of the dawn is the same root used for splitting something open, which links this sentence to the previous verse about the seed and the fruit stone. The night is rent by the light in the same way that the seed is opened by the shoot, and the sūrah places the two images side by side so that the audience reads them together.

The Book uses the same root for the daybreak in other places, including the sūrah that opens with the seeking of refuge in the Lord of the daybreak. The ordinary event of the morning is thus treated as an act of God rather than as a mechanical occurrence, and the sūrah's chain of signs gains a second item that the audience had watched from childhood.

**The Night Made for Rest**

And has made the night for rest. The verse names a purpose for the darkness, and the Book states the same arrangement in the sūrah of the News, where it says that God made sleep for rest, the night as a covering, and the day for livelihood (78:9–11). The sūrah of the Discernment gives the same set of functions in slightly different words, saying that God made the night a covering, sleep a repose, and the day a rising (25:47).

The sūrah used this particular gift at length in the passage about God calling back the souls of people at night and reviving them by day (6:60), and it treated the alternation as a daily demonstration of the resurrection. Here the same gift is listed among the signs of the created order, which shows how firmly the sūrah's argument ties the ordinary rhythm of human life to its claims about the Hereafter.

**The Sun and the Moon With Precision**

And made the sun and the moon to travel with precision. The Book attaches the same description to the two luminaries in several places: the sūrah of the Most Compassionate says that the sun and the moon travel with precision (55:5); the sūrah of Yūnus says that God made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases so that people might know the number of years and the calculation of time (10:5); and the sūrah of the Troops says that the sun and the moon each orbit for an appointed term (39:5).

The precision in view is the order that makes calendars possible, and the audience, whose religious year depended on the moon, understood what it meant. The sūrah of the Cow records the question about the phases of the moon and answers that they are a means for people to determine time and the pilgrimage (2:189). The verse in front of us states the arrangement as a design rather than as a convenience, and the design is credited to the One whose signs the sūrah has been presenting.

**The Two Names That Close the Sentence**

That is the design of the Almighty, All-Knowing. The two names state the attributes that the created order displays: the power that holds the arrangement in place and the knowledge that measured it out. The Book attaches the same pair to the same subject in the sūrah of Yā-Sīn, where it says that the sun travels for its fixed term and that this is the design of the Almighty, the All-Knowing (36:38).

The consistency of the Book's language is worth noticing. Wherever it describes the regular motions of the heavens, it uses the vocabulary of measuring and decreeing, and wherever it names the attributes of God in those passages it names power together with knowledge. The sūrah's audience lived in a culture attentive to the stars, and the verses answer the attention by pointing it to the arrangement rather than to the objects.

**What the Sign Does Not Do**

The sūrah's description of the dawn, the night, the sun, and the moon is followed by the statement that God has made the signs clear for people who know (6:97). The sequence leaves open the outcome the sūrah has been documenting from its opening: the signs are clear, and clear signs do not compel a response. The sūrah has described people who saw the same sky and drew the conclusions the verses are correcting, and it has described people who read the signs and were led by them.

The difference between the two responses is the subject of the sūrah's constant attention, and this passage states the difference in terms of knowledge. The signs are made clear for people who know, and the sūrah's next verses supply the next sign in the series: the stars that guide travellers across land and sea.

**The Order of the Signs**

The order in this verse moves from the small to the vast. The seed and the fruit stone open the series, then the daybreak, then the night, then the two great luminaries whose motion measures the years. The sequence gives the audience a ladder of evidence from the field outside their walls to the sky above them, and each rung is something they had handled or watched.

The next verse adds the stars, which are the complement of the sun and moon in the sūrah's argument. The two luminaries mark time, and the stars give direction, so the Book's catalogue covers both the calendar and the road. The audience that used both was being asked to acknowledge the One who made both, and the verse states the acknowledgement as a matter of knowledge rather than of ritual.
verses.97:
> And He is the One Who has made the stars as your guide through the darkness of land and sea. We have already made the signs clear for people who know

**The Stars as Guides**

And He is the One Who has made the stars as your guide through the darkness of land and sea. The sūrah has just described the sun and the moon marking time; this verse names the stars and gives them a different function, which is navigation. The Book uses the same image in the sūrah of the Bee, where it says that by landmarks and stars people find their way (16:16), and it repeats the phrase about the darkness of land and sea in the passage on the keys of the unseen (6:59).

The pairing of land and sea covers the two forms of travel the Makkans knew, and both depended on the night sky. A caravan crossing the desert steered by the stars, and a ship on the water did the same. The Book takes the most ordinary use of the heavens in the audience's daily economic life and presents it as a gift with a purpose, which is the same method it used with the seed, the dawn, and the night.

**The Stars as Subjected Creatures**

The Book's account of the stars in other sūrahs makes their status plain. The sūrah of the Heights describes the sun, the moon, and the stars as subjected by God's command and says that creation and command belong to Him alone (7:54); the sūrah of the Bee lists the stars among the things made subject for human benefit and says that in this there are signs for people who understand (16:12); and the sūrah of the Discernment describes the constellations God placed in the sky along with a radiant lamp and a luminous moon (25:61).

There is a pointed contrast between the Book's treatment of the stars and the practices of the audience. The Makkans venerated certain heavenly bodies and consulted astrologers about their influence, and the sūrah of the Cattle earlier showed Abraham testing the star and rejecting it when it set (6:76). The same objects that were folded into the region's astrology are presented here as servants of the travellers who used them.

**The Darkness That Requires a Guide**

The phrase about the darkness of land and sea deserves attention because the Book regularly uses darkness as an image of confusion.
