The sūrah described the man seduced by satans in the open country as one who has lost his way (6:71), and it uses darkness for the state of a person without guidance in several passages. The gift of the stars is therefore an image of guidance in the plain sense as well as a service to travellers.

The Book states that God guides the believers out of darkness into light in several sūrahs, and it describes the disbelievers as those in layers of darkness, one above another, so that a man cannot see his own hand. Against that background, the sentence about stars guiding through the dark is more than physical: it names the visible form of the guidance that the sūrah has been offering since its opening verse.

**The Signs Made Clear for People Who Know**

We have already made the signs clear for people who know. The sentence closes the verse with a statement about the audience's capacity rather than about the quality of the signs. The clarity has been supplied, and what the verse names is the kind of reader who benefits from it, which is the same qualification the sūrah attached to its earlier account of the varying of the signs (6:46).

The Book attaches the same qualification to other passages about its signs, saying that they are made clear for people who know, for people who understand, and for people who believe. The phrasing is the Book's way of stating that the evidence is not the variable. What differs between two people looking at the same sky is the knowledge they bring to it, and the sūrah has spent many verses describing what happens when that knowledge is absent.

**What the Audience Did With the Sky**

The sūrah has already recorded the audience's use of the heavens in the story of Abraham, where the star, the moon, and the sun were examined and abandoned as candidates for divinity (6:76–78). The same city that steered its caravans by the stars had also built its religion around them, and the two uses of the same objects are set side by side in the sūrah's argument. The verse in front of us names the gift of guidance through the night and leaves the reader to notice what the audience did with it.

That is the practical form of the sūrah's claim about knowledge. The stars were available to everyone in the region, and the difference between a traveller who reached his destination and one who lost the road lay partly in his ability to read them. The sūrah uses the image because it wants the audience to see the same arrangement in matters of revelation: the sign is there, and the reading of it is the work the Book asks for.

**The Series and Its Conclusion**

The passage that began with the seed and the fruit stone has now run through the daybreak, the night, the sun, the moon, and the stars, and each item has been an object the audience used or watched. The series is not a catalogue of wonders but a list of services: food from the soil, rest in the dark, a calendar, and a compass. The Book's argument in this sūrah typically proceeds in that way, since its aim is to show the audience that the powers they credited to other beings were exercised by the One who made them.

The verse ends with the audience's knowledge rather than with the signs themselves, and the sūrah's next verse continues the series with a different kind of evidence. Having described the order of the created world, the sūrah turns to the origination of human beings themselves, and it will make the same argument from the formation of a single person that it has just made from the sky.
verses.98:
> And He is the One Who originated you all from a single soul, then assigned you a place to live and another to ˹be laid to˺ rest. We have already made the signs clear for people who comprehend

**The Single Soul as the Origin of Humanity**

And He is the One Who originated you all from a single soul. The sentence introduces a new sign after the catalogue of the sky, and it turns from the heavens to the origin of human beings themselves. The Book states the creation from a single soul in several sūrahs: the sūrah of the Women opens with the command to be mindful of the Lord who created humanity from one soul and made its mate from it (4:1); the sūrah of the Heights gives the same account with the detail that the mate was made so that he might find comfort in her (7:189); and the sūrah of the Troops states it as the first item in a passage about the formation of human beings in the wombs (39:6).

The claim serves two arguments at once. It states God's power to originate a species from one beginning, which the sūrah uses as evidence for the power to raise the dead, and it states the common origin of all people, which the Book uses to deny the claims of superior descent that the sūrah has been dismantling throughout this chapter. The sūrah of the Chambers draws the conclusion explicitly when it says that God made people into nations and tribes so that they might know one another, and that the most noble among them is the most mindful (49:13).

**The Two Places Assigned**

Then assigned you a place to live and another to be laid to rest. The Book's commentators offered several readings of the two terms. Some took them as the womb and the grave, which are the two stations a person passes through; others took them as the settled dwelling and the place of rest in the earth; others applied the pair to the living and the dead among human beings; and some gave them a broader sense of the stations of the present life and the Hereafter.

What the readings share is a picture of human life as movement between two stations appointed by God. The sūrah has just described the soul taken at night and returned by day (6:60) and the angels taking the soul at death (6:61), and the pair of places in this verse continues the same account of a life that is measured out from beginning to end. The audience is being told that neither the arrival nor the departure is in its own hands.

**The Third Closing Formula**

We have already made the signs clear for people who comprehend. The passage that began with the seed, the dawn, the night, the sun, the moon, and the stars now carries a third qualification of its audience, and the word used here describes a kind of understanding that grasps relationships and draws conclusions. The previous verses addressed people who know, and this one addresses people who comprehend, while the verse that follows addresses people who believe.

The progression is worth noticing because it shows what the Book expects of its readers. The signs are not merely to be observed; they are to be understood in their connections, and the understanding is meant to produce belief. The sūrah's method in this section has been to present one ordinary phenomenon after another and to let the accumulation do the work, and the closing formulas mark the stages of reception.

**The Argument for Resurrection in the Origin of Life**

The sūrah has used several arguments for the resurrection in the course of its first hundred verses, and this verse's contribution comes from the beginning of human life. The sūrah of the Romans states the same case in a compact form, saying that He who originates the creation will repeat it, and that this is easy for Him. The sūrah also uses the revived earth, the seed that splits, and the daily return of consciousness, and each of these arguments works by pointing to a repetition the audience already accepted.

The argument from the single soul is the deepest of the series because it concerns the origin of the reader himself. The Book asks a person to consider that he was brought into being from a beginning he did not manage, and it treats the second bringing-forth as a smaller matter than the first, since the power that performed the first has already been demonstrated.

**What the Verse Says About Human Equality**

The sentence also states a fact about the human family that the sūrah's audience needed to hear. The Makkans divided their society by clan, wealth, and lineage, and the sūrah had already told the Prophet not to dismiss the poor believers at the request of the notables (6:52) and had described the differences of rank as a test (6:53). The claim that all people come from one soul cuts across every division the city maintained.

That claim is the ground on which the Book builds its repeated rejection of ancestral pride, and the sūrah has applied the same reasoning to the prophets in the catalogue of the previous verses, where the guidance was a gift given to men from different families and lands. The verse in front of us supplies the principle: one origin, one Lord, and a standing determined by mindfulness rather than by descent.

**The Series Continues**

The next verse adds the rain and the orchards to the catalogue of signs, and it does so with a wealth of detail about what the rain produces. The sūrah's method in this passage is to move from what the audience could observe in the sky to what they could handle in the field, and the closing formula shifts once more, so that the signs are described as clear for people who believe.

The whole series moves toward that last description. The knowledge of the sky, the comprehension of the human origin, and the observation of the harvest are all steps on a road whose destination is the community that accepts what the signs say about their giver.
verses.99:
> And He is the One Who sends down rain from the sky—causing all kinds of plants to grow—producing green stalks from which We bring forth clustered grain. And from palm trees come clusters of dates hanging within reach. ˹There are˺ also gardens of grapevines, olives, and pomegranates, similar ˹in shape˺ but dissimilar ˹in taste˺. Look at their fruit as it yields and ripens! Indeed, in these are signs for people who believe

**The Rain and What It Produces**

And He is the One Who sends down rain from the sky, causing all kinds of plants to grow. The sūrah moves from the origin of human beings to the provision that sustains them, and it does so with a description that is unusually detailed for this part of the chapter. Grain in clustered heads, dates hanging within reach, vineyards, olives, and pomegranates: the verse names the crops of the region and invites the reader to look at them.

The Book returns to this list of fruits in several places. The sūrah of the Bee describes the rain producing crops, olives, palm trees, grapevines, and every type of fruit, and calls it a sign for those who reflect (16:11); the sūrah of the Believers names gardens of palm trees and grapevines with abundant fruits (23:19); and the sūrah of the Thunder describes neighbouring tracts of land irrigated by the same water, with some fruits made better in taste than others, calling this a sign for those who understand (13:4). The details in this verse belong to a pattern the Book uses whenever it wants its audience to look at what they eat.

**The Pairing of Similar and Dissimilar**

Similar in shape but dissimilar in taste. The phrase appears in this sūrah's own passage on the gardens (6:141) and again in this verse, and the observation it records is one the audience could verify in any market. The sūrah of the Thunder makes the same point about the same water feeding different soils and producing different flavours (13:4), and it draws the conclusion that this is a sign for people who understand.

The choice of that particular observation shows the method at work. The Book is not pointing to a rare wonder but to a familiar contrast that a person stops noticing after childhood. Olive and pomegranate, similar in form and unlike in taste: the sentence asks the reader to treat that familiarity as evidence, and it does so in the middle of a passage about the resurrection and the power of God.

**"Look at Their Fruit"**

Look at their fruit as it yields and ripens. The command to look is the Book's ordinary way of directing attention, and it appears throughout the created-order passages. The sūrah of ʿAbasa tells the reader to consider his food and then describes the rain, the earth, and the crops that come from it (80:24), and the sūrah of the Cow gives the same sequence in a passage about the revived earth.

The instruction to watch the fruit as it yields and ripens is precise. The verse does not ask for an opinion about the origin of the world; it asks for attention to a process the reader can follow over weeks. The Book's arguments in this sūrah are built on the things people handled every day, and this verse's command makes the reader's own observation the evidence.

**The Signs for People Who Believe**

Indeed, in these are signs for people who believe. The clause closes the series that began with the seed by naming belief as the capacity in question, and it completes the progression across three verses. The signs of the sky were clear for people who know (6:97); the sign of the single soul was clear for people who comprehend (6:98); the signs of the harvest are clear for people who believe (6:99).

The variation in the closing clauses is not a stylistic flourish. The Book's vocabulary of reception moves from knowledge to understanding to belief, and it treats the last as the fullest response. A person may know that the rain produces the harvest, and understand that the same water feeds different soils; belief is what happens when he attributes the arrangement to the One the sūrah has been naming.

**The Verse and the Audience's Religion**

The crops named in this verse were also the crops the Makkans offered to their gods. The sūrah's later passages describe the shares they assigned to God and to their idols, and the Book's account of those practices includes the division of harvests between the Creator and the beings He had nothing to do with. The passage in front of us prepares the argument for that section by describing the produce as the gift of the One who sends the rain.

The sūrah is therefore laying out the evidence for the claim it will make in a few verses' time. The fruits the audience ate and offered had come from the sky and the earth in the order described here, and the Book's argument against the division of the harvest begins with the account of who produced it.

**The Completion of the Series**

The catalogue of signs that began with the splitting seed has now covered the sky, the human person, and the field, and it ends with the verse that follows it moving to the claims the audience made about the divine nature. The sūrah has provided the evidence and will now address the beliefs that ignored it, starting with the association of the jinn with God and the attribution of children to Him.

That transition gives the passage its shape. The created order, with all its provision and variety, is set before the reader; the reader is asked to look and to believe; and the sūrah then describes what the audience believed instead. The contrast is the argument.
verses.100:
> Yet they associate the jinn with Allah ˹in worship˺, even though He created them, and they falsely attribute to Him sons and daughters out of ignorance. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they claim

**The Jinn Associated With God**

Yet they associate the jinn with Allah in worship, even though He created them. The verse names a specific form of the audience's belief, and the Book records the same practice elsewhere. The sūrah of the Ranged says that the idolaters established a relationship between God and the jinn, and it notes that the jinn themselves know that those who say such things will be brought for punishment (37:158). The sūrah of the Jinn records the jinn's own declaration that their Lord has taken neither a mate nor offspring (72:3).

The claim being refuted took several forms in the region's religions: that the jinn were divine beings with a share in the rule of the world, that they were God's offspring, and that certain objects of worship were their representatives. The verse's answer to all of it is contained in a single clause: He created them. Whatever is created cannot be a partner of its creator, and the sūrah has been applying that reasoning to idols, celestial bodies, and prophets throughout the chapter.

**The Argument From Creation**

The phrase He created them is the same argument the sūrah used against the idols, where it said that the beings invoked besides God are created like their worshippers (7:194). What changes from one passage to the next is only the category of being: in each case the Book removes the possibility of divinity by stating the fact of creation.

The audience's error in this verse is worth stating plainly because it is not a crude mistake. They believed in unseen beings and in their influence, and the sūrah does not deny that the jinn exist. What it denies is the elevation of a created order to a share in the divine, which is the same error it has been correcting in every form of idolatry it has described.

**The Attribution of Sons and Daughters**

And they falsely attribute to Him sons and daughters out of ignorance. The Book records several versions of this claim. The sūrah of the Night Journey asks the pagans whether their Lord has favoured them with sons while taking angels as daughters, and it calls the claim outrageous (17:40); the sūrah of the Star records the same objection, asking whether they prefer sons for themselves while attributing daughters to God (53:21); and the sūrah of the Ornament says that they labelled the angels, who are servants of the Most Compassionate, as female, and asks whether they witnessed their creation (43:19).

The Book's response to the claim about the angels and the claim about Jesus follows the same line, and the sūrah of the Table and the sūrah of the Women address the Christian formulation directly by saying that the Messiah was a messenger of God and that God is far above having a son (4:171). To attribute offspring to God is, in the Book's account, to import the conditions of created life into the divine, and the verse names the source of that error as ignorance.

**The Phrase Out of Ignorance**

The word the translation renders as ignorance describes the absence of knowledge rather than a defect of intellect, and the sūrah has used the same charge repeatedly. It said that those who argued about the signs were following nothing but conjecture, and it said that the idolaters spoke about God what they did not know. The attribution of children to God is presented here as a claim made without evidence, and the Book's objection is to the presumption of speaking about God on the basis of inherited custom.

That charge is the sūrah's consistent method with the audience's theology. The Book never presents the Makkan beliefs as a rival system that has been examined and found wanting; it presents them as assertions inherited from ancestors and defended for reasons that had nothing to do with their truth.

**The Formula of Transcendence**

Glorified and Exalted is He above what they claim. The verse ends with the Book's standard declaration of God's transcendence, and the declaration is used throughout the Book at exactly these points, where a false claim about God has been described. The sūrah of the Cow records the claim that God has offspring and answers it with the same words before stating that everything in the heavens and the earth is subject to Him (2:116).

The formula is not a substitute for argument but the conclusion of it. Having stated what the audience claimed and why the claim conflicts with God's relation to His creation, the verse separates the Creator from the description entirely, and it does so with the vocabulary of exaltation that the Book uses in its descriptions of God's majesty. The next verse supplies the positive account of what God is, in a sentence built from the same argument.

**What the Verse Establishes for the Sūrah**

The passage that follows this verse states that God is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, that He has no mate, and that He created everything and knows everything (6:101). The two verses belong together, since the denial of offspring in this verse gives way to the explanation of why the claim is impossible in the next.

The sūrah is also closing the section of signs that ran from the seed to the harvest, and it does so by naming the beliefs that the signs should have corrected. The audience had watched the creation, the rain, the growth, and the harvest, and the verse states what they made of it: an association of created beings with the Creator and a set of claims about His family. The contrast between the two accounts is the argument, and the sūrah states it without further comment.
verses.101:
> ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and earth. How could He have children when He has no mate? He created all things and has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of everything

**The Originator of the Heavens and the Earth**

He is the Originator of the heavens and earth. The title is one the sūrah has used before, both in the command given to the Prophet to declare that he will take no guardian other than the Originator of the heavens and the earth (6:14) and in Abraham's declaration when he turned his face toward the One who originated the heavens and the earth (6:79). The Book uses the title consistently in the phrase Originator of the heavens and the earth, and the commentators noted that its root carries the sense of splitting open, which connects it to the image of the seed that splits at the beginning of this passage about signs.

The term describes a creator who brings things into being without a prior model, and the sūrah uses it here to answer the claim about offspring made in the previous verse. A being who originates the heavens and the earth has no need of a consort, and the sentence that follows states the reasoning plainly.

**How Could He Have Children?**

How could He have children when He has no mate? The question reduces the claim to an impossibility in a single clause, and the Book makes the same argument elsewhere in its own voice. The sūrah of the Cow answers the claim that God has offspring by saying that everything in the heavens and the earth is subject to Him (2:116), and the sūrah of Maryam states that it is not for God to take a son, since when He decrees a matter He simply says to it, Be, and it is (19:35).

The Book's argument about offspring rests on two observations: children are produced through the union of mates, and God has no mate; and everything other than God is created, whereas a child would have to share in the divine nature. The sūrah of Sincerity gathers the conclusion into a single declaration that God has never had offspring and was never born (112:3), and the sūrah of the Women addresses the same claim in its discussion of Jesus, saying that the Messiah was no more than a messenger of God and that God is far above having a son (4:171).

**The Claim About Jesus in the Sūrah's Setting**

The Makkans' claim about daughters and the Christians' claim about a son were both present in the region the sūrah addresses, and the Book treats them together as instances of a single error. The verse's question applies to both, since the reasoning does not depend on the identity of the offspring. What the sūrah denies is the dependence of God on anything at all, and the next clause states the positive basis of the denial.

The Book's statements about Jesus elsewhere uniformly preserve his honour while denying the claim about his nature, and the sūrah of the Table records his own declaration that he is a servant of God. The verse in front of us belongs to that pattern, and its argument applies to any creature that the audience might have placed on the divine side of the line.

**He Created All Things**

He created all things. The clause states the fact on which the argument turns. If everything besides God is created, then nothing besides God is ultimate, and the relations that belong to created things cannot be predicated of Him. The sūrah has used this reasoning in every form of the argument against idolatry it has presented: the idols are created like their worshippers (7:194), the jinn are created and therefore cannot be partners (6:100), and the angels are servants of the Most Compassionate (43:19).

The Book states the same principle in the sūrah of the Thunder, where it declares that God is the Creator of all things and the One, the Supreme (13:16). The sentence in this verse is therefore more than a statement of fact; it is the premise from which the sūrah's denials proceed, and the audience is expected to recognise it as the basis of everything the Book has been saying about worship.

**Knowledge of Everything**

And has perfect knowledge of everything. The verse closes with the attribute the sūrah has attached to God at several points in the chapter. It said earlier that God knows what is on land and sea and that not a leaf falls without His knowledge (6:59), and it described His knowledge as encompassing everything in the argument attributed to Abraham (6:80). The closing phrase here connects the account of creation with the account of the record, since the One who made all things is the One who knows all things.

The pairing of creation and knowledge appears in the Book's descriptions of God wherever it describes His relation to what He has made, and it appears in the sūrahs' closing formulas. The knowledge is not a general awareness but the knowledge of particulars, as the sūrah's earlier verses on the leaf and the grain made clear, and the phrase in this verse carries the same force.

**What the Verse Completes**

The verse completes the sūrah's answer to the claims made in the previous one, and it does so by supplying the positive account of God that the denials presuppose. The audience had associated created beings with God and attributed offspring to Him; the sūrah answers that God originates everything, needs no mate, creates all things, and knows everything. Each clause of the answer is a statement the sūrah has already made elsewhere in the chapter.

The next verse moves to a new subject and opens one of the sūrah's most striking passages, in which the Book describes the limitations of human sight and the reality of God's perception. The argument about God's nature has been stated in terms the audience could follow; the sūrah now turns to what can and cannot be seen.
verses.102:
> That is Allah—your Lord! There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him. ˹He is˺ the Creator of all things, so worship Him ˹alone˺. And He is the Maintainer of everything

**The Conclusion Drawn From the Argument**

That is Allah, your Lord! The sentence gathers the whole preceding account of the created order and attaches a name to it, and the Book's demonstrative form is the same one it used when it described the splitting of the seed and asked how the audience could be deluded (6:95). The verse identifies the subject of the signs: the One who originated, provided, guided, and knew, and it states the identity as a conclusion rather than as a new claim.

The passage has been building to this sentence for several verses. The sūrah described the sky, the human origin, the rain and the harvest, and then answered the claims about the jinn and about offspring, and the verse in front of us states what the audience should have concluded from all of it. The Book's method is to let the accumulation of evidence produce a declaration, and the declaration comes at the end.

**The Formula of Exclusive Worship**

There is no god worthy of worship except Him. The sentence is the Book's central confession, and it appears in this sūrah in the context of an audience that had many gods. The formula does not merely reduce the number; it denies the category, since the Book's claim is that everything the audience called divine lacked the standing the word implies.

The Book attaches the same formula to its conclusions about the created order in other passages, and it uses it as the boundary of the community's identity. The sūrah has already used it twice in its first hundred verses, and its reappearance here marks the end of a section of argument rather than the beginning of one.

**The Creator Who Is Worshipped**

He is the Creator of all things, so worship Him alone. The verse moves from the fact of creation to the command to worship, and the connection is the sūrah's persistent argument. The Makkans already accepted that God had created everything; their error lay in the conclusion they drew from the fact, and the verse states what the conclusion should be.

The Book makes the same connection in the sūrah of the Troops, where it states that God is the Creator of all things and the Maintainer of everything (39:62), and in the sūrah of the Thunder, where the acknowledgement of God as the Creator of all things is followed by the declaration that He is the One, the Supreme (13:16). The command to worship in this verse is the practical form of a fact the audience had already granted.

**The Maintainer of Everything**

And He is the Maintainer of everything. The Book's term describes the one who manages and arranges the affairs entrusted to him, and the sūrah has applied it to God at several points. The sūrah of the Troops uses the same title for God at the head of a passage on provision (39:62); the sūrah of Hūd states that God is the Trustee of all affairs (11:12); and the sūrah of the Confederates says that God is sufficient as a Trustee of affairs (33:3).

Attached to a passage about creation and worship, the title states that the arrangement described in the previous verses was not a single act that has since been left alone. The stars keep their courses, the rain comes, the harvest ripens, and the provisions of every creature arrive because the One who made the world continues to run it, and the verse names that ongoing management in a single phrase.

**Maintenance and the Everyday Evidence of It**

The title the Book attaches to God in this verse appears elsewhere in the context of provision. The sūrah of Fāṭir asks whether there is any creator other than God who provides for the audience from the heavens and the earth, and it follows the question with the same declaration of exclusive divinity that stands in this verse (35:3). The sūrah of Consultation says that God is kind to His servants and provides abundantly for whoever He wills, and it names Him the All-Powerful, the Almighty (42:19). Both passages join the act of providing to the title of maintainer, which is the pairing this verse makes.

The Book treats that pairing as the answer to the audience's practical worries. The sūrah of the Spider states that many creatures cannot secure their own provisions and that God provides for them and for the people who worry about them (29:60), and the sūrah of Hūd says that no creature on earth lacks a provision guaranteed by God and that everything is written in a perfect record (11:6). The Makkans who heard this verse lived from trade caravans and from the produce of the oases, and the Book's claim was that the arrangement behind both was the same arrangement described in the verses about the rain and the harvest.

**What the Verse Means for the Sūrah's Audience**

For the Makkans, the sentence was a direct challenge to their practice. They had their own answer to the question of creation, and the verse takes their answer and draws the conclusion they refused to draw. It does not ask them to accept a new fact about the origin of the world; it asks them to worship the being they already acknowledged as its maker.

The Book's argument in this chapter has proceeded in exactly that way throughout. It asked who provides, who rescues, who gives hearing and sight, and it recorded the audience's answers. The verse in front of us is the conclusion the sūrah has been working toward, and the verses that follow it turn to the question of whether God can be seen and to the responsibility of the people who have been shown the signs.
verses.103:
> No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision. For He is the Most Subtle, All-Aware

**The Verse That Says God Is Beyond Sight**

No vision can encompass Him, but He encompasses all vision. The sentence states a limit on human perception and a corresponding attribute of God, and the Book's commentators treated it as one of the most important verses in the Qur'an on the subject of seeing God. The Book says that eyes cannot reach Him and that His perception reaches everything, and it arranges the two clauses as a contrast between what creatures can do and what the Creator does.

The two verbs are the same in the Arabic, which is why the sentence has the shape it has: no vision encompasses Him, and He encompasses all vision. The verse does not simply deny that God is visible; it denies that any act of perception can take Him in, and it states that the relation of knowledge runs in the opposite direction.

**How the Companions Used the Verse**

The earliest community read this verse as a statement about the vision of God, and the reports about ʿĀisha are the clearest example. When she was told that some people claimed that the Prophet had seen his Lord, she rejected the claim and cited this verse, saying that anyone who told her that Muhammad had seen his Lord had told a lie, because God says that no vision can encompass Him. The report is recorded by al-Bukhārī and it shows how the verse functioned in the community's theology from the beginning.

ʿĀisha used the same style of argument against the claim that the Prophet had been shown the unseen, citing the verse that says none has knowledge of the unseen but God and the report about the five keys. The two verses together, this one and the one on the keys of the unseen (6:59), furnished the early community with its account of the limits of created knowledge.

**The Debate About Seeing God**

The verse entered the later theological discussions as one of the central texts. Some held that God cannot be seen at all, and they cited this verse together with the answer given to Moses when he asked to see his Lord and was told that he could not see Him, though the mountain was levelled when God appeared to it (7:143). Others held that the verse refers to the perception of the eyes in this world and that the believers will be granted the vision of God in the Hereafter, and they cited other passages for that hope.

What the verse itself settles is the inability of human perception to contain God, and the Book elsewhere states that no vision can reach Him while He perceives everything. The passage about Moses adds the detail that even a prophet's request was answered with a limit, and the two verses together define the discussion for every generation that has taken it up.

**The Names at the End**

For He is the Most Subtle, All-Aware. The two names explain why the contrast in the first half of the verse holds. The Most Subtle describes a being whose knowledge penetrates what is hidden from every other observer, and the All-Aware describes a knowledge of the inner reality of things. Together they state the reason that God perceives what no eye can reach.

The sūrah has attached the same vocabulary to God throughout its account of the hidden and the seen. It said that God knows what is on land and sea and that not a leaf falls without His knowledge (6:59); it described His knowledge as encompassing everything in Abraham's argument (6:80); and it stated that He has the keys of the unseen (6:59). The names that close this verse are the summary of that whole account.

**The Creation and the Knowledge of It**

The sūrah of the Kingdom puts the two halves of this verse's logic together in a single sentence, asking how the One who created could fail to know what He has made, and naming Him the Most Subtle, the All-Aware (67:14). That is the reasoning that stands behind this verse: the maker of a thing knows it in a way no outside observer can, and the knowledge described in the second clause is the knowledge of the one who formed what He sees.

The Book states the same principle through the image of the mustard seed in the counsel of Luqmān, where the father tells his son that a deed the weight of a seed, hidden in a rock or in the heavens or the earth, will be brought out by God, who is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware (31:16). The closing names of this verse carry the same scope, and the sūrah of the Women and the sūrah of the Confederates attach the pair to the recording of what people do. A perception that runs through rock and seed and sky is the perception the sūrah has claimed for God throughout, and this verse states it as the ground of the account that follows.

**What the Verse Does for the Sūrah's Argument**

Read in place, the verse answers a question the previous verses had raised. The sūrah had presented the audience with God as the Creator and Maintainer of everything, and the natural response of a person hearing that description is to look for the object described. The verse states that the search will not succeed and that the perception which matters runs from God toward the world rather than the other way.

That arrangement is what makes the record described in the previous verses possible. A God who is seen by His creatures could not know them as this sūrah has described Him knowing them, and the verse's second clause is the ground of the first. The Book's arguments about the leaf, the grain, and the deeds of human beings all rest on the fact that nothing is beyond His awareness.

**The Transition That Follows**

The next verse turns from the description of God to the responsibility of the people who have been given this knowledge, saying that insights have come from the Lord and that whoever chooses to see does so for his own good while whoever chooses blindness does so to his own loss (6:104). The verses function as a pair: the true account of God is stated, and the reader is told that the response to it is his own.

The sūrah has been making the same point since its account of the blind and the seeing (6:50), and the pairing in these two verses is its final statement of the principle in this section. What follows is a series of further signs, and the audience is left with a choice that the Book describes without pressure.
verses.104:
> Indeed, there have come to you insights from your Lord. So whoever chooses to see, it is for their own good. But whoever chooses to be blind, it is to their own loss. And I am not a keeper over you

**The Insights Given From the Lord**

Indeed, there have come to you insights from your Lord. The Book's word for what has come is a plural of perception or discernment, and the commentaries describe it as the clear evidences by which a person sees the truth of the message. The sūrah of the Story uses the same word for the Scripture given to Moses, calling it an insight for the people, a guide, and a mercy (28:43), and the sūrah of the Kneeling describes the Qur'an as an insight for humanity, a guide and mercy for people of sure faith (45:20).

The verse therefore describes the message as something the audience already possesses rather than as something still being offered. The signs have been recited, the argument has been made, and the insights have arrived. What the sentence does is place the responsibility for using them where it belongs, which is the subject of its next two clauses.

**Whoever Chooses to See**

So whoever chooses to see, it is for their own good. But whoever chooses to be blind, it is to their own loss. The two clauses use the language of sight and blindness, which the sūrah has already established in its earlier questions about whether the blind and the seeing can be equal (6:50). What the verse adds is the element of choice: the reader is described as the one who decides, and the consequences are attached to the decision rather than to the perception.

The Book states the same arrangement in several places. The sūrah of the Cave says that the message is the truth from the Lord and that whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve (18:29); the sūrah of the Ant has the Prophet told to recite and then to say that whoever chooses guidance does so for his own good and that the messenger is only a warner (27:92); and the sūrah of the Troops says the same about guidance and straying (39:41). The formula protects the freedom that the Book's invitations presuppose.

**The Language of Benefit and Loss**

The verse attaches the outcome to the person who chooses, and the attachment is stated in the vocabulary of personal profit and damage. The Book's ethical framework regularly describes the consequences of conduct in these terms, since it presents the commands of God as instructions for the good of the people addressed rather than as requirements that serve Him. The sūrah of the Bee states that whoever does right does so for his own soul and whoever does wrong does so against it.

The two clauses in this verse give the same structure to belief and denial. Seeing benefits the person who sees, and blindness harms the person who closes his eyes. Nothing in the sentence suggests that either outcome is a matter of indifference to God; the whole sūrah has been describing the consequences that follow from each choice, and the verse states the direction in which the consequences fall.

**"I Am Not a Keeper Over You"**

And I am not a keeper over you. The sentence returns to a refrain the sūrah has used twice before. The Prophet was told to say that he is not a keeper over the people at the end of a passage about the truth that had come to him (6:66), and the same denial appears in the account of his own announcement that he follows what is revealed to him (6:50 context). The sūrah of Yūnus and the sūrah of the Troops attach the same statement to the message (10:108; 39:41).

The repetition is a feature of the sūrah's method rather than a lapse, and it marks the points at which the audience is being told that the messenger's role has limits. The insights have come from the Lord, the choice belongs to the person who hears them, and the man who delivers them is not responsible for the outcome. What the Book does with this recurring statement is to remove the pressure that the Prophet's grief over his people had placed on him.

**What the Verse Assumes About the Reader**

The sentence assumes that a person can see and can refuse to see, and it treats the refusal as an act rather than as a condition. The sūrah's account of the deniers has consistently described them in the vocabulary of activity: they turn away, they argue, they deny, they mock, and they take the message as play. The choice in this verse is the ordinary form of all those actions, and the Book's ethical seriousness depends on it.

The verse also assumes that the reader has received what he needs in order to decide. The insights have come, and the Book's invitation is not to a leap in the dark. That is why the sūrah can state the consequences so plainly, and why it leaves the choice with the person who hears.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse describes the varying of the signs and the accusation that will follow from it: the disbelievers will say that the Prophet has studied the earlier scriptures, and the Book will answer that the message has been made clear for people who know (6:105). The two verses belong together, since both concern the response of the people who were receiving the clearest possible presentation of the message.

The sūrah's structure in this section is worth noticing. It states the message, states the freedom of the reader, states the limit of the messenger's responsibility, and then describes what the audience did with all of it. The response recorded in the next verse is an accusation about the source of the revelation, which is the same ground the sūrah has been covering since its opening verses.
verses.105:
> And so We vary our signs to the extent that they will say, “You have studied ˹previous scriptures˺,” and We make this ˹Quran˺ clear for people who know

**The Fourth Statement About Varying the Signs**

And so We vary our signs. The sūrah has used this vocabulary three times before. It described the varying of the signs when the audience turned away from the argument about hearing and sight (6:46); it used the same word when the explanation of the signs was said to make the way of the wicked distinct (6:55); and it used it in the warning about the punishments that could come from above, from below, or through the community's own divisions (6:65). The recurrence marks the stages of the sūrah's argument, and each occurrence states a different purpose.

The Book uses the same term elsewhere for the presentation of the message in many forms. The sūrah of the Heights and the sūrah of the Bee describe the signs as varied so that people might be mindful and give thanks, and the sūrah of the Ant speaks of the varying of the signs for a people who understand. What the term describes is a method of instruction rather than a rhetorical flourish, and the sūrah presents it as a deliberate provision for an audience that needed the argument in more than one shape.

**The Accusation That Will Follow**

To the extent that they will say, You have studied previous scriptures. The sentence states what the varying of the signs will produce in the audience, and it records the accusation in advance. The charge is that the Prophet had learned his material from the People of the Book, and the Book records the same charge in several passages: the sūrah of the Bee quotes it and answers that the person the accusers have in mind speaks a foreign tongue while the Qur'an is in eloquent Arabic (16:103); the sūrah of the Discernment records that they said the message was a fabrication made up with the help of others and that it consisted of ancient fables written down and rehearsed morning and evening (25:4–5).

The sūrah's inclusion of the accusation inside a statement of God's own activity is significant. The verse does not present the charge as an unexpected development but as something the varying of the signs would produce, which means the Book treats the accusation as part of the response its method would receive rather than as a refutation of that method.

**Why the Accusation Was Predictable**

The charge was predictable because the Qur'an contains the stories of earlier prophets, and the audience knew that the People of the Book possessed accounts of those figures. The Book's answer to the charge is not to deny that the stories are known but to point to what the revelation contains that no human source could have supplied, and to the fact that the man it accuses speaks a foreign language while the Qur'an is in the most eloquent Arabic.

The sūrah's own method makes the accusation inevitable in another way as well. The varying of the signs means the same truth is presented through the created order, the history of the earlier communities, the arguments of Abraham, and the conditions of the present. An audience determined to resist could always claim that one of those forms had been borrowed, and the Book responds by presenting the accusation rather than disputing it at length.

**The Clarity Given to People Who Know**

And We make this Qur'an clear for people who know. The sentence closes the verse with the same qualification the sūrah has attached to its other accounts of the signs: the clarity is real, and it is realised in people who know. The sūrah has used the phrase about the stars and the signs (6:97), and it has used the same construction at the end of the passage about the varying of the signs earlier (6:55).

The Book's use of this qualification consistently prevents the reader from turning the accusation into an argument against the message. If the audience says the Prophet has studied the earlier books, the answer is that the message has been made clear to those who know, which places the question of response back with the hearer. The clarification is God's act, and the knowledge of the clarified material is the reader's responsibility.

**The Sequence in Which the Verse Stands**

The verse follows the statement that the insights have come from the Lord, that the choice is the reader's, and that the messenger is not a keeper over the people (6:104). Read as a unit, the two verses describe the delivery of the message, the freedom of the response, the limits of the messenger's office, and the accusation that the Book knew would follow. The sūrah is preparing the reader for the rest of the chapter, which continues the argument with a people who had been shown the signs in every form.

The verses that follow turn to the subject of following what has been revealed and of the community that had been given the Book, and the sūrah will return to the guidance of Abraham once more. The pattern established in this passage governs the treatment of those subjects as well: the message is clarified, the response is counted to the person who makes it, and the messenger is a warner rather than a keeper.

**What the Verse Says About the Revelation's Source**

The verse's most important claim is contained in its first three words, since the varying of the signs is attributed to God. The audience's accusation concerned the human source of the message, and the answer given here is that the presentation of the message in different forms is itself the work of the One who sent it. Every new argument the Prophet brought was a fresh instance of that work.

The Book's confidence in this arrangement is part of what it says about the message's authority. A revelation that adapts its arguments to its hearers while keeping the same content is not a text that has been assembled from other texts; it is the address of a speaker who knows whom He is addressing. The sūrah states that in one sentence and leaves the accusation to be recorded beside it.
verses.106:
> ˹O Prophet!˺ Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord—there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him—and turn away from the polytheists

**The Command to Follow What Is Revealed**

Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. The command stands at the head of a passage in which the sūrah turns from the argument with the disbelievers to the instructions given to the Prophet himself, and its position is significant. After many verses of signs, refutations, and accounts of what the audience said, the sūrah states the one thing the messenger is to do with all of it, which is to follow the revelation.

The Book's use of this command elsewhere gives the phrase its force. The sūrah of the Cattle ends its long list of prohibitions with the instruction to follow the straight path and with the declaration that this is what God has commanded (6:153), and the sūrah of the Bee tells the Prophet that God has revealed to him to follow the way of Abraham, who was a man of pure faith (16:123). The command is the practical counterpart of the arguments that precede it.

**The Declaration That Accompanies It**

There is no god worthy of worship except Him. The sūrah inserts the confession in the middle of an instruction, and the arrangement shows how the Book treats the revelation and the declaration as one subject. To follow what is revealed is to act on the content of the message, and the content begins with the statement about God that the sūrah has been arguing for since its opening verses.

The sūrah has attached this sentence to several of its conclusions: to the account of the created order (6:102), to the description of the messenger's own position (6:19 context), and to the declaration of the truth that has come from the Lord. Here it accompanies the command to follow, and the two together state the terms of the Prophet's own obedience. What he is told to do is what every other person addressed by the sūrah was told to do, with the difference that his following includes the delivery of the message.

**The Instruction to Turn Away**

And turn away from the polytheists. The sūrah has issued a similar instruction at earlier points: it told the Prophet to leave those who took their religion as play and amusement (6:70) and it told him to say that he is not a keeper over the people (6:104). The command to turn away in this verse is not a command to abandon the argument, since the sūrah continues to address the audience's objections after it.

The Book's habit with this instruction is to distinguish between the prophet's responsibility for the message and his responsibility for the response. The sūrah of the Ranged tells him to turn away from them and to say peace, for they will come to know; the sūrah of the Pen tells him not to be distressed by those who deny. The turning away in each case belongs to the prophet's own conduct rather than to the mission, and the sūrah's next verse explains what the Prophet is not.

**What the Verse Establishes About the Messenger**

The verse places the messenger under the revelation in the plainest terms. He does not choose the content of what he teaches, and the instruction is given to him rather than to the audience, which is a pattern the sūrah keeps in the passages that address his situation directly. The Book records the same ordering in the sūrah of the Star, where the Prophet's utterance is described as nothing other than revelation sent to him (53:4).

The verse's second half then tells the Prophet how to live in a city that would not accept the message. The command to turn away is attached to a situation in which the Prophet had no power to compel belief and no responsibility for the failure of others to accept it. The sūrah treats that as a fact to be recognised rather than as a problem to be solved.

**The Verses That Define the Limits**

The verse that follows states the limits in a form that leaves no ambiguity: had God willed, they would not have been polytheists, the Prophet has not been appointed as their keeper, and he is not their maintainer (6:107). The two verses belong together, and they answer the question of how a person should act toward a community that has rejected the message he carries.

The Book uses the same structure in other sūrahs, joining a command to the Prophet with a statement about its scope. The sūrah of the Bee says God has guided whom He wills and that the Prophet's duty is to call people to the way of the Lord with wisdom and good instruction (16:125). This sūrah's version of the instruction is to follow, to declare, and to keep his own course, which is what the conclusion of the passage states.

**The Place of the Verse in the Chapter**

The sūrah has been moving through a section about the signs and the responses to them, and this verse begins the closing movement of that section. The arguments against the audience's theology have been made; the created order has been described; and the sūrah now turns to the practical form the message takes in the life of the man who receives it.

That turn gives the chapter its shape. What follows concerns the limits of the messenger's responsibility, the prohibition on insulting the objects the idolaters venerate, the oaths sworn by those who demand a sign, and the nature of what the witnesses among them testify to. Each passage continues the same argument from a different angle, and the instruction to follow what has been revealed remains the point from which they proceed.
verses.107:
> Had Allah willed, they would not have been polytheists. We have not appointed you as their keeper, nor are you their maintainer

**The Statement of Divine Will**

Had Allah willed, they would not have been polytheists. The sentence states that the existence of the audience's idolatry was permitted by God's will, and the sūrah has used the same form of statement elsewhere. It said that had God willed, the whole of humanity would have been one community, and it said that had God willed, no one would have associated partners with Him.

The Book's use of this statement is worth distinguishing from a claim the audience would later make themselves. In a verse near the end of this sūrah, the idolaters are recorded as pleading that if God had willed they would not have associated partners with Him or with Him forbidden anything, and the Book describes that argument as a lie (6:148). The Book makes the same claim as an acknowledgement of God's sovereignty and rejects it when it is offered by the idolaters as a justification for their conduct.

**Why the Two Uses Differ**

The difference between the two uses lies in who is speaking and to what end. When God states that the idolaters would not have disbelieved had He willed it, the sentence establishes His freedom and the inability of His creatures to compel anything. When the idolaters state the same fact, they use it to deny their own responsibility, and the sūrah's account of the final reckoning shows what that claim is worth.

The sūrah of the Bee records the same argument from the idolaters, who said that had God willed, neither they nor their ancestors would have worshipped anything besides Him (16:35), and the Book's answer is that the messengers were sent with clear proofs and that the communities' rejection did not alter the obligation to receive them. The verse in front of us belongs to that pattern, and it explicitly places the responsibility for rejection on the people who chose it, since the Book's very next words describe the Prophet's relationship to them as something other than supervision.

**The Keeper and the Maintainer**

We have not appointed you as their keeper, nor are you their maintainer. The verse names two roles and denies both to the Prophet, and the choice of the two words covers the two ways a person might imagine the messenger's authority. The keeper is the one set over a people to direct and manage them; the maintainer is the one responsible for their affairs and answerable for their condition.

The sūrah has already told the Prophet to say that he is not a keeper over the audience (6:104), and the repetition of the term in this verse joins the two passages as one teaching. The Book's description of the messenger's office elsewhere uses the vocabulary of reminding and warning rather than governance and responsibility: the sūrah of the Covering says that the Prophet is only a reminder and not a controller over the people (88:21–22), and the sūrah of the Prophets says that He was sent as a mercy to the worlds rather than as an enforcer of belief (21:107).

**The Comfort Contained in the Denial**

The sentence is addressed to a man whose people had rejected him, and its purpose is partly to lift a burden. The sūrah opened with the Prophet's grief over their refusal and its record of their arguments, and it has returned at several points to the fact that he does not carry their answer. The denial of the two roles removes from him the responsibility that his own compassion had put on him.

The Book returns to this reassurance in the passages where the Prophet's distress over his people is described. It tells him not to grieve over them and not to be distressed by what they plot, and it tells him that his duty is only the clear delivery of the message. The verse in front of us is one of the places where that reassurance is stated in terms of what God has not appointed him to be.

**The Order of the Two Verses**

Read with the verse that precedes it, the passage gives the Prophet three instructions and two denials. He is to follow what is revealed, to hold the confession, and to turn away from the polytheists; he is not their keeper and he is not their maintainer. The arrangement states what he is to do and then removes the anxiety that would otherwise have accompanied the doing of it.

That order is repeated in the Book's instructions to messengers at several points. The sūrah of the Anbiyā' and the sūrah of Hūd describe the messengers as delivering the message and leaving the outcome to God, and the sūrah of the Forgiver records a believer's appeal to his people with the words that the messengers have no duty other than clear notification. The sūrah has made the point concrete in a city where the messenger lived among the people who denied him.

**What the Verse Says About the Audience's Freedom**

The verse does not remove the audience's responsibility, since it is followed by verses that continue to address their conduct, their oaths, their insults, and their arguments. What the sentence establishes is that God has left the people to their own decisions in the present life, with the messengers sent to inform them of what those decisions entail.

The Book states the same arrangement in the sūrah of the Cave, where the truth is said to come from the Lord and each person is left to believe or disbelieve (18:29). The two verses that stand here combine that freedom with the messenger's own limits, and the sūrah proceeds to the next instruction, which concerns how the Prophet and the believers should speak about the gods the idolaters venerate.
verses.108:
> ˹O believers!˺ Do not insult what they invoke besides Allah or they will insult Allah spitefully out of ignorance. This is how We have made each people’s deeds appealing to them. Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do

**The Prohibition on Reviling the Idols**

Do not insult what they invoke besides Allah. The verse turns from the position of the Prophet to the conduct of the believers, and it issues a prohibition that runs against the obvious religious instinct. The audience of the instruction was a small community in a city whose gods stood in the sanctuary and whose tribes were tied to them, and the instruction told them not to attack those gods with their tongues.

The Book's reason for the prohibition is stated in the same sentence. The verse does not deny that the idols are worthless; it says that insulting them will produce a response that damages the cause of the message, since the idolaters will insult God spitefully out of ignorance. The instruction is therefore concerned with consequences rather than with the status of the objects, and the Book's habit elsewhere supports the reading.

**The Reason Given in the Verse**

Or they will insult Allah spitefully out of ignorance. The prohibition rests on the effect the believers' words would have on the people they were calling. A man who is told that his gods are worthless may respond by attacking the God he has been invited to worship, and the insult would be uttered in ignorance, which is the condition the sūrah has repeatedly attributed to the audience's theology.

The Book applies the same reasoning in its instructions about how the message should be delivered. The sūrah of the Bee commands the Prophet to call people to the way of the Lord with wisdom and good instruction and to argue with them in the manner that is best (16:125), and the sūrah of the Spider gives the same instruction for disputes with the People of the Book (29:46). The prohibition in this verse is the negative form of that method: what the believers were not to do was to speak in a way that made their hearers worse.

**The Conduct the Verse Was Answering**

The practice the verse corrected was a real one. The early community in Makkah had been denouncing the gods of the Quraysh, and the idolaters responded by reviling the God of the Muslims. Reports describe the leaders of the city approaching the Prophet's uncle with a proposal that both sides stop attacking the objects the other venerated, and the verse was understood as the instruction that settled the community's conduct in the matter.

The reports give the instruction a practical setting, but the principle the verse states is independent of that setting. Whenever the reviling of a false object strengthens the hearer in his falsehood, the sentence applies, and the Book's measure is the effect of the speech on the person addressed rather than the desert of the object abused.

**The Deeds Made Fair to Each Community**

This is how We have made each people's deeds appealing to them. The sentence explains why the insult forbidden in the first clause would have the effect described. The idolaters were not weighing the evidence; their practices had been made attractive to them, and the Book describes that condition in many places. The sūrah of the Family of Imran says that the disbelievers should not think that God's respite for them is good for them, since He grants them time only that they may increase in sin (3:178); the sūrah of the Ranged says that those who do wrong are misled in their ways; and the sūrah of the Bee records the idolaters' claim that God willed their practices.

The Book's statements on this subject take several forms. In some passages it attributes the beautifying of evil deeds to Satan, and in others, including this verse, it attributes the arrangement to God, who leaves people to what they have chosen as a test. The two accounts are not in tension in the Book's own presentation, since the testing of human beings includes the possibility of their being confirmed in what they have chosen.

**The Return and the Accounting**

Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do. The verse closes by referring the whole question to the judgment, and the Book uses the same formula at the end of its discussions of the idolaters' conduct. The sūrah of the Spoils uses the phrase after a passage about those who were left behind, saying that their return is to God and that He will inform them of what they did (9:94); the sūrah of Tobā gives the same statement about God's informing people of their deeds (9:105); and the sūrah of Yūnus, the sūrah of the Spider, the sūrah of Luqmān, the sūrah of the Troops, and the sūrah of the Congregation use the same formula in their own contexts.

The formula is the Book's way of closing an argument without forcing its conclusion. The believers are told not to insult the gods of their neighbours, and the outcome of the dispute is left to the day when God will state what each party did. That arrangement is what allows the community to live among people whose practices it rejects.

**Why the Verse Matters for the Community's Conduct**

The instruction has consequences that reach beyond the setting of Makkah. The Book has presented the message as a call addressed to people capable of accepting or rejecting it, and this verse recognises that the call can be defeated by the manner of those who deliver it. The prohibition on insulting what others venerate is thus a rule about the means by which the message should be carried, and it sits alongside the commands to argue in the best manner and to speak gently where harshness would fail.

The verse also protects the community from the illusion that zeal in denunciation is the same as service to God. What the Book requires here is restraint in speech for the sake of the hearer, and the next verse takes up the oaths by which the idolaters promised to believe if a sign came to them, which is another instance of the audience's response to the message.
verses.109:
> They swear by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a sign were to come to them, they would certainly believe in it. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Signs are only with Allah.” What will make you ˹believers˺ realize that even if a sign were to come to them, they still would not believe

**The Oath and What It Promised**

They swear by Allah their most solemn oaths that if a sign were to come to them, they would certainly believe in it. The verse records the terms on which the audience offered to accept the message, and the Book has recorded the same kind of oath elsewhere. The sūrah of Fāṭir says that they swore by God their most solemn oaths that if a warner came to them they would be better guided than any other community, and that when the warner came it only increased their aversion (35:42). The sūrah of the Table and the sūrah of Light record comparable oaths from those who claimed they would follow if only a sign were shown.

The Book treats the demand for a sign as a negotiating position rather than an expression of an open mind, and the oaths recorded in these passages are the clearest evidence for that judgement, since in every case the sign came and the oath was broken.

**The Answer Given to the Prophet**

Say, Signs are only with Allah. The instruction tells the Prophet how to answer, and the answer moves the question out of the hands of the messenger. The Book states elsewhere that no messenger could bring a sign except by God's permission: the sūrah of the Thunder says that a messenger is not able to bring a sign save by God's leave (13:38), and the sūrah of the Forgiver states the same (40:78). The sentence therefore answers the demand by placing the signs with the One who alone decides whether they will be shown.

The answer also removes the ground on which the audience was standing. The Makkans asked for a sign in order to settle the truth of the message, and the Book's response is that signs are not brought to order. They are granted or withheld by God, and the community that has received the Qur'an has already received what it needs.

**What Will Make You Realise**

What will make you realise that even if a sign were to come to them, they still would not believe? The second half of the verse is addressed to the believers, and the Book uses this form of address when it wants its readers to notice something they had not considered. The question is not a request for information; it is a statement that the audience's objection was never the real obstacle.

The sūrah has built the case for that judgement over many verses. It recorded the demand for the signs and the Book's refusal to produce them at the audience's command, and it recorded the response of those who had been shown the clearest kind of evidence. The verse closes the argument by naming the obstacle as the will of the people themselves, and the next verse will state that God turns their hearts away as a consequence of what they have chosen.

**The Reports About the Request for a Sign**

Reports connected with this verse describe the idolaters asking the Prophet to perform a miracle of the kind they had heard recounted of Moses and Jesus, and asking him to turn a hill near the sanctuary into gold. According to those reports the Prophet began to supplicate for what they requested and was then informed that such extraordinary signs were commonly followed by destructive punishment if they were rejected, so he ceased his request.

The report gives the verse a setting and explains the reference in the following verse to the punishment that would come with a sign if it were rejected. Whether or not the details are pressed, the Book's own statements in this passage and the one after it state the principle clearly: the sign would not have persuaded the people who demanded it, and its arrival would have made their position worse rather than better.

**The Pattern of Signs and Refusal**

The Book records a consistent pattern in the history of the earlier communities. The sign comes, the people who demanded it refuse it, and the refusal is punished, and the sūrah of the Children of Israel records that God refrained from sending the signs the audience asked for exactly because of what would follow their rejection. The sūrah of the Table gives the same reasoning in the account of the disciples' request for a table from heaven, and the sūrah of the Spoils states that God would not punish a people while the Prophet was among them.

The Book's treatment of the signs therefore turns on the responsibility that an unmistakable sign would create. The community that has received the Book without them is being shown mercy rather than being deprived, and the verse's question to the believers is meant to make them see the demand in that light.

**What the Verse Establishes for the Reader**

The verse establishes that the obstacle to belief lies in the people who refuse rather than in the evidence they have been given. The sūrah has described the signs that were already available in the created order, in the history of the earlier messengers, and in the revelation that was being recited to the audience. The demand for an additional sign did not arise from a lack of evidence but from a determination not to accept the evidence that had come.

That reading is confirmed by the verse that follows, which describes God diverting the hearts of the people who would not believe and leaving them in their transgression. The audience had made its decision, and the Book states what the decision produced, with the signs placed where the verse puts them, which is with Allah alone.
verses.110:
> We turn their hearts and eyes away ˹from the truth˺ as they refused to believe at first, leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance

**The Turning of Hearts and Eyes**

We turn their hearts and eyes away as they refused to believe at first. The verse states the consequence that follows a refusal, and it does so in the language of motion. The Book's word describes turning something over repeatedly, and the commentators read it as a swaying of the inner faculties, so that the hearts and eyes of the people who refused move from one state to another and never settle on the truth.

The sentence is the answer to the question the previous verse put to the believers: what will make you realise that even if a sign came the audience still would not believe? The verse in front of us supplies the reason, which is that the refusal had already occurred at the beginning, and the turning described here follows from it rather than causing it.

**The Reports About the Turning of Hearts**

The commentaries connect this vocabulary to a well-known report recorded in the Sunan of al-Tirmidhī. Umm Salama was asked which supplication the Messenger of God made most often in her presence, and she answered that it was, O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm in Your religion; when she asked him why he supplicated so often, he answered that every human heart lies between two fingers of the Most Merciful, who keeps firm whom He wills and turns aside whom He wills. The narration also appears from Anas ibn Mālik with the same phrases, and the reports describe the same divine action that this verse names.

What the verse and the reports together describe is God's complete disposal of human inward life. The Book states the same fact in its passages about the sealing of hearts, eyes, and ears, where those who persist in denial are described as unable to perceive what is addressed to them (2:7; 6:46), and the sūrah has used that description in its account of the people who turned away from the signs.

**Leaving Them in Their Defiance**

Leaving them to wander blindly in their defiance. The sentence names the condition in which the people who refused are left, and the Book's term for the wandering describes a state of confusion in which a person cannot find his way. The image belongs with the sūrah's earlier descriptions of those who walk in darkness: the man whom the satans have seduced in the open country and who has companions calling him to guidance he does not follow (6:71), and the people whose hearts and eyes were turned away in this verse.

The Book is careful to state that the wandering is the consequence of a choice, and the commentators explained the arrangement in that sense: God does not interfere with a person's decision, does not cut short his life to prevent further wandering, and does not compel the path he takes. The person who refused at the first opportunity is left to the road he has chosen, and the Book describes the road's condition rather than the man's fate.

**The Pattern of the Sealed Heart**

The sūrah has stated the same arrangement before, when it described the sealing of the hearts of those who denied the signs and the blindness that prevented them from seeing them (6:46; 6:25). The sūrah of the Cow states the pattern in its opening passage, where God is described as sealing the hearts of the disbelievers, covering their hearing, and placing a veil over their sight (2:7), and the sūrah of the Heights gives the same description with the detail that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.

The verses in this sūrah belong to that family, and the point they make is about the relationship between a person's first decision and his subsequent capacity. The Book presents the relationship as one of consequence rather than of arbitrary imposition: the people who refused to believe when the message first reached them are left without the disposition to believe when the signs appear later.

**Why the Verse Is Addressed to the Prophet's Audience**

The verse is part of a passage in which the Prophet is being prepared for the response he will receive. The sūrah has told him to follow the revelation, to turn away from the polytheists, and that he is neither their keeper nor their maintainer, and this verse supplies the explanation for the resistance he encountered. The people who demanded signs had already decided, and the turning of their hearts was the working out of that decision.

The Book's statements about the hearts of the audience are therefore not a claim that persuasion is impossible but a description of the people who had reached the point of refusal. The same sūrah presents the message as addressed to anyone who will hear it, and it asks questions that presume the capacity for a response.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The verse that follows states the case in the strongest possible terms: even if the angels had been sent to them, and the dead had spoken to them, and everything had been assembled before their eyes, they still would not have believed unless God willed (6:111). The two verses form a single argument, and together they close the discussion of the demand for signs that began with the oaths sworn by the idolaters.

What the sūrah will do next is turn to the Prophet's own situation among those who opposed him, describing the enemies appointed to every prophet and the whisperings of the devilish among humans and jinn. The discussion of signs ends, and the discussion of the messenger's company begins.
verses.111:
> Even if We had sent them the angels, made the dead speak to them, and assembled before their own eyes every sign ˹they demanded˺, they still would not have believed—unless Allah so willed. But most of them are ignorant ˹of this˺

**The Three Signs Named in the Verse**

Even if We had sent them the angels, made the dead speak to them, and assembled before their own eyes every sign they demanded. The sentence names the strongest evidence a person could imagine and treats it as insufficient. The three items are the angels coming in visible form, the dead rising to speak, and every remaining sign gathered together and set before the audience, and the verse states that even this would not produce belief.

The Book has described the audience's demand for exactly these kinds of evidence elsewhere. The sūrah of the Night Journey records their asking the Prophet to bring God and the angels before them or to send down a book they could read, and the sūrah of the Discernment records the demand that a treasure be sent down with him or that angels accompany him. The verse in front of us takes the demands at their full strength and states their result.

**The Refusal That Would Remain**

They still would not have believed unless Allah so willed. The exception clause keeps the statement from becoming an absolute claim about human nature, and it aligns the verse with the rest of the sūrah's teaching about God's will. Belief is possible when God wills it, and the people described here were not among those for whom that will had been exercised.
