The Book states the same exception in other places where belief is attributed to the will of God. The sūrah of Yūnus says that no soul can believe except by God's permission (10:100), and the sūrah of the Bee says that God guides whom He wills and that the Prophet's task is to convey the message. The verse here applies the principle to an audience that had seen enough evidence to believe and had refused it.

**The Ignorance of Most of Them**

But most of them are ignorant of this. The closing sentence explains why the demand for signs continued despite the answer the audience had received. The verse's claim is that the crowd did not understand what the signs were for: they treated the sign as a lever that would settle the matter, while the Book describes it as a gift that a willing heart receives and a reluctant heart resists.

The sūrah has used the charge of ignorance throughout its treatment of the audience. It said that they followed nothing but conjecture and that they spoke about God what they did not know; it described the attribution of children to God as a claim made out of ignorance (6:100); and it described the deniers as unable to perceive what was put before them (6:110). The sentence that closes this verse belongs to that pattern.

**The Reports About the Request and the Refusal**

The reports about the demand for a sign include the audience's request that a hill near the sanctuary be turned to gold, and they describe the Prophet beginning to supplicate for it before being told that such signs are followed by punishment when they are rejected. The verse's three items belong to the same family of demands, and the Book's answer is that they would have made no difference.

The Book's explanation for that judgement lies in its account of the audience's inner condition. The sūrah has stated that their hearts were turned away after their first refusal (6:110), and this verse supplies the consequence in terms of evidence. A person whose heart has been left to wander will interpret any sign he is shown in the terms of his existing position, and the Book describes that condition plainly.

**The Pattern in the Earlier Communities**

The Book states the same judgement in the sūrah of the Night Journey, where God says that nothing keeps Him from sending the demanded signs except that the earlier peoples had already denied them, and where the she-camel given to Thamūd is named as an example (17:59). The verse establishes both halves of the principle the sūrah is stating here: signs are withheld in mercy, and the communities that received them and refused were destroyed.

The Book applies that precedent to the audience's demands at several points, and it consistently treats the request for a sign as a claim on God that He answers as He chooses. The sūrah of Yūnus says that no soul believes except by God's permission and that His wrath falls on those who are unmindful (10:100), which is the same arrangement the verse in front of us describes when it makes belief contingent on God's will.

**What the Verse Says About Evidence and Belief**

The verse does not belittle evidence; it states its limits when it is offered to people who have already refused. The sūrah has spent its first hundred verses presenting evidence of every kind, and the created order itself has been laid out as a demonstration. What this verse adds is the recognition that evidence can be resisted, and that the resistance belongs to the will rather than to the intellect.

That recognition is the foundation of the Book's treatment of the earlier communities as well. The sūrah of the Cattle records the fate of the communities who saw the signs and did not believe, and it presents their destruction as the consequence of a decision they had made rather than of a deficiency in the evidence. The verse in front of us states the principle before the sūrah turns to the enemies that every prophet has had to face.

**The Transition to the Prophets' Enemies**

The next verse announces that God has appointed for every prophet enemies among the devilish of humans and jinn, who whisper to one another with elegant words of deception (6:112). The transition is natural: having described an audience that would not be moved by any sign, the sūrah turns to the mechanism by which such refusal is sustained and spread.

The two passages belong to the sūrah's larger purpose of preparing the messenger for the opposition he faced. The signs have been presented, the refusal has been explained, and the sūrah now describes the company of opponents and the instructions the Prophet receives about them. What follows is one of the sūrah's most striking accounts of how the message's enemies work against it.
verses.112:
> And so We have made for every prophet enemies—devilish humans and jinn—whispering to one another with elegant words of deception. Had it been your Lord’s Will, they would not have done such a thing. So leave them and their deceit

**The Enemies Appointed for Every Prophet**

And so We have made for every prophet enemies, devilish humans and jinn. The verse states a fact about the prophetic calling that the Prophet had not been told before in this sūrah, and it does so as a general law rather than as an account of his own case. Enemies are part of the work, and the work has always involved them. The Book announces the same fact elsewhere: the sūrah of the Ranged records that the enemies of the former messengers received a respite in the world, and the sūrah of the Forgiver tells the Prophet that the messengers before him were also called liars.

The phrase devilish humans and jinn names two orders of being in a single category, and the Book's account of temptation holds them together. The sūrah of the Jinn records a group of jinn listening to the Qur'an and believing, and it records others who mislead; the sūrah of the Cow records Satan's promise to lead people astray; and the sūrah of the Prophets describes how the prophets' enemies were made to incline toward one another. In this verse the hostility is shared between human beings and jinn who act in the same manner.

**The Whispering With Elegant Words**

Whispering to one another with elegant words of deception. The Book's word for the whispering describes the secret communication by which a person's resolve is undermined, and the sūrah of the Cow uses it for the prompting of Satan and for the suggestions of the malicious. The description of the words as elegant refers to their form rather than their content, and the phrase indicates the method: the enemies of the prophets do not usually present their case as opposition to God, since they dress their proposals in language that sounds persuasive.

The Book's treatment of persuasive speech in the sūrah of the Cow is instructive, since it records the beauty of the speech of the hypocrites while stating that their hearts are divided. The verse in front of us supplies the mechanism of that persuasion in the case of the messengers, and it locates the danger in the attractiveness of the formulation rather than in the honesty of the argument.

**What the Enemies Do With the Message**

The verse describes the activity that surrounds the delivery of a revealed message. The enemies do not destroy the message; they surround it with alternatives, interpretations, and proposals, and they make those alternatives attractive to their hearers. The sūrah will describe the same activity in the next verse, where the evil suggestions are said to find their way into the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter.

The Book's account of the earlier communities includes this activity in detail. The sūrah of Hūd describes the leaders of the people who said that they had heard a man speaking ideas that were no more than the words of other men, and the sūrah of the Family of Imran records the practices of those who were given a share of the Book and who twisted its words after understanding them. The enemies described in this verse are the human and unseen agents of that work.

**The Instruction Given to the Prophet**

Had it been your Lord's will, they would not have done such a thing. So leave them and their deceit. The verse gives the Prophet the same answer the previous passages gave him: the opposition exists by God's permission, and the Prophet's responsibility is to carry on with the message rather than to defeat the opposition. The instruction to leave them is not a withdrawal from the field but a refusal to make the enemies' conduct the measure of his own.

The sūrah has issued the same instruction twice already, telling him to leave those who take their religion as play (6:70) and to turn away from the polytheists (6:106), and the words are used again in the sūrah of the Bee, where the Prophet is told to strive against the disbelievers and hypocrites. The pattern is consistent throughout the Book: the messenger continues to speak, and the outcome is left to God.

**Why the Announcement Was a Consolation**

The announcement that every prophet has had enemies carries a consolation that a simple instruction would not. A man who finds himself opposed might suppose his mission is failing, and the verse tells him that opposition is the ordinary condition of the work rather than a sign against it. The Book makes the same point in its accounts of the earlier messengers, where each of them is described as encountering denial from his people.

The sūrah of the Ranged lists the messengers who were told they were liars and states that the word of punishment was fulfilled for them, and the sūrah of Yā-Sīn records God's regret over the servants to whom He sent messengers and whom they mocked. The verse in front of us places the Prophet's experience inside that long history, and the instruction that follows sends him back to the work.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The verse that follows states the purpose of the whispering in its own terms: the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may receive it, be pleased with it, and become persistent in what they are doing (6:113). The passage therefore describes a mechanism with a target, and the target is the inner disposition of the people who have already turned away.

That description completes the sūrah's account of how refusal is produced and sustained. The signs are presented and rejected, the hearts are turned aside, and the messengers' enemies continue the work of persuasion. The sūrah states each stage plainly, and it does so while giving the Prophet the instructions that ordered his own conduct inside a city where all of it was taking place.
verses.113:
> so that the hearts of those who disbelieve in the Hereafter may be receptive to it, be pleased with it, and be persistent in their evil pursuits

**The Purpose Clause of the Previous Verse**

So that the hearts of those who disbelieve in the Hereafter may be receptive to it. The verse states the outcome of the whispering described in the previous sentence, and it names the people in whom the whispering takes effect. The message of the enemies of the prophets reaches the people who have already denied the Hereafter, and the denial is given as the reason the message finds a place in them.

The connection between the denial of the Hereafter and the reception of deceptive speech is a theme the sūrah has been developing. The people who live only for the present life have no measure by which to test a proposal, and their judgement of what to accept is confined to what serves them now. The Book states the same connection elsewhere, and it treats the rejection of the Hereafter as the root from which other errors grow.

**The Three Terms of the Sentence**

The verse describes three effects in sequence, and each one deepens the hold of the deception. The first is that the hearts incline to the whispering and give it a hearing; the second is that they are pleased with it, so that the hearing becomes acceptance; and the third is that they persist in what they were already doing, so that the acceptance hardens into a settled course. The sentence therefore describes a process rather than a moment, and the process has the shape of a decision that becomes a habit.

The Book describes the same progression in its account of the people who did not expect to meet God. The sūrah of Yūnus says that those who do not hope for the meeting with God and who are content with the life of this world have their deeds made fair to them and are left in their confusion (10:7), and the sūrah of the Ants describes those who do not believe in the Hereafter as people whose deeds have been made attractive to them and who wander blindly (27:4).

**The Receptivity the Verse Describes**

The Book's word for the heart's reception describes the opening of a container to what is poured into it, and the image appears in the sūrah of the Prophets, where the Prophet's enemies are described as listening to the message while covering their hearts so that they might not understand it (17:46). The verse in front of us states the opposite condition in the people who receive the whisperings, and the reading of the two verses together shows what is at stake.

The Book attaches the same condition to the hearts of those who reject the Hereafter in several passages. The sūrah of the Troops says that when God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who disbelieve in the Hereafter are filled with disgust, while the mention of the other gods brings them joy (39:45), and the sūrah of Fussilat states that God assigned to the deniers companions who made their conduct appear fair to them, so that they would be among those for whom the word was fulfilled (41:25). The verse in front of us states the arrangement in its most compact form.

**The Persistence That Follows**

And be persistent in their evil pursuits. The sentence ends with the activity the audience had already been engaged in, and the Book describes the enemies' work as aimed at maintaining that activity rather than at creating it. The whispering does not produce a new direction; it supplies reasons for continuing in the direction already taken.

The Book's account of the people who persist in denial uses the same language in the sūrah of the Troops and the sūrah of the Cave, where those who turned away are described as pursuing what they had been doing. The verse in front of us names the mechanism that keeps a person in that pursuit, and it places the mechanism in the company of the whisperers rather than in the person himself.

**What the Verse Says About the Audience's Condition**

The verse states that the enemies of the prophets are not the cause of the audience's disbelief but the means by which it is confirmed. The people described here had already disbelieved in the Hereafter before the whisperings reached them, and the whisperings found in them a disposition that was prepared. The Book's presentation of the two orders of causes is consistent: the enemies work, and God permits the work, and the person who receives it does so because of what he has already chosen.

The Book's language about the hearts of these people also explains the audience's resistance to the arguments the sūrah has been making. The signs, the history of the earlier communities, and the confession of the earlier scriptures were all present, and none of them reached a heart that had been closed to what comes after death.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The verse that follows turns from the enemies' deception to the Book's authority, with the Prophet commanded to say that he will not seek a judge other than God, who has revealed the Book perfectly explained (6:114). The two verses stand in deliberate contrast: the whisperings produce hearts that receive falsehood, and the clearly explained Book is what the Prophet is told to hold to.

That contrast runs through the rest of the chapter, which continues to describe the audience's demands and the Book's answers. The sūrah has now completed its account of how the refusal of the message is produced among people who have denied the Hereafter, and it turns to the authority that stands over the whole dispute.
verses.114:
> ˹Say, O Prophet,˺ “Should I seek a judge other than Allah while He is the One Who has revealed for you the Book ˹with the truth˺ perfectly explained?” Those who were given the Scripture know that it has been revealed ˹to you˺ from your Lord in truth. So do not be one of those who doubt

**The Question Put to the Audience**

Should I seek a judge other than Allah? The sentence is a question addressed to the audience on the Prophet's behalf, and it follows a passage in which the people had been asking for signs and swallowing the whisperings of the satans among men and jinn. The demand behind their requests was a ruling: they wanted the matter settled by something they could see, and the question names the absurdity of looking for an arbiter beside the One who had already given His answer.

The Book places the same question in other settings. The sūrah of the Table tells the Prophet to judge between the People of the Book by what God has revealed, and asks who could be a better judge for a people who are certain (5:50). The sūrah of Yūnus ends its account of the revelation with the instruction to follow what has been revealed and to be patient until God passes his judgement, since He is the best of judges (10:109). The question in this verse is the sūrah's own version of that appeal.

**The Book Perfectly Explained**

While He is the One Who has revealed for you the Book with the truth perfectly explained. The second half of the question supplies the reason there is no need for another arbiter: the Book was sent down with the truth and set out in full detail. The Book uses the same description of itself in the sūrah of Fussilat, which calls it a Book whose verses are perfectly explained, a Qur'an in Arabic for people who know (41:3), and the sūrah of the Cattle itself says that God has already explained what He has forbidden (6:119).

The phrase also answers the audience's complaint about the message's content. The sūrah of Yūnus states that the Qur'an is a confirmation of what came before it and a detailed explanation of the Scripture, with no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds (10:37). What the verse in front of us says is that the guidance is complete in itself, and that a court of arbitration beside it would be asking for something already provided.

**The Testimony of Those Given the Scripture**

Those who were given the Scripture know that it has been revealed to you from your Lord in truth. The sentence turns from the audience's demands to the testimony of the communities that possessed earlier revelation. The Book records that testimony in many places: the sūrah of the Stories says that those to whom the Scripture had been given before believe in the Qur'an and declare on hearing it that this is the truth from their Lord, which they had already submitted to (28:52–53); the sūrah of the Night Journey says that those gifted with knowledge before it fall on their faces when it is recited to them; the sūrah of the Table describes the tears of those who recognise the truth; and the sūrah of the Family of Imran speaks of those among the People of the Book who believe in what has been revealed to the believers (3:199).

The Makkans lived alongside Jewish and Christian communities, and the sūrah has already appealed to the knowledge of the earlier scriptures in the argument about revelation (6:91–92). The verse in front of us states that the people who know those scriptures recognise the Qur'an's origin, which leaves the audience resisting a message that the other communities recognised.

The sūrah had already made the point at close range. It said in its earlier verses that those to whom God had given the Scripture recognise the Prophet as they recognise their own children, and that a group of them hides the truth knowingly (6:20; 2:146). The verse in front of us is the same argument applied to the origin of the Book rather than to the identity of the messenger, and it uses the witness of the same people.

**The Command Not to Doubt**

So do not be one of those who doubt. The instruction is addressed to the Prophet, and the Book gives similar instructions in other passages. The sūrah of Yūnus tells him that if he is in doubt about what has been revealed to him, he should ask those who read the Scripture before him, since the truth has come from his Lord (10:94). The command in this verse is not a suggestion that the Prophet wavered; it is the Book's way of stating the firmness that the revelation itself supplies.

The sūrah of the Cow gives the same instruction to the believers at the end of its accounts of the earlier scriptures: the truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters (2:147). The Book's habit of addressing its firmest reader with this command shows that the command concerns the message rather than the man, since what is being established is the certainty that the revelation carries with it.

**What the Verse Answers in the Sūrah's Argument**

The verse answers the demand for a sign from a direction the audience had not considered. They wanted a demonstration that would settle the question between them and the messenger, and the Book replies that the arbiter is already present in the revelation they could read or hear. The perfect explanation of the Book and the testimony of the earlier communities are offered as the answer, and both were available in Makkah without a miracle.

The passage that follows this verse states that the word of the Lord has been perfected in truth and justice and that none can change His words (6:115). Together the two verses establish the authority that stands over the whole dispute the sūrah has been describing, and they do it by pointing to what the audience already possessed.
verses.115:
> The Word of your Lord has been perfected in truth and justice. None can change His Words. And He is the All-Hearing, All- Knowing

**The Perfected Word**

The Word of your Lord has been perfected in truth and justice. The verse states that God's word has reached its completeness, and it names the two qualities in which that completeness consists. The Book uses the same verbal form in the sūrah of Hūd, where it says that the word of the Lord will be fulfilled, and in the sūrah of Yūnus, where it says that the decree of the Lord has been proven true against the rebellious (10:33). What the verse in front of us states is the finished character of the revelation rather than its arrival at a future point.

The two qualities named here cover the two sides of what a revealed Book contains. Truth belongs to what the Book says about God, the unseen, the past, and the reckoning; justice belongs to what it commands and forbids. The sūrah has been treating both throughout, and the sentence that gathers them states that neither side is defective.

**Truth and Justice Together**

The pair of terms describes the Book as both accurate and fair, and the Book uses the two together in other passages about its own character and about the conduct it requires. The sūrah of the Table says that God revealed the Book in truth and that it guides to a straight path (5:16 context), and the sūrah of the Troops says that God revealed the Book to the Prophet with the truth for humanity (39:41). The sūrah of the Cattle itself commands the Prophet to judge with justice in other passages.

The combination matters for the audience the sūrah is addressing. People who questioned whether the message was true were being told that its reports are accurate, and people who found its commands burdensome were being told that its rulings are just. The verse states both as features of the Word itself rather than as claims made on its behalf.

**None Can Change His Words**

None can change His Words. The sentence states the security of the revelation, and the Book repeats it in several places. The sūrah of the Cave commands the Prophet to recite what has been revealed to him from the Book of his Lord and states that none can change His words, nor can any refuge be found besides Him (18:27). The sūrah of Yūnus declares that there is no change in the promise of God and that this is the great triumph (10:64), and the sūrah of the Cattle earlier says that none can change the words of God and states that messengers before the Prophet endured rejection until God's help came (6:34).

The Book sets its own preservation against what it says happened to the earlier scriptures. The sūrah of the Table states that the People of the Book distorted the words of the Scripture and forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of (5:13); the sūrah of the Cow pronounces woe on those who write the Scripture with their own hands and then say that it is from God, seeking a fleeting gain (2:79); and the sūrah of the Women records those who take words out of their context and alter them (4:46). The sentence in this verse is the contrast to all of that.

**The Two Names That Close the Verse**

And He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing. The two names correspond to the two qualities named at the beginning of the verse: the One who hears what is said and knows what is done is the One whose word is true and whose commands are just. The Book attaches this pair to statements about decrees and knowledge in many places, and its use here ties the perfection of the revelation to the attributes of the One who sent it.

The names also answer the situation of the Prophet among a people who argued with him and denied his message. Nothing that they said escaped the One who hears, and nothing about their condition was hidden from the One who knows, which is the same ground the sūrah established when it described God's knowledge of the leaf that falls and the grain in the darkness (6:59).

**What the Verse Adds to the Passage**

The verse closes the passage that began with the demand for a judge and the testimony of those given the Scripture (6:114). Having established that the Book is fully explained and that the earlier communities recognise its origin, the sūrah states that the word itself is complete, incorruptible, and grounded in the attributes of the One who sent it. The dispute about the message is therefore not a dispute about a defective or partial revelation.

The Book makes the same claim about the guidance it contains in the passages about its own preservation, and the sūrah will return to that theme. What the verse provides here is the framework for the instructions that follow, in which the Prophet is told not to follow the majority of the people on earth and is told that his Lord knows best who has strayed and who is guided, so that the reader can weigh the crowd against the Book.

**The Transition to the Next Verses**

The next verse says that if the Prophet were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead him away from the way of God, since they follow nothing but assumption and do nothing but lie (6:116), and the verse after it states that God knows best who has strayed and who is guided (6:117). The two verses take up the question of authority from the side of numbers, and the Book answers it by pointing again to the knowledge of the One whose word has been perfected.

The connection between the two passages is direct. The Book has just been shown to be the arbiter, complete in truth and justice, and the sūrah now states that the majority of people are following conjecture. The answer to the crowd is the Book, and the answer to the Book's opponents is the One who hears and knows.
verses.116:
> ˹O Prophet!˺ If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah’s Way. They follow nothing but assumptions and do nothing but lie

**The Warning Against Following the Majority**

If you were to obey most of those on earth, they would lead you away from Allah's Way. The sentence is addressed to the Prophet, and it states a principle that the Book repeats in many places: the majority provides no measure of truth. The warning is not that the Prophet was tempted to follow the crowd but that the crowd's position carries a weight that the community around him felt, and the Book names the danger in the plainest terms.

The sūrah's audience was a society in which the majority held the ancestral religion, and the small community of believers lived inside that majority. The Book tells the Prophet that compliance with the majority would not merely have modified his message; it would have taken him off the way altogether. The verse therefore treats the pressure of numbers as a claim to authority and denies it outright.

**The Assumption That Stands in Place of Knowledge**

They follow nothing but assumptions and do nothing but lie. The two clauses name the ground and the consequence. The Book's word for assumption describes the surmise a person inherits or inherits by habit, and the sūrah of Yūnus states that most people follow nothing but inherited assumption and that assumption cannot replace the truth (10:36); the sūrah of the Star makes the same statement in the context of the claim that the angels are daughters of God (53:28); and the sūrah of the Cow describes the illiterate among the People of the Book as knowing nothing of the Scripture except lies and living on speculation (2:78).

The second clause raises the charge from error to falsehood. What the audience affirmed about God, about the idols' power to intercede, and about the resurrection was not merely an unproven opinion; the Book treats it as a statement about God made without warrant, which is the offence this sūrah has been describing since its claim that the idolaters invent lies against Him.

**The Book's Use of This Argument**

The Book makes the majority's position a subject of remark in several passages, and it never treats numerical support as evidence. The sūrah of Yūsuf says that most people will not believe no matter how keen the messenger is (12:103), and it says that most of them do not believe in God without associating others with Him (12:106). The sūrah of the Cattle itself states at the end of the passage about signs that most of the audience are ignorant (6:111), and the sūrah of the Women and others describe the majority in similar terms.

The argument is not a rejection of consensus in favour of idiosyncrasy. What the Book rejects is the use of numbers as a criterion of truth, and it supports the rejection by pointing to the content of the majority's belief rather than to its size. The Makkan majority was large, established, and confident, and the verse says that its followers were following conjecture.

**What the Warning Meant in Makkah**

The warning had a practical edge for the Prophet and for the community that had joined him. The majority controlled the city's worship, its trade, and its kinship structures, and a person who accepted the message faced the loss of all three. The verse tells the Prophet that the majority's way is not a path to be accommodated, and its statement that the majority's followers do nothing but lie gives the reason.

The Book's accounts of the earlier messengers show the same situation. The sūrah of Hūd describes Noah's people rejecting him on the ground that only the lowest among them had followed him, and the Book records communities that measured a claim by the standing of the people who made it rather than by what was said. The verse in front of us states the Book's position on that assumption without qualification.

**The Verse's Relation to the One Before It**

The verse follows the statement that God's word has been perfected in truth and justice and that none can change His words (6:115). The pair establishes the standard by which claims are measured: the perfected word on one side, and the conjecture of the many on the other. The sūrah has already told the Prophet to seek no judge besides God, and this verse removes the most obvious alternative, which is the opinion of the people around him.

The verse that follows answers the warning by stating that the Prophet's Lord knows best who has strayed from His way and who is rightly guided (6:117). The two verses together leave the question of standing where the sūrah has consistently placed it, in the knowledge of God rather than in the counting of heads.

**What the Verse Teaches the Reader**

The instruction concerns the community that would read the Book after the Prophet. Every generation faces the same pressure, and the sūrah's answer is the same in each case: the way of God is known from the revelation, and the size of the company that travels another road is not an argument. The Book states this principle in its accounts of the communities that were destroyed and in its descriptions of the small groups of believers who were saved.

The sūrah has spent much of its length distinguishing between the two roads, and the closing verses of this section continue the contrast with an account of the dietary laws, the divisions among the earlier communities, and the testimony that the Prophet is a warner rather than a keeper. The verse in front of us supplies the criterion by which the two roads are told apart, and the criterion is the revelation rather than the multitude.
verses.117:
> Indeed, your Lord knows best who has strayed from His Way and who is ˹rightly˺ guided

**The Formula and Where It Appears**

Indeed, your Lord knows best who has strayed from His Way and who is rightly guided. The sentence closes the warning about the majority with a statement about knowledge, and the Book repeats it almost word for word in other places. The sūrah of the Pen uses it to answer those who accused the Prophet of being a madman, saying that his Lord knows best who has strayed from His way and who is rightly guided (68:7). The sūrah of the Star uses the same words at the end of its discussion of the people who followed assumption (53:30). And the sūrah of the Bee attaches the sentence to the command to invite people to the way of the Lord with wisdom and good instruction (16:125).

The repetition tells the reader how the Book wants the division between belief and disbelief treated. Both passages in which the formula appears most fully are answers to disputes in which the audience was claiming to know who was on the right road, and the Book's reply moves the question to the knowledge of God.

**The Name of the Way**

The verse speaks of God's Way, and the sūrah has used the same expression in the sentence before it, warning the Prophet that the majority would lead him away from the Way of God (6:116). The Book's term describes the road rather than the destination, and its usage throughout this chapter has been developed through the imagery of paths and travellers. The straight path is described at the end of the sūrah's long passage of prohibitions (6:153), and the sūrah of the Bee's version of this formula follows a command about inviting people to the Way of the Lord.

The same noun serves both verse halves here: there is one Way, and people either follow it or wander from it. The verse does not divide humanity into categories of temperament or standing; it describes them in relation to a road, and the road is the one the revelation marks out.

**The Two Groups Named**

The verse names two conditions rather than two classes of people, and the Book's descriptions of the two are stated throughout the sūrah. The people who strayed are the ones whose conduct the chapter has described in detail; the people who are guided are those who hear the message and follow the best of it, as the sūrah of the Troops describes them. The sentence states that the membership of each group is known with certainty, and the knowledge is God's.

That arrangement removes the judgement from human hands without removing the distinction itself. The Book tells the Prophet not to be a keeper over the people and not to claim purity for himself, and it tells the community that the final sorting belongs to the day when every person's deeds are presented. The formula in this verse is the positive statement of that arrangement: the distinction is real, and the knowledge of it is complete in one place.

**What the Verse Meant for the Prophet**

The Prophet lived among people who had committed themselves to denying his message, and the formula was given to him as a form of relief. He was not required to determine the standing of each person he met, and he was not required to secure the outcome of the dispute. The sūrah had already told him that he was neither keeper nor maintainer over the people who denied his message (6:107) and that the matter would be settled on the day when God informs them of what they did.

The Book gives the same relief in the sūrah of the Bee's version of the formula, which stands at the end of a passage on how the message is to be delivered: the invitation is made with wisdom and the outcome belongs to God. What the verse in front of us adds is the statement that the outcome is already known to God, which means the uncertainty belongs only to human observers.

**The Knowledge Claim in the Sūrah's Argument**

The claim that God knows the two groups is continuous with the sūrah's account of His knowledge in other passages. The sūrah stated that God knows the secret and the open, that not a leaf falls without His knowledge, and that He is the one who has the keys of the unseen (6:59; 6:60). The formula in this verse applies that knowledge to the question of guidance, and it does so in the context of the warning that the majority would lead the Prophet away from the Way.

The Book's arguments against the audience's religion have rested on the audience's ignorance of the unseen, and the contrast between human assumption and divine knowledge has run through the passage since the demand for signs. The verse states the contrast in a single sentence: the people are following assumptions, and the Lord knows.

**The Transition to the Passage That Follows**

The next verse returns to the dietary practices of the audience, commanding the believers to eat of what the name of God has been mentioned over and forbidding what has been dedicated to other than Him, and then describing the people who argue about it. The subject changes, but the argument continues along the same lines, since the dietary rules concerned claims about what God had permitted and forbidden.

The verse in front of us supplies the framework for that passage. The audience's practices rested on inherited assumption; the guidance rested on revelation; and the difference between the two roads is known to the One who made both claims possible. The Book states the framework once here and proceeds to another instance of the same dispute.
verses.118:
> So eat only of what is slaughtered in Allah’s Name if you truly believe in His revelations

**The Command About Food**

So eat only of what is slaughtered in Allah's Name if you truly believe in His revelations. The verse states a dietary rule in the form of an instruction, and it attaches the instruction to belief in the revelation. The rule concerns meat in particular, since it is over the animal that the Name is invoked at slaughter, and the Book's commentators understood the command to forbid the eating of carrion, which had not been slaughtered with the invocation at all.

The Makkan audience lived with a set of inherited customs about which animals could be eaten and which could not, and the sūrah has been dismantling those customs and replacing them with rules that rest on the Name of God. The verse before this one described the majority as followers of assumption, and the dietary command is the practical form of the difference between inherited practice and revelation.

**What the Rule Requires**

The rule requires that the Name of God be invoked over the animal, and the invocation is what marks the meat as food for the community that believes. The sūrah of the Table sets the same requirement inside a wider list of restrictions, forbidding the flesh of animals that died of themselves, blood, swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God, with an exception for the person compelled by hunger. The sūrah of the Bee gives the same instruction to eat of what God has provided and to be grateful, and it repeats the prohibition and the exception.

The commentators observed that the rule concerns the act of slaughtering rather than the kind of animal alone, since the same species becomes permitted or forbidden according to what is said over it. The Book's concern throughout this passage has been with the authority behind the rules, and the invocation of the Name is what places the meal inside that authority.

**The Condition Attached to the Command**

If you truly believe in His revelations. The verse makes the dietary command a test of belief, and the Book attaches similar conditions to other commands. The sūrah of the Cow tells the believers to eat of the good things provided and to give thanks, and it makes the instruction part of the covenant that the community has accepted. What the condition in this verse states is that the rejection of the rule is not a matter of taste but of the standing of the revelation that carries it.

The audience had argued about food on the basis of ancestral custom, and the Book's answer is that the rule is bound to belief in what has been sent down. The sūrah has already stated that the people who follow assumption do nothing but lie (6:116), and this verse makes the practical consequence of that statement plain for the table.

**The Argument in the Audience's Practice**

The sūrah's later verses describe the audience's own rules about livestock in detail: the animals they set apart, the ones they forbade to certain people, and the shares they assigned to God and to their idols (6:136–139; 6:143–144). The command in front of us stands at the head of that whole section, and it states the principle that the section applies. What the audience did with their herds and flocks was governed by claims about what God had permitted and forbidden, and those claims were inherited rather than revealed.

The Book's account of the audience's system names some of its details: the animals whose backs were declared off limits, the livestock that no one was to eat, and the shares assigned to God and to the idols (6:136; 6:139). The sūrah sets those practices beside the command to eat of what the Name of God has been mentioned over, and the contrast between the two bodies of rules is the argument the section is making.

The Book's treatment of those claims follows the pattern the sūrah has established. It states what God has actually forbidden, it exposes the invention that has grown up around it, and it leaves the responsibility for the invention with the people who made it. The verse in front of us supplies the positive rule for food, and the passages that follow describe the inventions the rule replaced.

**What the Verse Says About Gratitude and Law**

The instruction to eat of what the Name has been mentioned over connects the meal to the acknowledgement of the One who provided it. The Book's dietary rules are not concerned with purity in the abstract; they concern the recognition of God's authority over what a person consumes, and the invocation at slaughter is the moment at which that recognition is expressed. The sūrah of the Bee states the same connection when it tells the believers to eat of what God has provided and to be grateful for His favours (16:114).

The Book's language about food elsewhere attaches the act of eating to worship, and the verse in this sūrah belongs to that usage. The command is addressed to a community forming around the revelation, and the rule tells it how the most ordinary act of the day is related to its confession.

**The Verses That Continue the Section**

The verse that follows asks why the believers should not eat of what has been slaughtered in God's Name when God has already explained what He has forbidden, with the exception of what compulsion requires (6:119). The two verses state the rule and then answer the objection to it, and the answer includes the observation that many people mislead others by their desires out of ignorance.

The sūrah therefore treats the dietary question as one instance of the argument it has been conducting throughout the chapter. The subject is food, and the question is the same one the sūrah asked about the signs, the idols, and the demand for miracles: whether the community's practice will rest on the revelation or on the inherited assumptions of the majority.
verses.119:
> Why should you not eat of what is slaughtered in Allah’s Name when He has already explained to you what He has forbidden to you—except when compelled by necessity? Many ˹deviants˺ certainly mislead others by their whims out of ignorance. Surely your Lord knows the transgressors best

**The Question Put in the Verse**

Why should you not eat of what is slaughtered in Allah's Name when He has already explained to you what He has forbidden to you, except when compelled by necessity? The sentence answers an objection to the previous command, and the objection was about the food the community might eat. The verse's answer is that the rule has been stated by God, that the permission is clear, and that the exception has been made for the person who has no alternative.

The structure of the answer is worth noticing. The Book does not argue the case from the audience's customs or from the judgment of the community; it refers the question to what God has explained, which is the standard the sūrah has been applying to every subject it has treated in this chapter.

**The Explanation Already Given**

When He has already explained to you what He has forbidden. The sūrah refers to a body of rulings that the audience had received, and the commentators discussed whether the reference is to the detailed dietary laws given later in the sūrah of the Table or to the principle stated in this very passage. The Book's own statement in the sūrah of the Cattle is that God has explained what He has forbidden (6:119), and the sūrah goes on in later verses to list the prohibitions concerning dead animals, blood, and swine.

What matters for the argument is that the explanation exists and that the community has access to it. The Book's position throughout this section is that the rules come from God rather than from the customs of a region, and the verse states that the rulings have already been set out.

**The Exception for Necessity**

Except when compelled by necessity. The exception appears in the Book's dietary passages generally, and it is one of the features that distinguishes the rules from the arbitrary taboos of the audience's tradition. The sūrah of the Cow permits the person in danger of death to eat what is otherwise forbidden without incurring sin, and the sūrah of the Table and the sūrah of the Bee state the same exception in the same terms.

The Book's treatment of necessity shows the purpose the rules serve. They are not a burden designed to test endurance to the point of death, and the Book states elsewhere that God does not impose on a soul more than it can bear. The exception in this verse is stated as a fact of the law rather than as a concession wrung from it, and the audience's arguments about food are answered on that footing.

**The People Who Mislead by Their Desires**

Many deviants certainly mislead others by their whims out of ignorance. The sentence identifies the people who were pressing the objection, and it describes their teaching as the pursuit of desire rather than the weighing of evidence. The commentators understood the reference to include those who argued that carrion, which had died without human slaughter, was preferable to meat that a person had killed himself, and the argument was based on inherited assumptions rather than on the revelation.

The Book's description of the misleaders repeats the terms it has used throughout this section. The sūrah has described the audience as following assumption and lying (6:116), and the verse before us states the same condition in the vocabulary of desire. What changes from passage to passage in this sūrah is the subject under discussion, and the characterization of the people who argue against the revelation remains constant.

**The Closing Statement About Knowledge**

Surely your Lord knows the transgressors best. The verse closes with the same kind of statement that ended the previous passage about the majority, where the sūrah said that the Lord knows best who has strayed and who is guided (6:117). Here the object of the knowledge is the transgressors, and the sentence leaves their identification to God rather than to the community.

The repetition of the formula in consecutive verses serves the sūrah's argument by keeping the judgment where it belongs. The community is given its rules and told to keep them; the people who oppose them are described; and the final assessment of who has overstepped the limits is stated as a matter of God's knowledge.

**What the Passage Establishes About Law and Custom**

The two verses together state the Book's position on the relationship between revelation and inherited practice. Food that has been consecrated to God is permitted, what has been forbidden is forbidden, necessity is recognised, and the people who teach otherwise are following their desires. The sūrah has applied this reasoning to the idols, to the signs, and to the requirement of a judge, and it applies it here to what the community puts in its mouth.

That application matters for the way the chapter's later passages about livestock and harvests are to be read. The audience had built an elaborate system of shares and prohibitions, and the sūrah will describe it in detail, but the criterion for judging it has already been stated in these two verses: what God has explained and what people have invented.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse commands the community to shun open and secret sin and states that those who commit sin will be punished for what they earn (6:120). The command follows naturally from the dietary instruction, since the sūrah has just been describing conduct that rests on the desires of those who mislead, and the new sentence broadens the subject from food to the whole of a person's conduct.

The section that continues from here moves through the prohibition of what has not been consecrated to God, the whisperings of the devils and their associates, and the errors of the audience's dietary system, and it ends with directions about the path of God and the testimony of the Book. Each of these passages rests on the same foundation, which is the explanation God has given and the responsibility of the people who receive it.
verses.120:
> Shun all sin—open and secret. Indeed, those who commit sin will be punished for what they earn

**The Command to Shun Sin**

Shun all sin, open and secret. The verse moves from the specific dietary rule to a general command, and it covers the two ways in which a person's wrong conduct can be conducted. The open sin is visible to others and is judged by them; the secret sin is hidden from the community, and the Book states that both are equally subject to the command.

The sūrah's treatment of the audience's conduct throughout the chapter has dealt with the hidden as well as the visible. It said that God knows what they conceal and what they disclose, and it described the whispering of the satans among humans and jinn as a hidden activity (6:112). The command in this verse addresses the whole field in which those activities occur.

**What the Book Means by the Two Kinds**

The commentators explained the open sin as the wrong that is done in public and the secret sin as what a person hides in his own conduct, and some applied the pair to the acts of the limbs and the intentions of the heart. The distinction appears in the Book's other passages about conduct, and the Book's word for the hidden covers both the concealment of an act and the inner intention behind it.

The Book treats the two together because its account of accountability includes intention as well as action. The sūrah of the Cow states that God will bring to account what people reveal and what they conceal, and the sūrah of the Family of Imran states that He knows what is in the hearts of His servants. The command in this verse assumes that the concern of the law reaches the place where no witness from the community can see.

**The Reason the Command Is Stated So Broadly**

The verse is stated broadly because the dietary question that precedes it was a fragment of a larger system. The audience had built rules around food while other conduct went unchecked, and the sūrah's argument has been that the religion is not a matter of selected observances. The command to shun sin in both its forms states the scope of the requirement.

The Book's addresses to the community elsewhere make the same point about partial observance. The sūrah of the Cow criticises those who accept part of the Scripture and reject part, and the sūrah of the Women records the same complaint. The command in front of us sets the whole of a person's conduct under the rule.

**The Statement of Punishment**

Indeed, those who commit sin will be punished for what they earn. The second sentence supplies the consequence and states it in the Book's vocabulary of earning. The Book frequently describes reward and punishment as the produce of what a person has collected for himself, and the same language is used in the sūrah's accounts of the day of judgment, when each person is confronted with what he has sent ahead.

The sūrah has described the audience's reckoning in several earlier passages: God knows what they do, their deeds will be recorded, and they will be informed of what they used to do (6:60; 6:108). The sentence in this verse states the same fact in terms of the sin itself, and it applies it to the open and the hidden alike.

**The Pairing of the Verse With Its Neighbours**

The verse stands between the dietary command and its defence and the prohibition of what has not been consecrated to God. The three verses form a single unit in which food, conduct, and ritual are treated by one standard. What God has permitted is permitted; what He has forbidden is forbidden; and the whole of a person's conduct, visible or concealed, is subject to the command.

The Book's habit of placing an ethical generalisation beside a ritual rule appears throughout the chapter, and it serves to show that the two belong to the same authority. The sūrah has already joined the confession of God's unity to commands about food, and it will continue to move between the two registers, since its argument is that both come from the same Lord.

**What the Verse Says About the Concealed Act**

The mention of the secret sin is significant in a passage addressed to a community that lived in close association with people who watched it. A community concerned only with its public standing could satisfy the visible requirements and leave the hidden ones untouched, and the Book's mention of the hidden sin prevents that reading. Nothing in the audience's conduct escaped the One who was being worshipped.

The sūrah has stated the same fact about knowledge in the passage on the keys of the unseen, where God knows the secret and the disclosure, the leaf that falls, and the grain in the darkness (6:59; 6:60). The command in this verse rests on that knowledge, and the punishment it states is the consequence that knowledge produces.

**The Transition to the Following Verse**

The next verse returns to food and forbids what has not had the Name of God mentioned over it, describing that as disobedience and connecting it to the whisperings of the devils and their associates (6:121). The shift back from general conduct to diet shows that the sūrah is treating the dietary system of the audience as one item in the register of conduct the Book is correcting.

The two verses together supply the standard for assessing the practices the sūrah will describe in the passages about livestock and harvests. Sin, whether open or hidden, is what the command excludes, and the following verse states how the concrete practice of the audience stands in relation to it.
verses.121:
> Do not eat of what is not slaughtered in Allah’s Name. For that would certainly be ˹an act of˺ disobedience. Surely the devils whisper to their ˹human˺ associates to argue with you. If you were to obey them, then you ˹too˺ would be polytheists

**The Prohibition Stated in the Negative**

Do not eat of what is not slaughtered in Allah's Name. The verse states the prohibition that corresponds to the command given a few verses earlier, and the Book uses the same form in the sūrah of the Table, where the list of forbidden foods includes what has been dedicated to other than God. The audience's herds produced both kinds of meat, and the rule tells the community which of them belongs to the food of the believers.

The commentators connected the rule to the practice of the Makkans, who ate animals that had died of themselves and animals over which the names of their gods had been invoked. The verse's prohibition covers both, and the reason given in the same sentence is that such food is disobedience.

**The Meaning of the Charge of Disobedience**

For that would certainly be an act of disobedience. The Book uses the same word for the person who leaves the bounds set by God, and the charge here attaches the eating to a departure from what has been commanded rather than to a defect in the food as a substance. The sūrah has been treating the audience's dietary rules as a system of invented restrictions, and this verse states that the eating they permitted was itself an offence.

The Book's usage attaches the term to the person who oversteps in a matter where God has given a rule, and the eating of what has not been consecrated is described in those terms because the Name was withheld deliberately. Where the invocation was not made, the person who killed the animal had chosen to omit it, and the food is the sign of that choice.

**The Whisperings of the Devils**

Surely the devils whisper to their associates to argue with you. The verse names the source of the arguments the community was facing, and the sūrah has described the same activity a few verses earlier, when it said that God made for every prophet enemies among devilish humans and jinn who whisper to one another with elegant words of deception (6:112). The whisperings in the two passages are the same activity directed at the same object.

The Book's account of the devils' associates appears elsewhere in its descriptions of the people who follow the promptings against the message. The sūrah of the Ornament describes God's placing a devil as a companion to the person who turns away from the Reminder of the Most Compassionate (43:36), and the sūrah of the Poets records the Book's denial that the devils brought the revelation down and its description of the ones on whom they actually descend (26:210; 26:221). The argument that the audience raised about food is presented here as something the devils inspired, and the association gives the dispute its place in the sūrah's larger account of how denial spreads.

**The Consequence of Obeying Them**

If you were to obey them, then you too would be polytheists. The sentence states the outcome of accepting the argument, and the identification of the outcome is exact. The audience's position was that the invocation of the names of their gods over an animal made its meat lawful, which is to say that beings other than God had a share in the authority over what may be eaten. To accept the reasoning would be to grant those beings the authority the sūrah has denied them throughout.

The Book's logic here is the same as in its treatment of obedience to any authority that contradicts the revelation. The sūrah of the Troops says that the worship of God is the only alternative to following the false, and the sūrah of the Cattle earlier said that whoever gives up the worship of God and follows the idols has strayed from the level path. The sentence in this verse applies that principle to the dinner table.

**What the Verse Says About Authority Over Conduct**

The section that runs from the dietary command to this prohibition states a single principle in several forms: what a person eats is determined by God's ruling, and the ruling is carried by the Name invoked over the animal. The Book's treatment is not a matter of ritual purity for its own sake but a statement about whose authority governs conduct. The invocation of the Name and the refusal to invoke anything else are the visible form of that statement.

That is why the verse ends with the identification of the alternative as polytheism. The argument the audience pressed was not an argument about hygiene or taste; it was a claim about who has the right to declare food lawful, and the sūrah treats the claim as an act of association with God.

**The Place of the Verse in the Section**

The passage that follows this verse turns to the details of the audience's system: the livestock they dedicated, the animals they set apart, the rules about who might eat what, and the shares assigned to God and to the idols (6:136–139; 6:143–144). The verse in front of us states the principle by which all of that is judged, and the sections that follow apply it.

The sūrah thus completes the first stage of its treatment of food. The believers are told what they may eat, why they may eat it, what is forbidden, and that the arguments offered against the rule come from the whisperings of the devils and their associates. The rest of the chapter takes the audience's own rules one by one and leaves the reader to measure them against the standard just supplied.
verses.122:
> Can those who had been dead, to whom We gave life and a light with which they can walk among people, be compared to those in complete darkness from which they can never emerge? That is how the misdeeds of the disbelievers have been made appealing to them

**The Parable of the Dead and the Living**

Can those who had been dead, to whom We gave life and a light with which they can walk among people, be compared to those in complete darkness from which they can never emerge? The verse states a comparison and leaves the answer to the reader, and the images it uses are the sūrah's own vocabulary from its earlier verses. The person who was dead and received life is the one who heard the message and responded; the light he walks by is the guidance; and the person in the darkness is the one who has been left in the condition described in the passage about the turning of the hearts.

The Book uses the same language about life and light in several places. The sūrah of Fāṭir says that the dead and the living are not equal and that God makes whom He wills hear (35:22); the sūrah of the Cow describes God as the guardian of the believers, bringing them out of darkness into light, while the disbelievers have their guardians in false gods who lead them from light into darkness (2:257); and the sūrah of the Cattle itself uses the phrase about walking among people in the present verse.

**The Light and the Darkness**

The two images are the Book's standard figures for guidance and its absence. To walk among people by a light is to move through the world with a course set and a destination known, and the Book contrasts that condition with the man who gropes in a darkness from which he cannot emerge. The sūrah of the Cattle earlier described the person whom the satans have seduced in the open country, calling to others who call him back to guidance he does not follow (6:71), which is the same condition stated by a different image.

The Book's use of light for revelation appears throughout its descriptions of the earlier scriptures as well. The sūrah of the Table describes the Torah as containing guidance and light (5:44), and the sūrah of the Cattle will later describe the Book given to Moses as a light and guidance for people (6:91). The verse in front of us treats the effect of that guidance on a person's conduct, which is the light by which he walks.

**The Deeds Made Appealing**

That is how the misdeeds of the disbelievers have been made appealing to them. The sentence explains the condition of the second figure in the comparison, and it uses the same vocabulary as the earlier passages about the enemies of the prophets and the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter (6:112–113). The Book's account of the made-appealing of evil conduct appears at several points in this chapter and outside it, and it is always attached to the people who have chosen their course.

The commentators described the appeal of the deeds as something produced by God's granting of respite and prosperity, which leads the people to suppose that their way is approved. The Book describes the same arrangement in the sūrah of the Family of Imran, where the disbelievers are warned against thinking that the time granted to them is good, since they are given time only to increase in sin. The verse in front of us states the arrangement as a fact of the disbelievers' condition rather than as a future threat.

**What the Two Conditions Mean for the Audience**

The comparison in this verse is addressed to people who were making the judgement implied by the question. The members of the audience who had denied the message judged the believers to be the losers, and the verse asks them to state whether the two conditions are alike. The Book uses this form of argument at several points, and it usually states the answer inside the question.

The verse's force lies in the change of perspective it requires. The person who walks by a light is the one whose way leads somewhere, and the person in the darkness is the one whose movement has no direction. The audience's assumption was that the established position of the majority constituted the direction, and the verse states the opposite in terms of sight and walking.

**The Book's Use of This Comparison**

The comparison between the living and the dead and between light and darkness runs through the Book's descriptions of the two responses to revelation. The sūrah of Fāṭir states that the dead and the living are not equal, and it places the statement in the context of God's making whom He wills hear, since the Prophet cannot make those in the graves hear (35:22). The sūrah of the Cow makes the same distinction at the end of its account of the covenant.

The verse in front of us therefore expresses a contrast the Book draws everywhere. What the sūrah has been describing since its opening verses, through the argument about the signs and the accounts of the earlier messengers, is how the two conditions are produced: the guidance comes from God, and the people who are left in their darkness have refused what was offered.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The verse that follows states that God has placed in every society the most wicked of its people to conspire in it, and that they plot only against themselves without perceiving it (6:123). The two verses belong together, since the darkness described here is the condition of the people who conspire in the next verse: they are active opponents of the message, and the sūrah describes them as plotting against their own interest.

That transition continues the sūrah's account of the opposition to the messengers. Having described the individual conditions of the guided and the lost, the chapter turns to the corporate activity of the people who work against the message, and it treats their activity with the same knowledge of the outcome that the earlier passages supplied.
verses.123:
> And so We have placed in every society the most wicked to conspire in it. Yet they plot only against themselves, but they fail to perceive it

**The Wicked Placed in Every Society**

And so We have placed in every society the most wicked to conspire in it. The verse states a fact about the societies to which the message came, and it does so as a general pattern rather than as a description of Makkah alone. Every community has had its leaders in opposition, and the Book connects the statement to the earlier verses about the enemies appointed to every prophet (6:112).

The Book's account of the opponents in other sūrahs identifies them with the same word the translation renders as the elite. The sūrah of Saba' says that whenever a warner was sent to a society, its elite said that they rejected what he had been sent with (34:34), and the sūrah of the Ornament records the same response, with the elite saying that they had found their forefathers following a way and would follow in their footsteps (43:23). The sūrah's audience, which took its direction from the leading families of the city, is being shown the pattern of that leadership.

**What the Conspiracy Consists In**

The verse describes the activity of these people as conspiring or plotting, and the Book uses the term for the schemes by which the messengers were resisted. The sūrah of the Prophets records the plan that Abraham's people made against him and the response that made them the worst losers (21:70), and the sūrah of the Cattle has recorded several of the audience's own schemes in its accounts of their demands and objections.

The Book treats the plotting as the work of the people it names, and it does not attribute it to the whole of a society. The elite are described as the ones who conspire, and the sūrah of the Ornament has them appealing to the ancestors' custom rather than to any argument. The verse in front of us states that this group exists in every community, and the sūrah's audience is told that its own leadership belongs to the pattern.

**They Plot Only Against Themselves**

Yet they plot only against themselves, but they fail to perceive it. The sentence states the outcome of the plotting, and the Book's claim is that the harm returns to the people who plan it. The sūrah of Fāṭir states that evil plotting only backfires on those who plot, and it attaches the conduct to the people who behaved arrogantly in the land (35:43); the sūrah of the Ants records the plan made by a community against the messenger and says that God made a plan while they were unaware (27:50); and the sūrah of the Family of Imran tells the believers that if they are patient and mindful of God, the schemes of their enemies will not harm them (3:120).

The Book's reasoning for that claim lies in its account of God's power over what is planned. The schemes of the elite succeeded in delaying the acceptance of the message, and they failed in the matter that counted, which was the progress of the revelation and the establishment of its community. The sentence in this verse describes the outcome from the standpoint of the schemers' own interest, and it says that they did not see what their effort was producing.

**The Failure to Perceive**

The closing clause adds the reason the schemers continued: they did not perceive what they were doing to themselves. The Book attaches the same inability to the people whose conduct it has been describing. The sūrah has said that they follow assumption and lie (6:116), that their conduct has been made appealing to them (6:122), and that their hearts were turned away after their first refusal (6:110). The verse in front of us states the practical consequence of that condition in the field of action.

The inability to perceive is not presented as a lack of intelligence, since the leaders of the Quraysh were capable and experienced. What the Book describes is a blindness about the direction of their own conduct, and it states that the blindness is the product of the choices the people had made.

**What the Verse Says to the Prophet and the Believers**

The verse answers the situation in which the small community found itself. The leading families controlled the resources of the city, and their opposition determined the terms on which the community lived. The Book tells the Prophet that this arrangement is neither peculiar to his city nor a sign that his mission has failed, since the pattern belongs to every society to which a warner has been sent.

The book has given the same assurance in its accounts of the earlier messengers, where the opposition is consistently presented as coming from the established families of the people and not from the community as a whole. The sūrah of Hūd records the leaders of Noah's people rejecting him on the basis of the standing of his followers, and the same pattern is traced through the histories that follow. The verse in front of us states the pattern in a single sentence.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse records the response of these people to the signs: whenever a sign comes to them, they say that they will never believe until they receive what God's messengers received (6:124). The demand is for the gift of prophethood itself or for the authority that came with it, and the verse answers that God knows best where to place His message.

The sequence of the two verses is exact. The elite plot within their society, and their plotting takes the form of a demand that the message be delivered by people of their own choosing. The sūrah has answered the demand for a sign, and it now answers the demand for a different messenger.
verses.124:
> Whenever a sign comes to them, they say, “We will never believe until we receive what Allah’s messengers received.” Allah knows best where to place His message. The wicked will soon be overwhelmed by humiliation from Allah and a severe punishment for their evil plots

**The Demand Made at Every Sign**

Whenever a sign comes to them, they say, We will never believe until we receive what Allah's messengers received. The verse records the demand of the elite described in the previous verse, and the demand is not for evidence but for standing. What the messengers received was the message itself and the authority that accompanied it, and the audience's position was that they would accept revelation only if it came down to them personally.

The Book records the same disposition in other places. The sūrah of the Night Journey records the demand of the audience that the Prophet bring down a book they could read (17:93), and the sūrah of the Family of Imran records the claim of those who said that God had commanded them not to believe in any messenger unless he brought an offering consumed by fire from the sky (3:183). The verse in front of us states the demand in its clearest form, since the audience wanted the office rather than the proof.

**The Answer Given to the Demand**

Allah knows best where to place His message. The sentence answers the demand by referring the matter of appointment to the One who makes it, and the Book states the same principle elsewhere in its accounts of the prophets. The sūrah of the Pilgrimage says that God selects messengers from both angels and people, for He is All-Hearing and All-Seeing (22:75), and the sūrah of the Cow records God's testing of Abraham and His promise to make him a leader for the people (2:124).

The answer also addresses the assumption behind the demand, which was that the leading families of a city were the natural candidates for any great mission. The Book's choice of messengers from among the shepherds, the traders, and the communities without standing was a standing provocation to the elite, and the sūrah of the Ornament records their complaint that the Qur'an should have been sent down to a great man of one of the two cities. The verse in front of us states that the placement of the message belongs to God's knowledge.

**The Humiliation and the Punishment**

The wicked will soon be overwhelmed by humiliation from Allah and a severe punishment for their evil plots. The verse closes by stating what the demand will produce, and the terms it uses are the ones the sūrah has applied to the opponents of the message throughout. Humiliation is the condition of the people who set themselves against the message, and the punishment is attached to the plotting described in the previous verse.

The Book's statements about the outcome of the plotters appear in several passages. The sūrah of Fāṭir states that evil plotting only backfires on those who plot (35:43); the sūrah of Tā-Hā records the magicians falling in prostration and believing after the sign was shown to them (20:70); and the sūrah of the Cattle has already described the wrongdoers in the throes of death and the torment that follows (6:93). The sentence in this verse attaches the same outcome to the demand for the messenger's office.

**The Reasoning in the Verse**

The verse sets two kinds of knowledge side by side. The audience claimed to know who should receive the message, and the Book states that God knows where to place it. The difference between the two is the difference between assumption and knowledge that the sūrah has been stating since its warning about following the majority.

The verse's arrangement also explains the audience's persistence. A people who believed that the position of their families entitled them to the leadership of any movement would not accept the message of a man from outside that position, and the Book presents their rejection as a response to the messenger's standing rather than to the content of what he brought. The verse states the correction directly, and it leaves the outcome with God.

**What the Verse Says About the Messengers**

The sentence about placing the message is the Book's answer to every objection based on the messenger's social position. The Book's narratives of the earlier prophets consistently present the same objection from the elites: that the messengers were ordinary men, that they ate food and walked in the markets, that they were not accompanied by angels, and that their followers were the weak. The verse in front of us treats all such objections under one principle.

The Book's own account of the Prophet's standing belongs to the same argument. The sūrah of the Family of Imran tells the believers that God has favoured them by sending a messenger from among themselves, and the sūrah of the Repentance states that a messenger has come to them from among their own number who is pained by their hardship. The message's placement among a particular people is presented as a mercy rather than as an accident.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse states the arrangement by which the two responses are decided: whoever God wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam, and whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted as though he were climbing into the sky (6:125). The two verses answer the same question from different sides, and the sūrah completes its account of guidance and its refusal.

The passage therefore ends with the division it has been describing throughout: a demand answered by God's knowledge, and a response settled by God's will. The sūrah's next verses return to the created order and to the signs, and they bring the chapter's argument back to the evidence that was available to the audience all along.
verses.125:
> Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens their heart to Islam. But whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes their chest tight and constricted as if they were climbing up into the sky. This is how Allah dooms those who disbelieve

**The Opening of the Heart**

Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens their heart to Islam. The verse states the arrangement by which guidance occurs, and it does so in the physical language the sūrah has used before.
