The heart that is opened receives what is presented to it, and the same image appeared in the previous passage about the hearts of those who disbelieve in the Hereafter being receptive to the whisperings of the devils (6:113). The two verses describe the same faculty receiving two different things.

The Book uses the opening of the heart for the effect of the message on believers in other places. The sūrah of the Troops asks whether the person whose heart God has opened to Islam, so that he walks in light from his Lord, is like the person whose heart is hardened (39:22), and the sūrah of the Cattle earlier described the light by which the believer walks among people (6:122). The verse in front of us states the divine act that produces that condition.

**The Constricted Chest**

But whoever He wills to leave astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted as if they were climbing up into the sky. The second half of the verse describes the condition of the person who is left in his error, and the image is one of breath. The comparison with the climber who cannot draw air describes the difficulty such a person experiences when the message is presented to him, and the sūrah of the Troops asks the same question from the other side, contrasting the opened heart with the hardened one.

The Book uses the image of the chest in its accounts of the Prophet's own experience as well, and the sūrah of Tā-Hā records his request that his chest be expanded for the task given to him (20:25). The verse in front of us states the same faculty in its closed condition, and the two images together give the Book's picture of the inner life as a space that can be opened or narrowed.

**The Language of the Verse and Its Source**

The verse's closing sentence states that this is how God dooms those who disbelieve. The commentators noted that the description of the constricted chest was familiar to the Arabs as an image of extreme difficulty, and that the verse is one of the clearest statements in the Book of the relationship between God's will and a person's condition. The Book elsewhere describes God as the one who guides whom He wills and leaves astray whom He wills, and it presents the two outcomes without concealing either.

The sūrah of the Troops gives the fuller statement to which this verse belongs: those whose hearts God has opened walk in light, while those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of God are in manifest error (39:22). The Book's language in both passages joins the inner condition to the response, and it treats the guidance as a gift rather than as a reward for the person's prior merit.

**The Two Conditions and the Sūrah's Argument**

The verse completes the answer to the demand recorded in the previous verse, in which the elite said they would not believe until they received what God's messengers received. The answer given here is that belief is a matter of the heart's condition rather than of the messenger's standing, and the persons who make the demand are described as unable to breathe in the presence of the message.

The sūrah's account of the two conditions has run from the beginning of the chapter. It described the sealing of the hearts of those who denied the signs (6:46), the turning of the hearts and eyes after the first refusal (6:110), and the receptivity of the hearts of those who denied the Hereafter to the whisperings of the devils (6:113). The verse in front of us states the principle that governs all of those passages.

**What the Verse Says About the Prophet's Task**

The verse relieves the Prophet of a burden that the sūrah has been addressing throughout the passage. He had been told to follow what was revealed, to turn away from the polytheists, and that he was neither keeper nor maintainer over the people (6:106–107); now he is told that the opening of the heart is God's act. The messenger delivers; the response is produced by a cause beyond his control.

The Book states the same arrangement in the sūrah of the Stories, where the Prophet is told that he cannot guide whom he loves but that God guides whom He wills (28:56). The two verses together define the limit of the prophetic office, and the sūrah's later instructions to the Prophet rest on that limit.

**The Transition to the Following Verse**

The next verse names the path that is described in this passage and announces that it belongs to God: this is the path of your Lord, straight, and the signs have been detailed for people who remember (6:126). The two verses belong together, since the opening of the heart and the constriction of the chest describe the two responses to the path, and the sūrah states the path's character as the standard by which the responses are measured.

The sūrah then continues with the promise of the home of peace with God as a protector, the day when the wrongdoers will be gathered to the fire, and the final passages about the jinn, the livestock, and the dietary system. The verse in front of us completes the section on guidance, and the chapter returns to the theme of the signs and their explanation for people who remember.
verses.126:
> That is your Lord’s Path—perfectly straight. We have already made the signs clear to those who are mindful

**The Path Named**

That is your Lord's Path, perfectly straight. The verse identifies the way that the sūrah has been describing. The demonstrative reaches back through the passage about the opening of the heart and the constriction of the chest, and it gathers the whole account into a single noun: the path of the Lord. What the sūrah has been offering the audience is not a set of arguments alone but a road, and the sentence names it.

The Book's language of paths appears throughout its addresses to the community. The sūrah of the Cattle itself returns to the image at the end of its long passage of prohibitions, where God tells the Prophet that this is His path, straight, and commands the community to follow it while warning against the paths that branch off and separate those who take them (6:153). The sūrah of the Family of Imran gives the same instruction in the prayer that God guide the believers to the straight path, and the opening sūrah of the Book asks for guidance upon it.

**The Straightness of the Path**

The Book's use of the image in the opening sūrah shows how central it is to everything the revelation asks. The prayer for guidance upon the straight path stands at the head of the Book (1:6), and the sūrah of the Family of Imran closes the declaration attributed to Jesus with the same phrase, telling its hearers that God is his Lord and theirs, that they should worship Him, and that this is the straight path (3:51).

The description of the path as straight states its function: it leads to the destination without deviation. The sūrah of the Family of Imran calls the message itself a way that is straight, and the sūrah of the Consultation states that God guides whom He wills to a straight path and that the revelation is a light by which He guides His servants (42:52). The Book's repeated use of the image shows that its concern is with the direction in which a person is travelling rather than with the opinions he holds in isolation.

For the Makkan audience, the claim had a specific force. Their city was a place of pilgrimage roads, and the metaphor of the travellers' routes was part of ordinary life. The Book tells them that a single road leads to the Lord, and that the practices they inherited had taken them off it. The sentence names the road and leaves the choice of travelling it with the hearer.

**The Signs Made Clear for the Mindful**

We have already made the signs clear to those who are mindful. The clause closes the passage with the fourth and last form of the formula the sūrah has used after its accounts of signs. The stars and the darkness were made clear for people who know (6:97); the sign of the single soul was for people who comprehend (6:98); the harvest was for people who believe (6:99); and the path described here is for people who are mindful.

The progression moves from the faculty of knowledge to the action of remembering, and the sūrah's vocabulary marks the difference between receiving information and holding it present. The Book's commands to remember occur throughout its addresses to the community, and the sūrah of the Cow attaches the guidance of the Book to those who are mindful of God.

**What the Verse Says About the Signs and the Path**

The verse joins two statements that the sūrah has kept together throughout: the road exists, and its signs have been made clear. The Book's claim is not that the path is hidden or that the guidance is inscrutable. The signs are set out for anyone who will pay attention, and the responsibility of the reader is stated in the description of the people for whom they are clear.

The audience had asked for signs of a particular kind and had been told that signs are with God. The verse in front of us supplies the answer to that demand in its own terms: the signs that lead along the path are already present, and the person who is mindful of God will find them where they have been placed.

**The Place of the Verse in the Sūrah's Structure**

The verse marks the end of the section that began with the command to follow what was revealed (6:106). That section has moved through the limits of the messenger's responsibility, the prohibition on reviling the idols of others, the oaths of those who demanded signs, the enemies appointed to every prophet, the deception of the whisperers, the authority of the Book, the warning against the majority, the dietary rules, the conditions of guidance and error, and now the naming of the path.

The sūrah's second half will move to the account of the gathering of jinn and humans, the reckoning of the communities, and the final passages on the dietary system and the covenant. The verse in front of us closes one movement of the chapter and states its conclusion: the path is God's, it is straight, and its signs have been made clear to the people who remember them.

**The Verse and the Reward That Follows**

The next verse states that the people who follow the path will have the Home of Peace with their Lord, and that He will be their guardian because of what they used to do (6:127). The two verses are joined in the way the sūrah has joined its statements throughout: the road and its destination, the guidance and the meeting with the guide.

That pairing gives the sūrah's argument its shape. The signs, the path, and the Home of Peace are presented as a single arrangement, and the audience is addressed as people capable of walking it. The Book's closing of the passage with the description of the mindful hearer states once more where the responsibility lies.
verses.127:
> They will have the Home of Peace with their Lord, Who will be their Guardian because of what they used to do

**The Home of Peace**

They will have the Home of Peace with their Lord. The verse names the destination of the road described in the sentence before it, and the name it gives the destination is the Book's own. The sūrah of Yūnus states that God invites all people to the Home of Peace and guides whoever He wills to the straight path (10:25), and the sūrah of the Troops describes the arrival of the mindful at the gates of the garden, where the keepers greet them with the word of peace and tell them that they have been made pure (39:73).

The pairing of the home's name with the word the Book uses for peace is deliberate. The Book's peace is the condition in which a person is free of fear and loss, and the sūrah of the Cow attaches that condition to those who follow the guidance, saying that they will have no fear and no grief (2:62). The home named in this verse is the place where the condition is complete, and the sūrah places it at the end of the road it has just described.

**The Home and Its Lord**

With their Lord. The phrase attaches the reward to the presence of the One who gave it rather than to a location, and the Book uses the same construction in its descriptions of the reward of the believers throughout. The sūrah of the Troops ends its description of the garden with the declaration that the believers have attained what they hoped for, and the Book's accounts of the Hereafter consistently present the meeting with God as the substance of the reward that the images describe.

The verse has already described the path as the path of the Lord, and the destination named here is the same Lord's home. The sūrah's arrangement is therefore a single movement from the guidance of the path to the presence of the guide, and the two sentences belong to one statement about the community that responds.

**The Guardian**

Who will be their Guardian because of what they used to do. The Book's term for the guardian describes the one who takes charge of another's affairs, and the sūrah of the Cow uses the same word for God at the end of its passage on light and darkness, saying that God is the Guardian of the believers who brings them out of darkness into light (2:257). The sūrah of the Kneeling states that God is the patron of the righteous while the wrongdoers are patrons of one another (45:19).

The Book's use of the term in this verse completes the description of the reward: the people who followed the path are not only admitted to the home but placed under the care of its owner. The state described is one of dependence fulfilled, since the person who has been guided through the world arrives at the end under the protection of the One who guided him.

**Because of What They Used to Do**

The clause attaches the reward to the conduct of the people who receive it, and the Book uses the same formula at the end of many of its promises. The sūrah of the Bowing states that no soul can imagine the delights kept in store for the believers as a reward for what they used to do (32:17), and the sūrah of the Prophets says that those for whom the finest reward has been destined will be kept far away from the fire (21:101). The formula is the Book's way of stating that the reward corresponds to the conduct it follows.

The Book's teaching on the relationship between deeds and reward appears throughout its addresses to the community. Its statements about forgiveness and grace stand alongside its statements about recompense, and the two belong together in a scheme in which the believers are told that their efforts are not disregarded and that what they send ahead will be found with God (73:20). The verse in front of us states the principle in its compact form, and the sūrah's later passages apply it to the reckoning of the communities.

**What the Verse Establishes for the Reader**

The verse closes the sūrah's section on guidance with a statement of what the guidance leads to. The Book has described the opening of the heart, the straightness of the path, and the signs made clear for the mindful; the reward named here is the end of that whole arrangement. A reader who has followed the sūrah's argument from its opening verses now sees the destination attached to the road.

The placement of the verse also prepares the reader for the passages that follow. The sūrah turns immediately to the gathering of the jinn and their human associates, the address to the communities at the resurrection, and the account of what the people with the most wealth and the greatest standing will bring with them. The Home of Peace stands at the head of those passages as the alternative they define.

**The Contrast With What Follows**

The next verse records the day when God will gather the beings together and address the jinn as the ones who misled great numbers of human beings, and the human associates will reply that they benefited from one another and have now reached the term appointed for them (6:128). The two verses set the two destinies side by side: the community of the path and the community of mutual deception.

The sūrah has been building toward that contrast since its treatment of the enemies of the prophets and the hearts that received their whisperings. What the verse in front of us supplies is the end of the road for the people who accepted the message, and it does so in terms that the sūrah's audience, familiar with the conditions of travel and hospitality, could measure against the alternative.
verses.128:
> ˹Consider˺ the Day He will gather them ˹all˺ together and say, “O assembly of jinn! You misled humans in great numbers.” And their human associates will say, “Our Lord! We benefited from each other’s company, but now we have reached the term which You appointed for us.” ˹Then˺ He will say, “The Fire is your home, yours to stay in forever, except whoever Allah wills to spare.” Surely your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing

**The Gathering and the Address**

Consider the Day He will gather them all together and say, O assembly of jinn! You misled humans in great numbers. The verse opens one of the sūrah's accounts of the resurrection, and it begins with an address to the jinn as a body. The Book's word for the gathering of a whole order of beings at once is used elsewhere for the assembly of the communities, and the sūrah of the Cattle records a comparable address a few verses later, when both the jinn and human beings are asked whether messengers did not come to them from among themselves (6:130).

The Book's accounts of the partnerships between the jinn and human beings appear in several places. The sūrah of the Jinn records that some men used to seek refuge with some jinn, so that they increased one another in wickedness (72:6); the sūrah of Saba' records the disavowal of the jinn on the day of judgment, when they declare that it was the people who followed them and not the reverse (34:41); and the sūrah of the Heights describes the entry of the evil groups of jinn and humans into the fire together (7:38). The address in this verse belongs to that family of passages.

**The Admission of the Human Associates**

And their human associates will say, Our Lord! We benefited from each other's company. The reply admits the relationship and describes it as a mutual advantage. The Book's statements elsewhere fill in what the advantage consisted of: the humans received the jinn's services in fortune-telling, protection, and ritual instruction, and the jinn gained followers and influence among the people. The sūrah has already described the association of the jinn with God by the audience (6:100), and the sentence in front of us gives the human side of the arrangement.

The Book treats the partnership as a real one rather than as a metaphor, and it records the jinn's own report of it in the sūrah that bears their name. The admission in this verse is the voice of the people who had made the arrangement, spoken at the moment when its consequences are being drawn.

**The Term Appointed**

But now we have reached the term which You appointed for us. The reply ends with the acknowledgement that the arrangement has run out. The Book's word for the term is the one it uses for the fixed span of every community and person, and the sūrah of the Cattle has already described God's holding of the souls and His revival of them by day within the span He has set (6:60). The sūrah of the Heights and the sūrah of Yūnus state that every community has its term which cannot be advanced or delayed (7:34; 10:49).

The sentence gives the scene its shape. The partners in the worldly arrangement have arrived at the end of it, and the usefulness they found in one another has expired. What the Book presents is a reckoning in which the relationships that organised life in the world are dissolved, and the verse's speakers state the fact of the dissolution as their own admission.

**The Sentence Passed**

Then He will say, The Fire is your home, yours to stay in forever, except whoever Allah wills to spare. The sentence states the outcome of the partnership, and it includes an exception clause. The Book uses the same form in the sūrah of Hūd, where the duration of the punishment is described as lasting while the heavens and the earth endure, except what the Lord wills (11:107), and the exception is understood in the light of the Book's statement that God does what He intends.

The commentators discussed the exception at length, and they connected it to the possibility of God's mercy reaching those whom He chooses. What the verse states is the permanence of the fire for the people described and the absolute freedom of God in the matter, and the attributes that close the sentence support the reading.

**The Names at the End**

Surely your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing. The two names explain the judgement that has just been pronounced: the knowledge that saw the arrangement in its reality and the wisdom that made the sentence fit it. The Book attaches this pair to its accounts of the reckoning in many places, and the sūrah has used the vocabulary of God's knowledge throughout its treatment of the hidden and the open.

The names also answer the objection that a person might raise about the length of the punishment. The Book's statements about the fire are always accompanied by its statements about the justice and knowledge of the judge, and the verse in front of us follows that pattern. The God who sentences is the God who knows what each partner did and who has measured the response.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse states that God makes the wrongdoers allies of one another because of what they have earned (6:129). The sentence follows the scene of the partnership and the judgement, and it generalises the arrangement: the mutual support of the wicked is itself a feature of the order that the Book describes, and it is a consequence of their deeds rather than a description of their strength.

The sūrah's account of the reckoning continues with the address to the communities and the confessions of the inhabitants of the fire, and the passage as a whole serves the argument the chapter has been making since its opening verses. The verse in front of us supplies the first scene of that account and states the end of the partnership the audience had entered with the unseen.
verses.129:
> This is how We make the wrongdoers ˹destructive˺ allies of one another because of their misdeeds

**The Alliance of the Wrongdoers**

This is how We make the wrongdoers allies of one another because of their misdeeds. The verse states a general principle after the account of the partnership between the jinn and their human associates, and it describes the companionship of the wicked as something God brings about. The sentence presents the alliance as an arrangement rather than as an accident of temperament, and it attaches the arrangement to the deeds of the people involved.

The Book's word for the ally covers the patron who takes charge of another's affairs and the friend who stands with him. The sūrah of the Kneeling uses the pair of terms in a single sentence, saying that the wrongdoers are patrons of one another while God is the patron of the righteous (45:19), and the verse in front of us states the first half of that contrast as a fact of the present order.

**The Book's Descriptions of the Wicked Company**

The Book returns to the company of the wicked in its accounts of the day of judgment, and it describes the company dissolving there. The sūrah of the Ornament states that close friends will be enemies to one another on that day except the righteous (43:67), and the sūrah of the Heights describes the groups of jinn and humans entering the fire together and cursing one another as they follow one another in. The sūrah of the Cattle has already described the partners in deception arriving at their term and being told that the fire is their home (6:128).

The companionships described in these passages share a feature: those who supported one another in the world are described as turning on one another when the support is no longer useful. The verse in front of us states the arrangement that produces those companionships, and the account of their end appears in the sūrahs that describe the reckoning.

**The Reason Attached to the Sentence**

Because of their misdeeds. The clause attaches the alliance to the conduct of the people, and the Book's statement is that the companionship of the wicked is itself a consequence of their wrongdoing. The sūrah has described the whisperings of the satans among men and jinn as an activity that targets the hearts of those who disbelieve in the Hereafter (6:113), and the sentence in front of us states that the participants in that activity are joined to one another.

The Book's reasoning follows the pattern it has established throughout the chapter. The people who choose a course are confirmed in it, and the confirmation includes the company they keep. The verse states the arrangement as one of the ways in which a choice is made to hold, and it presents the company of the wicked as a feature of the condition they have chosen.

**What the Verse Says About the Strength of the Wicked**

The sentence describes an alliance that is real but ruinous, and the translation's word for it carries the sense of mutual destruction. The Book's accounts of the powerful in the world do not deny their power; the sūrah of Saba' and the sūrah of the Ornament describe the elites of the communities as established and confident. What the Book denies is that their alliance can secure them against the judgement that follows.

The sūrah has made the point in its passages about the plotters who did not perceive that they plotted against themselves (6:123) and about the elite who demanded the messenger's office (6:124). The verse in front of us states the same fact about the alliances those people formed, and it describes the mutual support as a mutual harm that they did not see.

**The Verse in the Sūrah's Argument**

The verse stands between the account of the partnership between the jinn and the people and the address to both assemblies at the resurrection, and it supplies the general statement that binds the two passages together. The jinn misled human beings and the human beings benefited from the jinn, and the alliance that grew from that arrangement belongs to the wider pattern of alliances among the wrongdoers.

The Book's presentation is therefore not limited to the case of the jinn. The same sentence applies to every company formed around a course that the revelation condemns, and the sūrah's audience, organised as it was around clans and interest, is addressed by the principle in its own terms.

**The Contrast With the Community of the Believers**

The Book sets the mutual support of the wrongdoers against another kind of company, and the contrast shows what the verse is describing. The sūrah of the Chambers states that the believers are but one brotherhood and commands them to make peace among themselves (49:10); the sūrah of the Family of Imran tells the community to hold firmly to the rope of God and not to be divided, and it recalls the favour by which their hearts were united after enmity (3:103); and the sūrah of the Spoils says that God brought the hearts of the believers together when no amount of wealth could have done it (8:63).

The difference between the two companies lies in what holds them together. The alliance described in this verse rests on misdeeds and dissolves when its usefulness ends, while the brotherhood described in the other passages rests on a shared response to the message and is described as a gift from God. The sūrah's audience knew both kinds of bond, since the message had begun to create a community out of the tribes of a city organised around rivalry.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse records the address to the assembly of jinn and humans, asking whether messengers did not come to them from among their own people, proclaiming the revelations of God and warning them of the coming of the day, and it records their answer that they testify against themselves (6:130). The address follows the principle stated here, since the alliance of the wrongdoers does not remove the warning that was given to every community.

The sūrah thus completes its account of the responsibility of the people who were gathered. The partnership, the term, the fire, the alliance, and the confession follow one another as a sequence, and the verse in front of us states the law that governs the company of the people who chose the path the sūrah has been describing.
verses.130:
> ˹Allah will ask,˺ “O assembly of jinn and humans! Did messengers not come from among you, proclaiming My revelations and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours?” They will say, “We confess against ourselves!” For they have been deluded by ˹their˺ worldly life. And they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers

**The Address to Both Assemblies**

O assembly of jinn and humans! Did messengers not come from among you, proclaiming My revelations and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours? The verse records the address given to the assembled orders of created beings, and its form is a question that contains its own answer. The Book's word for the assembly is the one used in the previous address to the jinn (6:128), and the two sentences together frame the scene: the partners are gathered, and both are asked about the warning they received.

The Book states the universality of the warning in several places. The sūrah of Fāṭir says that the Prophet was sent with the truth as a deliverer of good news and a warner and that there is no community which has not had a warner (35:24); the sūrah of the Bee says that God has sent a messenger to every community with the command to worship God and shun false gods (16:36); and the sūrah of the Women says that messengers were sent with good news and warnings so that humanity should have no excuse before God after the coming of the messengers (4:165).

**The Argument From the Messengers' Coming**

The question's purpose is to establish the justice of the judgement, and the Book builds its account of the reckoning on the prior delivery of the message. The sūrah of the Cattle itself records the words of the people of the fire, who will say that they had no messenger come to them, and the Book's answer anticipates that claim with the address in this verse.

The mention of messengers coming from among the people addresses a point the sūrah has been making about the prophetic office. The Book's messengers are drawn from the communities they address, and the sūrah of the Family of Imran states that God favoured the believers by raising a messenger from among them (3:164). The question in this verse therefore states that no community was left without a spokesman of its own kind, and it leaves the assembled people to acknowledge the fact.

**The Confession**

They will say, We confess against ourselves! The answer admits the truth of the accusation without argument, and the Book records similar admissions at other points in its accounts of the judgement. The sūrah of the Heights describes the cry of the people overwhelmed by the punishment, saying that they had been wrongdoers (7:5); the sūrah of the Kingdom says that they will confess their sins and that the residents of the blaze are far from mercy (67:11); and the sūrah of the Prophets records the declaration of those who had taken lords besides God, freeing God of any partnership and confessing that they had been the ones at fault (25:18).

The sūrah of the Cattle has already described an audience that would deny everything at the resurrection, with their only argument being an oath that they were never polytheists (6:23). The verse in front of us supplies the other response, which is the confession that the sūrah's account of the judgement requires for its justice to be visible.

**The Delusion of the Worldly Life**

For they have been deluded by their worldly life. The sentence gives the reason the confession comes so late, and the Book's word for the delusion describes being taken in by something that appears substantial. The sūrah's earlier passage used the same vocabulary for the people who took their religion as play and amusement and were deluded by the life of this world (6:70), and the two passages belong to the same account of what the world's attractions do to a person's judgement.

The Book's treatment of the worldly life is consistent across the sūrahs. It describes the life of the world as a pasture and a passing enjoyment, and it contrasts it with what is with God, without denying its reality. The verse in front of us states the effect of that life on the people who were addressed by the messengers and remained where their desires had placed them.

**The Testimony Against Themselves**

And they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers. The verse closes with the completion of the admission, and the Book presents the record of a person's conduct as testimony that he gives against himself. The sūrah of the Night Journey states that every human being's destiny is bound to his neck and that a record will be brought out for him on the day of judgment, with the command to read it and the statement that the person is sufficient as an accountant against himself (17:13–14).

The sūrah has described the recording of deeds in its earlier passages, where the angels write down what the people do (6:61), and the verse in front of us shows the record being used. The testimony is not extracted by force; it is given by the people whose deeds it contains.

**What the Verse Establishes**

The verse establishes the terms on which the judgement of the gathered orders proceeds. Messengers came, revelations were proclaimed, warnings were delivered, and the people who were addressed were left without an argument. The confession that follows is the acknowledgement of that record, and the sūrah treats it as the final answer of the people who had argued throughout their lives.

The passage that continues from here returns to the theme of the Hereafter and the conduct of the people who denied it, and it moves toward the end of the sūrah's long middle section. The verse in front of us completes the sequence begun with the address to the jinn, and it states the principle on which the whole reckoning rests.
verses.131:
> This ˹sending of the messengers˺ is because your Lord would never destroy a society for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware ˹of the truth˺

**The Reason for the Sending of the Messengers**

This is because your Lord would never destroy a society for their wrongdoing while its people are unaware of the truth. The verse states the principle that stands behind the address to the assembled jinn and humans, and it explains why the warning was delivered before the reckoning. The sending of the messengers is presented as the arrangement by which the judgement is made just, and the verse attributes the arrangement to the Lord's dealings with the societies He has addressed.

The Book states the same principle in several places. The sūrah of the Night Journey says that God would never punish a people until He has sent a messenger to warn them (17:15), the sūrah of the Stories says that the Lord would never destroy a society until He has sent a messenger to its capital reciting His revelations (28:59), and the sūrah of the Poets declares that God has never destroyed a society without warners (26:208). The verse in front of us gives the same assurance in the context of the reckoning, where the confession of the assembled people has just been recorded.

**The Warning Preceding the Judgement**

The Book's accounts of the destroyed communities consistently attach the destruction to a warning that was rejected. The sūrah of the Cattle itself has described the fate of the communities that denied their messengers and the succession of the generations, and it has stated that God does not destroy a society unjustly. The verse in front of us gathers that teaching into a single sentence about the treatment of the people who are addressed.

The principle also answers the objection that the verse's own context raises. A community that was never told cannot be judged on the basis of what it was never told, and the Book's answer is that no community has lacked a warner. The address to the jinn and humans in the previous verse is the application of the principle, and the sentence in front of us states the reason the address was given.

**What the Verse Says About Ignorance**

The Book's word for the unawareness of the people describes the condition of those who have not been reminded, and the sūrah has used it for the people who turn away from the signs. The verse's point is that the warning removes the condition, and the Book's messengers are sent precisely so that the people who receive them can no longer plead that they did not know.

The Book's statements about responsibility elsewhere rest on the same arrangement. The sūrah of the Women says that messengers were sent with good news and warnings so that humanity should have no excuse before God after their coming (4:165), and the sūrah of Fāṭir states that there is no community without a warner (35:24). The verse in front of us states the purpose those verses describe, and it states it as a feature of the Lord's justice rather than as a record of the particular missions.

**The Justice Implied in the Sentence**

The sentence presents the destruction of a society as something that could not be charged to God without the warning that preceded it, and the Book's arguments for the justice of the judgement rest on that foundation. The sūrah has described the destruction of the earlier communities in its accounts of the generations, and it has stated that each was given its messenger and its term.

The Book's treatment of the communities that were destroyed is presented in the same terms. The sūrah of the Prophets describes the destruction of the towns whose people were wrongdoers, and the sūrah of the Cattle states that God does not destroy a society while its people are unaware. The verse in front of us supplies the principle in a form that applies both to the past and to the reckoning described in the surrounding verses.

**The Place of the Verse in the Sūrah's Argument**

The verse follows the account of the gathered assemblies and their confession, and it precedes the statement that each person will be assigned ranks according to what he has done (6:132). The three verses together present the judgement as a sequence: the warning, the acknowledgement, and the assignment of ranks. The sentence in front of us explains the first stage, and the verses that follow state the other two.

The sūrah's larger argument also benefits from the statement. The audience in Makkah had received the messenger, which means that the condition described in the verse was fulfilled for them, and the sūrah's warnings about the fate of the earlier communities were addressed to people who could no longer claim ignorance of the message. Nothing in the phrasing limits the principle to the past: the same measure is applied to every community, and no people will be judged against a message that never reached them.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse states that each person will be assigned ranks according to his deeds and that the Lord is not unaware of what they do (6:132). The verse completes the account of the reckoning with the statement of the degrees that distinguish one person's outcome from another, and it attaches the knowledge of God to the assignment.

The passage that follows tells the Prophet that his Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy, and able to replace a people with another if He wills (6:133). The warning, the ranks, and the sufficiency of God together give the sūrah's audience the full measure of their position, and the verse in front of us supplies the assurance that the reckoning will be conducted on the basis of what was delivered.
verses.132:
> They will each be assigned ranks according to their deeds. And your Lord is not unaware of what they do

**The Assignment of Ranks**

They will each be assigned ranks according to their deeds. The verse states the outcome of the reckoning for the assembled people, and it does so in the vocabulary of ranks or degrees. The Book uses the same term in its other accounts of the Hereafter: the sūrah of the Sand Dunes says that each of the two groups will be ranked according to what they have done so that God may fully reward all of them and that none will be wronged (46:19); the sūrah of the Family of Imran states that they each have varying degrees in the sight of God and that God sees what they do (3:163); and the sūrah of the Repentance places those who believed, emigrated, and strove with their wealth and their lives in greater rank before God (9:20).

The Book's teaching on ranks appears in its treatment of the present life as well. The last verse of this sūrah states that God has placed human beings as successors on earth and elevated some of them in rank above others as a test (6:165), and the sūrah of the Ornament says that God has distributed among people their livelihood in the present life and raised some above others in degrees. What the verse in front of us states is the arrangement of the Hereafter, where the ranks correspond to deeds rather than to the circumstances a person was given.

**The Correspondence Between Deeds and Ranks**

The sentence states that the assignment follows what each person did, and the Book's accounts of the reward and the punishment consistently describe the outcome as measured to the conduct. The sūrah of the Sand Dunes adds the declaration that none will be wronged, and the sūrah of the Cattle states elsewhere that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom.

The Book's emphasis on that correspondence serves its argument about the justice of the reckoning. The verses that surround this one describe the warning given to the communities and the confession of the people who received it, and the sentence in front of us states that the response to the warning is what the ranks measure. Nothing in the arrangement depends on the standing a person held in the world or on the family into which he was born.

**The Knowledge Attached to the Sentence**

And your Lord is not unaware of what they do. The clause states the ground on which the ranks are assigned, and the Book uses the same formula at the end of many of its passages about the deeds of the people it addresses. The sūrah of the Cow uses it after describing the hardness of hearts and the corruption of the Scripture (2:74; 2:85), and the sūrah of the Family of Imran attaches it to its statement about the varying degrees.

The formula is the Book's way of closing an account of human conduct without leaving the impression that the conduct goes unobserved. The sūrah has described God's knowledge of the leaf that falls and the grain in the darkness (6:59), and the sentence in this verse applies that knowledge to what people do, which is the point on which the assignment of ranks depends.

**What the Verse Says About the Reckoning**

The verse presents the judgement as a settlement in which every person's situation is placed where it belongs. The Book does not describe the Hereafter as an undifferentiated reward or punishment; it describes degrees and orders, and it attaches them to the deeds of the people who receive them. The sūrah's audience, which measured standing by descent and wealth, is being told that the ranks of the Hereafter are produced by a different measure.

The Book's descriptions of the day of judgement include the same feature in other sūrahs, where people are said to be shown their records and to be sorted according to what they did. The sūrah of the Emissaries and the sūrah of the Inevitable describe the people of the right hand and the people of the left as distinct groups, and the sūrah of the Cave states that God has prepared for the believers the highest place in the garden.

**The Verse's Place in the Passage**

The verse follows the address to the assembled jinn and humans and their confession, and it precedes the statement that the Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy, able to replace a people with another (6:133). The three verses give the reckoning its context: the warning that makes it just, the ranks that make it exact, and the sufficiency of God that makes it independent of the people who are judged.

The passage therefore completes the section that began with the gathering of the jinn and their human associates. The partnership, the term, the fire, the alliance, the address, the confession, the ranks, and the sufficiency of God follow one another as a single account, and the verse in front of us states the measure by which the account's outcome is set.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse tells the Prophet that his Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy, and that if He wills He can do away with the audience and replace them with whoever He wills, just as He produced them from the offspring of other people (6:133). The statement of God's self-sufficiency follows directly from the assignment of ranks, since the judgement described in this verse is not a transaction that benefits God or diminishes Him.

The sūrah's later verses continue with the promise that what the audience has been warned about will come to pass and that they will have no escape (6:134), and then with the instruction to the Prophet to tell his people to persist in their ways while he persists in his (6:135). The verse in front of us supplies the measure for the reckoning those passages announce.
verses.133:
> Your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy. If He wills, He can do away with you and replace you with whoever He wills, just as He produced you from the offspring of other people

**The Self-Sufficient Lord**

Your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy. The verse states two attributes together, and the pairing carries the argument of the passage. The Self-Sufficient describes a being who has no need of anything He has made, and the sūrah of Fāṭir addresses humanity with the same contrast, telling them that they are the ones who stand in need of God while He is the Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy (35:15). The sūrah of Luqmān states that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and that He is truly the Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy (31:26).

The two attributes appear together in the Book's treatment of human ingratitude and divine patience. The sūrah of Ibrāhīm records Moses saying that if the people and everyone on earth were ungrateful, God would still be Self-Sufficient and Praiseworthy (14:8), and the sūrah of the Cow states that kind words and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, since God is Self-Sufficient, Most Forbearing (2:263). The verse in front of us names the same independence and joins it to mercy, and the combination is what makes the sentence that follows intelligible.

**The Power to Replace a People**

If He wills, He can do away with you and replace you with whoever He wills. The sentence states the consequence of God's self-sufficiency for a community that rejects His message. The Book makes the same statement in several places: the sūrah of the Women says that if it is God's will He can remove humanity altogether and replace them with others, and that He is most capable of that (4:133); the sūrah of Fāṭir says that if He willed He could eliminate them and produce a new creation (35:16); and the sūrah of the Repentance tells the believers that if they do not march forth, God will afflict them and replace them with another people, and that they will not harm Him at all (9:39).

The Book's statements about replacement are addressed both to the community that receives the message and to the community that rejects it. The sūrah of Muhammad tells those who are invited to spend that whoever withholds does so to his own loss, and it states that God is self-sufficient while they are the ones in need. What the verse in front of us states is the possibility of replacement as a fact about God's freedom rather than as a threat that depends on the audience's importance.

**The Precedent of the Generations**

Just as He produced you from the offspring of other people. The clause supplies the evidence for the power being described, and the Book returns repeatedly to the succession of generations. The sūrah of the Cattle states at its end that God placed human beings as successors on earth and raised some of them above others in rank as a test (6:165), and the sūrah of the Human states that God created them and perfected their form and that if He willed He could replace them with others (76:28).

The Makkans' confidence rested on their position in the region and on the continuity of their community, and the Book's answer is that the same power which brought them into being after another people can bring another people into being after them. The clause treats the present generation as one in a series rather than as a permanent arrangement, and the sūrah has been describing the fate of the earlier communities throughout the chapter.

**What the Verse Says About the Audience's Standing**

The verse removes the assumption that the community's existence matters to God in a way that would make the judgement negotiable. The Book states that God has no need of His creation and that the mercy by which He deals with it is a gift rather than an obligation. The two attributes in the first sentence carry the whole argument: the self-sufficiency means the judgement is not a transaction, and the mercy means that it is not arbitrary.

The Book makes the same point in its address to the people who imagine that their wealth or their power gives them standing with God. The sūrah of Saba' states that God gives provision abundantly to whom He wills and measures it out, and the sūrah of the Cattle states that God has elevated some people in rank in this life, which is itself a test. The verse in front of us supplies the principle behind those statements.

**The Comfort Contained in the Sentence**

The verse is addressed to the Prophet, and it is one of several passages in which the sūrah prepares him for the possibility that his people will not believe. The statement that God could replace them is not a threat directed at the Prophet; it is the assurance that the mission is not dependent on the response of a particular community, and that if the message is rejected God's purpose is not defeated.

The sūrah has given the same assurance in other forms. It told the Prophet that he was not a keeper over the people (6:107), that God knows best where to place His message (6:124), and that the opening of hearts belongs to God (6:125). The verse in front of us states the same fact about the outcome of the mission, and it grounds the statement in the attributes of the One who sends it.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse states that what the audience has been promised will certainly come to pass and that they will have no escape (6:134). The two verses form a pair: the Lord is self-sufficient and free to replace them, and the promise he has made will be fulfilled regardless of their response. The passage then turns to the instruction given to the Prophet about how to conduct himself among the people who persist in their ways (6:135).

The sūrah's argument in this section is therefore complete. The reckoning is just because the warning was delivered, the ranks correspond to deeds, and the power of God is not constrained by the community that denies Him. The verse in front of us states the middle term of that argument and connects the freedom of God to the mercy by which He acts.
verses.134:
> Indeed, what you have been promised will certainly come to pass. And you will have no escape

**The Certainty of What Was Promised**

Indeed, what you have been promised will certainly come to pass. The verse states the certainty of the outcome that the sūrah has announced throughout, and it addresses the audience directly. What was promised was the judgement, the resurrection, and the reckoning described in the surrounding verses, and the sentence removes the option of treating them as remote possibilities.

The Book's language about the promises of God is consistent: what God has promised comes to pass, and there is no alteration in His words. The sūrah has already declared that none can change the words of God (6:34) and that the word of the Lord has been perfected in truth and justice (6:115). The sentence in this verse applies that guarantee to the warnings the audience had received, and it states them as a fact of the future rather than as a threat contingent on their conduct.

**The Plain Statement of the Future**

The Book's habit in these passages is to state the coming of the judgement without argument, and the sūrah has used the same directness in its earlier warnings. It described the day when the wrongdoers will be gathered and told that the fire is their home (6:128), and it recorded the confession of the assembled jinn and humans when they are asked about the messengers (6:130). The verse in front of us states the same event in a single sentence and leaves the details to the passages around it.

The Book's announcements of the reckoning appear in every part of the Qur'an, and the language of certainty is attached to them throughout. The sūrah of the News says that the day is the ultimate truth and that whoever wills may take the path back to his Lord (78:39), and the sūrah of the Resurrection states that there will be no refuge on that day (75:11). The sentence in front of us belongs to that family of statements.

**You Will Have No Escape**

And you will have no escape. The second sentence names the condition of the people who were addressed, and the Book's word describes the impossibility of finding a place from which the reckoning can be avoided. The Book uses the same idea in its descriptions of the day, and the sūrah's audience, which understood the geography of retreat and refuge, is told that none of the familiar routes will be available.

The claim is connected to the sūrah's account of God's knowledge. The Book has stated that God knows what is on land and sea, that nothing is hidden from Him, and that the record of every person's conduct is kept (6:59–61). The sentence in front of us draws the consequence: what is known cannot be escaped, and the person who is not beyond God's knowledge cannot be beyond His judgement.

**What the Verse Says About the Delay**

The sentence answers the attitude that the sūrah has documented in its audience, which was the assumption that the warnings were addressed to a distant future and could be met at leisure. The Book's answer in other places is that every matter has its set time (6:67), and the sūrah has already stated that the community has a term that cannot be advanced or delayed (7:34; 10:49).

The sentence in this verse does not specify when the promise will be fulfilled. What it states is that the fulfilment is certain and the escape impossible, and the Book leaves the timing with God, as it does in its other announcements of the day. The audience is left with the certainty of the event rather than with a date it could prepare for at the last moment.

**The Verse in the Sequence of the Passage**

The verse follows the statement that the Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Full of Mercy, able to replace a people with another (6:133), and it precedes the instruction to the Prophet to declare to his people that each side will persist in its way (6:135). The three verses form the sūrah's final word to the audience within this section: God has no need of them, what He has promised will come, they will not escape, and the Prophet is to carry on with his task.

The passage that follows turns to the dietary system of the audience and to the shares they assigned to God and to their idols (6:136). The shift of subject does not break the sequence, since the sūrah's case against the audience's religion has been built on both the arguments about the signs and the examination of their practices.

**What the Verse Requires of the Reader**

The verse requires the reader to treat the judgement as settled. The sūrah's audience had asked for signs and had been told that the signs were with God; they had asked for the messengers' office and had been told that God knows where to place His message; and the sentence in front of us removes the last resort, which was the hope that the whole matter could be avoided. The Book's invitation throughout the chapter has been addressed to people who were assumed to be able to respond, and the verse states the outcome of the response they give.

The Book's treatment of the day of judgement consistently pairs the certainty of the event with the freedom of the person who is to meet it. The sūrah of the News states the truth of the day and then states that whoever wills may take the path to his Lord, and the two statements together are the Book's way of presenting the matter.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse gives the Prophet the words he is to say to his people: that they should persist in their ways while he persists in his, and that they will soon know who will fare best in the end, since the wrongdoers will never succeed (6:135). The instruction follows the statement in this verse, and together they close the section with the two parties left in their positions and the outcome left with God.

The sūrah has now completed its treatment of the audience's demands, their theology, their practices of deception, and their dismissal of the messengers. What remains in the chapter is the detailed examination of their ritual and dietary system, the closing instruction to the Prophet, and the final testimony that the Book contains. The verse in front of us marks the end of the argumentative section and states its conclusion.
verses.135:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O my people! Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine. You will soon know who will fare best in the end. Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed.”

**The Declaration Given to the Prophet**

Say, O my people! Persist in your ways, for I too will persist in mine. The verse instructs the Prophet to address his people with a declaration that both sides will continue as they are, and the Book gives the same words to other messengers. The sūrah of the Troops records the instruction with the addition that the audience will soon come to know who will be visited by a humiliating punishment and an everlasting torment (39:39–40); the sūrah of Hūd gives the words to Shuʿayb with the same conclusion (11:93); and another verse of the same sūrah instructs the Prophet to tell those who disbelieve to persist in their ways while the believers persist in theirs (11:121).

The declaration is not a threat of violence or a challenge to a contest of power. It is the Book's way of closing a dispute that has been conducted with arguments: each side has stated its position, and each will continue in the way it has chosen, and the outcome will show which of them was right.

**The Meaning of Persisting**

The Book's word for persisting carries the sense of working and acting within a chosen station, and the verses that use it consistently describe the two parties engaging in their own kinds of activity. The sūrah's audience was continuing in its worship, its customs, and its opposition to the message; the Prophet was continuing in the delivery of the revelation and in the conduct that belonged to it. The sentence states that both will proceed rather than that either will be coerced.

The Book's treatment of the matter elsewhere gives the reader the same picture. The sūrah of the Bee tells the Prophet to call people to the way of the Lord with wisdom and good instruction and to argue in the best manner, and it adds that the Lord knows best who has strayed and who is guided (16:125). The declaration in this verse is the form that instruction takes in the case of a people who have refused.

**The Outcome Left to the Future**

You will soon know who will fare best in the end. The sentence states that the outcome will be evident, and the Book's word for the end describes the final consequence of a course of action. The passages that use the same formula attach it to the same question: which of the two parties enjoys the security and the success that the message promises, and which is overtaken by the punishment the messengers announced.

The Book's accounts of the earlier communities supply the answer in historical terms. The sūrah of Hūd describes the destruction of the people who rejected their messenger and the rescue of those who followed him, and the sūrah of the Poets tells the Prophet that he will see the fulfilment of what was promised them. The verse in front of us leaves the matter at that point: the outcome will be known, and the knowledge will come to both parties.

**The Wrongdoers Will Never Succeed**

Indeed, the wrongdoers will never succeed. The verse closes with the declaration of the outcome, and the sūrah has used the same sentence before. It appears at the end of the verse about the people who fabricate lies against God or deny His signs (6:21), and again in the words of Moses in the sūrah of the Stories, where he says that his Lord knows best who has come with true guidance and who will fare best in the end, adding that the wrongdoers will never succeed (28:37).

The sentence states the outcome in the form of a general law rather than as a prediction about particular people. What the sūrah's audience was being told is that the category to which their conduct belonged has a fixed end, and the declaration does not depend on the identity of any individual or community. The Book's confidence in this statement rests on the attributes the previous verse named: the Lord who is self-sufficient and merciful is also the Lord who brings the affair to its conclusion.

**What the Verse Requires of the Prophet**

The instruction gives the Prophet a way to conduct himself in a city that would not accept his message. He is not to abandon his people, since he addresses them as his own; he is not to pretend that the disagreement has been settled; and he is not to force the issue. He states the position of each side and continues with his work, and the outcome is left to God.

That pattern is consistent with the sūrah's earlier instructions: the command to follow what was revealed and to turn away from the polytheists (6:106), the reminder that the Prophet is neither keeper nor maintainer (6:107), and the statement that God's will decides who believes (6:111). The verse in front of us gives the practical form those instructions take in the Prophet's relationship with his own people.

**The Section That Follows**

The next verse begins the sūrah's detailed treatment of the audience's ritual system, describing the shares they assigned to God and to their idols from the crops and livestock and the claim they made about the arrangement (6:136). The verse in front of us closes the long section of argument that has run from the sūrah's opening, and it hands the reader over to an examination of the practices themselves.

The passage that follows will continue for many verses, treating the assignment of shares, the rules about livestock, the animals set apart for certain people, and the claims made about what God had permitted. Each of those passages applies the principles the earlier section established, and the declaration in this verse is the point from which the reader enters them: each party persists in its way, and the outcome belongs to God.
verses.136:
> The pagans set aside for Allah a share of the crops and cattle He created, saying, “This ˹portion˺ is for Allah,” so they claim, “and this ˹one˺ for our associate-gods.” Yet the portion of their associate-gods is not shared with Allah while Allah’s portion is shared with their associate-gods. What unfair judgment

**The Shares Assigned to God and the Idols**

The pagans set aside for Allah a share of the crops and cattle He created, saying, This portion is for Allah, so they claim, and this one for our associate-gods. The verse opens the sūrah's detailed treatment of the audience's ritual economy, and it describes a practice in which the produce of the land and the herds was divided between the Creator and the beings associated with Him. The Book records the same custom elsewhere, saying that the idolaters assign to the idols, who know nothing, a share of what God has provided for them (16:56).

The phrase so they claim marks the practice as an invention, and the Book's commentators noted that the arrangement had no basis in any revealed command. What the audience had done was to take a custom inherited from their ancestors and to place it beside the worship of God as though the two belonged to the same system.

**The Asymmetry in the Practice**

Yet the portion of their associate-gods is not shared with Allah while Allah's portion is shared with their associate-gods. The sentence describes how the arrangement worked when the portions were disturbed, and the commentators explained the two halves: if part of what had been set aside for the idols fell in with the portion belonging to God, the people returned it to the idols' share; but if part of God's portion fell in with the idols', they left it where it landed, saying that God was self-sufficient and had no need of it.

The reasoning they offered revealed the actual ordering of their loyalties. A practice that treated one party's property as recoverable and the other's as forfeit was not a division of equals, and the Book states the arrangement in order to show which of the two the audience actually served.

**The Judgement Passed on the Practice**

What unfair judgment! The sentence closes the verse with the Book's assessment, and the term describes a ruling that is wrong in itself rather than merely inaccurate. The Book's word for judgement has been used throughout the sūrah in the discussion of the arbiter and the perfection of God's word, and the verse in front of us applies it to the audience's arrangement of their own offerings.

The Book's method in these verses is to let the practice testify against the people who defended it. The shares were assigned in God's name, and the way they were administered showed what the assigners believed about the two parties. The sentence the Book pronounces is a conclusion drawn from the arrangements the audience had made themselves.

**The Offence in the Arrangement**

The offence that the sūrah is describing is not only the association of other beings with God but the redirection of provision that God had given. The Book states that the crops and cattle were created by God, which establishes the claim of the Creator to what His creation produces, and the sūrah of the Bee records the charge that the idolaters assign shares to beings that know nothing of the gift.

The Book's treatment of offerings elsewhere makes the same point about the direction in which gratitude should run. The sūrah of the Cattle will later say that the audience forbade what God had provided, attributing the prohibition to Him without warrant (6:140), and the verse in front of us shows the same system operating in the opposite direction, with gifts directed to the idols instead of to their maker.

**The Place of the Verse in the Section**

The verse begins a passage of several verses that examines the audience's rules about crops, cattle, and the offspring of the herds (6:136–139). Each verse takes up a particular practice, states it in the audience's own words, and passes judgement on it. The arrangement is the sūrah's method of showing the reader what the religion of the Makkans looked like when it was examined piece by piece.

The passage also continues the argument the sūrah has been conducting about authority. The verses about guidance and error established that the path belongs to God and that its signs are clear; the verses about the dietary rules established that permission and prohibition belong to God; and the passage that opens with this verse shows the audience transferring that authority to beings of their own invention.

**What the Verse Says About Custom**

The verse shows a community carrying out a practice under the name of God while its structure contradicted what they claimed for it. The Book's term for their own description of the arrangement, "so they claim", separates the custom from the revelation, and the reader is left with a practice that had no sanction other than inherited usage.

That separation is the sūrah's constant concern in its dealings with the audience's religion. The chapter has argued against their theology, their demand for signs, their dietary rules, and their associations with the jinn, and it now shows how the same habits of invention shaped the offerings they brought to their gods.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse describes the effect of the evil associates on the audience, saying that they made the killing of their own children appealing to them and that this led to their destruction and to confusion in their faith, before instructing the Prophet to leave them and their falsehood (6:137). The two verses belong together, since both describe the influence of the associated beings on the community's conduct.

The sūrah thus moves from the division of harvests to the destruction of children, and the passage as a whole shows the consequences of the religion the audience had inherited. What the verses state is the practical result of the associations the sūrah has been examining since its account of the jinn (6:100).
verses.137:
> Likewise, the pagans’ evil associates have made it appealing to them to kill their own children—only leading to their destruction as well as confusion in their faith. Had it been Allah’s Will, they would not have done such a thing. So leave them and their falsehood

**The Killing of Children**

Likewise, the pagans' evil associates have made it appealing to them to kill their own children. The verse names the practice that the sūrah condemns in several later passages, and it attributes the impulse to the associates the audience had taken. The Book's word for the associates is the one it uses for the partners associated with God, and the same verse's opening connects the practice to the influence those partners had on the community.

The practice was the burial of infant daughters, which the audience carried out for reasons of poverty and honour, and the Book names the reason in its later prohibition: do not kill your children for fear of poverty, since God provides for them and for their parents (17:31). The sūrah of the Cattle's closing list of prohibitions repeats the command against killing children, and the sūrah of the Folding Up describes the day when the girl buried alive is asked for what crime she was put to death (81:8–9).

**The Leading to Destruction and Confusion**

Only leading to their destruction as well as confusion in their faith. The sentence states the two consequences the practice produced, and the Book's word for the second describes a division or splitting in the community's religion. The killing of children divided a community against itself, since the practice was applied to one sex and not the other, and it separated the people who carried it out from the guidance that the messengers brought.

The sūrah of the Cattle's later passage states the same consequence in another form, saying that the people who killed their children out of ignorance and forbade what God had provided have certainly strayed and are not guided (6:140). The verse in front of us supplies the description of the practice as a work of the associates, and the later verse states the loss that follows from it.

**The Standard the Book Exposes**

The Book returns to the practice and to the attitude behind it in several passages. The sūrah of the Bee describes the man who is given the news of a baby girl, whose face grows gloomy as he suppresses his rage, and who hides from his people wondering whether to keep her in disgrace or bury her alive, and the verse ends by calling the judgement of such people evil (16:58–59). The sūrah of the Ornament gives the same description of the man given news of what he attributes to the Most Compassionate (43:17), and the sūrah of the Star asks the audience whether they prefer sons for themselves while attributing daughters to God (53:21).

The Book's answer to the attitude is stated in the sūrah of Consultation, where God is described as creating whatever He wills, blessing whom He wills with daughters, blessing whom He wills with sons, granting both to whom He wills, and leaving whom He wills infertile, for He is All-Knowing and Most Capable (42:49–50). The verse in front of us describes the practice that the Book's statements about daughters answer, and the passage places the killing of children inside the larger account of the audience's false attributions.

**The Statement About God's Will**

Had it been Allah's Will, they would not have done such a thing. The sentence repeats the formula that the sūrah has used before in answering the audience's conduct, and its placement here is important. The same statement was made about the idolaters' association of partners with God (6:107), and the sūrah will later record the audience using the same plea as an excuse for their practices and rejecting it (6:148).

The formula states the dependence of everything on God's will, and the Book uses it in the passages that describe the resistance of the community to the message. What the sentence does not do is to excuse the practice. The Book elsewhere makes the same statement and then states the punishment, and the two belong together in its account of human responsibility.

**The Instruction to Leave Them**

So leave them and their falsehood. The verse closes with the instruction the Prophet has received twice already in this sūrah, when he was told to leave those who took their religion as play and amusement (6:70) and to leave the enemies with their deceit (6:112). The instruction in each case concerns the Prophet's own conduct rather than the abandonment of the mission, since the sūrah continues to address the audience's practices in the verses that follow.

The Book's use of this instruction is a feature of the sūrahs revealed in Makkah, where the community was small and the opposition was strong. The Prophet is told that the conduct of the people he addresses is not his to correct by force, and the sūrah's statement of the practices continues so that the reader knows what the message has come to replace.

**What the Verse Says About Inherited Practice**

The practice described in this verse was inherited, and the Book presents it as the product of the community's own invention and of the influence of the beings they associated with God. The sūrah's treatment of the audience's system has followed the same pattern throughout: the practices are stated in the community's own words, their origins are identified, and their results are described.

The verse's mention of the associates shows how the sūrah connects the different parts of the audience's religion. The same beings whose partnership with God was refuted in the earlier verses are described here as the source of a practice that destroyed families, and the Book treats the theology and the social consequences as parts of one system.

**The Passage That Follows**

The next verses continue the examination with the audience's rules about the cattle and the crops, the animals reserved for certain people, and the offspring of the herds (6:138–139), and the passage ends with the declaration that those who have murdered their children and forbidden what God provided have strayed (6:140). The verse in front of us introduces the theme of the section, which is what the community's false attributions produced in practice.

The sūrah has been laying out the audience's religion in pieces since its account of the jinn, and the passage that follows completes the survey. The reader who has followed the argument now sees the full shape of the system the message was addressing, and the verses state both what the system claimed and what it cost.
verses.138:
> They say, “These cattle and crops are reserved—none may eat them except those we permit,” so they claim. Some other cattle are exempted from labour and others are not slaughtered in Allah’s Name—falsely attributing lies to Him. He will repay them for their lies

**The Rules About the Herds and the Crops**

They say, These cattle and crops are reserved, none may eat them except those we permit, so they claim. The verse continues the sūrah's examination of the audience's dietary system, and it records a rule the community had adopted about its own property. Certain animals and certain produce were set aside, and access to them was restricted to the people the community designated, which meant that the poor and the outsiders were excluded from what the system had reserved.

The phrase so they claim again marks the rule as an invention, and the Book's treatment of the practice follows the pattern established in the preceding verse. The audience attributed the restriction to a divine command, and the sūrah states that the attribution was their own.

**The Cattle Exempted From Labour**

Some other cattle are exempted from labour and others are not slaughtered in Allah's Name. The sentence names two further features of the system, and the commentators explained them as rules about which animals might be used for work and which might be killed without the invocation. The exemption from labour placed certain animals in a category of their own, and the omission of the Name placed others in a category that the sūrah's earlier verses had forbidden.

The two rules together show how far the community's practice had moved from the principle the sūrah stated when it commanded the believers to eat of what has been slaughtered in the Name of God (6:118–119). The system the audience had inherited produced both an excess of restriction and a licence to eat what had not been consecrated.

**The Charge of Attribution**

Falsely attributing lies to Him. The sentence states the offence that underlies the whole system, and the Book uses the same charge throughout the chapter. The sūrah has said that the idolaters invent lies against God (6:21), that those who fabricate revelation are the greatest wrongdoers (6:93), and that the audience attributes to God sons and daughters out of ignorance (6:100). The practices described here are the practical form of the attribution: what was forbidden by custom was presented as forbidden by God.

The Book's objection is not to the existence of rules but to the claim of divine authority made on behalf of rules that God had not given. The sūrah has already established the standard for such claims when it stated that God has explained what He has forbidden (6:119), and the verse in front of us measures the audience's system against that standard and finds it wanting.

**The Promise of Repayment**

He will repay them for their lies. The verse closes with the statement of the consequence, and the Book's language of repayment describes the correspondence between conduct and outcome. The audience had constructed a system of permissions and prohibitions and had placed the authority for them with God, and the sentence states that the false attribution will be answered.
