The sūrah uses the same closing formula in the verse that follows, where the audience's rule about the offspring of the herds is answered with the same promise of repayment (6:139). The two verses form a pair, and the repetition of the formula binds the passage together as a single indictment of the community's dietary rules.

**What the System Revealed About the Community**

The rules described in these verses show a community in which the management of food had become a way of maintaining status. The animals reserved for the community's own people, the produce withheld from general use, and the categories created by custom all served to distinguish those inside the system from those outside it, and the Book's criticism reaches the social arrangement as well as the theology behind it.

The sūrah's treatment of the meals of the community elsewhere makes the same point from the other side. The sūrah of the Cow instructs the believers to eat of the good things provided and to give thanks (2:172), and the sūrah of the Bee commands the same and forbids the practices that restrict what God has given. The verses in front of us state what those commands were replacing.

**The Place of the Verse in the Section**

The verse stands between the description of the shares assigned to God and to the idols (6:136) and the rules about the offspring of the herds (6:139), and it deals with the same system from the standpoint of the community's own table. The sūrah has been examining the audience's religion piece by piece since it turned from the argument about the signs, and this passage examines the part of it that governed daily life.

The treatment is not incidental to the chapter's purpose. The sūrah's claim throughout has been that the authority to permit and forbid belongs to God, and the passage that begins with these verses shows what happens when that authority is claimed by custom instead.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse records the rule the audience applied to the offspring of their herds, reserving it for the males and forbidding it to the females, with the qualification that a stillborn animal could be shared by all (6:139). The detail completes the survey of the system, and the verse closes the section with the statement that God will repay the audience for their falsehood and with the declaration that He is All-Wise, All-Knowing.

The passage that follows moves to the audience's practice of killing their children and forbidding what God has provided, and it states that those who do so have strayed (6:140). The sūrah's survey of the inherited system is therefore complete once these verses are read together, and the reader is left with the account of a religion that had replaced the law of God with the rulings of custom.
verses.139:
> They ˹also˺ say, “The offspring of this cattle is reserved for our males and forbidden to our females; but if it is stillborn, they may all share it.” He will repay them for their falsehood. Surely He is All-Wise, All-Knowing

**The Rule About the Offspring**

They also say, The offspring of this cattle is reserved for our males and forbidden to our females. The verse records another of the community's rules, and this one governs the young of the animals they had set apart. The males of the community were permitted to eat the offspring, and the women were not, which made the rule a matter of the household's internal order as much as of food.

The Book records the same kind of regulation elsewhere. The sūrah of the Table lists the set-apart animals of the Arabian system, naming the animals freed in the name of the gods, those dedicated to them, and the males reserved from work and from slaughter, and it states that the disbelievers invented these categories (5:103). The system described in the verse in front of us belongs to the same family of practices.

**The Exception for the Stillborn**

But if it is stillborn, they may all share it. The sentence states the qualification the community attached to its rule, and the qualification exposes the arbitrary character of the whole arrangement. The same animal was reserved for the men if it was delivered alive and shared by everyone if it was not, which means that the permission depended on a circumstance that had nothing to do with the eater.

The commentators noted the inconsistency as part of the sūrah's argument. A rule that distinguished between people by sex and then dissolved the distinction in the case of a dead animal was not a law but a set of inherited usages, and the Book's presentation lets the reader see the incoherence without adding a comment.

**The Charge Reiterated**

He will repay them for their falsehood. The sentence repeats the formula that closed the previous verse, and the repetition binds the two rules together as a single offence. The audience's system attributed to God a set of regulations that He had not given, and the Book states that the attribution will be answered by the One who knows what they said.

The Book's treatment of such attributions appears in several passages. The sūrah of the Bee tells the audience not to utter falsehoods about what God has permitted and forbidden and to attribute the rulings to Him (16:116), and the sūrah of Yūnus asks the audience whether God has given them permission for what they have made lawful or unlawful, or whether they are inventing the rulings themselves (10:59). The verses in front of us state the practice those passages address.

**The Attributes at the End of the Verse**

Surely He is All-Wise, All-Knowing. The two names answer the regulations the verse has described. The wisdom belongs to the One whose rulings are ordered to their purposes, and the knowledge belongs to the One who knows what the audience said and why they said it. The closing formula stands in deliberate contrast to the rules just recorded, which were neither wise nor founded on knowledge.

The same pair of names appears at the end of the sūrah's accounts of the reckoning, where the judgement is attributed to the One who knows what each person did. The sūrah's use of the names in this verse therefore connects the dietary system to the larger account of accountability that runs through the chapter.

**What the Rule Revealed About the Community**

The regulation described here used food as a way of ordering the community's members, and the distinction it drew fell along lines of sex and household standing rather than along lines of conduct. The Book's own regulations in this sūrah run in another direction: what is permitted is what God has permitted, what is forbidden is what God has forbidden, and the rules apply to the believers alike.

The sūrah of the Cattle's later passage about the gardens instructs the community to eat of the fruit they bear and to pay what is due at the harvest, without adding any of the distinctions the audience had built into its system (6:141). The verses in front of us show what the message was replacing, and the contrast is presented in the book's own account of provision rather than in a comment on the audience's customs.

**The Place of the Passage in the Sūrah**

The passage that begins with the shares assigned to God and the idols (6:136) and continues through the killing of children, the reservation of the herds, and the rule about the offspring ends with the declaration that those who killed their children and forbade what God provided have strayed and are not guided (6:140). The four verses form a survey of the audience's dietary and domestic system, and each of them states a practice and the judgement it receives.

The sūrah's argument has been building toward the declaration of what God has actually forbidden and commanded, which appears in the long passage beginning at 6:151. What the passage in front of us provides is the negative side of that instruction: the system that the revelation came to replace, presented in the audience's own terms.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse states that those who murdered their own children foolishly out of ignorance and forbade what God has provided have certainly strayed and are not guided (6:140). The sentence gathers the offences described in the preceding verses, and it passes the final judgement on the community that built its religion on them.

The sūrah then turns to a series of declarations about the created order and to the announcement of what God has actually forbidden and commanded, and it concludes with the testimony of the Book. The verse in front of us completes the survey of the inherited system, and the reader who has followed the passage now knows what the message had come to correct.
verses.140:
> Lost indeed are those who have murdered their own children foolishly out of ignorance and have forbidden what Allah has provided for them—falsely attributing lies to Allah. They have certainly strayed and are not ˹rightly˺ guided

**The Verdict on the System Just Described**

Lost indeed are those who have murdered their own children foolishly out of ignorance and have forbidden what Allah has provided for them. The verse gathers the offences described in the preceding passage and states their result, and the Book's word for the lost describes a loss that cannot be recovered. The killing of children was described in the earlier verse as the work of the associates who made it appealing (6:137), and the prohibition of God's provision was described in the rules about the herds and the crops (6:138–139). The sentence in front of us states what the whole system produced.

The verse's order is worth noticing. The murder of children comes before the forbidding of provision, although the sūrah described the dietary rules first, and the arrangement places the gravest offence at the head of the list. The Book's scale of seriousness is stated throughout its treatments of the audience's practices, and the killing of the community's own children is presented here as the culmination of a religion built on invention.

**The Two Charges and Their Ground**

The clause foolishly out of ignorance names the cause of the killing, and the Book's word for the ignorance describes conduct undertaken without knowledge rather than a simple lack of information. The practice was carried out for reasons of poverty and honour, and the Book's later prohibition addresses the poverty directly, telling the audience not to kill their children for fear of want since God provides for them and for their parents (17:31).

The second charge, that they forbade what God provided, is attached to the same ignorance, and the sūrah's earlier verses have shown what the prohibition consisted of: the animals reserved from labour and from the invocation of the Name, the produce withheld from general use, and the offspring forbidden to the women (6:138–139). The verse's sentence treats the two practices as products of one condition.

**The False Attribution**

Falsely attributing lies to Allah. The clause names the act that made the system a religious offence rather than a local custom. The audience had attached the authority of God to regulations they had invented, and the sūrah has stated the same charge at each stage of its examination: the shares assigned to the idols (6:136), the killing of children (6:137), the reservation of the herds (6:138), and the rules about the offspring (6:139).

The Book's treatment of the charge of attributing lies to God runs through the chapter, and the sūrah has described the fabrication of revelation and the claim to have received it as the worst of offences (6:93). The verses in front of us apply the same charge to the community's regulation of its food, which shows how seriously the Book treats the claim of divine authority made on behalf of human invention.

**The Statement of Straying**

They have certainly strayed and are not rightly guided. The verse closes with the declaration of the outcome, and the two clauses state the condition in both directions. The people described have left the path, and they are not being guided back onto it, which is the condition the sūrah has described in its account of those whose hearts were turned away after their first refusal (6:110).

The Book's statements about guidance and straying appear throughout the sūrah, and the verse in front of us applies them to the community's practices. The people who built a religion out of inherited custom had removed themselves from the guidance that the message brought, and the sentence states the consequence as a settled fact.

**What the Verse Says About the Cost of the System**

The verse presents the audience's religious system as destructive to the community that maintained it. The practices described in the preceding passage divided families, restricted food by sex and status, and took the lives of children, and the sentence in front of us names the loss that resulted. The Book's treatment of the system is therefore not only a matter of doctrinal correctness but of the welfare of the people who lived under it.

The Book's account of the community that accepts the message presents the opposite condition. The sūrah of the Cattle's later passage about the gardens instructs the believers to eat of the produce and to pay what is due at the harvest without waste (6:141), and the sūrah of the Bee tells them to eat of what God has provided and to be grateful. The contrast between the two arrangements is one the sūrah's readers were expected to see.

**The Place of the Verse in the Sūrah**

The verse closes the passage that began with the shares assigned to God and the idols (6:136), and it states the judgement on the whole system the passage examined. The sūrah has been conducting its survey of the audience's practices for several verses, and the sentence in front of us supplies the conclusion that the survey was building toward.

The chapter then turns to the created order and to the food that God has actually provided, describing the gardens, the palms, the crops, the olives, and the pomegranates (6:141), and it follows that description with the instruction to eat of what God has given and not to follow the footsteps of Satan (6:142). The verse in front of us marks the turning point of the section, and what follows supplies the positive account of the provision the audience had been managing by custom.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse describes the gardens that God produces, both cultivated and wild, with their palms and their crops of different flavours, and it instructs the community to eat of the fruit and to pay the dues at harvest without waste (6:141). The shift from the audience's rules to the provision that God has made is the sūrah's way of answering the system it has just condemned.

The passage that follows continues with the pairs of livestock and the argument about which animals God has forbidden (6:143–144), and it closes with the declaration that those who fabricate lies against God to mislead others will not be guided. The verse in front of us therefore stands at the head of the sūrah's positive account of what God has given, and the account is set against the system the previous verses described.
verses.141:
> He is the One Who produces gardens—both cultivated and wild—and palm trees, crops of different flavours, olives, and pomegranates—similar ˹in shape˺, but dissimilar ˹in taste˺. Eat of the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest, but do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful

**The Gardens and Their Produce**

He is the One Who produces gardens, both cultivated and wild, and palm trees, crops of different flavours, olives, and pomegranates, similar in shape but dissimilar in taste. The verse returns to the theme of provision after the passage on the audience's regulations, and it lists the produce of the region in the detail the sūrah has used before. The gardens appear in the sūrah's earlier account of the rain that produces green stalks, clustered grain, dates hanging within reach, vineyards, olives, and pomegranates (6:99).

The phrase both cultivated and wild covers the two kinds of planting the audience knew, and the description of the fruits as similar in shape and dissimilar in taste repeats the observation the sūrah made in its earlier passage. The Book's method in these verses is to lay the provision before the reader as evidence of the provider, and the variety of the produce is part of the demonstration.

**The Command to Eat and the Dues**

Eat from the fruit they bear and pay the dues at harvest. The verse attaches a command to the description, and the command includes both the permission to eat and the obligation to give. The Book's word for the dues describes what is owed from the produce, and the commentators understood it as the share due at the time of harvesting, which the community was required to set aside.

The Book's treatment of the duties attached to wealth appears throughout its instructions to the community. The sūrah of the Cow describes the believers as those who spend from what God has provided and sets out the kinds of giving the community was to undertake, and the sūrah of the Bee commands the believers to eat of what God has provided and to give thanks. The verse in front of us joins the permission and the obligation in a single sentence, and the arrangement reflects the Book's treatment of provision as a gift held in trust.

**The Prohibition of Waste**

But do not waste. Surely He does not like the wasteful. The sentence closes the verse with a prohibition, and the Book's term for waste describes spending beyond what is needed or destroying what could be used. The prohibition appears in the Book's instructions about wealth in several places, and the sūrah of the Night Journey includes waste among the practices it condemns, describing the wasteful as brothers of the devils.

The prohibition attaches to the harvest that the verse has just described, and the connection between the two sentences is practical. The produce that God has given is to be eaten, shared, and used, and what is left over is not to be destroyed. The Book's approach to provision is that it is received for use rather than for display, and the sentence states the limit.

**What the Verse Says About the Present Order**

The verse describes the created provision without attaching it to the audience's rules, and the omission is part of the argument. The gardens, the palms, the crops, and the fruits are produced by God, and the command that follows concerns eating and giving rather than the classification of the produce into permitted and forbidden categories. The sūrah has just finished describing the system the audience had built around those categories, and the verse in front of us states the simple arrangement the Book puts in its place.

The Book's treatment of the subject elsewhere makes the same contrast. The sūrah of the Heights asks who has forbidden the adornments and the good provisions that God has brought forth for His servants, and it answers that they belong to the believers in this world and will be theirs alone on the day of resurrection (7:32). The verse in front of us belongs with that passage, and the two together state the Book's position on the goods of the world.

**The Link to the Earlier Passage on Provision**

The verse echoes the sūrah's earlier account of the rain and the produce of the earth (6:99), and the two passages share the same details: the palms, the crops, the olives, the pomegranates, and the observation about the similarity of shape and the difference of taste. The earlier passage closed with the statement that these are signs for people who believe, and the verse in front of us closes with the command to eat, to give, and not to waste.

The repetition gives the sūrah its shape. The provision was presented first as evidence of the provider, and it is presented here as the material of the community's obligations. The movement from sign to duty is the pattern the sūrah follows in its treatment of everything it describes.

**What the Verse Says to the Audience**

The audience had spent its ingenuity on rules governing the produce of its fields and herds, and the verse tells the people who made those rules what the provision is for. What God has given is to be eaten, what is due from it is to be paid, and what remains is not to be squandered. The three instructions stand in place of the elaborate system that the sūrah has just examined and condemned.

The Book's treatment of the community's use of wealth elsewhere supplies the wider framework. The sūrah of the Cow commands the believers to spend from what they have been provided before the day comes when there will be no trade, no friendship, and no intercession, and it presents the giving as a feature of the community's life rather than as an occasional act. The verse in front of us states the same principle at the point where the harvest is gathered.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse returns to the livestock, stating that some cattle are fit for labour while others are too small, and it instructs the community to eat of what God has provided and not to follow the footsteps of Satan, who is an avowed enemy (6:142). The pair of verses covers the produce of the fields and the produce of the herds, and the instruction in both cases is the same.

The passage that follows takes up the argument about the pairs of animals and the claim that God had forbidden certain of them (6:143–144), and it answers the claim by asking the audience for the knowledge on which it rests. The verse in front of us supplies the positive command that the argument presupposes, and the verses that follow remove the false restrictions that had been placed on the provision.
verses.142:
> Some cattle are fit for labour, others are too small. Eat of what Allah has provided for you and do not follow Satan’s footsteps. Certainly, he is your sworn enemy

**The Cattle Given for Use**

Some cattle are fit for labour, others are too small. The verse returns to the livestock after the description of the gardens, and it names the two ways the herds served the audience. The larger animals carried loads and worked the land; the smaller ones were kept for their meat, their milk, and their hides. The Book's other passages describe the same provision, saying that God created the cattle as a source of warmth, food, and other benefits (16:5), and that they carry loads to distant lands that people could not otherwise reach without hardship (16:7).

The verse thus presents the herds as a gift with functions, and the functions are the ones the audience depended on. The sūrah's earlier account of the audience's rules about the animals had examined the categories they had invented for these same creatures (6:138–139), and the sentence in front of us states the plain arrangement that the categories had obscured.

**The Command to Eat and the Warning**

Eat of what Allah has provided for you and do not follow Satan's footsteps. The sentence joins permission to a prohibition, and it uses the formula the Book applies to the food of the community in several places. The sūrah of the Cow instructs humanity to eat from what is lawful and good on the earth and not to follow the footsteps of Satan, describing him as an avowed enemy (2:168); the sūrah of the Table tells the believers to eat of the good things provided and to be mindful of God (5:88); and the sūrah of the Bee gives the same command with the addition that the eater should give thanks (16:114).

The warning about Satan's footsteps is attached to the dietary instruction in each of these passages, and the connection is the same in all of them. The footsteps are the practices that lead away from what God has provided, and the sūrah in front of us has just finished describing the system the audience had built in place of the plain command.

**The Enemy Named at the End**

Certainly, he is your sworn enemy. The clause identifies Satan, and the Book states the same fact in its addresses to humanity in several places. The sūrah of Yā-Sīn records the question put to the children of Adam on the day of judgement, asking whether they were not commanded not to follow Satan, since he is their avowed enemy (36:60), and the sūrah of the Heights describes the enmity declared at the beginning of human life. The sūrah of the Cow's dietary instruction ends with the same description.

The sentence gives the warning its reason. The practices that the sūrah has been describing were not neutral customs; they were the means by which the community was led away from the provision of God, and the Book names the agency behind them. The identification of Satan as an enemy rather than as a tempter emphasises that the guidance being rejected was for the benefit of the people being addressed.

**What the Verse Says About Custom and Its Sources**

The verse sets the provision of God and the footsteps of Satan in opposition, and the arrangement gives the reader a way of assessing the practices the sūrah has examined. The herds were given for labour and for food; the rules that restricted them had no source in that gift; and the sentence that forbids following Satan's footsteps places the rules in the category of things from which the community was being turned away.

The Book's treatment of the audience's customs follows this pattern throughout the sūrah. The practices are stated, their attribution to God is shown to be false, and the guidance that replaces them is presented as the plain use of what God has provided. The verse in front of us states the choice in the form of a command and a warning, and the reader is left with the two options.

**The Provision and the Community's Gratitude**

The command to eat of what God has provided belongs to the Book's teaching about gratitude, and the sūrah has attached gratitude to the created order since its description of the harvest. The verse does not present the herds as a reward or as a possession to be managed by the community's own rules; it presents them as provision, and the response the Book asks for is the recognition of the provider.

The Book's statements about the world's goods elsewhere carry the same emphasis. The sūrah of the Bee tells the believers to eat of the lawful and good things and to be grateful for God's favours if they worship Him, and the sūrah of the Table gives the same command with the addition of mindfulness. The verse in front of us belongs with those instructions, and its warning about Satan's footsteps states what gratitude excludes.

**The Place of the Verse in the Passage**

The verse stands between the description of the gardens and the argument about the pairs of animals, and it functions as the general instruction that the following verses apply. The sūrah has examined the audience's rules about the herds in the preceding passage, and it will now take up their specific claim that God had forbidden certain animals and answer it with a demand for evidence.

The two verses that follow record that answer, asking the audience whether it was the males, the females, or what was in the wombs that God had forbidden, and requiring them to produce the knowledge on which their claim rested (6:143–144). The verse in front of us supplies the command that the argument presupposes, and the challenge that follows removes the ground on which the audience's rules had been built.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse names the pairs of animals and puts the question to the audience about which of them had been forbidden, ending with the demand that they produce knowledge if they are truthful (6:143). The sentence begins the sūrah's final treatment of the dietary system, and it proceeds by requiring the audience to state the basis of rules it had never examined.

The sūrah's method here is characteristic. It does not simply declare the audience's rules void; it asks the people who made them to explain them, and the question is framed so that the explanation cannot be given. The verse in front of us prepares the reader for that argument by stating the provision that the rules had presumed to regulate.
verses.143:
> ˹Allah has created˺ four pairs: a pair of sheep and a pair of goats—ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Has He forbidden ˹to you˺ the two males or the two females or what is in the wombs of the two females? Tell me with knowledge, if what you say is true.”—

**The Pairs and the Question**

The verse opens the sūrah's final treatment of the dietary rules by taking up the claim that certain animals had been forbidden, and it puts the question to the audience through the Prophet's instruction. The created animals come in male and female, and whatever is carried in the womb belongs to the female of the pair, so the categories of the created order are only three. If a prohibition had been given, it would have attached to one of them, and the verse asks the audience to identify which. The passage begins a two-part argument in which the claim that God had forbidden certain animals is tested by a question the audience could not answer.

The Book's word for the pairs describes a male and a female of each kind, and the four pairs named across this verse and the next are the sheep, the goats, the camels, and the oxen. The sūrah of the Troops states that God produced four pairs of cattle for humanity and that He creates people in the wombs of their mothers in stages, and the verse in front of us belongs to the same account of creation as provision (39:6).

**The Structure of the Question**

The question offers three possibilities and excludes the rest. If God had forbidden some of these animals, the prohibition would have to attach either to the males, to the females, or to what was carried in the wombs. The audience's rules did not correspond to any of the three, since they distinguished among animals by the kinds of distinctions the sūrah has already described: which animal was set free, which was reserved, and which was shared.

The sentence therefore asks the audience to state a rule in terms of the categories they themselves used, and the categories do not produce the rule they claimed. The Book's method is to accept the framework of the audience's practice for the sake of argument and then to show that the practice cannot be expressed within it.

**The Demand for Knowledge**

Tell me with knowledge, if what you say is true. The clause demands evidence, and the demand is the same one the sūrah has made throughout its treatment of the audience's claims. The sūrah has described the majority as followers of assumption who do nothing but lie (6:116), and it has stated that assumption cannot replace the truth (10:36). The sentence in front of us applies that standard to the audience's dietary rules.

The Book's use of the demand for knowledge in its arguments with the audience is consistent. It asks the people who claim that God has forbidden something to produce the revelation or the reasoning on which the claim rests, and it leaves them without either. The clause in this verse states the challenge in its shortest form.

**What the Argument Assumes About God's Commands**

The question assumes that a command of God would be knowable, and the assumption runs through the Book's treatment of the subject. The sūrah has stated that God has explained what He has forbidden (6:119), and it has recorded the revelation of the rules that the community actually received. A prohibition that could not be traced to the revelation, could not be derived from the categories of the created animals, and could not be stated in the terms of the audience's own practice had no claim to be a command of God.

The Book's positive statement of the forbidden things appears later in this sūrah, where the Prophet is told to declare that he finds nothing forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine, and what has been offered in the name of other than God, with the exception of necessity (6:145). The verse in front of us prepares the reader for that declaration by removing the invented prohibitions that had surrounded it.

**What the Verse Says About the Audience's Authority**

The verse addresses the audience as people who claimed to know what God had commanded, and it asks them to account for the claim. The sūrah has examined the shares they assigned to God and their partners (6:136), the killing of their children (6:137), and the rules that restricted their herds and crops (6:138–139), and it now asks them to state the basis of the system as a whole.

The Book's treatment of false attribution to God runs through the chapter, and the sūrah has described the claim to have received revelation as one of the gravest offences (6:93). The claim that God had forbidden certain animals belongs to the same family of assertions, and the question in front of us exposes it by requiring the claimant to produce the foundation of his claim.

**The Verse's Place in the Argument**

The verse forms a pair with the one that follows, which names the camels and the oxen and repeats the question with the addition of a further challenge: were the audience present when God gave them this commandment (6:144)? The two verses together complete the argument, and the second closes with the declaration that those who fabricate lies against God to mislead others will not be guided.

The sūrah's treatment of the dietary system therefore ends with the audience's claim left unsupported and the Book's declaration of the actual prohibition. What the verse in front of us provides is the first half of the challenge, and it does so by taking the audience's own categories and showing that they cannot carry the weight placed on them.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse names the second pair of animals and repeats the question about males, females, and wombs, before asking whether the audience was present when God gave the commandment and declaring that no one does greater wrong than the person who fabricates lies against God to mislead others without knowledge (6:144). The two verses are a single argument, and the second supplies the conclusion.

The passage that follows records the Prophet's declaration of what is actually forbidden and the rules that apply to the person compelled by necessity (6:145), and it then turns to the dietary practices of the Jewish communities and the guidance that the earlier scriptures contained. The verse in front of us stands at the head of that final treatment of food, and the challenge it issues governs everything that follows.
verses.144:
> and a pair of camels and a pair of oxen. Ask ˹them˺, “Has He forbidden ˹to you˺ the two males or the two females or what is in the wombs of the two females? Or were you present when Allah gave you this commandment?” Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah to mislead others without ˹any˺ knowledge? Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

**The Second Pair and the Completed Enumeration**

And a pair of camels and a pair of oxen. The verse completes the list of the animals whose status the audience had regulated, and the four pairs named across this verse and the one before it are the sheep, the goats, the camels, and the oxen. The Book's account of the created order elsewhere states that God made spouses for human beings and mates for the cattle (42:11) and that He created all things in pairs (36:36), and the enumeration in this passage belongs to that account of creation.

The sūrah of the Troops states that God produced four pairs of cattle for humanity and joins the statement to its account of the creation of human beings in the wombs (39:6). The passage in front of us draws the animals into the argument about what God has forbidden, and the enumeration supplies the field within which the audience's claim must be examined.

**The Repeated Question**

Ask them, Has He forbidden to you the two males or the two females or what is in the wombs of the two females? The question is put a second time over the second pair, and its repetition shows that the argument covers every kind of animal the audience's system had regulated. The three categories remain the same: the males, the females, and the unborn.

The Book's method in repeating the question is to leave the audience no category in which its rules might be located. The rules they had adopted distinguished among animals by whether they had been set apart, whether their backs had been declared off limits, and whether their offspring had been reserved for the men, and none of those distinctions corresponds to the categories the question proposes.

**The Challenge About the Commandment**

Or were you present when Allah gave you this commandment? The clause adds a second challenge, and it addresses the claim of divine authority directly. The audience asserted that God had forbidden certain animals, and the sentence asks whether they had witnessed the giving of such a command. The Book's answer to the claim is that no such revelation had been delivered to them, and the question requires them to say whether they were present at a moment no one had reported.

The Book's challenge to the audience's claims of knowledge appears throughout the chapter. The sūrah has told the Prophet to say that he has no knowledge of what the audience asserts and has described them as followers of assumption (6:116), and the verse in front of us puts the same challenge in the form of a question about witnessing.

**The Charge at the End**

Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah to mislead others without any knowledge? The sentence is the sūrah's repeated formula, and it adds the element of misleading others. The sūrah used the formula at the beginning of the chapter, in the verse about those who invent a lie about God or deny His signs (6:21), and it used it in the passage about those who claim to have received revelation (6:93). The form in front of us identifies the harm the fabrication does to the community that accepts it.

The clause without any knowledge returns to the theme the sūrah has developed since its warning about the majority. The people who invented the restrictions had no revelation and no evidence, and the sentence states the effect of their invention on the people who followed them.

**The Declaration About Guidance**

Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people. The verse closes with the statement about guidance that the sūrah has attached to several of its condemnations. The pairing of wrongdoing with the withholding of guidance appears in the Book's statements about those who persist in denial, and the sūrah has described the hearts of such people as turned away after their first refusal (6:110).

The sentence is not a statement about the audience's capacity but a declaration about the outcome of their chosen course. The sūrah has been careful to state that the signs were clear and that the responsibility belonged to the people who received them, and the verse in front of us applies the same principle to the fabricators of the dietary rules.

**What the Passage Establishes**

The two verses together remove the audience's dietary system from the realm of divine command. The animals were created in pairs, the rules the audience applied to them cannot be stated in the terms of the created kinds, no revelation had been given on the subject, and the people who invented the rules did so to mislead others. What remains is the position the sūrah will state in the next verse, where the Prophet declares what is actually forbidden.

The Book's treatment of the subject is therefore complete at this point in the argument, and the verses that follow supply the positive account. The sūrah has been examining the audience's religion piece by piece, and the passage in front of us closes the section on food with the claim of divine authority left unsupported.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse records the Prophet's declaration that he finds nothing forbidden to eat in what has been revealed to him except carrion, running blood, swine, and what has been offered in the name of other than God, with the exception of the person compelled by necessity (6:145). The declaration answers the fabricated rules with the actual prohibition, and it states the limits of what the revelation forbids.

The passage that follows turns to the restrictions imposed on the Jewish communities and to the mercy that the sūrah's audience was receiving, and it then addresses the polytheists' argument about God's will (6:146–148). The verse in front of us closes the sūrah's challenge to the audience's dietary system, and the declaration that follows supplies what the system had obscured.
verses.145:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine—which is impure—or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah. But if someone is compelled by necessity—neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need—then surely your Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

**The Declaration of What Is Forbidden**

Say, I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to eat except carrion, running blood, swine, which is impure, or a sinful offering in the name of any other than Allah. The verse gives the Prophet the words that answer the audience's dietary system, and the answer is drawn from the revelation rather than from inherited custom. The four categories named here are the prohibitions the Book states in its other dietary passages as well: the sūrah of the Cow lists carrion, blood, swine, and what has been slaughtered in the name of other than God, and it adds the exception for the person compelled (2:173); the sūrah of the Table gives the same list; and the sūrah of the Bee repeats it with the same qualification (16:115).

The familiar phrase I do not find in what has been revealed to me places the whole question within the revelation. What the Prophet is instructed to report is what has been sent down, and the audience's rules have no place among its contents.

**The Four Categories**

The verse names the prohibited things in an order that moves from the animal that died without slaughter, to the blood that pours from a slaughtered animal, to the swine, and finally to the animal offered to a being other than God. The Book's word for the third item describes it as impure, and the fourth is described as an offering made in disobedience. The sūrah has already forbidden the eating of what has not been slaughtered in the Name of God (6:121), and the list in front of us states the same principle in its full form.

The categories show what the Book's dietary law actually contains. It is not a system of inherited taboos about particular animals, and it does not rest on distinctions between the males and the females or on the condition of the unborn. It rests on the condition of the animal at the time of its death and on the name invoked over it, which is the principle the sūrah stated when it commanded the believers to eat of what has been slaughtered in the Name of God (6:118).

**The Exception for Necessity**

But if someone is compelled by necessity, neither driven by desire nor exceeding immediate need, then surely your Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The exception states the two conditions that qualify it: the person must be driven to eat by necessity rather than by appetite, and he must not take more than the immediate need requires. The Book's other dietary passages state the same exception more briefly, and the version in front of us adds the description of the person who may use it.

The Book's treatment of necessity in its legal passages shows the purpose the exception serves. The rules are not intended to destroy the person who is forced to break them, and the qualification keeps the permission from becoming a general licence. The names that close the sentence, All-Forgiving and Most Merciful, state the ground on which the exception rests.

**What the Verse Answers in the Sūrah's Argument**

The verse answers the audience's system with a list rather than with a rebuttal, and the list is short. The sūrah has spent several verses describing the shares assigned to the idols, the reservation of the herds, the killing of children, and the rules about the offspring of the animals, and the declaration in front of us states the four prohibitions that God has actually given. The difference in length is part of the answer.

The Book's treatment of the earlier communities' laws makes the same point from the other side. The verse that follows this one describes the restrictions placed on the Jewish communities and the reasons for them (6:146), and the sūrah of the Women states that God forbade the Jews certain foods that had been lawful for them because of their wrongdoing and their hindering others from the way of God (4:160). The community addressed in this sūrah was receiving a law that was lighter than what had preceded it, and the declaration in front of us states its substance.

**What the Verse Says About the Revelation's Authority**

The sentence's reference to what has been revealed to the Prophet is the ground on which the whole dietary question is settled. The audience had appealed to the customs of their ancestors, and the Book answers with the content of the message. The sūrah has stated that God has explained what He has forbidden (6:119), and the verse in front of us states what that explanation contains.

The Book's use of the formula in other contexts shows that it is not a denial of the revelation's completeness but a statement of where the rulings are to be found. The sūrah of the Cattle itself will later say that the Book is fully explained and that nothing has been omitted from it (6:38), and the declaration in front of us belongs to that account of a revelation that states what it requires.

**The Place of the Verse in the Section**

The verse stands between the challenge to the audience's dietary system (6:143–144) and the account of the restrictions imposed on the Jewish communities (6:146), and it supplies the answer that the challenge required. The sūrah's examination of food is complete once the positive statement of the law has been given, and the verses that follow show how the community's law relates to the laws given before it.

The passage that continues from here returns to the theme of the audience's arguments, with the polytheists claiming that God's will was behind their practices and the Prophet told to answer that God has the conclusive argument (6:148–149). The verse in front of us therefore closes one movement of the sūrah and prepares the reader for the next, and it does so by stating the law in its simplest form.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse describes the restrictions that were imposed on the Jewish communities, naming the animals with undivided hoofs and the fat of oxen and sheep with the exceptions attached to it, and it states that the restriction was a recompense for their violations (6:146). The contrast with the four brief prohibitions of the previous verse is the point of the passage, and the sūrah will go on to state that the community addressed in the Qur'an was receiving a lighter burden.

The Book's treatment of the earlier laws appears in several of its passages, and the sūrah of the Family of Imran states that all food was lawful for the children of Israel except what Israel made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed (3:93). The verse in front of us supplies the ruling for the community that received the Qur'an, and the passage that follows explains why the ruling differs from what the earlier communities were given.
verses.146:
> For those who are Jewish, We forbade every animal with undivided hoofs and the fat of oxen and sheep except what is joined to their backs or intestines or mixed with bone. In this way We rewarded them for their violations. And We are certainly truthful

**The Restrictions Placed on the Jewish Communities**

For those who are Jewish, We forbade every animal with undivided hoofs and the fat of oxen and sheep except what is joined to their backs or intestines or mixed with bone. The verse turns from the law of the community addressed in the Qur'an to the restrictions that had been imposed on the Jewish communities, and it states them in detail. The animals with undivided hoofs were forbidden, and the fat of the oxen and the sheep was forbidden with the exception of the fat attached to the back, the intestines, and the bone.

The Book records the same restrictions elsewhere. In the sūrah of the Women, God states that He forbade the Jews certain foods that had been lawful to them because of their wrongdoing and because they hindered many from the way of God (4:160), and the sūrah of the Bee says that to the Jews God forbade what had been related before and that they did not wrong God but wronged themselves (16:118). What those passages describe is set out in detail here.

**The Reason Given in the Sentence**

In this way We rewarded them for their violations. The sentence states the reason for the restriction, and the Book's account of the matter is that the prohibitions were imposed as a consequence of the community's conduct. The same connection appears in that sūrah's passage about the wrongdoing of the Jews, their taking of interest, and their consuming of people's wealth unjustly (4:160–161).

The Book's treatment of the earlier laws does not present them as burdens imposed without cause. The sūrah of the Family of Imran states that all food was lawful for the children of Israel except what Israel made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed, and it invites the audience to bring the Torah and recite it if they are truthful (3:93). What the restriction in this verse represents is a penalty attached to a community's violations, and the Book states it as a fact of the history it recounts.

**The Testimony Attached to the Verse**

And We are certainly truthful. The sentence closes the verse with the Book's testimony about its own account, and the Book uses this form of statement when it reports matters that the audience could dispute. The sūrah has been answering the audience's claims about the dietary rules of the earlier communities, and the sentence in front of us states that the account given in the revelation is accurate.

The Book's practice of testifying to its own truthfulness appears at the end of passages that correct the audience's understanding of the earlier scriptures. The sūrah of the Cow uses the formula in its account of the covenant, and the sūrah of the Cattle itself uses a comparable statement earlier in the chapter. This declaration closes the passage on the Jewish restrictions, and the reader is left with the revelation's account rather than with the one the audience had inherited.

**What the Verse Says About the Two Communities' Laws**

The passage that includes this verse sets the community's law beside the law given to the Jewish communities, and the comparison is deliberate. The four prohibitions stated in the previous verse are few and simple, while the restrictions described here are detailed and attached to a particular history. The sūrah's audience is being shown that the burden it was being asked to carry was lighter than what had been imposed on those who came before.

The Book states the same comparison in other passages. The sūrah of the Cow describes the covenant with the children of Israel and the severity of its terms, and the sūrah of the Table describes the obligations that were laid upon them. What this verse adds is the dietary portion of that history, and its statement that the restrictions were a recompense for violations explains the difference between the two arrangements.

**The Relation of the Verse to the Audience's Practice**

The audience had built a system of its own restrictions, and the sūrah has just answered the system with the four prohibitions stated in the previous verse. Its function in the passage is to show that restrictions attached to a community's wrongdoing are not a model for other communities to copy, and it states the reason the earlier community was given a heavier law.

The Book's treatment of the people who impose restrictions that God has not imposed is direct elsewhere in the sūrah. The verse that follows the passage about the Jewish restrictions states that if the audience denies the Prophet, he should say that the Lord is infinite in mercy and that His punishment will not be averted from the wicked (6:147), and the passage after that records the polytheists' argument that God's will lay behind their practices (6:148).

**The Place of the Verse in the Sūrah**

The verse completes the sūrah's treatment of food, which has run from the command to eat of what has been slaughtered in the Name of God (6:118) through the examination of the audience's system (6:136–144) to the declaration of what is actually forbidden (6:145). The passage in front of us adds the account of the earlier community's law, and the section is complete once the comparison has been made.

The sūrah's argument in this section has followed a consistent method. The audience's practices are stated in their own terms, the revelation's ruling is given, the earlier communities' laws are explained, and the responsibility for the practices is left with the people who adopted them. The last of those elements is supplied here, and the passage that follows returns to the audience's own arguments about God's will.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse tells the Prophet that if they deny him, he should say that the Lord is infinite in mercy but that His punishment will not be averted from the wicked people (6:147). The sentence follows the account of the restrictions and the testimony attached to it, and it states the two attributes that frame the audience's position: a mercy that gives time and a punishment that is not withdrawn from those who persist.

The passage that follows records the polytheists' argument that God's will lay behind their association of partners with Him and their prohibitions, an argument the sūrah answers by asking whether they have any knowledge to produce (6:148). This sentence stands between the two, and it states the position of the community that has received the revelation and the law in its plain form.
verses.147:
> But if they deny you ˹O Prophet˺, say, “Your Lord is infinite in mercy, yet His punishment will not be averted from the wicked people.”

**The Instruction for the Case of Denial**

But if they deny you, say, Your Lord is infinite in mercy, yet His punishment will not be averted from the wicked people. The verse gives the Prophet the words for the situation in which the audience rejects the message, and it is placed immediately after the account of the earlier communities' dietary laws and the testimony that closed it. The instruction covers both sides of the matter in a single sentence: the mercy that gives the deniers their time and the punishment that remains in place for those who persist.

The Book's habit of pairing the two attributes is consistent throughout. The sūrah of the Rocky Tract tells the Prophet to inform the servants that God is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful, and that His torment is the most painful (15:49–50); the sūrah of the Forgiver describes God as the Forgiver of sin, the Accepter of repentance, the Severe in punishment, and the Infinite in bounty (40:3); and the sūrah of the Heights records God's answer to Moses that His mercy encompasses all things while His punishment falls on those who persist (7:156). The verse in front of us states the pair in the context of the Prophet's own situation.

**The Mercy That Is Infinite**

The Book's word for the mercy here describes a quality without limit, and the phrase appears elsewhere in the Book's statements about God. In the sūrah of the Heights, God tells Moses that His mercy encompasses all things, and the sūrah of the Troops asks the audience whether they despair of the mercy of God. The verse in front of us states that the mercy is the reason the punishment has not yet arrived.

The Book's teaching about the delay that mercy produces appears in its accounts of the communities that were given time. Āl ʿImrān warns the disbelievers not to think that the respite granted to them is good for them, since they are given time only to increase in sin, and Sūrat al-Kahf states that God has overlooked much of what people have done. The sentence in this verse states the arrangement in the form of an answer the Prophet is to give.

**The Punishment That Is Not Averted**

Yet His punishment will not be averted from the wicked people. The second half of the sentence states the limit of the delay, and the Book's word for the wicked describes those who persist in wrongdoing. The sūrah has described the same outcome for the communities that rejected their messengers, and it has stated that the destruction of a society is not attributed to God before the warning has been delivered (6:131).

The Book's statements about the punishment attached to persistent denial appear throughout the chapter. The sūrah has described the wrongdoers in the throes of death and the torment that follows (6:93), the humiliation and severe punishment awaiting those who demanded the messenger's office (6:124), and the fire described as the home of the people who misled and were misled (6:128). The sentence in front of us states the same outcome in the form of an answer to denial.

**Why the Verse Is Addressed to the Prophet**

The instruction is given to a man whose people had rejected him, and its purpose is to place the matter where the sūrah has consistently placed it. The Prophet is not told to defend himself or to secure a verdict; he is told what to say, and what he says is a statement of the two attributes by which God deals with those who persist and those who turn.

The Book's instructions to the Prophet in similar situations follow the same pattern. The sūrah of the Prophets tells him that he is a warner and that the outcome belongs to God, and the sūrah of the Troops tells him that his duty is only to remind. The verse in front of us supplies the content of the reminder in this particular case, and it does so by stating the mercy and the punishment together.

**What the Verse Says About the Audience's Opportunity**

The sentence states that the audience's position was not yet settled. The mercy that gives time is named first, and the punishment is attached to the wicked rather than to the people who have merely heard and not yet responded. The verse therefore leaves the possibility of turning open, and the sūrah has made the same point throughout its treatment of guidance and refusal.

The Book's addresses to the community that had not yet accepted the message consistently leave the door open in this way. The sūrah of the Cave states that the message is the truth from the Lord and that whoever wills may believe, and the sūrah of the Troops tells the Prophet to inform the servants of the mercy before it states the severity of the punishment. The verse in front of us follows the same order, and the order is the point.

**The Place of the Verse in the Section**

The verse stands between the account of the earlier communities' dietary restrictions and the testimony that the revelation's account of them is true (6:146), on one side, and the polytheists' argument that God's will lay behind their practices (6:148), on the other. It functions as the answer the Prophet is to give when the account is denied, and it prepares the reader for the fuller argument about divine will and human responsibility that follows.

The sūrah's treatment of the audience's appeal to God's will is one of the most important passages in the chapter, and the verse in front of us states the framework within which that appeal is answered. The mercy and the punishment are the two terms of the arrangement, and the audience's plea does not remove them.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse records the polytheists' argument that if God had willed, neither they nor their forefathers would have associated others with Him or made anything unlawful, and it states that earlier communities made the same argument before they tasted the punishment (6:148). The passage that follows asks whether the audience has any knowledge to produce and states that they follow nothing but assumptions.

The two verses belong together, since the appeal to divine will is the denial the previous verse anticipated, and the answer to it occupies the verses that follow. The sūrah's treatment of the subject ends with the declaration that God has the most conclusive argument and that He could have imposed guidance on everyone had He willed (6:149), and the verse in front of us opens that final exchange.
verses.148:
> The polytheists will argue, “Had it been Allah’s Will, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated others with Him ˹in worship˺ or made anything unlawful.” Likewise, those before them rejected the truth until they tasted Our punishment. Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? Surely you follow nothing but ˹false˺ assumptions and you do nothing but lie.”

**The Argument of the Polytheists**

The polytheists will argue, Had it been Allah's Will, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated others with Him in worship or made anything unlawful. The verse records the audience's appeal to the divine will as an excuse for their conduct, and the appeal is one the sūrah has already anticipated. The sūrah stated that had God willed, the idolaters would not have associated partners with Him (6:107), and it made the same statement about the killing of children (6:137); the verse in front of us shows the audience turning that statement into a defence.

The Book records the same argument from other communities. The sūrah of the Bee states that the polytheists said that had God willed, neither they nor their ancestors would have worshipped anything besides Him, nor would they have forbidden anything (16:35); the sūrah of the Ornament records their claim that if the Most Compassionate had willed they would never have worshipped the idols (43:20); and the sūrah of the Cow records the answer of those who were invited to follow the revelation, that they would follow only what their forefathers followed (2:170). The argument appears in each passage as the last resort of a people who have no evidence.

**The Precedent of the Earlier Communities**

Likewise, those before them rejected the truth until they tasted Our punishment. The sentence places the audience's argument in the history of the communities that preceded them, and it states that the same plea was made before the punishment arrived. The sūrah has described the destruction of the earlier generations in several passages, and the sentence in front of us connects the argument to the fate that followed it.

The Book's accounts of the destroyed communities include the excuses they offered before their destruction. The sūrah of the Poets records the denials of the peoples of Noah, Hūd, and Ṣāliḥ, and the sūrah of the Heights records the arguments of the communities that rejected their messengers. What the verse in front of us states is that the plea of the audience in Makkah belonged to a pattern that had already been tested.

**The Demand for Knowledge**

Ask them, Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? The question turns the appeal back on the people who made it, and it asks them to produce something that would support their claim. The Book's word for the knowledge in question covers any evidence or revelation that would establish that God had willed their practices in the sense they claimed.

The demand is the same one the sūrah made when it challenged the audience's dietary rules and required them to state the basis of their claim (6:143–144). The method is consistent: the audience is asked for the foundation of its position, and the absence of any foundation is then stated.

**The Charge of Assumption and Falsehood**

Surely you follow nothing but false assumptions and you do nothing but lie. The sentence states the result of the challenge, and it uses the same vocabulary the sūrah has applied to the audience throughout. The verse about the majority said that they follow nothing but assumptions and do nothing but lie (6:116), and the sūrah of Yūnus states that most of them follow nothing but assumption and that assumption cannot replace the truth (10:36).

The two charges correspond to the two parts of the audience's conduct. The assumptions are the beliefs they inherited and never examined, and the lies are the claims they made about God on the basis of those beliefs, including the claim that He had forbidden certain things and willed their practices.

**What the Verse Says About the Appeal to God's Will**

The verse does not deny that God's will stands behind everything that occurs. The sūrah has stated the same fact about the idolaters' association of partners and about the killing of children, and the verse in front of us quotes the audience stating it. What the Book rejects is the use of that fact to remove responsibility, and the answer it gives is that the audience has no knowledge that would support the inference they draw from it.

The Book's resolution of the matter appears in the verse that follows, where God is said to have the most conclusive argument and to have been able to impose guidance on everyone had He willed (6:149). The divine will and human accountability are both affirmed, and the appeal that would use one to cancel the other is answered by the statement that God's case is complete and that the messengers were sent so that no one would have an excuse (4:165).

**What the Verse Says About Inherited Religion**

The audience's argument rested on the practices of their forefathers, and the sentence records the connection explicitly. The Book's answer to inherited practice appears in the sūrah of the Cow, where the people who are invited to follow the revelation reply that they will follow what their forefathers followed, and the sūrah asks whether they would do so even if their forefathers understood nothing and were not guided (2:170).

The verse in front of us applies that answer to the audience's appeal to God's will. The practices were inherited, the claim that God had willed them was the audience's own inference, and the sūrah's charge is that the inference rested on nothing but assumption.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse gives the Prophet the declaration that God has the most conclusive argument and that He could have imposed guidance upon all people had He willed (6:149). The sentence completes the answer to the audience's appeal, and it states the ground on which the argument between the messenger and his people is settled.

The passage that follows continues with instructions about the path of God and the prohibitions that the sūrah lists in its closing verses. The verse in front of us supplies the audience's final argument and the Book's answer to it, and the reader is left with the knowledge that the assumption on which the argument rested had no foundation.
verses.149:
> Say, “Allah has the most conclusive argument. Had it been His Will, He would have easily imposed guidance upon all of you.”

**The Conclusive Argument**

Say, Allah has the most conclusive argument. The verse gives the Prophet the declaration that closes the exchange with the polytheists, and the Book's phrase describes a case that is complete and leaves no room for an answer. The term belongs to the Book's language about proof and disputation, and it states that the argument on God's side has reached its end.

The declaration answers the audience's appeal to the divine will. The audience had argued that God's will lay behind their practices, and the Book replies that God's case is conclusive, which means the point they raised does not leave the matter unresolved. The sūrah's earlier verses have stated the evidence of the created order, the testimony of the earlier scriptures, the mission of the messengers, and the clarity of the Book, and the sentence in front of us gathers the whole into a single declaration.

**The Counterfactual About Guidance**

Had it been His Will, He would have easily imposed guidance upon all of you. The clause states what God could have done, and the Book makes the same statement in several places. The sūrah of Yūnus asks the Prophet whether he would compel people to believe after stating that all the people of the earth would have believed had his Lord willed (10:99); the sūrah of the Adoration says that had God willed, He could have imposed guidance on every soul (32:13); and the sūrah of the Cattle itself, in its account of the Prophet's distress over the denial of his people, states that God could have guided them all had He willed (6:35).

The clause is the answer to the audience's argument in its own terms. If God's will were the standard by which conduct is excused, then the fact that He could have compelled belief shows that the present arrangement is not compulsion. The audience was left free, and the choice they made was theirs.

**What the Book Says About Compelled Belief**

The Book's statements about guidance consistently distinguish between the power to compel and the decision to leave people free. The sūrah of the Cave states that the truth is from the Lord and that whoever wills may believe, and the sūrah of the Bee tells the Prophet that his duty is to invite and that God knows best who has strayed and who is guided (16:125). The declaration in front of us belongs to that account of the relationship between God and human beings.

The Book's treatment of the earlier communities makes the same point from the other direction. The messengers were sent with clear proofs and were rejected, and the Book describes their people as having chosen their course. The sentence in this verse states the possibility of compulsion in order to make clear that the outcome the audience experienced was not compulsion.

**The Place of the Verse in the Exchange**

The verse completes the passage that began with the audience's appeal to God's will (6:148). The audience had argued that they were not responsible for their practices, and the Book's answer runs through the verse that preceded this one and this verse itself. The audience has no knowledge to produce, they follow nothing but assumptions, they do nothing but lie, God's argument is conclusive, and He could have imposed guidance on everyone had He willed.

The exchange therefore ends with the responsibility placed where the sūrah has placed it throughout: the message was delivered, the evidence was presented, and the response belonged to the people who heard it. The Book's claim in the next verse takes up the same subject from a different angle, with the Prophet told to demand witnesses from those who claim that God has forbidden certain things (6:150).

**What the Verse Says About the Audience's Excuse**

The audience's argument was an attempt to transfer responsibility to God, and the declaration in this verse removes the transfer without denying God's sovereignty. The Book affirms that God's will stands over everything and denies that the affirmation relieves the people who made the choice. The two statements are held together in a single sentence, and that arrangement is characteristic of the sūrah's treatment of the subject.

The Book's statements about the day of judgement give the same account. The people who are questioned at the resurrection are questioned about what they did, and the confession they make is their own, as the sūrah's earlier verse described when the assembled jinn and humans testified against themselves (6:130). The verse in front of us states the principle before the scene is described.

**What the Verse Requires of the Reader**

The verse requires the reader to accept both facts: God's power is complete, and human responsibility is real. The sūrah has described the guidance that God grants and the error that He permits, and it has stated throughout that the signs were made clear to people who were capable of receiving them. The declaration in front of us prevents the reader from using either fact to cancel the other.

The Book's addresses to the community return to the pairing repeatedly. The sūrah of the Troops states that God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, and it commands the Prophet to remind, since he is only a reminder. The verse in front of us states the same arrangement in the form of a declaration the Prophet is to make in answer to the audience's plea.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse tells the Prophet to demand witnesses who can testify that God has forbidden the things the audience claimed were forbidden, and it instructs him not to testify with them, not to follow the desires of those who deny the proofs, disbelieve in the Hereafter, and set up equals with their Lord (6:150). The demand for witnesses continues the challenge the previous verses began, and it returns the discussion to the dietary rules the audience had invented.

The passage that follows begins the sūrah's long recitation of what God has actually forbidden, running through the commands about parents, children, indecency, life, the property of orphans, honest measure, and the path of God (6:151–153). The verse in front of us closes the debate about the audience's appeal and hands the reader over to the positive statement of the law.
verses.150:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Bring your witnesses who can testify that Allah has forbidden this.” If they ˹falsely˺ testify, do not testify with them. And do not follow the desires of those who deny Our proofs, disbelieve in the Hereafter, and set up equals with their Lord

**The Demand for Witnesses**

Say, Bring your witnesses who can testify that Allah has forbidden this. The verse gives the Prophet a demand that turns the audience's claim into a matter to be proved, and the Book uses the same form of challenge in its arguments about the revelation. The sūrah of the Cow tells the doubters to produce a sūrah like the revelation and to call their helpers besides God if they are truthful (2:23), and the sūrah of the Ants asks whether another god could originate creation, resurrect it, and provide from the heavens and the earth (27:64).

The witness the verse demands is a person who can testify that God forbade the animals the audience had declared unlawful. The sūrah has already asked whether the audience was present when the commandment was given (6:144), and the demand for witnesses completes the challenge: the claim of a divine prohibition requires witnesses, and none exist.

**The Instruction About False Testimony**

If they falsely testify, do not testify with them. The sentence instructs the Prophet to refuse to join the testimony, and the Book treats the bearing of false witness as a serious offence. The sūrah of the Distinguisher includes among the qualities of the servants of the Most Compassionate that they do not bear false witness and that they pass by falsehood with dignity (25:72), and the sūrah of the Pilgrimage includes the avoidance of false testimony among the commands given to the community.

The instruction protects the Prophet from the appearance of agreement. The audience would have been willing to produce witnesses for a claim that served their interests, and the sentence tells him that his presence would be taken as confirmation. The sūrah's method in such cases is to leave the opponents to their own devices while the Prophet holds to the revelation, as it did when it told him to leave those who took their religion as play (6:70).

**The Instruction Not to Follow Desires**

And do not follow the desires of those who deny Our proofs, disbelieve in the Hereafter, and set up equals with their Lord. The sentence names three characteristics of the people whose desires the Prophet is not to follow, and each characteristic corresponds to a feature of the audience's position that the sūrah has documented. They deny the signs, which the sūrah has described at length in its accounts of the demand for miracles; they disbelieve in the Hereafter, which the sūrah identified as the condition of those who receive the whisperings of the devils (6:113); and they set up equals with God, which is the charge that runs through the whole chapter.

The Book's warnings against following desire appear in several places. The sūrah of the Cattle itself tells the Prophet to say that he will not follow the audience's desires, since doing so would lead him astray from the guidance of God (6:56), and the sūrah of the Kneeling describes those who have taken their own desires as their god and whom God has left to stray knowingly (45:23). The instruction in this verse belongs to that group of passages, and it is addressed to the Prophet at the point where the dietary dispute has reached its end.

**The Reasons for the Instruction**

The Book gives the Prophet reasons for the limits it places on his engagement with the audience's claims. The sūrah has told him that he is not a keeper over the people (6:107) and that the hearts of those who refuse are left in their condition (6:110), and the sentence in front of us adds that the desires of such people are not to become the measure of his conduct. The instruction is a protection for the message as much as for the man who carries it.

The Book's treatment of the community's relations with people of other religions elsewhere is built on the same principle. The sūrah of the Spider tells the believers to argue with the People of the Book in the best manner and to state their belief in what has been revealed to them and to the earlier communities (29:46), and the sūrah of the Clearing forbids the believers from allowing the hostility of others to drive them into injustice. The verse in front of us states the negative form of the same rule.

**What the Verse Says About the Dietary Claim**

The verse settles the dietary dispute by requiring proof, and the proof does not exist. The audience's rules rested on the claim that God had forbidden certain things, and the sūrah has examined the claim from every angle: the categories of the created animals do not produce it, the revelation does not contain it, and no witness can testify to it. What the sentence adds is the instruction to the Prophet about how to conduct himself while the claim is made.

The Book's statements about the actual prohibition are given in the verses that follow, where the Prophet is told to recite what God has forbidden: the association of others with Him, the failure to honour parents, the killing of children, indecency, the taking of life, the property of orphans, dishonest measure, and the breaking of covenants (6:151–152). The passage states the law that the audience's invented rules had obscured, and the verse in front of us clears the ground for it.

**What the Verse Says About the Prophet's Standing**

The instruction places the Prophet outside the contest over the audience's claims. He is not to be a party to a false testimony, and he is not to adopt the desires of the people who made the claim. What he is to do is stated in the verses that follow, and the arrangement leaves him free to deliver the law without being drawn into the dispute about the audience's rules.

The Book's treatment of the Prophet's position in disputes of this kind is consistent.
