The verse that follows adds the denial of any partner and the statement that the Prophet has been commanded and is the first to submit (6:163), and the sūrah then returns to the accountability of every person and to the ranks in which people have been placed (6:164–165). The declaration in front of us supplies the middle term of that closing arrangement, and the reader is left with the direction the revelation asks of him.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse completes the declaration with the statement that God has no partner, that the Prophet is commanded, and that he is the first to submit (6:163). The three elements answer the audience's association of partners with God, state the ground of the Prophet's conduct, and identify the religion by its character of submission.

The sūrah's closing verses then take up the question of accountability from the side of every person, stating that the Lord of everything is the one to whom people return and that differences will be settled before Him (6:164). The verse in front of us supplies the dedication that the message requires, and the verses that follow state the terms on which the dedication is judged.
verses.163:
> He has no partner. So I am commanded, and so I am the first to submit.”

**The Denial of Any Partner**

He has no partner. The verse opens with the negation that governs the whole declaration, and the sūrah has built its case on the same negation from its first verses. The audience associated beings with God in worship, consulted the jinn, divided their harvests between God and their idols, and attributed offspring to Him, and the sentence in front of us states the denial in its barest form. The Book's statement of God's unity elsewhere gives the same negation in the sūrah of Sincerity, where God is declared one and indivisible and where the denial of offspring follows (112:1–3).

The placement of the negation inside the declaration of dedication gives the two halves of the speech their connection. The Prophet has said that his prayer, his worship, his life, and his death belong to God, and the sentence that follows states why no other being could share in that dedication. The two verses together present the religion as a whole: the worshipper is devoted to the One who has no partner.

**The Command and the Response**

So I am commanded. The sentence states that the Prophet's declaration is not a personal choice but an instruction he has received, and the Book's commands to him elsewhere use the same form. The sūrah of the Troops tells him to say that he is commanded to worship God, being sincerely devoted to Him alone, and that he is commanded to be the first of those who submit (39:11–12); the sūrah of the Cattle itself has placed a series of commands before him in its earlier verses, from following what is revealed (6:106) to declaring that God's argument is conclusive (6:149).

The phrase describes the Prophet's relation to the revelation in the plainest terms. He does not choose the religion he follows, and the declaration he makes is the content of what has been sent down to him. The Book's account of the messenger's position in this sūrah has been consistent on that point, and the sentence in front of us states it at the close of the chapter's teaching.

**The First to Submit**

And so I am the first to submit. The Book's word for submission describes the surrender of the person to God's command, and the religion itself is given that name in other passages. The sūrah of the Family of Imran states that God's only way is Islam (3:19), and the sūrah of the Table records God's declaration that He has chosen submission as the religion of the community (5:3). The Prophet's statement that he is the first of those who submit places him at the head of the people who accept that religion.

The Book's use of the phrase elsewhere appears in the commands given to the Prophet. The sūrah of the Troops joins the command to be the first of those who submit to the command of sincere worship (39:12), and the sūrah of the Cattle's opening verses record the Prophet's declaration that he is commanded to be the first of those who submit. The precedence is a precedence in time and in commitment, and the community that follows him is described in the Book as the people who submit.

**What the Declaration Answers in the Sūrah**

The three-verse declaration answers the audience's religion in its parts. The guidance declared in the first verse answers the audience's claim to the heritage of Abraham; the dedication of the second answers the division of worship and sacrifice between God and the idols; and the denial of partnership in this verse answers the association that the sūrah has described in its accounts of the jinn, the idols, and the fabricated rules. The declaration is therefore the sūrah's positive statement of what the message requires, set against everything the chapter has examined.

The Book's treatment of the audience's practices in the sūrah has moved from the theological to the practical and back. The chapter began with the argument about God's unity and the signs of His power, examined the audience's dietary and ritual system, and now closes with the Prophet's declaration of the religion in its simplest form. The reader who has followed the argument sees the contrast between the two systems stated in a few lines.

**Submission as the Religion's Name**

The name the verse gives the religion is the one the Book uses for the response of the person who accepts the message. The sūrah of the Cow describes Abraham and Ishmael praying that their descendants be a community submitting to God (2:128 context), and the sūrah of the Family of Imran states that whoever follows a religion other than submission will not have it accepted of him (3:85). The Book's use of the term covers the conduct as well as the confession, since the person who submits is the one who acts on what has been sent down.

The sūrah's audience is therefore addressed as people who are offered a place in that submission. The Prophet declares that he is the first of those who submit, and the Book's commands to the community elsewhere attach the same description to the believers who respond. The verse states the identity the message confers, and it does so in the middle of the declaration that closes the sūrah's teaching.

**The Place of the Verse in the Sūrah's Close**

The verse completes the declaration that began with the Prophet's statement of the guidance he has received (6:161) and continued with the dedication of his prayer, worship, life, and death (6:162). The three verses are a single speech, and the last of them supplies the negation, the basis, and the name that the speech requires. The sūrah's argument with the audience is finished, and the Prophet's own religion has been stated.

The verses that follow turn to the accountability of every person, stating that no one reaps except what he sows and that no soul will bear another's burden, and they close with the ranks in which people have been placed on the earth and with the two attributes that end the sūrah. The declaration in front of us supplies the Prophet's own position, and the closing verses state the terms on which everyone else is judged.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse gives the Prophet the question about whether he should seek a lord other than God while God is the Lord of everything, and it states that no one reaps except what he sows, that no soul bears another's burden, and that all people will return to their Lord and be informed of their differences (6:164). The passage turns from the Prophet's declaration to the accountability of the audience, and the two themes are joined by the statement about the Lord of everything.

The sūrah then closes with the verse about the successors placed on the earth and the ranks in which they have been set, and with the declaration that the Lord is swift in punishment and All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (6:165). The verse in front of us completes the Prophet's declaration, and the reader is left with the message in its final form: one Lord, one worship, and a submission that the messenger himself has embraced.
verses.164:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Should I seek a lord other than Allah while He is the Lord of everything?” No one will reap except what they sow. No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another. Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of your differences

**The Question About Another Lord**

Say, Should I seek a lord other than Allah while He is the Lord of everything? The verse gives the Prophet a question to put to the audience, and the question returns to the ground on which the whole sūrah has stood. The Book's opening command to the Prophet in this sūrah was to declare that he would not take any guardian other than the One who originated the heavens and the earth (6:14), and the sentence in front of us states the same position in the form of a question.

The Book uses the question in other sūrahs as well. In the sūrah of the Troops, the audience is asked whether it is urging the Prophet to worship anyone other than God, and it is addressed as ignorant (39:64); the sūrah of the Forgiver records the Prophet's declaration that he has been forbidden to worship what they worship besides God since the clear proofs have come to him. The verse in front of us belongs with those passages, and it puts the matter in the form that leaves the audience to answer for itself.

**The Lord of Everything**

The question rests on the statement that God is the Lord of everything, and the sūrah has established the claim throughout its account of the signs. The stars, the rain, the harvest, the herds, and the human beings themselves have been presented as the provision of one Lord, and the sūrah has stated that God is the Creator of all things and the Maintainer of everything (6:102). The phrase in front of us supplies the reason no other lord can be sought.

The Book's statements of the same fact appear in its descriptions of God's relation to creation, and the sūrah has supplied them in its accounts of the origin of human life and the ordering of the heavens. The sentence in front of us applies the fact to the question of worship, and it leaves the audience with the choice between the Lord of everything and the beings who own nothing.

**No One Reaps Except What He Sows**

No one will reap except what they sow. The sentence states the arrangement of the reckoning, and the Book attaches the same principle to the accountability of every person. The sūrah of the Star declares that each person will have only what he endeavoured towards (53:39), and the sūrah of Fussilat says that whoever does good does so for his own benefit and whoever does evil does so to his own loss (41:46). The sūrah of the Cattle itself has stated the two measures of reward and punishment in the verse before this passage (6:160).

The image of reaping describes the relation between conduct and outcome, and the Book uses it to place responsibility on the person who acted. The sūrah has described the audience's appeal to its ancestors and its reliance on the practices it had inherited, and the sentence in front of us removes the support that such an appeal provides.

**No Soul Bears Another's Burden**

No soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another. The sentence states the same principle in the language of carrying, and the Book repeats it in several places. It is stated in the sūrah of the Star that no soul burdened with sin will bear the burden of another (53:38); the sūrah of Fāṭir says the same and adds that a soul crying out for help with its burden will not be relieved, even by a close relative (35:18); the sūrah of the Troops states that no bearer of burdens bears another's (39:7); and the sūrah of the Night Journey gives the same statement in its account of the responsibility of every person (17:15).

The Book's rejection of substitution extends to the intercession that the audience expected from its idols. The sūrah has already stated that no protector or intercessor besides God will help the people who are warned (6:51) and that the intercessors the audience claimed will be absent on the day of judgment (6:94). The sentence in front of us states the principle that underlies those passages, and the sūrah of the Cow's warning about the day when no soul will be of help to another adds the same list of things that will not be accepted (2:48).

**The Return and the Settlement of Differences**

Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of your differences. The sentence closes the verse with the statement of the outcome, and the Book uses the same formula in its accounts of the disputes among the people of the earlier books. The sūrah of the Table states that God will inform people of what they differed about (5:48), the sūrah of the Pilgrimage says that God will judge between them on the day of judgement regarding their differences (22:69), and the sūrah of the Troops states that their differences will be settled before their Lord.

The sūrah's own treatment of the divisions among the communities appears in the previous passage, where the judgment of those who split into sects is left with God (6:159). The sentence in front of us completes that arrangement by stating that the differences which occupied the people of the earlier books will be presented and explained, and it leaves the community with the revelation it has received.

**What the Verse Answers in the Sūrah**

The verse answers the audience's position on three points that the sūrah has been examining. It answers the association of other lords with God by naming Him the Lord of everything; it answers the reliance on inherited religion and on intercession by stating that each person reaps only what he sows; and it answers the disputes among the communities by referring them to the day when God will inform people of what they differed about. The Prophet's declaration in the verses above is followed by the terms on which everyone else is judged.

The Book's habit of closing a long argument with a summary of accountability appears in several sūrahs, and the sūrah of the Cattle supplies its own version here. The reader who has followed the argument from the signs to the dietary rules and the covenant is left with the plainest statement of what a person carries to his Lord.

**The Transition to the Next Verse**

The next verse states that God has placed people as successors on the earth and elevated some of them in rank above others so that He may test them with what He has given them, and it closes the sūrah with the declaration that the Lord is swift in punishment but All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (6:165). The sentence takes up the theme of the ranks and the test, and it supplies the two attributes that frame the sūrah's final word.

The two verses together bring the chapter to its end. The accountability of the individual is stated, the difference of ranks is explained as a test, and the attributes of the Lord are named. The reader is left with the Book, the path, and the reckoning that the sūrah has described from its opening verses.
verses.165:
> He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth and elevated some of you in rank over others, so He may test you with what He has given you. Surely your Lord is swift in punishment, but He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**The Successors Placed on the Earth**

He is the One Who has placed you as successors on earth. The verse opens the sūrah's final statement with the theme of succession, and the Book uses the same description in several places. The sūrah of Fāṭir states that God has placed people as successors on the earth and that whoever disbelieves bears the burden of his own disbelief (35:39); the sūrah of the Cow records God's announcement to the angels that He would place a successive authority on the earth (2:30); and the sūrah of the Cattle itself told the Prophet earlier that God could do away with the audience and replace them with whoever He wills (6:133). The sentence in front of us states the arrangement in the form of a description of the audience's position.

The succession is presented as a fact about the audience's standing, and the sūrah has used the history of the earlier communities to show what it means. The generations that came before had their turn on the earth and were replaced, and the sūrah has described their destruction in its accounts of the peoples who rejected their messengers. The sentence in front of us places the audience within that history, and the verses that follow state the purpose for which the succession was given.

**The Elevation in Ranks**

And elevated some of you in rank over others. The sentence states the differences that exist among people in the present life, and the Book attaches the same fact to the distribution of livelihood in several passages. According to the sūrah of the Ornament, God has distributed people's livelihood in this world and raised some of them in rank above others so that they may serve one another, and the passage asks whether it is the audience who distribute the mercy of their Lord (43:32). The sūrah of the Cattle itself states at its close that God has raised some above others in rank, and it has already stated that the ranks of the Hereafter are assigned according to deeds (6:132).

The two arrangements belong together in the sūrah's teaching. The differences of the present life are described as a distribution rather than a judgment, and the differences of the Hereafter are described as the consequence of what each person did. The verse in front of us states the first arrangement and the purpose attached to it, and the earlier verse has stated the second.

**The Test in What Has Been Given**

So He may test you with what He has given you. The clause states the purpose for which people have been placed on the earth and given their differences, and the Book attaches testing to the gifts of the present life in several passages. In the sūrah of the Kingdom, God states that He created death and life in order to test which of the people is best in deeds (67:2); the sūrah of the Cave says that God has made what is on the earth an adornment for it in order to test which of them is best in deeds (18:7); and the sūrah of the Cattle says that God has tested some people by means of others (6:53). The sentence in front of us states the purpose in the plainest terms.

The Book's treatment of the test gives the audience's position its meaning. What a person has been given is not a mark of his standing with God, and the differences in wealth, strength, and rank are the field on which conduct is examined. The sūrah has described the audience's pride in its standing and its resistance to a messenger from outside its leading families, and the sentence in front of us states the terms on which that standing will be assessed.

**Swift in Punishment**

Surely your Lord is swift in punishment. The attribute opens the sūrah's closing declaration, and the Book attaches it to the warnings about the communities that persisted in denial. God's declaration in the sūrah of the Heights is that He would send against the people of the earlier books those who would make them suffer terribly until the day of judgment, and that verse closes with the statement that the Lord is swift in punishment and All-Forgiving, Most Merciful (7:167). The sūrah of the Thunder states the same pair in its answer to those who ask for the torment to be hastened before the grace (13:6), and the sūrah of Fussilat names the Lord of forgiveness and painful punishment (41:43).

The sūrah's own account of the punishment extends through its accounts of the destroyed communities and of the reckoning described in its closing passages. The attribute in front of us states the speed with which the punishment arrives, and the Book's use of it in the passages about the earlier generations gives it content.

**All-Forgiving, Most Merciful**

But He is certainly All-Forgiving, Most Merciful. The second half of the declaration states the attribute that balances the first, and the sūrah has ended its description of the punishment with the same pair in other passages. Within the sūrah of the Heights, the two names stand together at the end of its warning (7:167), and the sūrah of the Troops tells those who have exceeded the limits against their own souls not to despair of the mercy of God, for He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful (39:53); the Book's habit of placing mercy alongside severity is one of its most consistent features.

The pairing in front of us gives the sūrah its final word, and the arrangement matches the chapter it closes. The sūrah has described the signs, the arguments, the destruction of the communities, the rules of the covenant, and the reckoning; it ends with the two attributes that frame the whole: a severity that is not idle and a mercy that is not exhausted. The community that receives the Book is left between the two.

**What the Closing Verse Says About the Audience**

The verse states the position of a generation that has inherited the earth from those who came before it, and it tells that generation what its standing means. The audience was proud of its continuity, its sanctuary, and its position among the tribes, and the sentence in front of us describes those advantages as a test. Nothing in the verse suggests that the standing is secure, and the sūrah has already told the audience that God could replace them with whoever He wills (6:133).

The Book's closing verses in other sūrahs give the same account of the present life. The sūrah of the Cave states the purpose of the world's adornment in the language of testing, as does the sūrah of the Kingdom, and the sūrah of Fāṭir joins the succession of generations to the statement that each person bears his own burden. The verse in front of us states the arrangement for the audience addressed by the Qur'an, and the reader is left with the account of what has been placed in his hands.

**The Sūrah's Ending**

The verse closes the chapter with a description of the human position and a declaration of the two attributes of the Lord, and the combination is characteristic of the sūrah. The chapter began with praise of the One who created the heavens and the earth, made darkness and light, and then made those who disbelieve equal others with Him (6:1). It ends with the successors on the earth, the ranks they have been given, the test in what they hold, and the mercy and severity that will meet what they do.

The sūrah's argument has moved from the signs of the created order through the accounts of the messengers, the divisions of the communities, the dietary and ritual practices of the audience, the covenant of the commands, and the closing declarations of the Prophet, and the final verse gathers the whole into a statement about the people who receive it. What has been given is a Book, a path, a set of obligations, and a reckoning; and the last words of the chapter are the names of the Lord who gives, commands, tests, punishes, and forgives.
